News.title: Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya
News.content:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also hit a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.

Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Police investigate unknown substance that caused Manchester's Co-op Live evacuation
News.content:
Thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester after an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.

It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with music fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood".

One person was taken to hospital while more than 80 people were assessed for "eye and respiratory symptoms", the North West Ambulance Service said.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said a major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.

The force said 12,000 people had been evacuated and one fan told of "distressing scenes" with people "choking" and coughing as they left the venue.

Some fans have complained about security and a lack of searches going in to the concert.

Joey Howe said the incident happened 30 or 40 minutes in.

The 22-year-old told BBC Radio Manchester: "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.

"The lights have come on and he is being rushed off stage.

"That horrible smell just hit you."

News.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
News.content:
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."

"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.

Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

News.title: Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis
News.content:
Tyson Fury says he was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.

British heavyweight Fury, 38, says he heard voices in his head threatening to hurt him and his family.

In a documentary which will be released by Netflix on Friday, Fury and wife Paris describe how he was diagnosed after being admitted to hospital with a suspected heart attack in June 2016.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.

"It was like a living version of the pits of hell. I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.

"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."

Doctors said Fury had suffered an anxiety attack.

Fury recalls hearing the radio talking to him, and begging Paris to get him out of the hospital because "the Illuminati" wanted him.

In the period after his victory over Klitschko, Fury gained weight and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

"It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind," he says.

"I wouldn't be able to sit and have a conversation because I'd be hearing stuff in my mind.

"I didn't know where to turn and no-one knew what to do. I really needed help, or check into rehab or something.

"I never got a break from it for years. I wanted to be what I thought was normal again."

After Fury was released from hospital, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder was confirmed.

The NHS describes schizophrenia, external as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech. It says the main symptom of bipolar disorder, external is extreme changes to your mood.

Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween.

"I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," he says.

"I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on.

"I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'."

He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.

It resulted in another world title when he beat Deontay Wilder in 2020.

Fury is preparing for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.

The fight will be broadcast live on Netflix.

News.title: NHS launches world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial
News.content:
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.

AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.

Recruitment to the EDITH trial , externalhas already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.

Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.

At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.

About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.

It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

News.title: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
News.content:
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim â and one that needs examining.

The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.

So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?

It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.

You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.

News.title: Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?
News.content:
Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about Â£18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a Â£22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for Â£1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.

A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.

Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

News.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
News.content:
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.

"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."

He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform in an attempt to reduce the welfare bill by Â£5bn a year.

More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.

The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.

News.title: Mild Atlantic air collides with cold air across the UK, a recipe for some snow
News.content:
The UK is in the grip of the coldest spell of autumn so far, but will it result in snow?

Mild Atlantic air that arrived in the south-west of the UK over the weekend is pushing eastwards, coming up against colder Arctic air.

In this setup, the meteorological ingredients for snow are in place; however, there remains uncertainty in where the boundary between the cold and mild air will sit.

Even small shifts in temperature could make a significant difference to what falls from the sky and, crucially, the chances of snow.

News.title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
News.content:
Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise Â£190m to bolster its finances.

Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.

One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

News.title: Woman faces hour-long drive to give birth as hospital suspends maternity services
News.content:
A couple who are expecting their first child have said their excitement has turned "into complete worry" because of the suspension of maternity services at their local hospital.

Shelly Magee was due to give birth in Newry's Daisy Hill Hospital in County Armagh in January but from Monday, the Southern Trust is moving all hospital-based births to Craigavon, about 20 miles away.

Her partner, Clinton McKeever, said the journey from their home in Mullaghbawn could take them up to 90 minutes in bad weather or heavy traffic.

The Southern Health Trust apologised to families facing longer journeys but said the shortage of obstetricians meant services must be temporarily concentrated at one hospital.

"We mean it when we say it's temporary - we're going out to make further attempts to recruit," said its chief executive, Steve Spoerry.

From Monday, all expectant mothers who receive treatment from the trust have been advised to go to Craigavon Area Hospital - not Daisy Hill - for all labour and birthing services, inpatient maternity care and emergency gynaecology support.

It added that patients would receive the same high standard of care from experienced specialists, including staff from Daisy Hill who are relocating to Craigavon.

News.title: 'I was left broken' - Woman taking civil case against 'church that failed her'
News.content:
Warning: This article contains details that some readers may find distressing.

A woman who is taking a civil case against her former church, over an allegation that she was groomed and sexually abused by a youth leader when she was a teen, has said she was failed by those who should have protected her.

Jessica, not her real name, had been a member of a youth group in a Church of Ireland parish in County Antrim when she said she was first sexually assaulted at the age of 17 by a much older, married man.

After she turned 18, she said she went on to become his "toy" and was coerced into months of what she described as non-consensual sex.

The Diocese of Connor, which oversees Jessica's former church, said it would be "inappropriate" to comment on the allegations given the matter was the subject of legal proceedings.

The alleged abuse happened about 20 years ago but a survivors' advocate warned that grooming continues to happen in faith settings, where young people are particularly vulnerable.

Nikella Holmes, who is a survivor of sexual abuse and who supports others with similar experiences, said more learning was needed in churches in order to protect young people from potential predators.

Jessica did not initially disclose her alleged abuse herself.

It was the youth leader who told the County Antrim church that the pair had been having a consensual affair.

Jessica said he had made the disclosure while he was under scrutiny for a separate unrelated issue, for which he was stood down from his youth leader role.

According to Jessica, the church wrongly accepted this at face value and did not view his disclosure as a safeguarding issue.

Years later, when she confronted a senior member of the church about how the matter was handled, she said they told her she had been viewed as someone who had been "groomed and taken advantage of".

Despite this, the church is defending Jessica's civil claim against it.

Jessica is now in her 30s and after years of therapy and support from her loved ones said she was finally "in a good place".

But the abuse she said she was subjected to had left her a "broken, young girl" and, at one point, feeling suicidal.

Jessica said that when the abuse began she had been having a hard time and that the youth leader offered her spiritual support and prayer.

She said he was someone in a "position of authority", whom she "looked up to and trusted and respected".

"I believe he saw my vulnerability. He was witness to what was going on in my life and how I was struggling to cope with various things," she said.

"It's only been in hindsight that I've realised that actually that behaviour from him was in fact grooming, and that was him manipulating me and getting alongside me for the wrong intentions."

She said: "He betrayed me spiritually, emotionally and physically."

News.title: Househunter swaps Australia for Wales's most affordable town - where locals are struggling to buy
News.content:
A house-hunter has moved 10,000 miles (16,000km) from Australia to Wales' most affordable town because the properties are so cheap.

James Brown, 56, spotted the three-bed house in Tylorstown, near Ferndale, Rhondda Cynon Taf, online for Â£80,000 and put an offer in.

"It's ideal if you're commuting, and everything's virtually on your doorstep, so a really affordable area to come to," he said.

But some people who live in Ferndale - dubbed Wales' most affordable town with an average property price of Â£116,200 - say they are still struggling to buy homes.

Zoopla says a typical home in Ferndale costs "less than twice the annual wages of two full-time workers".

The property selling website said its analysis shows this is the most affordable town in Wales.

Residents have described how they have had to travel to work in England to afford a home in the area, while an estate agent said the low prices attract investors and buy-to-rent landlords from outside south Wales.

Originally from Gloucester, when Brown moved back from Australia he decided to move to the south Wales valleys because of the property prices.

He said the equivalent property in his home region would have cost him Â£200,000.

Brown said: "It's definitely a lot of outside buyers buying properties in Wales which I suppose in some ways is not helping the local people get on the ladder, but like I said, the affordability is just unreal in south Wales."

News.title: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat plane, air chief says
News.content:
Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.

Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".

His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.

The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest, is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.

Writing in the Telegraph, external, Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.

He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."

Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.

The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a Â£4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.

According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.

Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.

In October, Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK government would "seek to progress" Germany joining GCAP. He said the partnership could also support cooperation on issues including "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

News.title: Russell Brand's wife says she'll honour prison rules after message row
News.content:
The wife of disgraced comedian Russell Brand says she will "honour" the rules of his prison, a week after she read a message from her husband proclaiming his innocence.

Laura Brand, 39, drew criticism from ministers after reading out the message from inside HMP Littlehey last week, prompting the government to seek to have the episode removed from social media platforms.

She said on Sunday that she would continue to defend her family and herself over her portrayal in the media during the couple's weekly podcast, which she now presents alone.

Russell Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura Brand said during this week's episode of Sunday Service.

"Now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that."

In the relayed message last week, Russell Brand had said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".

Laura Brand said she had spoken to him at the Cambridgeshire prison and said he was "OK".

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

Further allegations have since been reported about him and some have called for consent laws to be revised.

His conviction has renewed conversation about safeguarding in the media industry, and whether some celebrities are still able to use their fame to prey on women and then silence them.

Ministers have pointed out that inmates are prohibited from making statements that are likely to cause their victims distress and have said Brand's message was being investigated.

A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16, but who was not among the women whose accusations led to his conviction, said his prison message was "upsetting" and "really shocking".

The government attempted to have the podcast removed from YouTube, but this was refused by its owner Google. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged social media companies to "show some decency and take these videos down".

On Sunday, Laura Brand also said that Sunday Service would be a place where she would "continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media's image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny".

She expressed feeling a mixture of "grief", "absence", "desolation" and "loneliness" since her husband's imprisonment.

News.title: Boss of British Gas owners Centrica 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
News.content:
The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.

Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by Â£443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get Â£100 to help with bills, but one Citizens Advice adviser said it was a "drop in the ocean" while a pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.

"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about Â£1.50, Â£1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".

The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit Â£5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.

News.title: Voices: Ukraine is taking its war against Russia far beyond the battlefield – and the West is worried
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Blown up by a Ukrainian attack, the Russian warship Merkury, listed, capsized and sank in Libya’s Benghazi port, where only its bow is now visible in a strike Volodymyr Zelensky called an “exemplary operation” and which Libya’s government condemned.

It is the latest in an expanding number of tightly targeted Ukrainian operations, mostly at sea, involving Kyiv special forces including Spain, Malta, Turkey, Italy, Senegal, Mali, Niger, Sudan, Greece and Syria and the Baltics.

Largely unnoticed, until the latest assaults on ships off the coast of Finland and Libya, Ukraine’s secret units have been fighting a covert war against Russia, and Moscow’s mercenary forces in what was the Wagner group, since 2022.

This month there has been a surge in activity. Some of which risk friction with close allies in Ukraine because they could involve the territorial violation of a Nato member.

The increased tempo and reach of the Ukrainian attacks outside the ground war against Russia and conflict over the Baltic Sea is a product of necessity and apacity.

open image in gallery Footage shows moment of the attack on a Russian cargo ship, off the coast of Benghazi, Libya November 22, 2026 ( Libyan National Army )

This month, Ukraine's secret service accepted responsibility for multiple drone strikes on the Buyan-M class in the Gulf of Finland, Russian ships which carry the hypersonic Kinzal missiles Vladimir Putin has used against Kyiv. The corvette sailed away under its own power, but casualties are believed to have been inflicted.

Also in the Gulf of Finland, ten days later on November 21, the cargo ship Sparta was hit by drones, caught fire and its crew rescued. It was under US sanctions as part of Russia’s military transport system.

Finland has been publicly relaxed about these attacks, in international waters, because it cannot be directly accused of helping the Ukrainians.

Libya is not in that category. Ukrainian drone units have been in the west of the country, with the knowledge and support of the government in Tripoli for at least three years.

The Ukrainian drone experts have been useful in meeting the threat from Libyan eastern warlord Kalifa Hiftar, who is known to have support from Russia (and the United Arab Emirates) in his civil war against the UN recognized government.

On the same day that the Merkury was sunk, the nearby Russian-linked cargo ship the Sacalon, which was carrying Russian military supplies, was also attacked.

Russian forces have used the east of Libya as a staging point for operations south, through formal military forces or more often through mercenary companies connected to the Kremlin. These have gold mining interests in Sudan and have backed the murderous Rapid Support Forces (once known as the Janjaweed). Ukraine helped the government forces there, again with drone experts.

open image in gallery Zelensky has hailed the attack on the Russian ship in Libya ( Getty )

So far Ukraine’s involvement in Africa, aside from Libya, has been relatively low key. But it illustrates the political risk to Kyiv that expanding operations can bring.

In backing rebels who fought against government forces in northern Mali because the central government there was supported by Russian “mercenaries” authorized by the Kremlin, Mali and Niger - another new Russian ally - cut ties with Kyiv in 2024.

After the latest Ukrainian assault in Libya, Tripoli complained that it “should not be allowed to become an arena for external conflicts”.

Russian-linked attacks on ships have proliferated in recent years. In November 2025 the Turkish flagged Mersin, which had been loaded with Russian fuel and was anchored off Dakar on the Senegalese coast with 39,000 tons on board, suffered a series of mysterious blasts in its engine room. Its operator announced soon after that it would no longer take on Russian business because of security risks.

Ukraine did not comment on the striking of a cargo ship off Spain in December 2024, the damage to a Turkish tanker the following month, the targeting of another Libyan tanker off its coast in February 2025, another off Italy in the same month, and another engine room incident off Libya that June.

open image in gallery This aerial photo taken on March 15, 2026 shows the wreck of Russian liquified natural gas (LNG) carrier Arctic Metagaz, which is adrift between Malta and Lampedusa ( AFP/Getty )

But Ukraine calls these types of operations “kinetic sanctions”. They are designed to make it impossibly expensive, because of rocketing insurance fees, to ship Russian goods or support Russian operations. Insurance on Russian ships in the Black Sea has risen by around 40 times in the last year. Russian vessels that do not use western insurance companies risk being directly attacked.

Such operations appeared, until the assaults in the Gulf of Finland, to have been heavily concentrated close to Libya and nearby Malta. Over the last 11 months, a total of seven vessels were disabled with drones including an LNG carrier, a vehicle transport cargo ship and a crude oil tanker.

With Russian hybrid warfare now being described by Wes Streeting, the UK’s defence minister, as “state sponsored terrorism, Ukraine’s widening of the regions where it will fight its war will be met with great sympathy - and growing fear that Russia will do the same.

News.title: Stay humble, Max? The true sentiments behind Verstappen’s inexorable George Russell tirade
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

There’s nothing quite like kicking a man when he’s down. Forlorn once again after a dismal late shunt, George Russell had swiftly completed his media duties and, if he had any sense, was heading straight to Harry Reid International Airport for the first flight back to London when Max Verstappen, gleeful and exuberant after what was undoubtedly a brilliant grand prix win in Las Vegas, entered the FIA press conference room.

After 15 minutes of preamble came the bait: Max, was it nice to get one-up on Russell after his remarks – the Briton said Verstappen “screwed him over” and “walks around like he’s bigger and better than everyone else” after a clash in practice which the Dutchman was served an official warning for – on Saturday?

Cue Verstappen, vocalising his tried-and-true stream of consciousness. “The thing is… he speaks a lot next to the track,” he said. “And honestly, for me, it doesn’t really bother me because he’s so far below my level that it doesn’t make any sense for me to challenge that.”

open image in gallery Max Verstappen: George Russell is ‘so far below my level’ ( Getty )

He goes on. “And today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in the mirror and I saw what was happening [Russell’s crash]. I was like ‘fantastic, my day is only getting better’ – and then when I crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

Moments earlier, in the TV pen, Verstappen had not needed a leading question in discussion with Dutch broadcaster ViaPlay as he labelled Russell’s season a “complete joke.” Backed up by his victory, swatting Russell’s challenge to the wayside, this was a Verstappen tirade at its most inexorable.

As you can imagine, the largely vitriolic world of social media lapped it up. “Tears for George”; “inject this s*** into my veins”; “there’s levels to this game, Max is generational”. And the rest.

In one respect, the problem for Russell is that, as per his own words, Verstappen really is better than virtually everyone else on the grid. Only Lewis Hamilton can stake a claim to be in the Dutchman’s sphere of aptitude and, even then, many rate the four-time world champion’s raw talent and pure speed above that of Hamilton.

And this is not finishing school; this is elite-level sport. You can immerse yourself in all the mind games and media back-and-forth but, ultimately, your performance dictates everything. You have to back it up. And with his clumsy attempt to pass 20-year-old world champion teammate Kimi Antonelli on the third-last lap and a bump into the barriers, Russell lost a whole load of credibility on Saturday night. For the Briton, now an astonishing 138 points behind Antonelli, it has been nothing short of a disastrous season at the wheel.

However, there is still something to be said for a degree of sportsmanship and good grace. And, look: these two clearly don’t get on. Yet even then, rubbing more salt in what is the saltiest of wounds does show a lack of class; a class that is still refreshingly prevalent in other sports. Verstappen does not need to actually state that he is a level above the Briton; the results and records speak for themselves. Wins: 75 vs 8. Podiums: 140 vs 32. Championships: Four vs zero. But in actually vocalising with a wry smile such brutal frankness – not in the excusable heat of the moment environment, either, but with a good hour of reflection – displays something a little more malicious.

open image in gallery Verstappen and Russell at the front in Las Vegas in a battle that the Dutchman won ( Getty )

open image in gallery Russell has endured a chastening season ( AP )

Of course, unapologetically, Verstappen is who he is – and the majority of Formula 1 fans love him for it. It can go both ways, though.

It wasn’t so long ago that the 29-year-old was petulantly threatening to walk away from the sport (again) in a rant about the 2026 breed of cars. Martin Brundle was one of many pundits who told Verstappen to stop moaning. On the same weekend in Japan, he banned a British journalist from his media session. A few months later, he signed a new contract at Red Bull until 2030. The Dutchman’s forthright post-race interviews have been a hallmark snippet of a largely forgettable season. And, much like two years ago, this argy-bargy with Russell is intoxicating content for Formula 1 in its era of unrelenting content. However, at times, is it all a bit much?

Yet ahead of the penultimate round in Qatar this weekend – with Russell set to respond on Thursday – two thoughts spring to mind. First: where does Toto Wolff stand in all this? Frustratingly, the Mercedes team principal completed his own media duties in Vegas before Verstappen’s remarks. At that point, he said of the feud: “I think it’s probably a bit of cat and mouse. These provocations, on either side, is another good factor of the entertainment.” Hardly the staunchest of defences.

In 2024, Wolff stood by his driver (literally) as he lambasted Verstappen for his behaviour, including a remark that he’d “put my f***ing head in the wall.” You’d hope Wolff, who has long flirted with poaching Verstappen, would come out in defence of his driver in this scenario too, especially given how Russell now finds himself at the very lowest of ebbs. As he looks to 2027, Russell must use this situation as a deep-lying fuel for motivation.

Second: on a weekend where Ferrari again gave Hamilton cause to lose his mind, the Briton was largely reflective, resisting the urge to twist the knife in deep at his team and under-fire teammate Charles Leclerc. One of Hamilton’s most amiable attributes has been his regular shows of graciousness, never displayed better than when he shook Verstappen’s hand after seeing a record-breaking title snatched away from him in Abu Dhabi in 2021. Red Bull’s star man is indeed the driver of his generation; one of the best-ever; an athlete of immense talent, hunger and killer instinct. But when it comes to humility, Verstappen could take a lesson or two from the seven-time world champion.

News.title: Army veteran mom-of-three, 36, mauled to death by dogs in Georgia—just months before becoming a grandmother
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A 36-year-old mother of three who served in the US Army has died after being attacked by dogs in Georgia, and her daughter is calling for justice.

Allison Lynn Anderson was found dead in the yard of an abandoned house in Cartersville, a community 45 miles northwest of Atlanta, according to investigators. Her family remembered her as funny, outgoing and kind, and said she loved making people laugh.

She leaves behind three children: Miley and her two younger brothers, Lathem and Jaxon. The family said Allison had been looking forward to becoming a grandmother for the first time, with Miley expecting a baby early next year.

Allison Lynn Anderson, 36, was found dead in the yard of an abandoned house in the community of Cartersville, Georgia ( GoFundMe )

“If my mom knew that I was carrying her first grandchild she would be over the moon and full of excitement... ... I am so disgusted and absolutely heartbroken that the owners of these dogs did not have control over them. What my mom went through was torture,” Miley said in a statement.

“She deserves justice and even though what happened earlier this week was terrible, her heart is so pure she would forgive them,” the grieving daughter said in the release. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) said preliminary autopsy results showed Allison had suffered fatal injuries after being attacked by dogs.

Her body was discovered on Monday, 16 November, and a 911 call was made at around 9.10 am. Deputies, state troopers and investigators responded to the scene.

Several dogs believed to have been involved in the attack have since been located and are being held by Bartow County Animal Control. Anderson's family has set up a GoFundMe page. “With the holidays approaching, this tragedy has made an already devastating loss an even more difficult time for the family,” the page reads in part.

On a Facebook page that her family also set up, “Justice for Allison Lynn,” her relatives said that Anderson went by the name Allison Garner.

A neighbor, Betty Mathison, remembered the slain woman in an interview with Fox Atlanta. “I would see her she'd be walking the road; she'd stop by sometime and talk to me. She was a really sweet little girl, she was real sweet.”

“They talked to me. My grandson put me up some cameras so they looked at the cameras. It reaches to the road, so I'm hoping they can see something, and it might be helpful. To her family, I'm praying for them and I hope they get justice and get some kind of peace from it,” Mathison said.

According to the Fox Atlanta report, the case has sparked widespread speculation on social media, including about how many dogs were involved in the attack.

News.title: Prince William pens powerful foreword for new mental health book
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Prince of Wales has written the foreword to a book of letters written by strangers to people struggling with their mental health.

The collection, titled Reasons To…, grew out of the viral suicide prevention project Reasons To Stay, which campaigner Ben West launched at the start of the year.

Mr West began the initiative in honour of his younger brother Sam, who died by suicide at the age of 15 in 2018.

The book gathers letters from people all over the world, sharing wisdom, kindness, and reflections on grief, loneliness, joy, mental health and other life experiences.

William praised the project for creating space for open conversations about mental health, describing the need to feel connected as “profoundly human”.

Mental health campaigner Ben West’s new book Reasons To…

In the foreword, William wrote: “At its heart, this project is about starting conversations, however imperfect or uncomfortable they may feel.

“It connects those who write with those who read, people who may never meet, yet share something profoundly human: the need to feel connected.”

More than 5.7 million anonymous letters have been delivered to people visiting the free-to-access site reasonstostay.org since the initiative began in January.

Mr West said in a video on Instagram: “I want to say a massive thank you to Prince William for his incredibly kind and supportive words about that project and this book.”

The prince has long campaigned on mental health, and launched the National Suicide Prevention Network in 2025, and the On Your Side suicide prevention toolkit for people in sport in Liverpool, in September.

Mr West appeared as one of the panellists at the Liverpool launch.

William also met Mr West in 2025 during a visit to the 24/7 text crisis helpline Shout.

Reasons To… will be published by Penguin on January 14 2027.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.title: Tyson Fury opens up about schizophrenia diagnosis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tyson Fury was diagnosed with schizophrenia just a few months after becoming unified world heavyweight champion, his wife Paris has revealed.

After upsetting the odds to defeat long-reigning Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf in November 2015, Fury sunk into depression and has now said he heard “voices in my mind”.

Fury, who will take on Anthony Joshua in a long-awaited ‘Battle of Britain’ in Cardiff on December 11, made the admission in a Netflix documentary which will be released on Friday.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua answer questions during a press conference at British Airways ARC at the Olympia, London on Wednesday, as the countdown started on their ‘Battle of Britain’ clash in Cardiff on December 11.

“Words can’t explain the darkness I was in,” he said.

“I came from the living version of the pits of hellfire. And I 100 per cent thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.

“I was waking up in the night (and) the anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it. Completely gone, and that’s when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London.

“She asked me like a gazillion questions and stuff, and I ticked all the boxes, whatever was going on. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder…”

Fury’s wife Paris added: “He’s a mild schizophrenic and even then the penny didn’t drop.”

Fury has been open about his mental health struggles since beating Klitschko, after which he took a near three-year hiatus from boxing, with his weight ballooning to 27 stone, while he battled suicidal thoughts and alcohol addiction.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury, left, takes on Anthony Joshua on December 11 in Cardiff (John Walton/PA) ( PA Wire )

“It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind,” the 38-year-old said. “I wouldn’t be able to sit and have a conversation because I’d be hearing stuff in my mind.

“I think the turning point for me was Halloween night 2017 and I went out and I was embarrassed of how I looked, I was a fat mess and I had this big costume on, a glow in the dark skeleton suit and I thought no one would recognise me in this.

“And I looked around me and I could see all like young people and I thought, ‘I’ve had the world in my hands and I threw it all away. And now, I’m just a fat mess, addicted to alcohol’.”

It marked the start of Fury embarking on a successful comeback, becoming world heavyweight champion for a second time when he beat WBC champion Deontay Wilder in February 2020.

While he suffered a pair of twin defeats to Oleksandr Usyk in 2024 – the only losses in his 39-fight professional career – Fury could become a three-time world champion when he takes on Joshua with the vacant WBA title set to be on the line.

:: Call Samaritans for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org

News.title: India gives Nepal £1.2bn for flood recovery as it seeks to counter China’s influence
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

India announced a $1.6bn (£1.2bn) package to help Nepal rebuild after deadly floods earlier this year killed 1,500 people, left more than 5,200 missing, and wiped out entire settlements.

Indian prime minister Narendra Modi announced the package on Monday after meeting his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah in Delhi.

The floods in August destroyed roads, bridges, power plants, farms, and homes, causing an estimated $4.7bn (£3.6bn) in losses, according to Nepalese authorities.

A study by World Weather Attribution in September found that human-caused climate change was a key factor in destabilising the mountainside whose collapse triggered the floods. Rising temperatures had thinned glaciers and thawed permafrost, weakening the ice and frozen ground that helped hold mountain rock in place.

open image in gallery Balendra Shah and Narendra Modi remotely inaugurate a train service between India and Nepal after their meeting in Delhi on 23 November 2026 ( AP )

Mr Modi said the assistance would help restore infrastructure, rebuild communities and support people who lost their homes and livelihoods.

Nepal earlier received an allocation of $20m (£1.5m) from the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, established to help vulnerable developing countries cope with the irreversible impacts of climate change.

The allocation, the fund’s first, was approved at an emergency board meeting in October. But it’s less than 1 per cent of Nepal’s recovery bill.

Nepalese officials and climate experts welcomed the decision but said the amount was a small fraction of what was needed.

Maheshwar Dhakal, a senior official in the climate and environment ministry, described the funding as small compared with the losses suffered by the country.

He argued, however, that releasing the money would send a message. “This shows that the global community can take the right decision at the right time to help those who are most vulnerable to climate change.”

open image in gallery Puppets symbolising victims of flash floods in Nepal lie on the ground as activists take part in a demonstration titled ‘Climate Justice for Nepal’ during the UN Climate Change Conference ( Reuters )

Member states have pledged more than $820m (£626m) to the UN fund, which has received 176 requests for support from developing nations totalling about $2.8bn (£2.1bn).

The fund’s board is due to meet in December to consider further requests.

In September, the Nepalese PM said at the UN that his country was paying a devastating price for a crisis it had barely contributed to causing. “We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” he said.

open image in gallery People cross a newly built suspension bridge next to houses damaged by the deadly flash floods in Nuwakot, Nepal, on 23 November 2026 ( Reuters )

Climate experts have said steep cuts to international aid budgets, including funding for the US Agency for International Development, have made it harder for nations like Nepal to prepare for and respond to climate-driven disasters.

In 2025, development assistance from major donor countries fell by 23 per cent, according to the OECD, with the US accounting for the largest reductions but Germany, France, Japan, and the UK cutting their aid budgets as well.

“The reality is that we need trillions of dollars every year, but developed countries have not met their obligation,” Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign, a global group that pressures governments to contribute to the UN fund, said earlier.

The funding shortfall comes amid broader divisions over how the international community should support countries bearing the brunt of climate change. At the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya in Turkey, which concluded on Sunday, member states failed to reach an overarching political agreement, with disagreements over climate finance, fossil fuels and how to address the impacts of global warming exposing deep divisions between developed and developing nations.

open image in gallery Nepalese lawmaker Sagar Dhakal speaks next to activist Greta Thunberg at Cop31 UNFCCC Climate Conference in Antalya, Turkey, on 12 November 2026 ( Getty )

India’s assistance also comes as Delhi seeks to strengthen its ties with Nepal amid China’s growing economic and infrastructure influence in the region.

India and Nepal have shared close historical, economic and cultural links, but relations have periodically been strained by political and territorial disputes.

The two prime ministers also launched several cross-border projects during Monday’s meeting, including a hydropower project, an oil storage facility, a pipeline, and a railway link.

Nepal remains heavily dependent on India for fuel and other essential supplies, but energy ties are becoming increasingly reciprocal, with India importing around 1,200 megawatts of electricity from across the border.

News.title: Poundland’s owners meet Business Secretary amid last-ditch rescue talks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Poundland’s owners are holding further talks with the Business Secretary as the race to stave off insolvency heats up, after a new bidder entered the fray just days before it faces collapsing into administration.

It emerged over the weekend that German investment firm Zachert Private Equity had made a last-minute proposal to buy the stricken retail chain, boosting hopes of a solvent deal.

Zachert is thought to be a credible suitor and joins three previous confirmed bidders, though it is unclear how the private equity firm’s deal would be funded.

The group’s interest comes as Poundland owners Gordon Brothers meet Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds again on Monday to update him on the process, which has become politically sensitive given the future of the firm and about 11,000 workers hangs in the balance weeks before Christmas.

Poundland gave itself more time to thrash out a rescue deal for the business earlier this month, when it filed for a second notice of intention (NOI) to appoint administrators after the first one expired.

This gave the business a further 10 days to secure a potential rescue deal, which will expire at midnight on Wednesday.

The low-cost chain filed the initial notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of October.

Gordon Brothers have faced mounting political pressure to protect the chain’s future and MPs have accused them of deliberately cutting off funds and pushing it to the brink of insolvency.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has stepped in to call for executives to work with the Government to find a solution that saves shops and jobs.

About 11,000 jobs and 600 shops in the UK remain at risk.

Time is running out for a deal as the firm also faces funding issues to restock its shelves in the busy festive trading period.

Advisers have been in talks with parties interested in buying the brand or parts of the business, such as swathes of shops.

It has held talks with potential bidders including Tesco over proposals to buy up to 150 stores, and other chains such as Iceland and Lidl.

Investment firm Xyra Holdings emerged recently as a potential buyer for the whole business, and Irish firm Martin Property Group is believed to remain interested.

Gordon Brothers previously rejected a takeover offer from Martin Property Group, but management named the firm as the preferred bidder last month.

Irish investment firm Innovest is also among possible buyers, although there are believed to have been questions over its funding.

If a rescue deal is not secured, it is expected that administrators would be appointed, and corporate advisory firm AlixPartners has been lined up.

News.title: Any regrets, Mauricio? Man Utd are deep in relegation battle after Anfield farce
News.content:
Bruno Fernandes says he has shelved talks over a new contract because it is not the “right moment” for discussions over his future as Manchester United captain.

Fernandes, 32, is out of contract next summer although United have a 12-month option to extend his deal to 2028.

The Portugal midfielder is understood to have rejected two contract offers from United since the summer but said all his focus needs to be on trying to help the team out of their current plight.

United head into Sunday’s game against Liverpool at Anfield second from bottom in the Premier League.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season,” Fernandes told Sky Sports.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

“The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”

Fernandes said claims he wants more money or a longer-term deal on offer are incorrect and that if finances were the issue he would have left Old Trafford before now. The captain has previously rejected lucrative offers from Saudi Arabia.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said.

“There’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that ‘He’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years’. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here.

“I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

“The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.”

United chief executive Omar Berrada said of Fernandes on Friday that it was “true that we’re having conversations about his new contract” but that the club preferred “to keep that private”.

Having been voted PFA Player of the Year last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off this term like that of the team.

He was dropped for the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth in the wake of a 4-1 drubbing by Como when he criticised the tactics and approach of then head coach Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino, Carrick’s successor, confirmed on Friday that Fernandes would remain as captain.

Fernandes said the United fans had been “far too patient with us” and hopes Pochettino - who wanted to bring the Portuguese to Spurs in 2019 - will bring a fresh energy.

“He’s someone that likes to bring a very good energy to the team, someone very positive, very strong, strict, said it straight away that he won’t allow us to not give him what he demands from the team, from each player,” Fernandes said.

“He wants the club to succeed so much, he wants to win games, and that’s pretty clear and obvious by the way he and his staff speak and want us to improve.

“Obviously [in 2019] I was a very young player that was eager to come to the Premier League. They had [Harry] Kane there, they had Dele Alli, Son, the chance of playing with those players in front was very attractive.”

News.title: Midges pose a growing health threat to Britons, experts warn
News.content:
Midges pose a growing health threat to people in Britain, experts have warned.

Like mosquitoes, midges can act as disease carriers, picking up pathogens when they bite infected animals and potentially passing them on when they feed on another host.

The UK is home to more than 650 species of midge, mostly concentrated in Scotland.

While some are harmless, others are already known to spread serious animal diseases, including Bluetongue and Schmallenberg – viruses that cause severe illness and, in some cases, death in livestock including cattle, sheep and goats.

“Most of the diseases transmitted by midges affect animals, but recently there has been evidence that they play more of a role in human disease,” Professor Heather Ferguson, an infectious disease ecologist at the University of Glasgow, told The Telegraph.

Last month, a man in France died after contracting the first-ever human case of Shamonda virus, a midge-borne disease previously only known to infect animals.

The virus, which is now widespread in European animals and was detected in British cattle earlier this month, has historically been confined to sub-Saharan Africa.

In other parts of the world, midges are already known to spread serious diseases to people.

Across South and Central America, thousands of people have been diagnosed with Oropouche virus in recent years, a midge-borne disease that is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and their unborn children.

Brazil – which has recorded more than 13,000 cases of Oropouche since 2023 – has launched a probe into the links between the virus and pregnancy.

It fears the disease could cause a tragedy similar to that of the 2015 Zika epidemic, which left more than 3,000 Brazilian children permanently disabled after being infected in utero.

“This midge-borne virus historically was thought to only be transmitted between animals and wildlife, mainly in forest areas,” Dr Christopher Sanders, an entomologist at The Pirbright Institute, told The Telegraph.

“But over the past couple of years, it has emerged in South America and parts of Central America where it’s actually being transmitted in cities and causing infections in humans, so that is obviously a concern”.

News.title: Verstappen mocks ‘absolute joke’ Russell after thrilling Las Vegas win
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix, coming to you from very early on a Sunday morning (if you are in the eastern hemisphere) and very late on a Sunday night (if you are in the western hemisphere).

It is a strange race in a strange place, but this is now the fourth edition of the race and it looks to be here to stay for all its strangeness. It does present the teams with problems and problems are there to be solved or negotiated as well as can be in F1. That is the name of the game.

In qualifying yesterday the world champion, Kimi Antonelli, did that expertly, sneaking in at the end to finish fastest. He does, however, take a five-place grid penalty, so will be starting in sixth. Taking first place on the grid will be the in-form Max Verstappen, followed by George Russell, who could do with a strong finish to the season.

Russell seemed miffed about missing out on pole position, particularly with how Mercedes managed the qualifying situation, particularly with how the tow was managed. Antonelli was always going to take a grid penalty, so why give him the tow, was Russell’s reasoning.

In any case, Russell has a good chance to take his third victory this season. At least on paper. Russell’s qualifying has probably been his strongest suit this season, but race days have let him down. Let us not forget that Lando Norris, who won last time out in Brazil, starts third.

There could be a bit of aggro on the first lap, given Russell and Verstappen’s “disagreement” yesterday, but let’s see. It may end up being a clean race.

It all starts in about an hour and we will be here for all the updates and reaction from the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix.

News.title: Wales ‘frustrated’ after being brought back down to earth by Wallabies
News.content:
Wales have a spring in their step coming into their game tonight as they host Australia at the Principality Stadium. Wales pulled off one of their best wins in recent memory last weekend, ending an over 70-year with for a victory over New Zealand. Despite pulling off that shock victory, Wales sit down in fifth in the northern hemisphere standings coming into this final round of fixtures. In all likelihood, they can only improve one spot. They have made four changes from the historic win over the All Blacks, with the likes of Josh Adams and Aaron Wainwright coming in.

“We were all immensely proud to make history last week,” Wales head coach Steve Tandy said. “There is a new opportunity and challenge for us against Australia and we are looking to back up our performance this weekend. It is our last home game of this competition. The support that fans give to the players and staff has been incredible and we cannot wait to get back out at Principality Stadium.

“We made nearly 350 tackles, the ball in play time was one of the highest in Test rugby in the last three years and we have got competition. The plan was always to freshen up and we are likely to do similar for the week after, because we need to find out about players. We have fresh and hungry players coming in, which will add the energy that we need at the weekend. The training environment is getting more competitive in certain positions we have the ability to put people in and feel confident about performance.”

News.title: Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode
News.content:
Speaking to Sky Sports, the Arsenal boss said: “My feeling is that we lost two points today. I think we were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.

“But it wasn’t. And when it wasn’t, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.

“And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it’s game on. And from that it became a very chaotic game. Every set-piece, we know that they are exceptional at it and we concede from a set piece.

“And then you have to react. And then we went back to the team that the exceptional team that we were in the first half again for another 25 minutes and we scored a great goal. We create infinity of openings to create and score the third goal, but we lack some time or to be precise, to make that count.”

News.title: ‘Remarkable’ Ireland deliver perfect riposte to Erasmus mind games
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Ireland vs South Africa from the Nations Championship in Dublin, with both teams harbouring hopes of finishing the day at the top of their respective tables.

Ireland and South Africa have both won four of their five games in the group phase of this year’s inaugural Nations Championship, and come into their last match before next weekend’s finals still in contention for the overall title.

Andy Farrell’s men begin the afternoon in third in the Northern Hemisphere table, but level on points with second-placed England, who are currently hosting New Zealand, and just one point behind leaders France, who take on Argentina this evening.

The reigning world champions, meanwhile, are guaranteed to at least remain in second in the Southern Hemisphere table, but are just one point behind the All Blacks at the top of the group, so will be hoping for a favour from Steve Borthwick’s men at Twickenham.

The Springboks will be without head coach Rassie Erasmus for today’s contest in the Irish capital, with the 54-year-old facing a six-match ban because of his criticism of officials following his team’s narrow defeat by France last weekend, including asking whether they were “match-fixing”.

“He’s been hands-on with our team, and we’re in a good space,” assistant coach Mzwandile Stick said of Erasmus on Friday. “Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure.”

In the same press conference, Erasmus predicted that Sam Prendergast would be cleared to play after being cited for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji. The Ireland fly-half escaped punishment from the independent panel and starts for Farrell’s side this afternoon.

News.title: Alonso heckled as Chelsea are humiliated by Leeds
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to coverage from the Premier League as domestic football returns after an international break.

We have five matches to bring you, including Chelsea vs Leeds, Aston Villa vs Sunderland and Tottenham vs Ipswich.

Xabi Alonso said his Chelsea side needs to learn to deal with the absence of Joao Pedro as the Blues struggle for goals in the absence of their injured striker.

The Brazilian has not played since the 2-0 win over Everton on October 17 and will be unavailable again today.

Without a focal point in the number nine position, Chelsea’s goal output has been dramatically reduced and they have dropped to fifth and having suffered two defeats in their last three games.

“(We need) the whole team for that,” said Alonso. “It’s not just the strikers that can score. We can score from set-pieces, from defenders, from midfielders.

“It’s teamwork. For sure Joao is an important player but we need to deal with this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying.

“We need to deal with it. It’s not that I’m going to look for one explanation. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.”

Tottenham will not have their manager, Roberto De Zerbi, on the touchline after receiving three yellow cards this season.

Gary O’Neil is targeting a “special” result at Tottenham, but promised Ipswich will not make any drastic changes after a four-match winless run.

Ipswich lost 2-1 at home to Bournemouth before the two-week break, which followed draws with Hull and Nottingham Forest along with a narrow defeat at Manchester City, but O’Neil is happy with his new-look group.

“There won’t be any drastic changes. The odd personnel change, (but) I don’t think it’s going to be a big shift for us,” O’Neil told a press conference.

“It’s a very well-balanced squad. There’s going to be no massive uplifts or downgrades when we have to change players within this group.”

Aston Villa will have Johan Manzambi available for the visit of Sunderland.

The midfielder did not feature for Switzerland during the recent international break because of a calf injury but he has trained with the rest of the squad and can feature today.

Villa can also call on right-back Aaron Wan-Bissaka after a muscle injury ruled him out for six matches. His return is timely as Matty Cash is unavailable.

Cash was suspended for Villa’s 4-4 draw with Manchester United before the international break but suffered a concussion while away with Poland.

Sports.title: Arsenal handed David Raya injury boost after arriving back from Newcastle draw
Sports.content:

ARSENAL have been handed an encouraging injury boost after David Raya was able to drive himself home following his shoulder scare against Newcastle.

The Gunners goalkeeper was forced off in the 70th minute of Saturday’s thrilling 2-2 draw at St James’ Park, sparking fears of a lengthy spell on the sidelines.



Raya appeared to hurt his left shoulder following a collision with Newcastle forward William Osula and looked in considerable pain as he was helped off the pitch by Arsenal‘s medical staff.

But SunSport understands the Spaniard was comfortable enough to drive himself home after the squad returned from their trip to the North East.



The 31-year-old did not require anyone to collect him from the club following the team’s return, offering some encouragement after his worrying departure.

Although being able to drive is no guarantee that Raya has escaped serious injury, it will provide a degree of reassurance to Arsenal supporters awaiting news of his condition.

The full extent of the damage remains unclear, with medical assessments and an MRI scan expected to establish whether the goalkeeper faces a spell on the sidelines.

He was absent from today’s training session, with Kepa arrizabalaga and Illan Meslier seen warming up together ahead of Arsenal’s clash with Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Raya has become one of Mikel Arteta‘s most indispensable players, with his exceptional distribution and composure in possession central to Arsenal’s style of play.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta is holding a press conference at 1:30pm and will provide a full extent of Raya’s situation.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The Spain international has been instrumental in the Gunners’ formidable defensive record, with the Premier League champions conceding just seven goals in their opening 11 league matches this season.

His importance was underlined by the concern surrounding his withdrawal against Newcastle, particularly with Arsenal facing a demanding run of fixtures in the coming weeks.

Arteta’s men face Borussia Dortmund and Real Madrid in the Champions League, alongside Premier League clashes with Manchester City, Brentford and Tottenham.



Kepa replaced Raya at St James’ Park and would be expected to deputise should his fellow Spaniard be ruled out.

The 32-year-old remains the most expensive goalkeeper in football history following his £72million move from Athletic Bilbao to Chelsea in 2018.
