Sports.title: Rumors Swirl Turki Alalshikh Could Walk After Fury vs Joshua Fight
Sports.content:
Johnny Nelson thinks boxing could go back to the “dark ages” if Turki Alalshikh steps away from the sport. Without Alalshikh putting up the massive purses to force big fights across the finish line, fans are going to struggle to see top matchups, even if plenty of spoiled stars have already been coasting for easy money on his cards.

Nelson believes Alalshikh will step away soon after the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua event.

“The rumor has it that Turki will be stepping away shortly after this at some point or another,” said Nelson to talkSPORT Boxing.

Big Purses And Flat Fights

Fans have gotten spoiled since 2024. Alalshikh has loaded cards with the biggest names in boxing, even when half of them turned in dull performances. Canelo Álvarez, Shakur Stevenson, Terence Crawford, Teofimo Lopez, Oleksandr Usyk, Devin Haney and Jai Opetaia all looked flat while collecting huge purses.

Maybe knowing the money is already in the bank takes away some of the urgency, or maybe they just had off nights, because it happened far too often with the best paid fighters on those shows. Only a handful of guys, like Ryan Garcia and Daniel Dubois, actually delivered real excitement for the money.

“We’ll not get the fights that we’ve been graced with,” said Nelson.

That is the real issue here. Once fighters get used to Alalshikh’s money, it will be hard to get top boxers to accept normal promoter purses again. They will turn their noses up at standard offers and sit on the shelf hoping he comes back.

The Purse Problem For Fighters

Look at Shakur Stevenson right now. He is already showing what happens when a fighter holds out for the big payday. The longer he waits around for the number he wants, the longer he goes without fighting a top opponent. You don’t get those prime years back, and nobody is going to bail him out once the Saudi money dries up.

The old promotional headaches will creep back in too. Eddie Hearn and Frank Warren both put on shows for DAZN, and they have done well for themselves working alongside Alalshikh over the last two years. Still, sharing a broadcaster settles nothing when one promoter holds a fighter the other needs.

Sports.title: Jermell Charlo Out Of December 5 Vergil Ortiz Fight
Sports.content:
Jermell Charlo will not replace Keith Thurman against Vergil Ortiz Jr. on December 5, according to Mike Coppinger. Good. Bringing a 36-year-old fighter out of mothballs with no tune-up after more than three years away would have been terrible optics. Charlo has not won a fight since May 2022, over four years ago. Is this really what Ortiz wants for his career at 28?

“Charlo indeed is not in the mix to fight Vergil Ortiz,” Coppinger wrote on X. Chris Mannix reported that Brian Mendoza and Eric Priest are the expected options after Thurman withdrew injured. Charlo is already set to face Brock Jarvis at 160 pounds on December 12 in Australia.

Poor Replacement Options For PPV

What about DAZN? They are charging fans $79.99 in the United States and £24.99 in the UK for the December 5 pay-per-view headlined by David Benavidez and Michal Cieslak. Ortiz was brought into the co-feature slot to liven things up, yet there is nothing sporting about feeding him either of these replacements.

Mendoza (23-5, 17 KOs) is no upgrade after dropping three of his last four fights. He caught lightning in a bottle with his seventh-round knockout of Sebastian Fundora in April 2023, though it has been all downhill since then with clear decision losses to Tim Tszyu, Serhii Bohachuk, and Yoenis Tellez.

Priest has spent six years fighting on small club cards without beating a single ranked contender, and Esneiker Correa even held him to a draw last November. Expecting fans to shell out $79.99 to watch Ortiz face a faded Mendoza or a club-level opponent like Priest makes zero sense for a pay-per-view show.

What Charlo Has Left At 160

Charlo has not stepped through the ropes since September 2023, when he jumped up two weight classes and lost a lopsided decision to Canelo Alvarez. Canelo dropped him in the seventh round and swept the cards by scores of 119-109 and 118-109 twice. Moving to 168 pounds was never going to be easy, yet Charlo spent the whole night in survival mode and gave Canelo zero reason to take his foot off the gas.

Coppinger noted that an Ortiz versus Charlo fight at 160 could happen in the first half of 2027 if both win next month. Beating Jarvis in Australia gets Charlo active again, though it still proves nothing against top middleweights.

Ortiz has already burned roughly 13 months since stopping Erickson Lubin in two rounds. His promotional dispute with Golden Boy helped kill talks for a fight against Jaron “Boots” Ennis, which would have answered every question about where Ortiz stands. Ortiz cannot afford to keep wasting his prime against short-notice fill-ins.

Sports.title: WBC Mandatory Challenger Souleymane Cissokho Wants To Face Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
The WBC world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia has mentioned the possibility of a fight with either Floyd “Money” Mayweather or Teofimo Lopez, but the WBC mandatory challenger is wondering when he will receive his shot at the title.

In some cases, a fighter can enter the sport of boxing and gradually build his pro career brick by brick. Once that fighter has earned the right to walk through the door of opportunity, a boxer with name recognition cuts the line.

Back in May 2025, Souleymane Cissokho was set to defend his WBC Silver welterweight title against Egidijus Kavaliauskas. In addition to being a fight for the Silver belt, this matchup also served as a world title eliminator bout.

In a very competitive 12-round contest, Cissokho defeated Kavaliauskas by way of unanimous decision. With the victory, Souleymane Cissokho officially became the WBC number one ranked welterweight contender.

Eleven days later, the then 46-year-old Manny Pacquiao announced he was ending his four-year retirement to fight for the WBC world welterweight title. In a match that ended up being a draw, the champion Mario Barrios held on to the belt.

Seven months after the Pacquiao fight, Ryan Garcia leaped over Souleymane Cissokho, and he was locked in to challenge Barrios for the title. At the time, Garcia was coming off a loss he suffered against Rolando “Rolly” Romero.

On February 21, 2026, Ryan Garcia defeated Mario Barrios via unanimous decision. After Garcia became the new world champion, it seemed like the path was cleared for Cissokho to finally receive his shot at the world title.

Unfortunately for Cissokho, another named person cut in front of him as Conor Benn was penciled in to challenge Ryan Garcia. In their world title fight, Garcia stopped Benn in the 2nd round.

Once again, Souleymane Cissokho is at the front of the line as it relates to the opportunity to fight for the world title. Now it appears Cissokho will get skipped for a fourth time.

The WBC welterweight world champion Ryan Garcia and his promotional company CEO Oscar De La Hoya have been very vocal regarding the next title defense being against Floyd “Money” Mayweather or Teofimo Lopez.

The current No.1 contender Souleymane Cissokho was born in Dakar, Senegal, but moved to France when he was 4 years old. He started boxing at the age of 14 and would go on to represent France and win a Bronze medal in the 2016 Olympics.

Now the undefeated Souleymane Cissokho (18-0, 9 KOs) is waiting to receive the world title bout he rightfully earned. Unfortunately for him, Mauricio Sulaiman and the WBC are known for having number one contenders who don’t receive title shots.

Mauricio Sulaiman has the authority to order a mandatory world title fight. Hopefully, in 2027, Sulaiman will step up and make the proper decision in favor of the number one-ranked WBC welterweight contender Souleymane Cissokho.

Sports.title: Josh Kelly Plans To Retire After Ennis And Fundora
Sports.content:
IBF junior middleweight champion Josh Kelly has come up with one of boxing’s unlikeliest exit plans. He wants to beat Jaron “Boots” Ennis, take the last belt off Sebastian Fundora, and walk away as undisputed champion.

“Yeah. No, it’s Boots, Fundora, and then sail into the sunset,” said Kelly to Fight Hub TV. Asked if he would call it a career after that, he said, “Yeah, bro. Yeah, I don’t need to do much after that.”

Running Will Not Beat Boots

What Kelly never answered is whether he plans to retire if he loses to Ennis. The interviewer dropped the ball by skipping the most obvious follow-up question on the board. Getting carved up by Boots the way Kelly was in his sixth round stoppage loss to David Avanesyan in 2021, when his corner threw in the towel with him a bloody mess, would leave his career in rough shape.

Ennis is up first on February 27 in Atlanta. Anyone who watched Kelly win the IBF belt off Bakhram Murtazaliev saw a twelve round track meet, and he used the same running routine to get past his last opponent. Kelly thinks he can read Ennis’s style because he uses similar moves in the ring. He also claimed he saw a few habits from the Xander Zayas fight that he is keeping quiet until the opening bell.

“It’s whoever can adjust first is going to get the better of the fight,” said Kelly. He expects the fight to shift from round to round and even within a round.

Kelly liked being the underdog against Murtazaliev and says he fights looser when people expect him to lose. Atlanta is a totally different problem. Boots cuts off the ring, switches stances effortlessly, and punishes fighters who try to survive on their bicycle. A counter Kelly lands in the third round could easily turn into a trap Ennis springs in the fourth.

At this point, Fundora is not even worth discussing yet. Kelly said he has enough left to fight until 36 or 37 if he wants. “Why spoil that? Why come back after something like that?” said Kelly.

He will not have to worry about retiring early. His whole exit plan ends in Atlanta against Boots, so the Fundora fight will never happen.

Sports.title: Agit Kabayel Wants Unification After Facing Nelson Hysa
Sports.content:
Agit Kabayel could not get the heavyweights he wanted for his first WBC title defense. Instead, he gets 42-year-old Nelson Hysa on November 28 in Düsseldorf. He is already looking past Saturday. Kabayel wants another belt next, though one possible opponent has to get through a fighter Kabayel already stopped.

“I want only the big fights, but none of the big guys are available. Now I will teach him respect,” said Kabayel in an interview with Queensberry Promotions. The unbeaten champion meets Hysa at Merkur Spiel-Arena, with DAZN streaming the main card from 1 p.m. ET.

Hrgovic Has Mandatory Ahead Of Unification

IBF champion Filip Hrgovic is one option, except Sky Sports reported he is headed toward a mandatory defense against Frank Sanchez in Croatia in early 2027. Hrgovic also wants WBO champion Daniel Dubois. The two faced off after Dubois defended his belt against Fabio Wardley in October.

Sanchez gives Kabayel plenty of reason to watch that IBF fight. Kabayel stopped Sanchez in seven rounds in 2024 on the Oleksandr Usyk vs. Tyson Fury undercard. If Sanchez beats Hrgovic, Kabayel could land a rematch with a second belt on the line. If Hrgovic wins, both Kabayel and Dubois will be chasing him.

Dubois holds the WBO title. He also shares promoter Frank Warren with Kabayel. That gives Warren a clean path to put two belts together while Hrgovic deals with Sanchez, provided both fighters want it. Dubois has also talked about a third fight with Usyk, so Kabayel is not the only name on his list.

What Kabayel Faces In Hysa

Kabayel (27-0, 19 KOs) sat ringside when Hrgovic stopped Moses Itauma for the vacant IBF belt in August. Hysa stopped Thomas Narmo in two rounds on that same undercard, then called out Kabayel and promised a knockout. Now Hysa (25-0, 23 KOs) gets his shot in Germany on Albanian Independence Day.

Hysa carries a streak of 19 straight knockouts into the ring, though he did not turn pro until age 37 and has spent four years beating regional club fighters and aging journeymen like Danny Williams and Patrick Korte. Kabayel stopped Arslanbek Makhmudov, Sanchez, Zhilei Zhang, and Damian Knyba in consecutive fights. He took the interim belt against Zhang before being elevated to full champion in June after Usyk vacated the WBC title.

“Nelson is my focus now. But after this fight, it’s a unification fight,” said Kabayel. Getting past Hysa is the easy part on paper, though a 42-year-old puncher who has never gone past six rounds still has to be put away before Warren can start calling Dubois.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua Eyes Retirement Ahead Of Tyson Fury Fight
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua says he expects to retire “pretty soon,” and beating Tyson Fury in Cardiff might give him an easier exit than another loss. At 37, Joshua gets his shot at settling an old score on December 11 at Principality Stadium. Netflix will stream the card.

“When am I going to retire? Pretty soon. I’m getting old now. From an athlete’s point of view, I’m getting old,” said Joshua in an interview with The Sun. He said he had few years left in boxing and brought up investing in longtime sponsor Under Armour once his career ends. He did not set a date.

Through much of his career, Joshua has been at the top of the heavyweight division since winning Olympic gold in 2012.

What A Fury Win Does For Joshua

Joshua stopped Wladimir Klitschko in 2017, outpointed Joseph Parker to pick up the WBO belt in 2018, then avenged his 2019 stoppage loss to Andy Ruiz Jr. six months later by boxing behind his jab for 12 rounds. He proved in that rematch he could stick to a disciplined game plan instead of trading hooks in the pocket.

Fury ended Klitschko’s title run in 2015 and built his reputation on two wins over Deontay Wilder. Both British heavyweights later lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk. Beating Fury settles who owns the head-to-head edge after years of stalled negotiations.

It is tempting to say age is catching up to Joshua, though his problems started back in 2017 when a 40-year-old Wladimir Klitschko put him on the canvas and nearly finished him. Two years later, fringe contender Andy Ruiz Jr. knocked him out in 2019. Then came two losses to Oleksandr Usyk and the fifth-round knockout against Daniel Dubois in 2024.

Joshua’s stamina and punch resistance flaws were there from the beginning, even if Eddie Hearn’s careful matchmaking hid them for years after Joshua’s disputed 2012 Olympic gold medal. Usyk and Dubois simply stripped away the cover. At 37, putting Joshua in with Filip Hrgovic, Agit Kabayel, Moses Itauma, or Frank Sanchez would go badly.

What Joshua Faces In Cardiff

Joshua’s exit would cost British promoters their biggest stadium draw, though that is their problem after December 11. Joshua’s problem is surviving 12 rounds against a 6-foot-9 heavyweight who still knows how to lean on smaller men and spoil their rhythm. He cannot afford to leave his chin up in the pocket the way he did against Dubois. If Joshua wins, he gets to walk away on his own terms. If Fury beats him, retirement stops being a choice he gets to time himself.

Sports.title: Aaron Pryor Overwhelms Gaetan Hart In Six Rounds
Sports.content:
Aaron Pryor never gave Gaétan Hart a chance to settle into their November 22, 1980 title fight at Riverfront Coliseum in Cincinnati. Pryor dropped the Canadian challenger three times and stopped him in the sixth round, keeping his WBA and The Ring junior welterweight belts.

Understandably, referee Roberto Ramírez Sr. stepped in at 2:09 to stop the contest. Hart was pinned in a corner, bleeding, and taking clean shots with nothing coming back.

At 25, Pryor was already a nightmare matchup for anyone at 140 pounds. He came into the fight with an unbeaten record, fresh off flattening Antonio Cervantes in four rounds in the same arena three months earlier.

Hart, a 27-year-old lightweight champion from Buckingham, Quebec, brought legitimate fight-ending power into his first world title shot. It didn’t matter. Pryor forced a pace that kept Hart in a constant state of defense, taking away his leverage before he could ever set his feet to throw heavy shots.

What Followed Hart To Cincinnati

Hart carried dark history into Ohio after two brutal fights in Canada earlier that year. In May, he stopped Ralph Racine in the 12th round of a Canadian lightweight title bout, putting Racine into a coma that ended his career. One month later in Montreal, Hart stopped Cleveland Denny in the 10th round. Denny died 16 days later.

Opponents in Canada made the mistake of letting Hart plant his feet and unload. Pryor never gave him the chance. He backed Hart up in the first round and dropped him 20 seconds into the second. Hart beat the count, then went down again before the bell. He was gassed out before the fight even got started.

Hart Couldn’t Survive Pryor’s Pace

Hart absorbed heavy shots in the third without going down and had a brief spell of offense in the fourth before Pryor took back control and knocked out his mouthpiece. Early in the fifth, a punch buckled Hart’s knees. He steadied himself and landed two crisp lefts that snapped Pryor’s head back, the exact kind of heavy shots that had ruined opponents in Canada. Pryor walked straight through them without getting hurt.

Hart landed first in the sixth, too. Pryor answered with a right hook that sent him down for an eight count, then chased him into the corner until Ramírez waved it off. Pryor was already running away on the cards, leading 50 to 45 on two and 50 to 43 on the third.

Pryor went to 27 and 0 and knocked out his next four challengers before stopping Alexis Argüello twice. He finished 39 and 1 with 35 knockouts and made the Hall of Fame in 1996. Hart never fought for a world title again and later turned up in the documentary The Steak. Nobody at 140 pounds could take Pryor’s punches or survive that pace in 1980.

Ghana News.title: MTN donates computers to UMaT as student population grows
Ghana News.content:
The University of Mines and Technology (UMaT), Tarkwa, is seeking to improve access to computer facilities after admitting more than 5,000 new students this academic year.

Vice Chancellor, Professor Bernard Kumi-Boateng, said the increase in enrolment had put pressure on the University’s ICT resources, making it difficult to provide adequate computer access for all students.

He was speaking at a presentation of computers and ICT accessories by MTN Ghana to the University as part of the telecommunications company’s 30th anniversary Acts of Kindness initiative.

Professor Kumi-Boateng described the donation as timely, saying the equipment would support teaching, learning and research while improving students’ access to essential digital tools.

He also commended MTN Ghana for its longstanding partnership with UMaT and its continued investment in education and technology.

Acting Senior Manager for MTN’s South West Region, David Woasey, said the donation formed part of the company’s Computers-4-Social-Good programme, which provides educational technology resources to selected institutions across the country.

He said digital skills were increasingly important in sectors such as mining, engineering, data science, cybersecurity and telecommunications, making access to technology essential for students.

Mr Woasey said MTN hoped the computers would strengthen UMaT’s learning environment and help prepare students to contribute to Ghana’s digital and industrial development.

The donation forms part of MTN Ghana’s 30th anniversary Acts of Kindness activities and its broader commitment to education and digital inclusion.

Ghana News.title: Endeavour Mining commits XOF 803m to health projects in three African countries
Ghana News.content:
Endeavour Mining has committed XOF 803 million to support health initiatives in Ghana's neighbouring countries, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and Senegal, in 2027.

The commitment was announced at the third edition of Speak Up Africa Day in Dakar, Senegal, where more than 400 stakeholders from government, business, science, civil society and the development sector gathered to discuss Africa's health, education and inclusion priorities.

The investment is expected to contribute to health interventions in the three countries, although details of how the funds will be distributed and the specific projects to be supported were not disclosed. The announcement came during a high-level engagement on the role of the private sector in malaria elimination and improving access to healthcare, particularly in communities where health needs remain greatest.

Speak Up Africa, the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene, and OSIDEA used the gathering to encourage businesses, especially those in the extractive industry, to make sustainable investments in public health. The event also saw the launch of the Private Sector Health Investment Barometer, a tool intended to document corporate contributions to healthcare and encourage more businesses to support national health priorities.

Four companies, Canal+, ICons, Boto S.A. and Endeavour Mining, were recognised for their contributions to the fight against malaria.

Elhadji Doucoure, Head of Monitoring, Evaluation, Surveillance and Digital Transformation at Senegal's National Malaria Control Programme, said private-sector involvement must translate into tangible investments that protect vulnerable communities.

"The private sector has an essential role to play in malaria elimination. The challenge is to translate this engagement into decisive investments that support national strategies and protect communities where needs are greatest," he said.

Beyond malaria, the event highlighted the need to protect African children against preventable diseases. Speak Up Africa, in partnership with the Basketball Africa League (BAL), launched the First Shot campaign on November 14 in Guédiawaye, Senegal, to strengthen public and political support for child health.

The campaign seeks to promote routine immunisation, malaria prevention and polio eradication, using sporting events and influential personalities to raise awareness. It is expected to run until the end of 2027. Former NBA player Ian Mahinmi, founder of the I AM Foundation, was among the personalities who supported the launch.

Marie Laurence Archambault, Director of Social Responsibility and Player Programs at the Basketball Africa League and NBA Africa, said millions of African children still lack essential protection against preventable diseases.

She said the partnership would use the influence of sport and its personalities to make child health a priority both within communities and at the policy level.

Education was also a major part of this year's gathering, with the launch of the Make It Count campaign, which advocates for every African child to acquire basic reading, writing and mathematics skills by the age of ten.

The campaign is being led by Speak Up Africa and its partners through the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Hub.

In Senegal, the Harmonised Model of Bilingual Education (MOHEBS) has reached more than 640,000 students and supported 12,116 teachers across the country's 18 education academies.

Fara Ndiaye, Co-Founder and Deputy Executive Director of Speak Up Africa, said governments must translate their commitments to foundational learning into adequate funding and measurable results in classrooms. The programme also highlighted the contributions of women and young people to Africa's development.

An intergenerational gathering brought together women leaders from different sectors to share experiences and strengthen networks, while Story Lab Next Gen created a platform for young people, advocates and content creators to explore new approaches to public advocacy.

Discussions also addressed reproductive health and family planning, with an emphasis on youth participation and access to essential information and services.

The 2026 edition, which marked 15 years of Speak Up Africa, ended on November 20 with two exhibitions celebrating individuals working to advance health, education and inclusion.

The exhibitions, titled "Jambaar" and "Leurs voix, nos regards", featured portraits of African sports personalities and women whose work is contributing to health and women's rights in their communities.

Ghana News.title: Mahama mourns former South African Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama has paid tribute to former South African Deputy President Dr Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka following her death, describing her as an influential African leader whose contributions to gender equality, peace and security will be greatly missed.

In a Facebook post on Monday, November 23, President Mahama extended his condolences to her family, the South African government and its people, highlighting her distinguished record in public service and her contributions to the continent and the international community.

He recalled Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka's service as South Africa's Deputy President and her subsequent leadership of UN Women as Executive Director, where she played a prominent role in championing gender equality and advancing the rights of women worldwide.

"Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka was a trailblazer whose impact resonated worldwide," President Mahama wrote.

The President also reflected on their professional association through the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, which he chairs and where the former Deputy President served as a board member.

He said the forum had benefited from her knowledge and experience, particularly her commitment to addressing issues of peace, security and development across the continent.

"Her Excellency's unwavering commitment to peace, security, and the development of our continent leaves a void that will be deeply felt," he stated.

Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka's work at UN Women earned her international recognition for her advocacy for gender equality and efforts to advance opportunities for women and girls.

Her contributions to both South African politics and international development made her a prominent voice in discussions on women's empowerment and Africa's progress.

President Mahama concluded his tribute with a message of sympathy to her family and the people of South Africa, praying for her peaceful repose.

Ghana News.title: Fire destroys offices of Northern Regional Minister and Chief Director in Tamale
Ghana News.content:
Fire has gutted parts of the Northern Regional Coordinating Council (NRCC) in Tamale, including the offices of the Northern Regional Minister and the Chief Director.

The fire reportedly broke out at about 5:30 a.m. today, destroying computers, office furniture, equipment and important documents.

The Chief Director's office was the worst affected, with no single item reportedly salvaged from the inferno. The Chief Director is a key administrative figure at the RCC, overseeing its day-to-day operations and coordinating the activities of the various departments.

It took the timely intervention of personnel from the Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) to bring the fire under control and prevent it from spreading to other parts of the facility. However, no casualties were recorded.

Briefing journalists after the incident, the Northern Regional Minister, Ali Adolf John, said he received information about the fire early in the morning. He noted that the incident had virtually grounded the operations of the RCC, considering the extent of the damage to offices and the destruction of essential equipment and documents.

The Minister said preliminary investigations suggested that the fire could have been caused by an electrical fault. He added that the GNFS had commenced investigations to establish the actual cause of the fire.

Ghana News.title: Government moves to ease port congestion, separates shipping line releases from cargo clearance
Ghana News.content:
Victor Baidoo speaking with GIFF members at the meeting

The government has directed the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) and terminal operators to separate shipping line release procedures from the cargo clearance process at the ports, in a move to reduce congestion and facilitate international trade.

Under the new arrangement, importers who have paid the required duties and completed all customs clearance procedures will be allowed to take delivery of their cargo without waiting for separate release approvals from shipping lines.

The measure is expected to eliminate procedural delays, improve the movement of goods and reduce the cost of doing business at the ports.

The Head of the Revenue Assurance Department at the Ministry of Finance, Victor Kofi Baidoo, disclosed this at a meeting with members of the Ghana Institute of Freight Forwarders (GIFF) at Tema. The meeting formed part of the ministry's engagements with freight forwarding stakeholders to discuss measures to improve port operations, address bottlenecks and facilitate trade.

Mr Baidoo explained that the directive was part of the government's efforts to streamline port operations by removing shipping line release procedures from the customs clearance chain. He noted that under the previous arrangement, importers who had paid their duties and completed the necessary customs procedures were still required to obtain separate release approvals from shipping lines before their goods could be evacuated.

Under the new system, customs clearance and shipping line transactions will be treated as separate processes. Once Customs has confirmed that the cargo has been duly cleared and the appropriate duties paid, importers can proceed to evacuate their goods while resolving any outstanding transactions with the shipping lines separately. Mr Baidoo said the government had communicated the directive to Customs and terminal operators for implementation.

Port Congestion

The separation of the two processes is expected to ease pressure on limited storage space at the ports by reducing the time cleared containers remain in the terminals awaiting shipping line approvals.

Faster evacuation of cargo could improve container turnaround, create room for incoming consignments and reduce the accumulation of containers within the port. It could also lower demurrage and other avoidable charges incurred by importers, while improving the overall efficiency of the supply chain.

Compare Couriers

A freight forwarder and leading member of GIFF, Johnny Mantey, welcomed the decision, describing it as a significant step towards addressing congestion at the Tema Port.

He said freight forwarders had, over the years, engaged various stakeholders on the need to separate shipping line release procedures from customs clearance, adding that the new arrangement addressed a longstanding concern within the industry.

However, Mr Mantey noted that delays in obtaining container releases from some shipping lines remained a major challenge, with importers sometimes having to wait between four and five days to He expressed concern about the increasing number of containers accumulating at the port, particularly empty containers awaiting return to shipping lines.

He said the situation was putting pressure on available storage space and could worsen congestion if urgent measures were not taken. Mr Mantey called for greater cooperation from shipping lines to ensure the timely evacuation and return of containers, adding that further engagements would be held with them to address the concerns and prevent the situation from escalating.

Ghana News.title: CDD-Ghana’s John Osae-Kwapong blames lack of sanctions for persistent absenteeism among MPs
Ghana News.content:
A fellow at the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana), Dr John Osae-Kwapong, has attributed persistent absenteeism among Members of Parliament (MPs) to the failure to hold lawmakers accountable for staying away from parliamentary sittings without reasonable explanations.

He argues that the absence of effective sanctions for MPs who disregard parliamentary attendance rules creates little incentive for them to change their behaviour.

Speaking on JoyNews AM Show on Monday, November 23, Dr Osae-Kwapong said the continued recurrence of the issue suggested that existing measures had not been effective in ensuring that lawmakers took their attendance obligations seriously.

He questioned why absenteeism remained a concern despite repeated discussions about the conduct of MPs, arguing that failure to enforce the rules could encourage further disregard for parliamentary responsibilities.

" If nothing is being done in terms of holding persons accountable for absenting themselves from Parliament without proper explanation or the proper excuse, then no one has the incentive to change behaviour," he said.

Dr Osae-Kwapong maintained that enforcing the existing rules and imposing appropriate consequences on MPs who failed to justify their absence could help reduce the practice.

He said lawmakers would be more inclined to comply with attendance requirements if they knew that staying away from parliamentary proceedings without an acceptable reason could attract sanctions.

The CDD-Ghana Fellow suggested that the Speaker's enforcement of parliamentary attendance rules should go beyond expressions of concern to include measures that hold offending MPs responsible for their actions.

He noted that such accountability could help address the recurring problem and reinforce the importance of MPs being present to perform their legislative duties.

Dr Osae-Kwapong's comments come amid renewed concerns about absenteeism in Parliament and calls for lawmakers to demonstrate greater commitment to their responsibilities in the House.

Ghana News.title: CSU Chancellor calls for support for private universities to strengthen national development
Ghana News.content:
The Chancellor of Christian Service University (CSU), Most Rev. Prof. Emmanuel Kweku Asante, has called for stronger government and stakeholder support for private tertiary institutions, arguing that they play a critical role in Ghana's human resource development.

Speaking at the university's 50th Congregation ceremony at the CSU durbar grounds, where more than 500 students graduated, Most Rev. Prof. Asante said private universities are not established solely for profit but contribute significantly to the training of skilled professionals for national development.

The ceremony, held under the theme “Expanding Beyond the Frontiers of Academic Excellence,” brought together university officials, parents, guardians and other stakeholders, with more than 500 students graduating.

He says private universities must be supported to expand access to higher education, particularly as public institutions alone cannot meet the country's growing demand for tertiary education.

“If you take away the private institutions, the public institutions alone cannot meet the needs. Look at the numbers,” he said, appealing to government to consider partnerships and support mechanisms for private universities.

The Chancellor also urged graduating students to move beyond acquiring certificates and focus on applying their knowledge to practical situations, insisting that education must produce graduates capable of delivering results in the workplace and contributing meaningfully to society.

He said the university expects its graduates to demonstrate excellence wherever they find themselves, whether in employment or entrepreneurship.

“People who come in here to study must not just acquire knowledge for the sake of knowledge, but they should be people who will be holistically educated,” he said.

Delivering the keynote address, High Court Judge, Justice Abdul-Hakeem Osman, has challenged graduates of Christian Service University (CSU) to look beyond academic certificates and focus on developing practical skills, integrity and innovation to address societal challenges.

He says academic qualifications alone are insufficient to guarantee success, urging graduates to translate the knowledge acquired in the classroom into practical solutions that contribute to national development.

Justice Osman said academic excellence must be complemented by leadership, emotional intelligence, creativity and the ability to solve real-world problems.

“A very high GPA is only a key, but not the final destination,” he emphasized.

He explained that the true purpose of education goes beyond passing examinations and obtaining certificates, stressing that graduates must demonstrate their ability to apply knowledge in their respective fields.

“In the classroom, success is measured by how well we absorb information. In the real world, success is measured by how effectively we apply that information to solve real-world problems,” he said.

Justice Osman further urged the graduates to embrace failure as part of the learning and innovation process, noting that major breakthroughs often come from individuals who are willing to take risks, learn from mistakes and persevere.

He also emphasised the importance of character and integrity, warning that intellectual ability without good character could undermine an individual's potential.

The ceremony also celebrated the achievements of graduates, including valedictorian Sophia Abena Agyaka, a midwife who pursued a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science.

She said her decision to combine healthcare experience with computing was driven by a desire to develop technological solutions to challenges in maternal and child healthcare, particularly in record-keeping and service delivery.

“I see me pursuing computer science would help solve problems in the midwifery sector, building technologies to solve problems with mother and children and making services easy for both mother and children,” she said.

Ms. Agyaka indicated plans to pursue a master's degree in Health Informatics to further combine technology and healthcare, describing improved documentation and digital systems as key areas where technology could enhance service delivery.

Ghana News.title: GPL: ‘We lost focus in the final minutes’ – Hearts of Oak’s Mohammed Hussein on draw with Aduana
Ghana News.content:
Mohammed Hussein and Samuel Boadu share a moment after Hearts of Oak's 2-2 draw with Aduana. Photo Credit: Reality Images

Hearts of Oak midfielder Mohammed Hussein says the team went to sleep in the final minutes of their Ghana Premier League game against Aduana Football Club, allowing the latter to claw back into the tie.

The Phobians gave up a two-goal lead in the matchday 12 fixture to pick up one point after the game ended 2-2 at the University of Ghana Stadium.

The draw sees Hearts now five points behind league leaders Medeama, who defeated AshantiGold in their game in Tarkwa.

Speaking following the end of the game, Hussein, who was adjudged Most Valuable Player of the Match, revealed the team's late switch-off allowed Aduana into the game.

"I think at the latter part of the game, we lost a bit of concentration that led to the 2-2 draw," he said.

"I know our supporters are not happy as they want; I am begging them on behalf of my teammates and the technical team. We will go back to the drawing board and correct our mistakes."

"It's not just a league; it's a marathon. The league is not yet ended. We still have a lot of games [to play], so we will go to the drawing and correct the mistakes."

Hearts will turn attention to FA Cup action this weekend when they come up against Accra Elite Academy.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Former Icelandic PM says world’s great powers are flexing their muscles
World.content:
Iceland’s former prime minister warns climate change remains an existential threat as global power politics sidelines action.

Iceland’s former prime minister says that although climate change has fallen lower down on the international political agenda, it remains an existential crisis.

Katrin Jakobsdottir says our warming world is not just a catastrophe for nature, but a health and security emergency that cannot be ignored.

Her country is on the front lines of that emergency, with the Arctic warming at four times the rate of the rest of the world.

Almost all of Iceland’s glaciers are rapidly retreating – one was declared “dead” in 2019.

Jakobsdottir says it all comes at a time when the world’s biggest powers are flexing their muscles – and the politics of compromise are being squeezed out.

World.title: COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
World.content:
UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in blow to climate agenda.

UN climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.

The talks in Antalya in Turkiye, known as COP31, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others ⁠⁠rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia.

It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark, which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.

So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?

Why did COP31 collapse?

The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.

Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture, the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.

Cosima Cassel, Programme Lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at ⁠⁠environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.



The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the ⁠⁠main driver of global warming.

The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after around 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.

On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.

“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”

Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.

Sebastien Duyck, Senior Attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.

“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”

What’s next for the UN process – and for the planet?

The collapse of climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.

The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.

Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.



“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.

However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process (UNFCCC) is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.

“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.

Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice (ICJ) advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.

Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.

Without any meaningful action, the planet will warm 2.3 to 2.5C (4.1 to 4.5F) by 2100, the report said.

Joeri Rogelj, Professor of Climate Science and Policy at Imperial College London, said a starting point would have been to renew commitments made at COP28 in Dubai, where nations had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.

Instead, “even simply echoing these agreed outcomes was politically too challenging for some countries with strong vested interests in fossil fuels,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The commitments needed are clear: global greenhouse gas emissions must decline to slow the rate of global warming,” Rogelj told Al Jazeera.

“This failure risks further delaying meaningful global emissions reductions, with the poorest and most vulnerable countries and communities bearing the greatest consequences.”

World.title: Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
World.content:
A series of drone strikes on Russian vessels in Libyan and Finnish territories fuels fears that the war in Ukraine is spreading.

Share Who’s behind drone attacks on Russian ships off Libya and Finland? on social media

Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.

“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.

The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.

The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.

The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.

What do we know about the attacks?

The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.

Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.

Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.

“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.

A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.



In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.

Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.

Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.

What have Libya and Russia said?

Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.

“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.

“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.

The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.

On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.

“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.

The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The origin of Sunday’s attack is still not confirmed.

How many Russian vessels have been attacked in recent weeks?

At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.



The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.

In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.

In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.

Is the Ukraine-Russia war expanding geographically?

Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.

“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.

He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.

Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.

“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.

The sinking of the Merkury, commissioned in 2023, would also weaken Russia’s naval capabilities, Muraviev said.

However, the academic warned that the Gulf of Finland was particularly sensitive because of its geography and the proximity of Russian and NATO forces.

“In my personal view, it is an area where a possible clash between Russia and NATO is quite possible,” he said.

Muraviev added that the attacks could have wider implications for global shipping, which is already facing heightened security threats around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.

“[The attacks] just add additional risks to marine operators from across the world,” he said.
