World.title: CAS decision on Senegal’s AFCON 2025 title appeal on Tuesday
World.content:
Senegal are contesting CAF’s decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal winning the final 1-0 in January.

The Court of Arbitration ‌for Sport (CAS) will release its decision on Senegal’s appeal against ⁠being stripped of ⁠this year’s Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title on Tuesday.

Senegal are contesting the decision of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal ⁠beating the hosts 1-0 in extra time in January’s final in Rabat, and the outcome will be announced on Tuesday, the court confirmed on Monday.

It did not give a time for the announcement.

CAS heard the arguments of Senegal, Morocco and CAF in Lausanne ⁠in early October.

It had initially promised a decision within days of the hearing on ‌October 8 but then decided to issue a complete ruling, including legal grounds, known as a CAS Award. That process requires several weeks.

CAS Awards hold the same value as a national court judgement, enforceable in accordance with the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. Awards may be enforced by sports federations or state courts, depending on the circumstances.

In the final, Senegal ⁠walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty ⁠was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.

Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal ⁠scored the winner to secure victory.



However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled ⁠that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off ⁠the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco.

Senegal appealed the CAF ruling to sport’s highest court, CAS, on March 25, but it was heard some six months later. The ‌basis of its arguments is that the referee’s decision is final and he allowed the match to be completed.

The CAS panel is presided over by French sports law ‌expert ‌Gerald Simon, with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich, Ulrich Haas.

World.title: Why is Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank under attack?
World.content:
One of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions has found itself at centre of political tensions amid protests and violence by supporters of ousted PM Sheikh Hasina.

Dhaka, Bangladesh – When attackers stormed a Grameen Bank branch in Kashiani last week, they did not just damage furniture and equipment. They also destroyed records accumulated over nearly three decades.

Solaiman Morol, the branch manager in Bangladesh’s Gopalganj district, said about a dozen men arrived on the afternoon of November 18 carrying machetes, petrol and tools to break the locks. Staff members were away on field visits.

The attackers looted the branch and tried to cut open its vault with a grinder. They took out about 40 sacks of vouchers and other documents and set them on fire. They also looted steel cupboards, filing cabinets, chairs, tables and other equipment. A staff member’s rice cooker was among the items taken away. “They said that after burning the records, nobody would have to repay their loans,” Morol said.

Videos of the attack later appeared online. Morol said he heard slogans including “Joy Bangla” and “Joy Bangabandhu”, associated with ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, as well as calls to burn what the attackers described as “Yunus’s den”.

The branch has not been able to resume normal operations. Staff members have received threats and customers are worried about the safety of their deposits and loan records.

“A bank depends on trust. This is impacting our customers’ confidence. People who have deposits with us are becoming frightened,” Morol said.

It wasn’t a one-off incident.

Grameen Bank under attack

The attack was part of a wider wave of violence against Grameen Bank. Its latest internal memorandum, dated November 23, records 97 attacks on branches and offices between November 10 and 23.



The attacks have put the Nobel Prize-winning institution founded by Muhammad Yunus at the centre of Bangladesh’s political tensions, months after he stepped down as chief adviser following Hasina’s removal from power in August 2024. Hasina supporters set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members in Faridpur and Narail.

In a statement on Monday, Yunus called “the systematic assault” on Grameen Bank “unbelievably shocking”, noting that bank officials and borrower-members “narrowly escaped fatal injury” in several incidents.

Grameen Bank is one of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions. It pioneered a model of microcredit that provides small loans to people who often cannot access conventional banking services.

About 90 percent of its ownership belongs to its borrower-members, while the government holds the remaining 10 percent. It has around 10.6 million members, most of them rural women, according to its managing director, Sarder Akhter Hamed. Around 5.5 million borrowers have outstanding loans worth more than Tk19,000 crore ($1.53bn). Members also hold deposits of around Tk25,000 crore ($2bn) with the bank.

“There are many people in the communities we serve whom other banks and financial institutions are unwilling to lend to. We stand beside them and provide access to credit,” Hamed said.

The attacks have disrupted the bank’s work and left staff members worried about their safety. Hamed said the institution has around 21,000 employees and that the violence had affected them psychologically. “There is a sense of insecurity,” he said.

Is the Awami League targeting Grameen Bank – and why?

The government has blamed the Awami League, the party of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, for the attacks.

“The government is making every effort to maintain law and order,” Ziauddin Ahmed, additional secretary in charge of the political wing at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Al Jazeera.

The attacks come amid renewed political activity by Hasina’s supporters, which has led to serious unrest in parts of the country, for example Gopalganj, her ancestral district. Hasina supporters have set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members.

Political analysts say Grameen Bank has become a symbol through which some Awami League supporters can direct their anger at Yunus, under whose interim rule Hasina’s party was banned from electoral politics. During Yunus’s stint as Bangladesh’s leader, Hasina was also convicted by a tribunal for massacres carried out against protesters who challenged her rule in 2024. Hasina faces a death sentence, but has recently asserted that she intends to return to Bangladesh from India, where she has lived in exile since she was ousted.



Mubashar Hasan, a researcher at the humanitarian and development research initiative at Western Sydney University, said the timing was significant.

“Her party has spent the week pushing for her return. Grameen Bank is the easiest symbol of Dr Yunus they can reach,” he said. “For the Awami League’s hardliners, Yunus is the face of their fall, so burning his bank is a way of hitting back at him.”

The attacks, Hasan argued, may also be intended to demonstrate that the party still has a presence on the streets, despite the ban. “Some of these attacks look like a performance of strength, especially in Gopalganj, to tell supporters ‘we are still here’,” he said.

Asif Mohammad Shahan, a professor in the department of development studies at the University of Dhaka, sees the violence as part of a broader political strategy.

He said the Awami League had two possible routes after the August 2024 uprising: acknowledge its mistakes and seek political rehabilitation, or try to force its way back into politics. In his assessment, the party has chosen the latter.

“The attack on Grameen Bank is actually an effort of sending a message of ‘politics of revenge’,” Shahan said.

He said the attacks could also be intended to provoke the government into a heavy-handed response, allowing the party to portray itself as a victim and challenge the government’s legitimacy.

Why is Grameen Bank particularly vulnerable, and who is paying the price?

The bank’s ownership structure makes the attacks especially consequential. Most of its shares belong to the poor women who depend on it for loans, savings and other financial services.

“When a branch burns, it’s their loan files, savings records and repayment schedules going up in smoke,” Hasan of Western Sydney University said.

He warned that disruption could push borrowers towards informal lenders and make it harder for them to continue their repayment cycles.

The damage is already affecting the bank’s operations. Hamed, the Grameen Bank managing director, said the institution had suspended the accrual of interest on outstanding loans at branches unable to operate because of the attacks.

The bank is also trying to protect its staff and property. Some branches have increased security and moved staff from locations considered particularly risky.

But the consequences extend beyond damaged buildings and lost records: At stake is also the confidence of customers in the bank.

Why is the BNP government struggling to stop the attacks?

The attacks have also raised questions about the ability of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government to maintain law and order.

Ahmed, the Home Ministry official, said “it would be wrong to say that the government is struggling to contain the situation”. Police headquarters told Al Jazeera that eight cases had been filed and eight people arrested in connection with the attacks. “The problem is that our police force is somewhat short of manpower,” Ahmed said.

Shahan said the government’s response was being constrained by the knowledge that a tough crackdown could give the Awami League the chance to play victim. “The Awami League is baiting the government into attacking it so that it can quickly switch to playing the victim and try to delegitimise the government,” he said.



Hamed said police had responded whenever the bank sought help and in some cases had provided advance warnings about possible attacks. “For the most part, however, we have had to remain alert and protect ourselves,” he said.

“If the law-and-order situation in the country improves, confidence and trust [in the bank, too] will automatically return,” he said.

World.title: Occupied West Bank ‘military zones’ become de facto Israeli settler land
World.content:
Closed military zones in the occupied West Bank are being seized by settlers and made into staging posts for pogroms against Palestinians.

Ramallah, Occupied West Bank – Saleh Zahran had a room on his family’s land with a television, a fireplace, a fridge and solar panels. The kids would play in the groves, and the men stayed up late at night watching the stars.

“We’d cook, eat, drink, spend a whole day from morning to sunset,” he says.

Zahran, 39, inherited the farmland, with 120 olive trees, in Deir Abu Mishal, a village west of Ramallah, from his grandfather and father, splitting it among his brothers.

Between 70 and 80 percent of people in the village, which falls in Area B, under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, live off the land, and just a few years ago, there were no settlers nearby.

“We’d come and go whenever we wanted, pick our fruit at our own pace, sell, build, and marry off sons from the olives. Now, it’s all gone,” he told Al Jazeera.

Since settlers set up an outpost in Area B about 1km from his land in June, nobody in his family had been able to reach it. Settlers attacked their cars, and his elderly father was pepper-sprayed while trying to reach the farmland, he says.

On November 10, an Israeli High Court decision granted the village two days of army “coordinated” harvesting, something once unthinkable in Area B.

Zahran set out with his brothers to reach their lands for the first time in five months, but about 20 settlers came at them. They threw stones, smashed the family’s truck and his brother’s four-wheeler and slashed the tyres. He saw no soldiers, and police never arrived despite their calls.

The next day, the army and its liaison office were present. But farmers were held up until about 9am, shown a map of permitted areas, and told to leave by 2:30pm. Ghiyath Nasser, their lawyer, says villagers could reach less than a third of the area in question, so Zahran could harvest only about 20 of his 120 trees.

After five months, Zahran finally reached the farm room that day only to find settlers had stolen or smashed his belongings and were drawing water for their sheep from the two wells he had restored. The saplings he had planted last year had died of thirst.



On paper, it is the settlers who are barred from the Zahran family’s property and the land around Deir Abu Mishal. But in practice, it is Palestinian owners like Zahran who are kept out.

Nasser says that after his first legal petition, the army twice demolished the outpost – which was immediately rebuilt both times – then declared the site a closed military zone for Israelis only. That, Nasser argues, means soldiers cannot demand permits or “coordination” from Palestinian owners – their job is to keep settlers out.

“Sometimes they declare an area closed to settlers, but in the application they close it to Palestinians,” said Wail Qut, a lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), who is from Madama, south of Nablus.

Kerem Navot and Peace Now’s July report found that, at the end of 2025, farm outposts effectively controlled more than 1 million dunams (247,105.4 acres), about 18 percent of the West Bank — roughly 750,000 dunams (185,329 acres) taken since late 2022.

‘A de facto closure’

In Madama, closures came first, and the outposts followed. Qut says its northern land was never declared a closed military zone, but the effect was the same.

About five years ago, the army gated the road from the village to Nablus, citing security concerns, he says. It was the only access to as much as a third of Madama’s land. The Israeli High Court dismissed the villagers’ petition after the army said farmers could reach the land on foot or by animal and apply for permits.

“It’s a de facto closure, though,” said Qut, with farmers still barred from entering.

Then, last April, an outpost of what Qut estimates are now 10 caravans appeared inside the closed area. He said the army suddenly reopened the gate for the settlers to use. Qut and his brother were stopped by a settler in the same area when they tried to pick olives there this year, forcing them to leave under armed threat.

Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, which tracks settler land takeovers, says such closures without orders are common across the occupied West Bank. “There is no vacuum in the West Bank,” he said. “Once an area is closed to Palestinian access, settlers sooner or later will come and take it over, and this is exactly what happened in Madama.”

But Qut finds the courts complicit too. When JLAC petitioned over the outpost north of Madama in September, the court gave the state until May 2027 to respond, rather than a few days, as Qut expected.



‘On the pretext of I don’t know what’

On November 13, a wedding was due to take place in al-Mughayyir, located at the northeastern edge of the Ramallah governorate. “Despite the pain and the suffering, people rejoice,” said Samir Abu Alia, 60, a village council member whose cousin’s son, Hassan Abu Alia, 30, was the groom. But soldiers violently cut the festivities short.

“The moment the patrols came down, they surrounded the hall, 20 army jeeps, and started throwing stun grenades between the men and the women,” recalled Abu Alia. Soldiers took the groom and relatives away from his bride for two hours. Abu Alia and others say the groom was beaten.

It began earlier that day on the eastern plain, when a settler grazing his flock inside a closed military zone claimed someone from al-Mughayyir had thrown firecrackers or shot at him, although he was unhurt. Soldiers accepted the settler’s claim at face value and then sealed and raided the village. The army quickly targeted the wedding, claiming there were gunshots and firecrackers, which attendees deny.

About 80 percent of al-Mughayyir’s 43,000 dunams (10,625.5 acres) lies beyond its eastern entrance, closed for years. Abu Alia says villagers can now move freely in only about 900 dunams (222.4 acres). “The rest of the land they’ve taken over, they stop people from reaching it, on the pretext of a military zone, on the pretext of security, on the pretext of I don’t know what.”

Here, the outpost came first. Village council member Marzouq Abu Naim says the first outpost on the eastern plain appeared in 2018 and has grown from 200 dunams to 5,000 dunams. He counts a dozen around the village. “One of the settlers comes, brings a tent, pitches it on a hilltop … the second day, the third day, you find there’s facilitation, something not normal: [authorities] run him water, they run him electricity, they lay a road to this tent,” he said.

According to Abu Naim, when villagers tried to use the eastern entrance about two months ago, settlers attacked and tried to burn cars and tractors, and the army did nothing to intervene.

Abu Naim, whose son, Jihad, 32, was shot dead by a settler during an invasion of the village school in April, also lost a 10-dunam grove of about 250 olive trees. “It wasn’t me who planted them, or my father — our grandfathers planted them.”

In August 2025, after a shooting wounded an Israeli teenager, the army ordered olive trees beside a settler road through the plain cleared as a “security threat”, and settlers joined in. Locals say more than 10,000 trees were eventually uprooted, including 230 belonging to Abu Alia.

Documents from the Israeli NGO Yesh Din show the area was closed for 30 days to “preserve the aims of the clearing”. Renewed in October 2025, the order extended to July 2026 with redrawn boundaries, and again through December.

The order bars everyone without a permit, settlers included. But Yesh Din’s legal objection says it is enforced only against the owners, while settlers graze, plough and build on their plots. When the army’s legal adviser declined to enforce the closure against settlers, he referred Yesh Din to the Israeli Defence Ministry’s legal adviser instead, which the NGO says was an effort to absolve the army of responsibility.



Lior Zur, a Yesh Din lawyer representing the petitioners, told Al Jazeera, “Through this policy of selective enforcement, the military turns closure orders into a mechanism for transferring possession of land from its lawful Palestinian owners to settler trespassers.”

The ‘height of injustice’

The pattern runs across the West Bank. In March, a closed zone around Duma was enforced against Israeli solidarity activists protecting Bedouin families, rather than settlers; after soldiers removed the activists, settlers invaded the encampment, forcibly displacing the community the next day.

In Burin, farmland sits in closed zones renewed every month or two; settlers have gutted five greenhouses in these closed zones already. In Taybeh, an August order barred Israelis and foreigners, but settlers and outposts remained, including one near the edge of Area B that led to another unevenly enforced closed zone.

Similar cases have occurred in Ein al-Duyuk, Qusra, Umm al-Khair and elsewhere. In closed and firing zones the Israeli army has not used for decades, Etkes said, settlers are “filling in”, even though the orders formally apply to settlers, too.

The result, this olive harvest season, has been unprecedented levels of violence and access restrictions. The United Nations Humanitarian Country Team for the occupied Palestinian territory said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks that caused casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season. The infrequent “coordination” access windows, it said, are often followed by “cancellations, denial of entry, expulsion or attacks”.

“What started as local initiative has been adopted by the military and is today, maybe not a declared policy, but an implemented policy,” said Etkes. The outposts are “not legal, but they are completely supported by the military, by the government, without officialising it”. The Israeli Civil Administration has leased large areas of the West Bank to settlers for grazing, which they never do for Palestinians, Qut said.

“Military closed-zone orders and settler takeovers of Palestinian land are two complementary practices,” said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for Israeli NGO B’Tselem. “The military uses these orders to drive Palestinians off their land, while settlers are frequently allowed to remain or establish outposts.”

Back in Deir Abu Mishal, olives are rotting on trees as the season ends. Zahran’s three young children ask why they cannot return to the farm room for barbecues and the olive harvest. He tells them it is too dangerous. “Four or five settlers stop a whole village, 5,000-6,000 people, from going to the land,” Zahran said. “We are living the height of injustice.”

World.title: Thousands displaced after deadly storm hits Brazil town
World.content:
NewsFeed Thousands displaced after deadly storm hits Brazil town

A powerful supercell storm devastated the Brazilian town of Tupancireta, where at least five people were killed and nearly all homes were damaged. Around 200 military personnel were deployed to help clear debris.

World.title: Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
World.content:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".

"That is the reality," he said on Monday.

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

World.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
World.content:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.

The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.

Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

World.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
World.content:
A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

In a Telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

World.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says
World.content:
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

On Sunday morning, the government that controls eastern Libya said there had been an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia.

Zelensky said the attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.

The health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

The Kremlin declined to comment on the attack.

In a statement on Monday, Zelensky praised an "exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war".

Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky wrote. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.

The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.

The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.

Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend". He said: "It is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."

Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships off Libya's coast and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.

The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".

"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X., external

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

World.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
World.content:
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco â no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles â be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come downâ¦ and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

World.title: Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
World.content:
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.

All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.

Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.

A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.

"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".

As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".

"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.

Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.

Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

World.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
World.content:
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna GnassingbÃ© as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

World.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
World.content:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.

Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.

The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

World.title: PT State of the Race: Atiku, Obi, Makinde’s ambitions test opposition unity
World.content:
Nigeria’s opposition parties are again attempting to build a common political front to challenge President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in the 2027 presidential election. But while negotiations are progressing towards a formal cooperation agreement, the competing ambitions of the parties’ presidential candidates are exposing the difficulty of translating calls for unity into a workable electoral arrangement.

The Coalition for Democracy, comprising six opposition parties and factions, has scheduled 30 November for its second summit in Abuja, where participating parties are expected to sign a formal agreement on political cooperation, democratic renewal and electoral integrity.

The meeting, initially scheduled for 23 November, was postponed after participating parties requested more time to accommodate their campaign schedules. The parties subsequently agreed to suspend their campaign activities on 30 November to attend the summit, where they are expected to sign a “Covenant for Democratic Renewal.”

Coordinated by Salihu Lukman, an African Democratic Congress (ADC) chieftain, the coalition brings together the ADC, Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), a faction of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and the Social Democratic Party (SDP).

However, the parties are approaching the negotiations with separate presidential tickets already on the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) list of candidates. The list names Atiku Abubakar and Rotimi Amaechi for the ADC; Seyi Makinde and Lawal Daura for the APM; Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso for the NDC; and Sandy Onor and Umaru Babangida for the PDP.

The proposed agreement is intended to establish a framework for cooperation without requiring participating parties to dissolve their structures or surrender their individual political identities.

But a major question has widely emerged on whether the opposition parties can go beyond electoral cooperation and agree on a common presidential candidate to challenge the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The difficulty is becoming increasingly apparent as Atiku, former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi and Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde continue to navigate their respective presidential ambitions, while negotiations over a common opposition platform remain inconclusive.

A unity coalition confronting individual ambitions

The latest developments surrounding Atiku have further exposed the competing interests within the opposition’s proposed arrangement.

On 21 November, a coalition of support groups that previously backed the former vice-president announced its endorsement of the Obi-Kwankwaso presidential ticket of the NDC, citing the need for opposition cooperation and considerations around regional power rotation.

Atiku subsequently dismissed reports that he had withdrawn from the presidential race, insisting that he remained in the contest and was determined to challenge Mr Tinubu.

In a statement issued through his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, the former vice-president rejected suggestions that he would abandon his ambition in favour of another opposition candidate.

“I do not need anyone to step down for me, and I am stepping down for no one,” he said.

The ADC’s spokesperson, Bolaji Abdullahi, also distanced the party from the statements, saying they were not authorised and should be disregarded.

Speaking via a phone call with PREMIUM TIMES on Friday, Mr Abdullahi said official communication concerning the party would always be issued only through authorised channels.

“The statements did not come from us. Whatever development involving our party will be communicated through official and authorised channels. Anybody can impersonate you and issue unauthorised statements capable of misleading the public or complicating issues,” he said.

The development illustrates one of the coalition’s central difficulties. While opposition politicians may agree on the need to cooperate against the APC, that agreement does not necessarily translate into a willingness to surrender their individual presidential ambitions.

For Atiku, who has contested the presidency several times and emerged as the ADC’s candidate in May as his fourth attempt, withdrawing in favour of another contender would require considerable political concessions. His emergence as the party’s flagbearer also means that any proposed arrangement must address the interests of the ADC and the political structure mobilised around his candidacy.

The latest development follows a leadership dispute within the ADC over the legitimacy of the party’s leadership under which Atiku emerged as its presidential candidate.

In a judgement delivered on 5 November, Justice Peter Lifu invalidated the David Mark-led ADC leadership and decisions taken under it, raising questions about the validity of the processes through which Atiku emerged as the party’s presidential candidate.

Last week’s edition of the PT State of the Race examined the 68-page published judgement, which, under Order 4, invalidated official acts performed by Mr Mark, Rauf Aregbesola and other national officers covered by the case from 29 July 2025.

Orders 7 and 8 also restrained INEC from recognising them as national officers and barred them from continuing to act in those capacities.

Although the judgement did not specifically direct INEC to remove all ADC nominees, including Atiku, Order 5 directed the electoral commission to recognise Nafiu Gombe as the sole elected member of the National Working Committee entitled to supervise the party’s affairs.

The interpretation and implications of the ruling for Atiku’s candidacy remain contested. The ADC’s lawyer, Kalu Kalu, argued on Channels Television that the judgement did not invalidate the former vice-president’s candidacy. The central dispute is whether the court’s orders invalidating decisions taken under the Mark-led leadership also affect the validity of nominations made during that period. The fact that Atiku was not expressly named in the orders does not, in itself, resolve that question.

The dispute later escalated when officials aligned with Mr Gombe, a former ADC deputy national chairman, called on Atiku to suspend his campaign. In a communiqué, they cited the judgement and claimed to have the backing of the party’s six zonal leaders.

Mr Gombe, however, offered a conditional path to reconciliation with Atiku in a Saturday interview with BBC Hausa, reported by PREMIUM TIMES on Sunday.

He said reconciliation would depend on compliance with what he described as the party’s membership and leadership requirements.

His remarks left open the possibility of internal political negotiations, although no settlement with Mr Mark was announced.

However, Mr Shaibu told PREMIUM TIMES on Thursday that Atiku had filed a 17-ground appeal at the Court of Appeal to overturn the November 4 judgement of the Federal High Court that nullified his nomination.

He added that the issue involving its leadership remains internal and could be resolved by the party’s concerned leaders.

“We are still on it, and we challenged the justification of the earlier orders at the appellate court,” he said.

He added that Atiku remains the party’s candidate and his appeal urged the court to examine whether the trial court had jurisdiction.

“It is left to the court to find out if the disputed evidence was properly assessed, and whether the sweeping orders made against the party can stand in law.”

Mr Obi’s emergence as the preferred candidate of some opposition support groups presents another dimension to the negotiations. The endorsement of the Obi-Kwankwaso ticket by groups previously aligned with Atiku demonstrates that some political constituencies are already considering alternatives to the ADC candidate.

The NDC, meanwhile, already has its own presidential ticket on INEC’s list, meaning that any agreement on a common candidate would have to accommodate the political interests of the party and its leadership.

These competing expectations make the search for consensus more complicated than securing endorsements from party leaders.

Makinde’s position adds another layer

Mr Makinde’s involvement in the coalition also illustrates the difficulty of reconciling the interests of the different presidential aspirants.

The Oyo governor, who is the APM’s presidential candidate, confirmed in a 13 November interview with ARISE News that opposition leaders were actively discussing a possible alliance.

Mr Makinde argued that the selection of a candidate should be based on evidence, including the aspirants’ manifestos, previous performance and public sentiment, rather than personal preferences or emotional considerations.

Asked whether he would work with Atiku if the available evidence established that the former vice-president was the appropriate candidate around whom the opposition should unite, Mr Makinde answered in the affirmative.

“Not only that I’m open, we’re actively discussing this,” he stated during the interview. “We just won’t say, ‘Oh, okay,’ take emotional decision and say, ‘Oh, it’s you.’ We have manifestos now; we have certain things in that manifesto. We will sit down; we have maybe historical performance. We also have the sentiment of the people. All of those things will come together and arrive at a decision.”

The governor’s position suggests an openness to cooperation, but it does not resolve whether he would eventually relinquish his own presidential ambition.

Indeed, the reported determination of the major contenders to remain in the race underscores the challenge confronting the coalition.

For Mr Makinde, the negotiations also offer an opportunity to participate in shaping the opposition’s political direction beyond his immediate political base in the South-West.

While Mr Makinde said he is “willing to work with any Nigerian” that emerged from its alliance through a thorough assessment of manifestos and past governance delivery, his involvement will ultimately be tested by whether he is prepared to accept an arrangement that does not produce him as the presidential candidate.

The same question applies to other aspirants involved in the coalition’s consultations, including former Cross River State Governor Donald Duke and former presidential candidate Adewole Adebayo, who are also in the presidential race under the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Social Democratic Party (SDP), respectively.

The narrowing window for a common candidate

Beyond the political disagreements, the opposition parties also face a legal and electoral timetable that could complicate efforts to produce a common presidential ticket.

Under Section 31 of the Electoral Act 2026, a candidate seeking to withdraw from an election must submit a written notice and sworn affidavit through the sponsoring political party to INEC not later than 90 days before the election.

For the 16 January 2027 presidential election, the deadline fell on 18 October 2026, challenging the chance of a common candidate that may be produced from the coalition.

Section 33 also restricts political parties from changing or substituting nominated candidates, except in cases of death or withdrawal, subject to the provisions of the law.

This means the participating parties cannot simply replace their presidential candidates through the ordinary withdrawal and substitution process at this stage. A formal merger of political parties is also a separate process governed by Section 81, which requires nine months’ notice and INEC approval.

The distinction is important because the coalition’s proposed cooperation agreement does not necessarily require a merger or the replacement of candidates on the ballot. Parties can still coordinate campaigns, endorse an existing candidate and collaborate on protecting votes while retaining their individual identities.

However, such an arrangement would not automatically remove the other candidates from INEC’s list or create a single joint ticket.

Adebola Bakare, a political scientist and director of the Institute of Legislative Studies at the University of Ilorin, said the opposition’s efforts to build a coalition could strengthen its chances of defeating the incumbent, but warned that competing political ambitions could undermine the arrangement.

Mr Bakare said that although the coalition was a significant step towards building a stronger opposition, the individual interests of the participating parties and their presidential candidates could complicate efforts to reach a common position.

He noted that the presidential candidates had already secured the confidence of their respective parties, built political structures and mobilised supporters around their ambitions, making it difficult for them to abandon their candidacies in favour of another contender.

“All of the presidential candidates have political structures, and nothing made them candidates other than the confidence of their respective parties that this is the person they believe can execute their mandate,” he said.

He, however, warned that agreeing to field a common presidential candidate could trigger another round of disagreements among the coalition members, particularly over who should emerge as the flagbearer.

“What will happen after their agreement to go for a common candidate is the beginning of another disagreement, because the question that will follow is: who would it be?” he said.

Mr Bakare also drew attention to the legal implications of the proposed alliance, saying the parties must clarify the nature of the electoral cooperation they intend to pursue and how they would reconcile their separate presidential nominations within the existing legal and electoral framework.

Lessons from the 2023 election

The opposition’s renewed search for a common platform is largely informed by the outcome of the 2023 presidential election, when the failure of major opposition parties to agree on a joint candidate resulted in separate contests against the APC.

In that election, PREMIUM TIMES reported that Mr Tinubu defeated 17 other candidates with 8,794,726 votes, while Mr Atiku secured 6,984,520 votes. Mr Obi polled 6,101,533 votes, and Rabiu Kwankwaso of the New Nigeria Peoples Party received 1,496,687 votes.

The combined votes of Atiku, Mr Obi and Mr Kwankwaso exceeded 14.5 million, substantially higher than Mr Tinubu’s total.

Although the combined figure does not establish that those votes would automatically have transferred to a single opposition candidate, it illustrates the scale of support distributed among competing political platforms.

The experience has since strengthened arguments among opposition politicians that greater coordination could improve their ability to challenge the ruling party.

Mr Bakare noted that the alliance of the opposition parties could be a lesson from their separate bids for the presidency to challenge the APC in 2023.

“I believe the coalition structure they are building now was informed by the 2023 presidential election when all the parties contested under their respective parties,” he said.

However, the circumstances of the 2027 election present a different set of political calculations.

The opposition is no longer simply attempting to persuade parties to abandon separate platforms. It must also reconcile the interests of politicians who have already secured presidential tickets, established campaign structures and mobilised supporters around their individual ambitions.

Consequently, the challenge is not merely to identify a candidate with broad appeal but to establish a process that the other aspirants and their political constituencies would consider legitimate.

Without such an arrangement, political experts noted that an endorsement of one candidate could emerge on paper without necessarily securing the cooperation of the supporters and political structures of those who retain their own tickets.

A test for signing agreement

The coalition’s 30 November summit will therefore be an important test of whether its members can move beyond consultations and establish practical mechanisms for cooperation.

Mr Lukman, during an interview with Arise News on Thursday, stated that the coalition has developed three documents: the National Covenant for Democratic Renewal, the Framework for Opposition Unity and the National Reform Programme.

“They have already agreed that 30th November will be the day they will publicly sign it,” he said.

The proposed framework is expected to establish principles for cooperation and mechanisms for managing disagreements, while the reform programme will outline minimum policy commitments expected of any government produced by the coalition.

Mr Lukman also disclosed that the parties were considering joint campaigns and the pooling of resources to protect votes at polling units, particularly in areas where individual parties lack the capacity to deploy sufficient agents.

These proposals could provide a basis for cooperation even if the parties fail to agree on a common presidential candidate.

Mr Lukman also noted that the coalition would demonstrate how its commitments can be implemented, including approaches to resolve any disagreement that could arise.

However, there is also the question of how the proposed agreement relates to the five documents initially envisaged at the coalition’s 31 August summit.

The earlier proposals included a Single-Term Transition Charter and a Roadmap to a Common Presidential Candidate, whose status remains unclear. The coalition has yet to explain whether the three documents now scheduled for adoption replace, combine or incorporate the earlier proposals.

The absence of a publicly established mechanism for selecting a common candidate is particularly significant because it concerns the most politically sensitive aspect of the alliance.

Mr Lukman has acknowledged that the coalition has yet to agree on such a mechanism, noting that the participating presidential candidates must be directly involved in the negotiations.

APC’s opportunity amid opposition divisions

While the opposition attempts to reconcile its differences, the APC is preparing to defend its control of the presidency.

Mr Tinubu’s campaign activities and efforts to consolidate support across political constituencies will take place against the backdrop of the opposition’s negotiations.

Experts noted that the ruling party could benefit politically if its opponents remain divided, particularly if competing presidential candidates continue to mobilise independently and their supporters disagree over who should lead the opposition.

“They have to handle their alliance with greater care because the ruling party could also seize the opportunity to build its own structure for victory,” Mr Bakare said.

Mr Bakare said that the existence of multiple opposition candidates does not automatically translate into an advantage for the APC. He noted that the candidates still have to persuade voters through their programmes, records and campaign activities, while the ruling party must defend its own record in government.

“If the opposition coalition couldn’t establish a credible framework for cooperation, it could make it more difficult to coordinate campaign resources, communicate a common message and build a consistent nationwide mobilisation structure,” he noted.

World.title: Why Kwankwaso didn’t join APC with me – Kano governor
World.content:
Kano State Governor Abba Yusuf has again dismissed allegations that he betrayed his political mentor, Rabiu Kwankwaso, by joining the All Progressives Congress (APC).

The governor said Mr Kwankwaso consented to moving into the APC with his followers until a backlash over his public utterances scuttled the plan.

Governor Yusuf said the defection from the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP) arose from a pact with President Bola Tinubu, which was initiated by Mr Kwankwaso, the party’s presidential candidate in 2023.

The former governor is now the vice presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC).

In a wide-ranging interview with BBC Hausa published on Monday morning, the governor addressed his political rift with Mr Kwankwaso, the ongoing Kano Emirate dispute, and preparations for the next general elections.

On the benefits of joining the federal ruling party, Governor Yusuf explained that operating outside the ruling party at the federal level created governance challenges for Kano State.

The pact to return to the APC

Governor Yusuf stated that Mr Kwankwaso sent him to seek an agreement with President Tinubu during the 2023 Kano governorship election litigation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the governor, while awaiting the Supreme Court verdict on the election petition, Mr Kwankwaso instructed him to meet with Mr Tinubu to urge the president not to interfere in the case and to pledge a merger with the APC if the election was not voided.

“He himself even sent me to Tinubu. He pleaded with me to go meet Tinubu and tell him—make this promise to him,” Governor Yusuf said.

“Even if it came down to it, I should take the Quran and swear an oath to President Tinubu at that time that if Allah granted us victory at the Supreme Court, he desired for us to join the APC and work together as one.”

Governor Yusuf noted that he delivered the message and reported President Tinubu’s positive reception back to Mr Kwankwaso, arguing that this timeline invalidates accusations of betrayal by Mr Kwankwaso and his Kwankwasiyya followers.

“Up until the very end, everything that was done was with Mr Kwankwaso’s full knowledge,” he added.

Breakdown of the talks

The governor also rejected public speculation that his rift with Mr Kwankwaso was a staged political strategy designed to maintain control over both the ruling party and the opposition in Kano.

Recounting the final stages of the realignment, Governor Yusuf stated that members of the state House of Assembly independently consulted Mr Kwankwaso regarding a return to the APC before Mr Kwankwaso approached him to facilitate a meeting with the president.

Governor Yusuf said he arranged a meeting in Abuja and informed Mr Kwankwaso, who initially expressed gratitude.

However, according to the governor, the plan collapsed after Mr Kwankwaso returned to Kano and made critical remarks about President Tinubu in an Hausa interview which were subsequently transcribed and sent to the Presidency.

“That is what further ruined things—he left, and we never heard from him again regarding the trip to see the president,” Mr Yusuf stated.

He said at this point he had no option but to continue the move to the APC even without Mr Kwankwaso, considering the agreement reached before the Supreme Court verdict.

On the Kano Emirate tussle

Commenting on the prolonged royal dispute involving reinstated Emir Lamido Sanusi and the dethroned Emir Aminu Ado Bayero, Governor Yusuf urged residents to remain calm and allow the judiciary to resolve the matter.

Describing all parties involved as “brothers” with a mutual understanding, the governor noted that the state government had fulfilled its constitutional duties and that the legal battle had now reached the Supreme Court.

“What I am calling for is for the public to set this emirate issue aside, and let us wait until the Supreme Court delivers its judgement,” he said.

Youth discipline and re-election prospects

Responding to criticisms regarding moral decadence, online defamation, and substance abuse among youths in the state, Governor Yusuf distanced his administration from political thuggery and verbal attacks, stating that anyone claiming to act on his behalf to insult others was lying.

To combat drug abuse, he highlighted establishing a task force led by a “seasoned, fearless individual,” (Muhuyi Magaji), noting that the agency’s efforts have drawn public commendation.

Looking ahead to President Tinubu’s re-election prospects, Governor Yusuf expressed confidence in the administration’s standing in Northern Nigeria.

He described the president as an elder statesman whose primary challenge is not a lack of performance, but insufficient public communication regarding his administration’s achievements.

“Well, I wouldn’t say there is any major challenge that we see. This man is an elder statesman. This man loves this country; this man loves the North. It is just that people have not understood him. The biggest challenge is simply the lack of people who will effectively publicise and communicate the good things he is doing,” Governor Yusuf said on President Tinubu.

World.title: Nigeria created over 27,000 jobs in data compliance sector in less than three years – NDPC
World.content:
The Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) has said the country’s data protection and compliance sector has created over 27,000 jobs in less than three years.

The commission said the development was part of efforts to support President Bola Tinubu’s campaign promise to create jobs for Nigerians through the digital economy.

The National Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer of the NDPC, Vincent Olatunji, projected that the sector could generate over 500,000 jobs, noting that the commission was working towards exceeding the target.

Mr Olatunji spoke on Friday at a sensitisation and awareness training on data protection and privacy organised by the commission for journalists in Abuja.

“You will recall when Mr President was running his campaign during the 2023 elections he promised two million jobs for the digital economy sector.

“And for this ecosystem, which is a sub-sector of the digital economy sector, we are saying that over 500,000 jobs are available in the data privacy ecosystem. And we are already pushing towards achieving that. If within the ecosystem we are doing over 27,000 jobs in less than three years, that is massive. That is very huge. But the target is to get to about 500,000, and even more,” he said.

Nigeria continues to grapple with unemployment, underemployment and a shortage of decent job opportunities, particularly among its youth population.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Although the country’s official unemployment rate has declined under the National Bureau of Statistics’ revised methodology, concerns persist over the quality, availability and security of jobs, with a significant proportion of employed Nigerians working in the informal sector.

The NBS, in its second-quarter 2024 Labour Force Survey, put Nigeria’s unemployment rate at 4.3 per cent, down from 5.3 per cent in the first quarter of the same year. However, the survey showed that 6.5 per cent of young Nigerians aged 15 to 24 were unemployed during the period.

The country’s employment challenge is also reflected in the prevalence of informal work. According to the NBS’ 2023 annual labour force report, about 92.2 per cent of employed Nigerians were engaged in informal employment, raising concerns about access to stable jobs, social protection and other employment benefits.

The digital economy has increasingly been identified as an avenue for expanding employment opportunities, particularly for young Nigerians, as businesses and government institutions adopt digital technologies and require specialised skills.

However, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) has identified skills mismatches, low labour productivity and structural weaknesses in the economy as some of the challenges affecting employment growth in Nigeria.

Strengthening capacity for data protection officers

The NDPC commissioner also spoke about the commission’s efforts to increase the number of certified data protection officers in the country.

He said when the commission was established in 2023, Nigeria had fewer than 1,000 data protection officers. However, the number has since increased to over 10,000 certified officers responsible for overseeing and supporting organisations on data protection matters.

“Section 32 of our law says that all data controllers and processors must engage the services of data protection officers. When we started, we had less than 1,000 data protection officers in all of this country. In the whole of the commission, I was the only certified data protection officer. But as we speak now at the commission, we have over 90 per cent of our staff who are certified.

“And in Nigeria, we have over 10,000 certified data protection officers. What do they do? They support organisations. They create awareness. They oversee their data protection activities, and this is a very scarce skill. They are doing what they are looking for data protection officers,” he said.

Mr Olatunji urged journalists who participated in the training to consider pursuing careers in the data protection and compliance sector.

Nigeria wins global privacy prize

Mr Olatunji also announced that Nigeria had won the Accountability Prize of the Global Privacy Assembly at its 48th annual conference held in Brussels, Belgium.

He said the Global Privacy Assembly comprises 145 countries with data protection laws and independent data protection authorities.

According to him, the assembly provides a platform for countries to exchange knowledge, conduct peer reviews, learn about emerging technologies and assess developments in the global privacy ecosystem.

The NDPC commissioner attributed Nigeria’s progress in data protection to its Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model, under which the commission licenses Data Protection Compliance Organisations (DPCOs) to carry out compliance activities on behalf of the government.

“And one thing that is really working for us in Nigeria is the PPP model. That’s the Public-Private Partnership model, where we license DPCOs to carry out compliance on behalf of the government. And the whole world has seen that model as very unique and impactful, and to a large extent, that has really accounted for the traction that we have achieved in Nigeria.

“The whole world actually celebrated Nigeria, and that wouldn’t have happened without your (journalists) input. No matter what we are doing back home here, if you (journalists) don’t put them out there, nobody will see, nobody will know it. But they saw the work, and through your effort, they were able to identify what we have done. Nigeria was placed on that global map. So we thank all of you for what you have been doing so far,” he said.

World.title: Bayelsa boat tragedy exposes questions over N844m budgeted for boat purchases
World.content:
Bayelsa State Government budgeted a combined N844 million for procuring marine vessels and boats across its 2025 and 2026 budgets.

However, a boat accident that killed 29 people in the state has raised questions about the availability of safe public water transportation.

The questions have become more pressing after President Bola Tinubu directed the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC) to procure boats for riverine communities in the state, alongside his approval of N250 million in financial assistance for families of the victims.

On 20 November, a passenger boat conveying mourners from Ayama community to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near Oweikorogha community in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area, leaving at least 29 people dead and over 50 survivors.

As reported by PREMIUM TIMES, Governor Douye Diri of Bayelsa said preliminary findings suggested that the tragedy could have been avoided if established safety regulations had been observed.

He said the boat was neither seaworthy nor suitable for river transportation and that the location where passengers boarded was not an approved government loading point.

The circumstances have raised questions about the availability of government-provided passenger boats, the regulation of commercial water transport and the government’s management of public investments in the marine sector.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Millions budgeted for boats

An examination of Bayelsa’s 2025 budget and budget performance records shows that the Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy had a N600 million allocation for the procurement of trawlers, heavy-duty river crafts, barges and self-propelled barges.

However, the records indicate that only N79.5 million was spent between January and September 2025 under the provision, leaving questions about whether the proposed vessels were procured and delivered.

Separately, N200 million was earmarked for the procurement of one trawler, one heavy-duty river craft and one self-propelled barge in the 2026 approved budget.

Also, N34 million was allocated to the Ministry of Special Duties, East Senatorial District, in the 2026 budget to purchase a sea boat for the three local government areas in the district.

In the 2026 budget, the Ministry of Community Development also budgeted N10 million for purchasing two sea boats for communities.

It remains unclear whether the vessels under these provisions were delivered, where they are currently deployed and whether they serve residents who depend on water transportation.

The 2026 Third Quarter Budget Performance Report also records N24.88 million spent on the purchase of sea boats between January and September 2026.

The expenditure raises further questions about the number of boats acquired with the money, their locations and the communities benefiting from them.

Government announces new vessels

The budgetary questions come against the backdrop of announcements by the state government about the acquisition of marine vessels.

On 18 January 2026, the Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy announced the arrival of a new 38-seater passenger ferry.

The Commissioner for Marine and Blue Economy, Faith Zibs-Godwin, said the vessel was in addition to an earlier batch of rehabilitated marine fleets, with more expected.

Barely three weeks later, on 4 February, the ministry announced the delivery of additional vessels, including a cargo barge, cruise boats, passenger ferries and water ambulances.

Mrs Zibs-Godwin received the vessels at the ministry’s jetty in Yenagoa and credited Governor Diri with supporting their acquisition.

A BusinessDay report also noted that Bayelsa took delivery of new marine transport fleets between late 2025 and February 2026.

However, the announcements did not provide a comprehensive breakdown of the number of passenger ferries acquired, their capacities, the communities where they were deployed or the extent to which they were made available for public transportation.

The state government has also not publicly reconciled the reported acquisitions with the amounts appropriated and recorded as expenditure for boat procurement in its budget documents.

Commissioner promises response

When contacted by PREMIUM TIMES, the Commissioner for Marine and Blue Economy, Mrs Zibs-Godwin, was asked to clarify whether the vessels for which N79.5 million was reportedly spent in 2025 were procured.

She was also asked about the status of the separate N200 million allocation for the trawler, heavy-duty river craft and self-propelled barge, and whether the N34 million sea boat for the three East Senatorial District local government areas was purchased and delivered.

The commissioner was further asked how many boats were purchased with the N24.88 million recorded in the 2026 Third Quarter Budget Performance Report, when they were acquired, where they were deployed and which communities benefited.

In her response on Monday, Mrs Zibs-Godwin asked the newspaper to visit the ministry for clarification.

“Feel free to visit the ministry for realistic response to your concerns.. thank you,” she said.

When PREMIUM TIMES explained that it was not immediately available in Bayelsa to visit the ministry and requested that the answers be provided by telephone or text message, the commissioner said the response would be given within the week.

As of the time of filing this report, she had yet to provide substantive answers to the questions.

Tinubu orders procurement of boats

During his condolence visit to Bayelsa on Sunday, Vice-President Kashim Shettima announced that President Tinubu had directed the NDDC to procure boats to improve transportation in the state’s riverine communities.

The president also approved N250 million to support families of the victims and directed relevant federal agencies to work with the state government to strengthen safety standards on inland waterways.

The intervention is happening in the face of renewed checks of the state’s marine transport infrastructure and the safety of residents who rely on boats to travel between riverine communities.

For many communities in Bayelsa, waterways remain essential routes to markets, schools, healthcare facilities and other public services.

While the presidential directive could improve access to boats, questions remain about the state government’s own investments in the sector, the deployment of vessels it says it has acquired and the availability of safe and regulated transport for residents.

The tragedy has renewed calls for accountability beyond the immediate circumstances of the accident but also over the government’s preparedness to provide safe water transportation for communities that have few alternatives.

World.title: OPay introduces Shield Pay, helping Nigerians trade with confidence
World.content:
You see an item you like online. The vendor sends you their account details; you transfer your hard-earned money, and then you wait. Hours pass, your calls go unanswered, your messages are ignored, and suddenly, the vendor’s account is nowhere to be found.

Sadly, this is an experience many Nigerians know too well.

From shopping online to paying for services, sending money to someone you have never met can be risky. You may see attractive photos and even receive an account number. But how do you know you can trust the vendor?

What happens when you pay and the vendor fails to deliver on their promise? Who helps you get your money back? Your hard-earned money deserves better, and so does your peace of mind.

This is why OPay introduces Shield Pay, a safer way to trade, with OPay protecting your payment from start to finish. With Shield Pay, you no longer have to send money to vendors and hope for the best. OPay safely holds your payment until the agreed conditions are met.

How Does Shield Pay Work?

Both the person making the payment (Payer) and the person receiving it (Payee) must have an OPay account. Before making a payment, you can find the vendor using their phone number or OPay account details. You can also check their trust level and reviews to help you make a more informed decision.

Once the Payer is ready to proceed, both parties agree on the payment amount, purpose and expected completion time. The Payee then sends a payment request, and the Payer has 24 hours to complete the payment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Here is where Shield Pay makes the difference. Instead of the money going directly to the Payee, OPay holds the funds safely until the agreed payment conditions are met.

Once the Payee completes their part of the agreement, they provide supporting information as proof. The Payer then has seven days to review the information and confirm that everything has been delivered as agreed. If more time is needed, the Payer may extend this period once by an additional 7 days.

Once the Payer confirms that the agreed conditions have been met, OPay releases the money to the Payee. The Payee can then withdraw the funds into their OPay wallet at no extra charge, provided no dispute has been raised.

What Happens When Something Goes Wrong?

With Shield Pay, you are not left on your own when a transaction does not go as agreed. If the Payee fails to deliver, delivers later than promised, provides something that does not meet the agreed terms, or scams or misleads the Payer, the Payer can raise a dispute.

Even after confirming that a transaction is complete, the Payer has up to 15 days to raise a dispute if they later discover that the agreed conditions were not met.

Once a dispute is raised, both parties must provide supporting evidence within 48 hours. OPay will review the payment transaction, assess the evidence provided by both parties and resolve the payment dispute.

With Shield Pay, you have more control over your payments, better protection against payment-related scams and greater confidence when trading. Whether you are making an online transaction or paying a vendor for a service, you deserve to know that your money is protected and that there is a clear process to follow if things do not go as planned.
