World.title: Like other Nigerians, I suffer from water challenges in Aso Rock – Tinubu
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has said he experiences water supply challenges as other Nigerians, recounting how water supply was interrupted while he was shaving at the Presidential Villa in Abuja last week.

Mr Tinubu said this on Sunday during a special prayer organised by the Tinubu Family of Lagos at the Yoruba Tennis Club in Onikan, Lagos State.

Recounting the experience, the president said the interruption occurred despite his residence being the seat of Nigeria’s presidency.

“If I tell you some of you, you know, on a Wednesday of last week, I was shaving and the water went off. In the Villa. You know, you want no punishment, they’re there too. The water went off,” he said.

The president acknowledged persistent infrastructure challenges, including unreliable electricity and water supply, but expressed confidence that his administration would address them.

“We will correct all these, no light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Mr Tinubu’s remarks come amid longstanding concerns over unreliable electricity and access to potable water across the country.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria continues to grapple with electricity supply challenges, with millions of households and businesses relying on alternative sources of power to meet their daily needs.

The president, however, did not explain whether the water interruption at the Presidential Villa was caused by a temporary technical fault or a broader supply problem. The Tinubu administration has also spent billions of naira to address electricity challenges in the Presidential Villa, including use of solar energy to allow the removal of the Villa from the national grid.

Nigerians react

Mr Tinubu’s account of the water interruption at the Presidential Villa has sparked reactions on social media, with some Nigerians questioning how the government could address the country’s infrastructure challenges when the president’s official residence also experiences water and electricity supply problems.

Reacting on X, some users mocked the president’s experience, while others used it to criticise his administration’s handling of basic infrastructure.

One user, Sir Ernest, wrote: “Imagine a whole President struggling with running water in Aso Rock. At this point, even the kitchen tap needs a new administration.”

Another user, Olaiya Taofeek, questioned the president’s ability to address the country’s challenges, “Tinubu can’t even fix the water supply in Aso Rock. How does he intend to fix Nigeria?” She asked.

Similarly, a user identified as Chiamaka said the president’s account raised questions about electricity and water supply at the seat of power, while another user suggested that the experience reflected the challenges faced by ordinary Nigerians.

Political mobilisation

At the gathering, President Tinubu also urged Nigerians, particularly his supporters in Lagos, to mobilise voters ahead of the forthcoming elections.

He challenged his supporters to ensure that eligible voters obtained their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), arguing that the state had not fully translated its large voting population into votes.

“How can you have seven million registered voters and produce 100,000, 200,000 votes? That’s failure. Even if you win, I say a win is a win, no. You have to generate the maximum,” he said.

He also urged aggrieved APC members to set aside their differences and work together, directing his Special Adviser on Political Affairs, Ibrahim Masari, to reconcile party members in Katsina and other states.

World.title: Gov Abba Yusuf: When ruthless 2027 respects no matrimony, friends, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
As if he had Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf and his estranged wife, Zainab, in mind, the retired American Air Force officer and poet, Stanley Victor Paskavich, once wrote: “Always remember when it comes to family arguments and disputes: blood is thicker than anger.”

Neither Governor Yusuf nor Zainab yielded to that counsel. Paskavich, who once declared that poetry was where he hid his demons, could hardly have imagined his words playing out with such modern clarity in the ancient city of Kano last week. Apparently miffed that a woman had dragged the majesty of his office through the mud by initiating a divorce, Governor Yusuf stood before a Government House gathering to announce, with theatrical finality and self-deprecating banter, the dissolution of his 20-year marriage. Immediately afterward, he was quoted as saying: “If what our opponents want is a divorce letter, then we have provided it. Let everyone rest. We have also directed the Commissioner for Information to issue an announcement so that we can find decent and respectable women to remarry.”

With that statement, it became unmistakably clear that the demon of 2027 election politics was the sole incubus behind the couple’s matrimonial disharmony. Their conjugal union, which produced six children and celebrated its second decade a couple of months ago, had ceased to be merely a marriage vow, transforming into an oath of political abidance.

Zainab’s secret filing for Khul’i at an Upper Area Court in Abuja was the first salvo heard from her flank. A bedrock of northern Islamic family law, Khul’i is a divorce initiated by a wife in exchange for financial compensation, often involving the return of her mahr, dowry to her husband.

Yusuf’s public confirmation sealed their fates. In what appeared to be political rather than domestic retaliation, the governor tossed a pebble at the porcelain of his 20-year matrimony, shattering it with a public, husband-initiated divorce called talaq. Turning a family dispute into political theater at a Government House event, Yusuf joked that he had been demoted from a “corporal” to a “constable” – from two wives down to one – before inviting fresh applicants to jostle for his heart. It was a textbook display of how Nigerian politicians weaponize populist banter to neutralise personal embarrassment and project strength in the face of ridicule.

At the center of this drama stood Zainab, niece and adopted daughter of Yusuf’s estranged political godfather, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso. Kwankwaso had given his late brother’s daughter, whom he raised as his own, to Yusuf, his longtime personal assistant, commissioner, and handpicked successor, as a seal on their political alliance and a totem of trust.

In this executive domestic saga, the Kano political class witnessed far more than a private separation. What Yusuf hoisted in public view was the fatal rupture of auren siyasa, the time-honoured Northern Nigerian tradition of dynastic marriage, where a political Malam gives his daughter to a protégé as an unspoken blood oath of loyalty.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Those privy to the turgid atmosphere inside Government House say the collapse was triggered by Yusuf’s daring decision to defect to the rival All Progressives Congress (APC), along with the bitter political brickbats that followed. The fallout underscores a timeless truism: wherever power and matrimony share the same roof, they breed a mutual discomfort the Yorùbá capture in the proverb of a hen perched on a taut rope. Neither is at ease – the rope strains under the hen’s weight, while the hen struggles to keep its balance. My people express this strain as “Adìyẹ bà l’ókùn, ara ò rọ okùn, ara ò rọ adìyẹ.” This typifies and exemplifies the Yusuf family. In a politically midwifed union like this, the couple is that hen and politics is the rope. Once Yusuf crossed party lines, the political tremor could not be kept outside the bedroom door.

Across Kano and the wider North, gifting a daughter to a key aide or anointed successor is a proven mechanism to ensure the protégé does not turn against his benefactor upon tasting power. When the protégé defects, however, the marriage ceases to be an alliance and becomes an active loyalty hazard. Zainab was apparently caught in a classic hostage dilemma, forced to choose between husband and father. Viewed with suspicion in her husband’s new camp, while her father’s political family expected unwavering fealty to the man who raised her, Zainab’s latter years trauma under a political captive was best imagined.

For two decades, Zainab served as the living axle binding Kwankwaso’s red-cap political empire to Yusuf. Indeed, Yusuf’s emergence as Kwankwaso’s successor rested squarely on that foundation; without the marriage, Kwankwaso would scarcely have hugged the porcupine by entrusting so vast a political destiny to an ordinary aide. Yet, the moment Yusuf crossed the Rubicon into his father-in-law’s rival party, playing Judas to his benefactor and apostate to a shared political dream, his home ceased to be a covenant of fealty and became a battleground until it caved in.

To the casual observer outside the North, the collapse of the Yusuf marriage might look like an isolated melodrama. In truth, across African history and statecraft, matrimony has rarely been matrimony simpliciter. From the diplomatic marriages of the 19th-century Sokoto Caliphate and the ọgọ in-law non-aggression pacts of pre-colonial Igboland, to the warlord alliances of the Old Oyo Empire and the 1962 Awolowo–Akintola fratricide that tore through Western Region parlours, marriage has long doubled as an instrument of statecraft.

In Northern Nigeria specifically, auren siyasa has functioned as a political glue across four distinct eras: pre-colonial, colonial, military, and the four Republics. Following the 1804 Jihad, Usman dan Fodio and his successor, Sultan Muhammad Bello, deliberately married their daughters and sisters to newly appointed emirs and flag-bearers in Kano, Katsina, Zazzau, Bauchi, and Adamawa, while taking wives from those ruling houses in return. Those unions forged a trans-emirate aristocracy that turned any rebellion against Sokoto into a violation of family bloodlines. Similarly, in emirates like Kano and Zazzau, where rival royal houses such as the Sullubawa, Dabo, and Mallawa competed for the throne, intermarriage softened succession bitterness and guaranteed losing factions continued proximity to the palace.

Centuries earlier, the Mais of the Kanem-Borno Empire routinely used marriages with the daughters of tributary chiefs like the Bulala and Mandara to secure frontier peace and trans-Saharan trade routes. Centuries later, during British Indirect Rule and into the First Republic, the Northern aristocracy used the same instrument to absorb the rising Western-educated commoner class – the talakawa intelligentsia – into their fold, bridging bureaucratic competence with aristocratic legitimacy.

While Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, was a blue-blooded descendant of dan Fodio, non-royals like Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa were brought into the establishment fold, and the broader Northern People’s Congress elite routinely cemented alliances between senior civil servants, ministers and traditional titleholders through marriage. Early Northern leaders institutionalized the gesture with an unspoken creed: “I trust you with my bloodline, so I can trust you with my political legacy.”

This Malam–protégé dynamic borrows directly from traditional Qur’anic schooling called tsangaya, where a revered scholar rewards his most loyal, brilliant and trustworthy almajiri disciple with his daughter’s hand. The pattern persisted into the military era, when prominent political, military, and business dynasties, the Yar’Aduas, Babangidas, Abachas, Buharis, Sarakis, Dantatas, and Indimis, intermarried across generations.

What makes the Yusuf–Zainab split so troubling is its departure from that historical norm. In traditional Northern political culture, marriages were designed to absorb political shocks, not get shattered under them. Even during the fierce First and Second Republic rivalries between the conservative NPC/NPN establishment and Mallam Aminu Kano’s radical NEPU/PRP movement, families rarely dissolved because matrimony straddled both camps. The Kano matrimonial rupture of the Yusufs signals a stark erosion of that old aristocratic code. It reveals that modern electoral survival and party defections have become so ruthlessly zero-sum that even a sacred Malam–protégé marital covenant can no longer withstand the shock of political betrayal.

History beyond Nigeria’s borders offers sobering parallels. In South Africa, while personal strains existed, the 1996 divorce of Nelson and Winnie Madikizela-Mandela was fundamentally accelerated by irreconcilable political divergence: Nelson’s post-prison commitment to reconciliation clashed head-on with Winnie’s militant populism, turning their marriage into an unsustainable political liability.

In politics, “till death do us part” often carries an unspoken codicil: “unless party realignment comes first.” A similar dynamic played out in Zimbabwe during ZANU-PF’s succession wars, where spouses within the party’s inner circle, particularly among allies of Jonathan Moyo and former Vice President Joice Mujuru, queued on opposing sides of the Lacoste (Mnangagwa) and G40 (Mugabe) factions, forcing public denouncements and separations.

Even in the United States, Arnold Schwarzenegger and Maria Shriver walked a 25-year tightrope between a Republican governor and a Kennedy Democrat, where constant ideological friction exposed how political identity can strain a union. The crucial difference is that while Western political marriages tend to fracture over ideology, African political divorces are far more often driven by patrimonial and factional survival, where loyalty to a godfather or political bloc outweighs personal vows.

As Nigeria navigates the crater-filled road to the 2027 general elections, the Yusuf–Zainab rupture is merely the most dramatic symptom of a wider trend. Across the country, prominent political families are splitting publicly along party lines, echoing Shakespeare’s “Et tu, Brute?” In November alone, Auwal Lawal Daura, an APC chieftain, publicly endorsed President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid even as his father, former DSS Director-General Lawal Daura, runs as the vice-presidential candidate on the APM ticket.

Similarly, while former President Olusegun Obasanjo remains a vocal critic of the APC administration, his son Olujonwo formally joined pro-Tinubu campaign ranks in November as Special Adviser on Political Affairs for the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement. And in Benue, House of Representatives member, Blessing Onuh sits on a different party platform from her father, former Senate President David Mark, who is now a central figure in the ADC, as she forges an alignment with APC and pro-Tinubu campaign efforts ahead of 2027.

Many commentators also suffer collateral damage from friends whose political parties they critique and those whose principals fall under the hammer of their commentaries. Friendships forged in the smithy when ambitions were mustard seeds, made realisable with the help of those friends, suddenly, on the cruel road to 2027, became leprosy and enmity of the Yusuf-Zainab kind.

Ultimately, the collapse of the Yusuf–Zainab union stands as a cautionary parable for Nigeria’s political class ahead of 2027. When matrimony is drafted as a foot soldier in partisan warfare, the home ceases to be a sanctuary. It becomes an extension of the campaign ground. It then becomes vulnerable to every shift in political wind. If the ancient covenant of auren siyasa can no longer shield bloodlines from the zero-sum ruthlessness of 2027 elections defections, then Nigerian politics has entered an era where no institution, not even the family altar, is sacred. Paskavich was right that blood ought to be thicker than anger. Yet in Kano’s executive theatre, among friends, raw political ambition proved thicker than blood and the sanctity of family altar.

Who Decides Nigeria’s 2027 President: Ballot or Bullet?

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 general elections, the familiar drums of political hostility are beating once again. Across the country, violent rhetoric, convoy attacks, and targeted intimidation, are casting a dark shadow over the democratic process. Since campaigns officially kicked off in August, at least eleven major incidents of electoral violence have been recorded. They range from the disruption of an NDC town hall in Lagos and attacks on party rallies in Enugu, to the obstruction of presidential candidate, Peter Obi’s convoy in Benue, as well as the October ambush on ADC senatorial candidate, Heberta Okonofua in Edo State.

While alarming, these incidents are neither isolated nor new. They are the latest symptoms of a violent political culture woven into the very fabric of Nigeria’s electoral history.Nigeria has at best a legacy of elections written in blood. The rain of political thuggery began beating Nigeria long before the Fourth Republic and even before independence. In 1953, when the Action Group (AG) toured Northern Nigeria to campaign for independence, the move triggered large-scale riots in Kano. Supporters of the Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU) and Southerners living in Sabon Gari, particularly the Igbo, bore the brunt of a conflict they did not start. Around the same period, the Tiv faced brutal suppression for opposing the Northern People’s Congress (NPC) regional government and demanding Middle Belt autonomy.

By the First Republic, electoral contests had fully degenerated into warfare. Ahead of the 1964/65 general elections, both the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP) and the AG, later allied under the United Progressive Grand Alliance, (UPGA) treated the ballot as a do-or-die affair.

Nigerian Tribune editions of the period read like war dispatches: On June 20, 1964, its lead story was, “Act of thuggery: NCNC fires Yoruba Obas.” It was a report which linked Chief S. L. Akintola’s government to political brigandage in the West. In its June 24 and 29, 1964 report, the newspaper’s banner headlines screamed: “NNDP thugs hit Ado, Ife.” It prompted a grim editorial comment in the newspaper on hooliganism. This forced a regional curfew and an emergency intervention in Lagos by ceremonial president, Nnamdi Azikiwe.

On 2 October, 1965, following UPGA’s failed court injunction to restrain the Electoral Commission under Mr. T. Esua from declaring candidates unopposed, the Tribune reported mass displacements across Osun, Ife, and Ilesa. In Osogbo, it reported that a Mrs. Fatoki, wife of an UPGA candidate, was severely macheted and that, in Ilesa, thugs smashed the vehicle of an UPGA candidate, Bola Sadipe.

As Professor Eghosa Osaghae notes in his Crippled Giant, (1998) while both sides deployed violence, the NNDP weaponised state incumbency to devastating effect. There is near-unanimous consensus among historians that the 1964/65 electoral crisis, marked by widespread fraud, arson, and the killing of over 200 people in the Western Region, directly triggered the collapse of the First Republic.

Why does this cycle of blood persist? Beneath the surface of Nigeria’s political turbulence lies a fundamental philosophical failure: the triumph of monism over pluralism. Long before the 17th-century philosopher, René Descartes formulated his theory of Cartesian dualism, the idea that reality consists of distinct substances, rather than a single monolithic truth, Yoruba philosophy captured the necessity of multiple perspectives through its proverb, “A kì í dúró ojú kan wò’ran eégún.” It translates to read that, one does not stand in a single spot to watch a dancing masquerade. Because a masquerade’s performance is dynamic and multifaceted, an observer must constantly shift angles to appreciate its full form.

In contrast, Nigerian politics is trapped in a rigid, monist worldview. It is a mindset of “I and I alone.” When political actors believe there is only one legitimate path to power and no room for opposition, democracy ceases to be a contest of ideas and becomes a zero-sum war for survival. Violence becomes the way out.

This monist mindset is reinforced by structural and historical forces that turn elections into existential battles. First, as scholars, Kelechi Ani and Dominique Uwizeyimana observe, British colonialism, the type Nigeria went through, was established through “naked brutality” and military subjugation. Rather than dismantling this coercive apparatus at independence, Nigeria’s political class inherited it, institutionalising violence and the militarisation of the polity as standard tools of governance.

Political scientist, Billy Dudley, also famously noted that Nigerian politicians view public office as an investment for acquiring extraordinary wealth unavailable through legitimate enterprise, stating this to be where “politics means money and money means politics.” Legendary political scientist, Claude Ake, also pushed this further by saying that in Nigeria, those who win state power can accumulate limitless wealth without working, while those who lose have no security even for wealth earned through honest labour. Consequently, to capture the state becomes a matter of life and death.

As a 2007 United States Institute of Peace (USIP) report highlighted, political parties often operate like mafia syndicates controlled by “godfathers.” These power brokers exploit Nigeria’s mass youth unemployment to recruit idle young men as political mercenaries for the purpose of snatching ballot boxes, assassinate rivals, intimidate electoral officials and deploy state security forces to suppress voters.

While it is possible to hold elections without democracy, it is impossible to sustain democracy without credible elections. Credibility, however, cannot exist where voters are governed by fear.

As 2027 draws near, Nigeria stands at a familiar crossroads. If Nigeria will escape the ghost of 1964, its political class must shift their gaze from the destructive zero-sum logic of political monism. True democracy requires the wisdom of the masquerade’s audience: the willingness to accommodate shifting viewpoints, respect the opposition and allow the ballot, rather than the bullet, to decide who leads Nigeria in 2027.

Olanipekun: Here Comes the Newest GCON

In a piece I wrote on 3 April, 2022, on the occasion of Chief Wole Olanipekun’s appointment as Chairman of the Body of Benchers, I began by writing as follows:

“Since his death in March 2005, not minding the galaxy of topnotch legal colossi that Nigeria has sired ever since, many schools of thought hold that Nigeria has not been able to reincarnate Chief Frederick Rotimi Alade Williams, QC, SAN. I argue to the contrary, however, that in Chief Wole Olanipekun, Williams is very much alive at the Nigerian Bar. The late Queen’s Counsel bestrode the legal firmament, both literally and with his immense physical stature.”

As President Bola Tinubu conferred on Olanipekun Nigeria’s second-highest national honour, the Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger (GCON) last week, I am forced to reproduce the piece thus:

“Like Williams, Olanipekun has also traversed the world of law. First Nigerian to become a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), a staunch member of the Action Group, Minister for Local Government, and Western Region’s first indigenous Attorney General—before becoming Minister of Justice in 1959, Williams also became President of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA). When lawyers cite groundbreaking precedents like Lakanmi v. Attorney General (Western State) and the landmark case involving the Oba of Lagos, Adeniji Adele, against the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP), Williams’s legal wizardry and imprimatur encompass them all.

Years after Williams’s departure, however, there is arguably no Nigerian lawyer who has traversed the firmament of law like the Ikere-Ekiti-born legal colossus, Olanipekun. Called to the Bar in July 1976 after graduating from the Nigerian Law School and becoming a SAN in July 1991, Olanipekun eventually became Ondo State’s Attorney General and Commissioner for Justice.

Perhaps the most talked-about period of his legal career, and his most profound engagement with the Bar, was in 2002 when he was elected President of the NBA. Legal pundits liken that period to the Alao Aka-Bashorun leadership of the Bar for its overarching impact on the profession and the lives of individual members. The year after, Olanipekun was appointed Vice President of the Pan African Lawyers Union (PALU) and, in January 2007, became a Life Bencher, one of the most prestigious heights of attainment in the legal profession.

The University of Ibadan still talks with nostalgia about his period as its Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of the Governing Council between 2004 and 2006. Apart from being a Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators (FCIArb), Olanipekun was also bestowed with the national honour of Officer of the Order of the Federal Republic (OFR).”

Same last week, Olanipekun unveiled a six-volume publication he entitled, Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases to mark his 50 years at the Bar. Called in 1976, Olanipekun has also spent 35 years as a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, having been elevated to the Silk rank in July 1991.

While conferring him with the GCON last week, President Tinubu affirmed my earlier tribute to Olanipekun, touching a part of the great elephant when he said: “I proudly celebrate Chief Wole Olanipekun, Senior Advocate of Nigeria, a phenomenon in Nigeria and an outstanding advocate who has fittingly stepped into the shoes of the acclaimed legends of the legal profession. He did not merely fill those shoes, but is walking with them into new territory.”

Tinubu also acknowledged the years of friendship, loyalty, and hard work that hallmarked his relationship with Olanipekun by saying, “On a personal note, I celebrate decades of loyalty, friendship, commitment and reciprocity between Wole Olanipekun and me.”

In conferring the GCON on Chief Olanipekun, the Nigerian state has merely placed its formal seal on a historical verdict which the Bar delivered before now. More than four years after I first argued that the spirit of Timi the Law lives on in this Ikere-Ekiti titan, that thesis stands vindicated. Its vindication is not merely the towering precedents Olanipekun has helped make in Nigerian courts, but in the institutional panache with which he continues to steer the legal profession.

For Olanipekun, the GCON does not confer merely a valedictory medal. It is also not an oar – which steers boats through water – to be rested upon. It is for this legal icon a fitting national salute, a medal hung on the lapel of a colossus who straddles the firmament of Nigerian law with purpose.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: Taming inflation: MPC’s November choice, By Posi Olatubosun
World.content:
The central question is whether the Central Bank can anchor inflation expectations firmly enough to ensure that disinflation withstands the election cycle, the fiscal pressures of 2027, and the next external shock — and thereby break the pattern of temporary relief followed by renewed price surges that has characterised Nigeria’s experience over the past two decades. Success will be measured over years, not months: monthly inflation consistently settling at low levels, real interest rates declining gradually rather than abruptly, and a credible path towards single-digit inflation under a formal inflation-targeting framework.

Inflation is at a six-year low. This week, the Central Bank must determine which economic reality to prioritise.

Today, 23 November, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Central Bank of Nigeria begins its final meeting of the year. The headline figures appear to support an easing of monetary policy. Inflation fell to 14.06 per cent in October from 14.63 per cent in September, while core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, declined to 10.78 per cent. However, the same report showed that prices were rising more rapidly month-on-month, and food inflation remains above 19 per cent. The naira is under renewed pressure, and the election season is approaching. The MPC faces a genuine dilemma, and the appropriate response may not be the one many market participants hope for.

The case for a further cut is compelling. In September, the MPC reduced the Monetary Policy Rate by 350 basis points, from 26.5 per cent to 23 per cent, describing the move as a reset intended to strengthen policy transmission. Even after that reduction, the policy rate remains approximately nine percentage points above headline inflation and more than twelve percentage points above core inflation. Real interest rates at this level are among the highest globally. They make credit prohibitively expensive for manufacturers, farmers and traders, while increasing the cost of servicing public debt. The bond market already anticipates lower rates: at the Debt Management Office’s auction on 16 November, the government borrowed at approximately 17 per cent, well below the policy rate. Fitch Ratings expects the policy rate to average 21.7 per cent in 2027 and 18.6 per cent in 2028. On these grounds, a further cut appears justified.

The case for caution is stronger, at least for now. Four risks argue against moving this week.

The first risk relates to momentum. Headline inflation is easing largely because prices were rising rapidly a year earlier. On a month-on-month basis, headline inflation accelerated to 0.43 per cent in October, up from just 0.06 per cent in September. Food inflation, at 19.13 per cent year-on-year, is higher than it was in October 2025. A Central Bank survey found that 77.2 per cent of households perceived inflation to be high in September, up from 67.2 per cent in August. Some economists have publicly questioned whether the official figures reflect the prices that families pay. When expectations are moving in the wrong direction, a central bank that eases policy too soon risks undermining the credibility it has spent three years rebuilding.

Election years have historically seen higher public spending, and this year is not likely to be an exception. The government has approved new allowances for workers, is borrowing heavily in the domestic market, and has sought approval for substantial new external loans. At the same time, oil prices have fallen sharply from their September peak, and crude output declined in October, weakening revenue. If fiscal policy eases while monetary policy also loosens, inflationary consequences could emerge in the first half of 2027 — precisely when the MPC would least want them.

The second risk relates to the naira. The official exchange rate has hovered around ₦1,358 to the dollar, while street dealers quote approximately ₦1,440, and the gap between the two markets has widened. Gross reserves have declined to about $54.8 billion, roughly $450 million below their late-October peak, partly because of Central Bank interventions. Analysts ascribe some of the pressure to seasonal import demand and pre-election demand for dollars. A rate cut now would narrow the return on naira-denominated assets just as demand for dollars is rising, leading to further depreciation and, through import prices, a renewed increase in inflation.

The third risk is fiscal. Election years have historically seen higher public spending, and this year is not likely to be an exception. The government has approved new allowances for workers, is borrowing heavily in the domestic market, and has sought approval for substantial new external loans. At the same time, oil prices have fallen sharply from their September peak, and crude output declined in October, weakening revenue. If fiscal policy eases while monetary policy also loosens, inflationary consequences could emerge in the first half of 2027 — precisely when the MPC would least want them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The fourth risk relates to timing. The September reset was substantial, and its effects are still working their way through the financial system. Monetary policy operates with a lag of several months. The MPC’s statement indicated that future decisions would be data-dependent. Data released since September are mixed rather than conclusive. Third-quarter growth figures will not be available until after this meeting. Under these circumstances, patience reflects discipline rather than timidity.

The Central Bank has rebuilt much of its credibility since 2023. Spending that credibility on a premature rate cut amid rising monthly inflation, currency pressures, and election-year spending would be an unfavourable trade-off. Holding firm now, while signalling a clear path to lower rates and unlocking bank lending through the reserve requirement, offers the best chance of turning inflation at a six-year low into a lasting reality that households can finally feel.

What, then, should the MPC do? In my view, it should maintain the Monetary Policy Rate at 23 per cent this week, while pairing that decision with two measures that support growth without creating instability. First, it should provide clear forward guidance. The Committee should state explicitly that it expects to resume easing in 2027, provided monthly inflation moderates and the exchange rate stabilises following the election period. Markets and businesses respond to credible signals, as well as to changes in interest rates. Clear guidance would help keep long-term borrowing costs on a downward trajectory without the risks associated with an immediate rate cut.

Second, it should begin a gradual, targeted review of the cash reserve requirement, which remains at 45 per cent for commercial banks. A requirement of that size locks away nearly half of bank deposits and is one reason the September cut has not reached small businesses. A modest, phased reduction, linked to verified lending to manufacturing, agriculture and small enterprises, would channel funds to productive activity, rather than to the currency market. It would also do more for the real economy than another headline rate cut that banks may simply not pass on. The Committee should also be frank about the limits of monetary policy. Interest rates cannot fix food supply disrupted by insecurity, transport costs driven by fuel prices or electricity shortages that raise every producer’s costs. Those problems belong to fiscal and structural policy. A central bank asked to compensate for them will either fail or overreach.

The true test of this decision extends well beyond the market’s reaction this week. The central question is whether the Central Bank can anchor inflation expectations firmly enough to ensure that disinflation withstands the election cycle, the fiscal pressures of 2027, and the next external shock — and thereby break the pattern of temporary relief followed by renewed price surges that has characterised Nigeria’s experience over the past two decades. Success will be measured over years, not months: monthly inflation consistently settling at low levels, real interest rates declining gradually rather than abruptly, and a credible path towards single-digit inflation under a formal inflation-targeting framework. The Central Bank has rebuilt much of its credibility since 2023. Spending that credibility on a premature rate cut amid rising monthly inflation, currency pressures, and election-year spending would be an unfavourable trade-off. Holding firm now, while signalling a clear path to lower rates and unlocking bank lending through the reserve requirement, offers the best chance of turning inflation at a six-year low into a lasting reality that households can finally feel.

Posi Olatubosun is a UK-based academic faculty member in accounting and finance.

World.title: Troops clear suspected IPOB/ESN camp, neutralise IEDs in Imo
World.content:
File image.

By Kingsley Omonobi

Troops of the Nigerian Army, working alongside other security agencies, have cleared additional sections of a suspected Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) and Eastern Security Network (ESN) camp in Imo State, uncovering and neutralising improvised explosive devices (IEDs).

The operation, conducted on November 21 around Awomama in Oru East Local Government Area, was part of ongoing security offensives launched on November 16 and 17, according to the Army.

The joint operation involved troops of the 34 Artillery Brigade and personnel of the Nigerian Navy, Nigerian Air Force, Nigeria Police Force, Department of State Services (DSS) and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).

Security sources said the joint team advanced into the Tango 2 and Tango 3 sections of the suspected camp at about 6:30 a.m., where they discovered that the locations had been heavily fortified with explosives.

With the support of Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) personnel, the troops located and successfully neutralised the improvised explosive devices.

The operation also led to the recovery of two battery components suspected to have been used to trigger the explosives.

The clearance operation is part of sustained efforts by security agencies to dismantle suspected criminal hideouts and prevent attacks in the area.

World.title: PANDEF mourns Bayelsa boat accident victims, urges coastal roads
World.content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) has mourned victims of the boat accident around Oweikorogha Community in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of Bayelsa State, which reportedly claimed several lives, including youths and children.

The socio-political organisation also renewed its call on the Federal Government and governments of oil-producing states to prioritise the construction of roads and bridges to connect isolated coastal communities and reduce their dependence on water transportation.

PANDEF, in a statement signed by its National Chairman, Ambassador Godknows Igali, said it received the news of the accident, which occurred on Friday, November 20, 2026, with shock and sadness.

The organisation described the incident as heartbreaking and commiserated with the affected families, the Bayelsa State Government, residents of Southern Ijaw and the affected communities.

It said the tragedy reinforced its longstanding position that inadequate road infrastructure had left many coastal communities with limited transportation options, making water travel a necessity for their residents.

According to PANDEF, the Federal Government should, as an interim measure, support state governments in acquiring adequate seaworthy vessels to meet the transportation needs of coastal communities.

The organisation also called on emergency relief agencies, security agencies and regulatory authorities to work with the Bayelsa State Government to provide assistance to survivors and bereaved families.

It urged the relevant authorities to strengthen enforcement of water transportation safety regulations, including compliance with passenger safety protocols, the use of appropriate safety equipment and the operation of vessels that meet prescribed seaworthiness standards.

PANDEF said measures must be taken to prevent a recurrence of such tragedies, stressing the need for improved transportation infrastructure and stricter safety standards across the coastal areas.

The statement read in part: “While mourning this tragic loss, PANDEF calls on the relevant emergency relief agencies, security agencies and regulatory authorities to work closely with the Bayelsa State Government to ensure that all necessary measures are taken to assuage the impact on survivors and bereaved families.

“More importantly, [they should] take all necessary measures to prevent a recurrence of such tragedies.”

The organisation expressed solidarity with the victims’ families and the people of Bayelsa State, praying for the repose of the souls of the deceased and comfort for those affected by the tragedy.

World.title: Alice Huang had contact with China spy agency during Nvidia boss affair – Report
World.content:
This screengrab from video footage by CTI obtained via AFPTV on November 9, 2026 shows Alice Huang (2nd R in pink), a Chinese executive linked to the data centre company called Megaspeed, attending a dinner hosted by Nvidia’s chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang (2nd L in black back facing camera) at a restaurant in Taipei on May 22, 2025, during Computex, the island’s top tech expo. Chip giant Nvidia’s board announced on November 8, 2026 it opened a probe into Huang after he acknowledged an affair with a woman US officials say was working for Chinese intelligence. The executive, Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen Huang — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said. (Photo by various sources / AFP) / – Taiwan OUT / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE – MANDATORY CREDIT “AFP PHOTO / CTI via AFPTV- NO MARKETING NO ADVERTISING CAMPAIGNS – DISTRIBUTED AS A SERVICE TO CLIENTS

Alice Huang, the alleged spy at the center of the Nvidia scandal, was in touch with an official from China’s top spy agency during an affair with the chip giant’s former chief executive Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday.

Alice Huang was this month outed as a suspected Chinese spy, accused of having an affair with Jensen Huang while digging up company secrets for Beijing.

She was in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the intelligence.

Alice Huang, who is no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based tech group under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia chips, possibly in violation of US export controls.

According to the Times, Alice Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency correspond to the affair as well as a period when Megaspeed was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips.

The Times also reported that US intelligence agencies have gathered evidence that Alice Huang’s business partner Kang Wei — who the newspaper said was often introduced as her husband — worked with the same Chinese spy agency.

Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive earlier this month, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang.

He is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.

The upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia which is at the center of an AI boom that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe.

World.title: Senegal to know fate of AFCON title appeal Tuesday – CAS
World.content:
Senegal and Morocco players clash during the Africa Cup of Nations (CAN) final football match between Senegal and Morocco at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat on January 18, 2026. (Photo by Abdel Majid BZIOUAT / AFP)

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) announced that a verdict on Senegal’s appeal of the decision to strip them of the Africa Cup of Nations title in favour of Morocco will come on Tuesday.

CAS’s ruling comes after a hearing of the case, over a chaotic AFCON final in January, which took place behind closed doors at its headquarters in Lausanne on October 8.

“The parties have been notified that the CAS decision will be rendered Tuesday 24 November 2026 in the course of the afternoon (GMT),” CAS said in a short statement on Monday.

At the January 18 final in Rabat, Senegal won 1-0 thanks to Pape Gueye’s extra-time goal, but the occasion was marred near the end of normal time when many Senegal players walked off the pitch in protest at the decision to award Morocco a penalty with the match still goalless.

Some Senegalese supporters also attempted a pitch invasion, and the game was held up for almost 20 minutes before the Senegal players returned.

In March, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) overturned that result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title.

In response, the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the ruling as the “most blatant administrative robbery in the history of our sport”.

The Senegal team even paraded the trophy to their supporters in Paris at the end of March.

World.title: Tinubu directed me to secure Yorubaland against terrorists – Igboho
World.content:
Sunday Igboho

…says President called for collaboration with security agencies to protect rural communities, urban centres, forests

By Adeola Badru

Yoruba nation activist and founder of the Iru Ekun Security Network, Chief Sunday Adeyemo, popularly known as Sunday Igboho, has disclosed that President Bola Tinubu directed him to sustain security operations across Yorubaland, with particular emphasis on protecting rural communities, urban centres and forests against terrorists from neighbouring African countries.

Igboho said the president gave the directive during a brief discussion lasting about five minutes inside his official car shortly after the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally held at Mapo Hall, Ibadan, the Oyo State capital, on Saturday.

According to him, Tinubu also emphasised the need for the Iru Ekun Security Network to maintain effective collaboration with the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigerian Army, the Department of State Services (DSS) and other relevant security agencies to prevent the infiltration of terrorists and other criminal elements into the South-West.

Igboho disclosed this in a statement issued by his media office on Monday, which quoted him as saying that the President’s directive was aimed at strengthening security across the region, particularly in rural settlements, urban centres and forest reserves.

He said, “After the Ibadan Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) rally on Saturday, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu called me into his car and instructed me to continue working with security agencies to ensure peace and stability in the South-West.”

“I was honoured by our President on Saturday when I had a brief discussion with him inside his official car before the presidential convoy moved out of the ancient Mapo Hall premises, Ibadan.”

“It vividly shows that Mr. President values our selfless efforts to galvanise and improve security and safety of our people.”

The Yoruba activist said the discussion, although brief, highlighted the importance the president attached to the security of the Southwest and the continued activities of the homegrown security initiative.

“Our discussion lasted for about five minutes. Mr President directed that we must sustain our operations by securing rural communities, urban centres and our forests in Yorubaland against terrorists from neighbouring African countries,” he said.

Igboho added that Tinubu specifically stressed the importance of cooperation between the Iru Ekun Security Network and established security agencies in tackling criminal activities across the region.

He said the president also directed the operatives to pay particular attention to agrarian communities and forest reserves, which could be vulnerable to infiltration by terrorists and other criminal groups.

“Mr President emphasised that Iru Ekun cooperation with all security agencies is germane to tackle criminalities in Yorubaland, including our agrarian settlements and forest reserves.”

“He said we should monitor all terrains with a view to preventing infiltration by terrorists from Lake Chad, Mali and other African countries,” he stated.

Igboho further disclosed that the President instructed the security network to provide protection for all Nigerians within its areas of operation, irrespective of their ethnic, religious or political affiliations.

According to him, Tinubu also stressed the need for the network to notify the relevant security agencies before carrying out its operations in order to ensure effective coordination and achieve the desired results.

“We were also instructed to provide security to all Nigerians within our jurisdictions, regardless of ethnic, religion and political divides.

“He stressed that our security duties must be carried out by informing security agencies ahead such that positive results and impacts can be achieved in restoring the confidence of the people in government’s responsibility of providing security for the citizenry,” the statement quoted Igboho as saying.”

Igboho said the brief encounter with Tinubu demonstrated the president’s recognition of the efforts of local security initiatives in supporting the protection of lives and property, while stressing that such efforts must remain coordinated with established security agencies.

He added that the directive was not limited to any particular community or group but covered all Nigerians within the operational areas of the Iru Ekun Security Network, regardless of their ethnic, religious or political differences.

Igboho reiterated the importance of collaboration between the network and conventional security agencies, particularly in securing vulnerable communities and preventing the infiltration of terrorists from neighbouring African countries.

He added that the security network would continue to work towards restoring public confidence in the government’s responsibility to protect citizens and maintain peace across Yorubaland.

World.title: Kipit Asset Management Appoints Mr. Luke Ofojebe, CFA, as Acting Managing Director
World.content:
As part of its strategic positioning, Kipit Asset Management Limited (formerly Fortuna Capital Limited), a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) licensed Fund & Portfolio Management Company, has appointed Mr. Luke Ofojebe, CFA, as its Acting Managing Director, with effect from 20 November 2026. The appointment is subject to the approval and confirmation of the SEC.

Luke joins Kipit from Zedcrest Group, where he most recently served as Chief Investment Officer (CIO), capping nearly a decade in investment research and portfolio management. His appointment reflects the seriousness with which Kipit is pursuing its strategy: building an asset management firm anchored on deep research, disciplined portfolio management and experienced leadership.

A Research-Led Portfolio Manager

Before becoming CIO at Zedcrest Group, Luke was Head of Research and Portfolio Management at Zedcrest Wealth, the Group’s Asset Management arm, where he led the team that designed and executed the strategies that significantly grew the firm’s assets under management. He managed money market, equity and proprietary portfolios during that time.

Earlier in his career, Luke headed equity research at Vetiva Capital Management and worked as an equity analyst at CardinalStone Partners. Those years gave him a deep, ground-up understanding of Nigerian companies, sectors and capital markets, and they still shape how he invests today.

In the market, Luke is known for a disciplined, evidence-driven approach to portfolio management, a sharp read of macroeconomic and market trends, and the ability to turn that insight into sound decisions for investors. He is a CFA charterholder.

A Statement of Intent

Kipit was built on a simple belief: managing wealth in Nigeria should be simple, transparent and worthy of trust. Attracting a leader of Luke’s calibre is a statement of how seriously the company takes that belief. As Acting Managing Director, Luke will lead Kipit’s engagement with regulators, clients, partners and the wider market, and will work closely with the Board and management to sharpen the firm’s investment offering and widen its reach.

Commenting on his appointment, Luke Ofojebe said:

“Kipit is one of the most exciting stories in Nigerian asset management right now. The ambition is real, and so is the commitment to doing right by investors. I joined because I believe Kipit can set a new standard for how Nigerians build wealth, and I look forward to working with the team, our regulators and our investors to make that happen.”

The Board of Kipit Asset Management welcomes Luke and looks forward to the value he will bring to the company and its investors.

ENDS

About Kipit Asset Management

Kipit Asset Management Limited is built to make wealth creation simple, transparent and trustworthy. Licensed by the SEC, the company offers both discretionary and non-discretionary portfolio management services and financial advisory services to individuals, businesses and institutions, to enhance their wealth for today and the future. Kipit prides itself on the security of its clients’ investments, combined with its expertise in delivering competitive returns, and treats every client as a partner in their wealth creation journey, guided by its mission: Build wealth, deliberately.

World.title: Pete Edochie commends son Yul’s restraint amid marital controversy
World.content:
Veteran actor Pete Edochie (Right) and his son, actor Yul Edochie.

Veteran Nollywood actor Pete Edochie has praised his son, Yul Edochie, for refraining from public outburst towards his wife, May, amid controversy surrounding his second marriage.

Edochie gave the commendation when he featured on Unfiltered with Ugo and Precious, an online interview series featuring candid conversations on relationships, public opinion, lifestyle and personal experiences.

Describing Yul as strong-willed, the veteran actor said his son had remained undeterred despite insults directed at him over his marital decisions.

“Yul is a very tough guy. You can never subdue him, no matter how much you try.

“He took a second wife; people have been insulting him, saying all sorts of things, and he has been living his life,” he said.

Explaining why he held his son in high regard, Pete said Yul had never publicly insulted May or accused her of wrongdoing.

“He has never insulted his wife for one day. Go and check everything that has been happening.

“He has never come out to say this woman is this or that. It shows somebody responsible,” he said.

Edochie also said May had equally refrained from making negative public comments about Yul.

“The wife too, on her own part, has not said anything against him,” he added.

He further alleged that award organisers had repeatedly excluded Yul from industry recognitions but said his son had continued to thrive.

“Each time awards are organised, they don’t include him. He hasn’t bothered. He’s doing very well. I can tell you that he’s my son.

“Yul has the best voice in the industry,” he said.

The embattled actor publicly introduced actress Judy Austin as his second wife in April 2022, while announcing the birth of their son.

The development has continued to attract public criticism on social media platforms, especially from supporters of May, with whom he has four children. (NAN)

World.title: Eisenkot, Netanyahu parties to meet again for Israel coalition talks
World.content:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot (left) and his opponent, incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. © Maya Levin, Jewel Samad, AFP

The parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, who is tasked with forming the next Israeli government, are due to resume coalition talks on Monday after negotiations a day earlier delivered no agreement.

The third round of talks comes as Eisenkot’s wide-ranging camp faces divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a national unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud.

Former military chief Eisenkot has until December 6 — a deadline which can be extended by 14 days — to form a government to replace Netanyahu after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.

Delegations from Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party and Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud are due to meet on Monday evening for a third round of negotiations, a spokesperson for Likud told AFP.

Representatives from each party met for nearly four hours on Sunday and laid out their positions “on a range of substantive issues,” with no sign of a breakthrough.

– Political ‘boycotts’ –

On Saturday, Yashar presented the talks as “a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government”, saying that Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options.

Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, including an end to “all personal attacks” and political “boycotts” targeting Netanyahu and his government.

Eisenkot’s 48-member bloc needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority and remains divided over how to build a coalition.

Short of 61 lawmakers, Eisenkot’s bloc could form a minority government.

The head of the left-leaning Democrats party, Yair Golan, on Monday called for an end to the “sham talks with Likud”.

Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow Netanyahu to keep his political leverage against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Eisenkot’s refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign.

Last week, Eisenkot said that he would be prepared to put forward a minority national emergency government for a parliamentary vote should efforts to create a broad-based government fail.

World.title: National Anthem: Northern Youth Assembly Gives Obi 72 Hours To Apologise
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

The Northern Youth Assembly has given former presidential candidate Peter Obi and some of his associates 72 hours to publicly apologise over a controversy surrounding the singing of Nigeria’s former national anthem at a political gathering in Lagos.

The group also demanded that Obi clarify his position on the recognition of Nigeria’s officially adopted national anthem, Nigeria, We Hail Thee, and reaffirm his commitment to national unity and constitutional order.

The demands were contained in a statement issued by the Assembly’s National Publicity Secretary, Comrade Adikwu Omaji Joshua.

The Assembly expressed concern over the incident at the Nigeria Democratic Congress town hall meeting in Lagos, where it alleged that some participants declined to sing the current national anthem and instead rendered the former anthem, Arise, O Compatriots.

It said the conduct was inappropriate, particularly at a gathering associated with a prominent political figure and presidential aspirant.

The group, however, acknowledged that Nigerians had constitutional rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and political association, but insisted that such freedoms should be exercised with respect for the country’s sovereignty and national symbols.

According to the Assembly, the national anthem represents Nigeria’s collective identity and should not be treated as a political campaign tool or an instrument for expressing grievances against the government.

It argued that national symbols should remain above partisan interests, ethnic affiliations and religious differences.

The organisation also said Obi’s influence in the country’s political space placed a responsibility on him to promote national cohesion and responsible citizenship.

It added that political leaders should demonstrate restraint and ensure that the enthusiasm of their supporters did not undermine national unity and peaceful coexistence.

The Assembly warned against a situation where political disagreements could be used to justify disrespect for national institutions and symbols.

It said Nigeria had experienced the consequences of disunity, ethnic divisions and separatist agitations, urging political actors not to encourage actions capable of worsening existing tensions.

Consequently, it asked Obi and others it said were directly involved in the incident to issue a public apology within 72 hours of the statement.

The group also demanded a clear declaration of their position on Nigeria’s officially recognised national symbols, alongside a reaffirmation of their commitment to the country’s unity, sovereignty and constitutional order.

It further urged the political figures to caution their supporters against turning political disagreements into hostility towards national institutions.

The Assembly said the ultimatum was intended to provide an opportunity for those involved to demonstrate patriotism and respect for Nigerians.

It warned that failure to receive a satisfactory response within the stipulated period could prompt it to pursue further lawful action.

The group, however, maintained that its position was not intended to suppress opposition or legitimate criticism of the Federal Government.

It called on political leaders, youth organisations and civil society groups to promote responsible citizenship and defend Nigeria’s unity across ethnic, religious and regional divides.

The statement said while political opposition and disagreements remained legitimate in a democracy, the country’s sovereignty, peace and national identity should not be compromised in the pursuit of political power.

World.title: 2027: Iyamu Gains Momentum in Oredo Reps Race, Towers Above ADC, NDC Rivals
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

With political activities gathering momentum ahead of the 2027 general election, indications have emerged that the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate for Oredo Federal Constituency, Dr. Paddy Emmanuel Iyamu, is consolidating his political base and emerging as a formidable contender in the race for the House of Representatives.

Iyamu, a grassroots politician and former Edo State Commissioner for Education, is believed to be gaining traction across different segments of Oredo, with endorsements and expressions of support reportedly coming from political stakeholders, traditional institutions and various community-based groups.

His closest rival, the incumbent Oredo Federal House of Representative member and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate, Hon. Uyi Frank Omosigho, is banking on his legislative experience. Observers are of the view that he may reap from the bandwagon effect and the popularity of Peter Obi as witnessed in 2023.

While the African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate, Dr. Osamwonyi Irowa, may be relatively unknown politically, analysts say his chance for the Oredo Federal House of Representative seat is slim.

Iyamu growing political profile, observers believe, is being strengthened by his record in public service, particularly his contributions to the education sector under the administration of Governor Monday Okpebholo.

As he intensifies consultations and campaign activities ahead of the 2027 polls, Iyamu has continued to highlight what he described as tangible achievements recorded during his tenure as Commissioner for Education, insisting that his experience in government has prepared him for effective representation at the National Assembly.

Speaking on his record in office, Iyamu said his administration at the ministry successfully reconstructed more than 100 schools across Edo State, many of which, according to him, were in various stages of dilapidation before the intervention.

He also disclosed that over 6,000 teachers were employed during his tenure, a development, he said, strengthened the state’s educational workforce and improved the learning environment for pupils and students.

“Under the administration of His Excellency, Senator Monday Okpebholo, we recorded tangible results that directly touched the lives of Edo people.

“As Commissioner for Education, we successfully reconstructed over 100 schools that were in various stages of dilapidation across the state. We also ensured that over 6,000 teachers were given full employment.

“This helped strengthen the foundation of learning in Edo State and created an environment where our children could compete favourably and win national awards,” he said.

The APC candidate maintained that his approach to governance was driven by direct engagement with the people rather than administrative convenience.

“I did not lead from behind a desk. I was always on the ground, supervising projects, engaging stakeholders and feeling the pulse of our people to ensure that government policies translated into real impact,” Iyamu stated.

He said the same commitment to accountability, hard work and people-oriented leadership would guide his aspiration to represent Oredo Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives.

According to him, his ambition is not merely about occupying a political office but ensuring that the constituency enjoys effective representation, access to federal opportunities and legislative interventions capable of improving the living conditions of residents.

“The work we started in Edo will continue, but this time on a bigger stage for the good people of Oredo. I am committed to bringing the same spirit of accountability, hard work and people-first leadership to Oredo Federal Constituency,” he added.

Political observers say the emerging contest in Oredo is expected to attract considerable attention as the APC, ADC and NDC position their respective candidates for the 2027 election.

However, Iyamu’s supporters believe his experience in government, grassroots connections and reported endorsements across different interest groups could give him an advantage in the contest.

With the 2027 elections approaching, the former commissioner appears determined to turn his record in public office and growing political consultations into electoral support, as the battle for the Oredo federal seat gradually takes shape.

World.title: Marketsquare Puts Customer Confidence at Heart of Quality Promise
World.content:
