World.title: LSU spent $150 million on Lane Kiffin and a new roster, it finished worse than under Brian Kelly | Ian Miller
World.content:
In the real world, early September was not so long ago. In the world of modern college football, it's been an eternity.

Just a few months ago, the UCLA Bruins were a punchline, not a contender to win the Big Ten Conference and potentially secure a first round bye in the College Football Playoff. The Ohio State Buckeyes were widely viewed as the best team in the country, thanks to quarterback Julian Sayin and elite talent on defense.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Then, there's the LSU Tigers.

LSU'S $40 MILLION FOOTBALL ROSTER MAY HAVE BEEN A MIRAGE, ACCORDING TO CFB EXPERT JOSH PATE

The Tigers made the biggest splash of the 2025-2026 offseason by hiring Lane Kiffin from Ole Miss to revitalize their program after firing Brian Kelly. Kiffin commanded an exorbitant salary, with nearly $100 million in guarantees. He hired the most expensive support staff in the country, with over $14 million in assistant salaries.

They revamped the roster too, putting together massive NIL deals and the No. 1 transfer portal class, with an estimated cost of around $40-50 million.

Then, week one. And boy, did it look like their decision-making had panned out. The Tigers beat Clemson 51-10 in a game that wasn't even that close. It was a complete demolition, and seemed to validate hiring Kiffin and their roster-building process. Kiffin even gave a typically sarcastic comment after the game, referencing the SEC's push to stop them from rostering players who'd formerly gone pro.

With a 31-3 lead at halftime, Kiffin told ESPN's Holly Rowe, "Imagine if we'd had pro players."

Essentially, "look how good we are already, we didn't even need them."

Fast-forward two months, and it turns out LSU might have needed them. Badly.

LANE KIFFIN TAKES THE SIDE EXIT AS TENNESSEE SENDS LSU HOME AND MOVES TO THE DOORSTEP OF CFP

The Tigers' loss to the Tennessee Volunteers in Knoxville put a final nail in the coffin of a dismal season. Yes, LSU will beat up on hapless Arkansas this weekend, but every single outcome that looked possible after that Clemson game has now officially fallen by the wayside.

LSU have had a difficult schedule, one of the toughest in the country, in fact, but managed to get the least out of it. There was the emotionally charged return to Oxford against Ole Miss, which it lost. It lost at Kentucky. Then it was blown out at home by Alabama. It had a late lead against Texas, only to give up a devastating touchdown to Arch Manning and Raleek Brown for another loss.

On Saturday, Tennessee simply dominated the LSU offense. A whopping eight sacks, 10 tackles for loss, and just 43 rushing yards allowed on 34 attempts. It was an ugly game with six combined turnovers, and Tennessee was fortunate to cross 100 passing yards, but once again, the Tigers came up on the wrong side of what should have been a competitive game.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Winning all five of these games against solid teams might have been too much to ask for any team, but elite programs could and would expect to win some of them. LSU won none. Just 3-5 in the SEC, with the three wins coming over a woeful Texas A&M team, Mississippi State without Kamario Taylor, and Auburn.

After all that talk, all the money, all the swagger and arrogance, they sit here in late November at 6-5 with one of the most disappointing seasons by any team in recent memory. And maybe even more frustrating, it's worse off than any full season under Brian Kelly.

Kelly went 10-4 in 2022, 6-2 in the SEC. He went 10-3 in 2023, once again 6-2 in the SEC. He was 9-4 in 2024 and 5-3 in the SEC. Then was 5-3 when fired during the 2025 season. So in three full seasons in Baton Rouge, Kelly lost seven games, total, in the SEC, with a 17-7 overall record. Kiffin's lost five of his first eight.

LANE KIFFIN BLAMES LSU'S $40+ MILLION ROSTER AFTER LOSS TO TEXAS: 'WE'LL HAVE BETTER ROSTERS’

$150 million, plus a $54 million buyout to Kelly, and they lost more SEC games in eight weeks than Kelly lost in two seasons.

Maybe even more frustrating, and damning for Kiffin, is that the Tigers, by computer models based on offensive, defensive and special teams efficiency, would still be expected to play like one of the top-15 teams in the country. Their losses, at least some of them, have been a result of not making plays when it matters, or getting hurt by costly mistakes. Like, say, 16 penalties for 98 yards against Tennessee. Some of that falls on the $150 million coaching staff.

Hard to get worse than that.



What's more incredible, even, is that this is who the Tigers are, and what the program has been. After the 2019 national championship winning team with Joe Burrow, it has been comparable to a mid-tier Big Ten program by most metrics: Minnesota.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

One Golden Gophers-focused account on X put together a table showing the similarity in outcomes between the two teams in recent years.

And yeah, that's really close. Despite Minnesota having far fewer resources available to them.

Some of this comes down to LSU playing tougher schedules; it's had 29 games against AP ranked teams compared to 19 for Minnesota, but it's won a lower percentage of those matchups, implying either a talent or coaching gap between them and their opponents.

It's hard to believe, but LSU just hasn't been the type of program that they, or many fans, think they are. Maybe Kiffin's second season in Baton Rouge will be different; they'll still have a big recruiting class, transfer portal group, and plenty of money. But spending $200 million, between coaches, players, and buyouts, and finishing 6-5? Even with underlying performance suggesting a top-15 team?

That's about as bad as it gets.

World.title: FBI warns AI hackers can breach systems in under 3 hours
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Your bank could spend millions protecting its computer systems. Your employer might have an entire cybersecurity team watching for suspicious activity. Yet hackers now have an AI-powered tool that can help them break into some organizations in less than three hours.

The FBI is warning that criminals are using the ARTEX AI hacking tool to automate cyberattacks against businesses around the world. Some attacks have moved from initial targeting to powerful administrator-level access in under three hours. That leaves companies very little time to recognize an attack and stop it.

If hackers reach a business that stores your personal information, you could end up dealing with the consequences. Here's how ARTEX works, why the FBI is concerned and what you can do to protect yourself.

No technical experience is needed.

AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS

What is the ARTEX AI hacking tool?

ARTEX started as a legitimate penetration testing framework. Cybersecurity professionals use these tools to find weaknesses in computer systems before criminals discover them. However, hackers have found ways to turn ARTEX against organizations without permission. The framework uses artificial intelligence to handle tasks that previously required significant hacking expertise. It can search for security weaknesses and attempt to exploit them. Once inside a system, ARTEX can work toward gaining higher levels of access and extracting sensitive information. What makes ARTEX particularly concerning is its ability to operate with limited human involvement. Attackers can give the software instructions, then let AI agents carry out much of the work automatically.

ARTEX also connects to external AI models, including OpenAI's GPT and Anthropic's Claude. It supports DeepSeek and several other models. These integrations allow the framework to process instructions and automate complicated hacking operations. Their availability does not mean the AI companies are directing the attacks. According to the FBI, the technology allows criminals with relatively little technical knowledge to launch sophisticated attacks against multiple organizations simultaneously.

FBI warns ARTEX hackers can gain access in under 3 hours

In a November 13, 2026, security advisory, the FBI warned that criminals have used ARTEX in cyberattacks since at least August 2026. The agency identified campaigns targeting financial institutions and healthcare organizations. Government agencies and technology companies have also appeared among the targets. The speed of these attacks is especially troubling. According to the FBI, some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. That means hackers obtained powerful permissions that could allow them to make changes inside compromised systems.

ARTEX can also identify weaknesses in systems that companies sometimes overlook. These include employee portals and older business applications. Criminals may exploit vulnerable third-party connections to reach organizations with stronger security. Although automated attacks can trigger security alerts, their speed creates another challenge. A company's security team might detect suspicious activity only after criminals have already gained access.

How hackers used ARTEX to attack Microsoft 365

One of the clearest examples involves Microsoft 365, the service millions of employees rely on for work email and company files. In October 2026, hackers exploited compromised application credentials associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup. The service, formerly known as SkyKick Cloud Backup, helps businesses back up Microsoft 365 information. Here's why that attack is so concerning. The compromised applications already had permission to access customer environments. Hackers took advantage of those existing permissions to authenticate without needing an employee to sign in. In an October 21 investigation, Microsoft attributed the campaign to a China-state-aligned hacking group it tracks as Storm-0940.

The group used ARTEX to speed up its operations and attempt access to more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments. Cybersecurity company Huntress reported unauthorized sign-ins across at least 162 customer environments during its initial investigation. However, the number of environments targeted does not represent the number where criminals stole information. Microsoft specifically warned that successful authentication does not automatically mean customer data was accessed or taken. The attack also did not result from a vulnerability in Microsoft's own systems or services. Hackers exploited permissions associated with a trusted third-party application. For businesses, that's a serious concern. Employees could have strong passwords and multifactor authentication enabled, yet criminals might still gain access through a compromised application the company already trusts.

ARTEX cyberattacks have already exposed personal information

The Microsoft 365 incident represents only part of the FBI's warning. In South Korea, hackers used ARTEX in attacks against financial institutions. Those attacks exposed personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people, according to the FBI.

In a separate investigation, South Korean authorities arrested seven suspects connected to attacks against more than 90 organizations. Police said the group stole approximately 8.2 million data records, with ARTEX reportedly used in many of the attacks. Researchers have also identified a separate international cyberespionage campaign.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked hacking group known as Vapor Panda used ARTEX in attacks targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. The campaign compromised at least nine organizations. The AI agents helped criminals identify vulnerabilities and obtain credentials. When one attack method failed, the software could attempt another approach. These incidents show how quickly AI-assisted hacking has expanded from individual targets to coordinated attacks against organizations around the world.

Why the ARTEX warning should concern you

You probably have never heard of ARTEX before now. But the businesses you depend on could become targets. Think about the information your employer keeps on file. It may include your Social Security number and banking details for direct deposit. Your healthcare provider holds sensitive medical information, while financial institutions maintain records connected to your identity. If criminals steal information from those organizations, they could use it to attempt identity theft or target you with convincing scams. A hacker who obtains your email address and details about your employer could create a phishing message that looks legitimate. A message mentioning a company you actually do business with may be harder to recognize as fraudulent.

There's another concern. Your personal information could be exposed through a company you barely remember giving it to. The FBI has not warned that ARTEX automatically compromises personal phones or home computers. Its advisory focuses on attacks against organizations and the systems they operate. Still, you don't have to be the direct target of a cyberattack to feel its effects.

NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH

Why removing ARTEX from GitHub hasn't stopped the attacks

The original ARTEX developer released the framework publicly in July 2026. After reports emerged that criminals were abusing it, the developer removed the original GitHub repository on October 8. However, the software remains available through archived copies and modified versions. The FBI also identified a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles. That figure refers to accessible framework interfaces, rather than 1,600 confirmed criminal operations. Removing the original project did little to eliminate copies already circulating online.

How to protect yourself from AI-powered cyberattacks

While companies are responsible for securing their systems, you can still take steps to protect your personal information and limit the damage if a business you trust gets hacked.

Use strong passwords and a password manager

If criminals steal login credentials from one organization, they may test those credentials against other accounts. Reusing passwords makes that easier. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A reputable password manager can generate secure passwords and store them for you. Start with your primary email account because criminals who gain access to it may be able to reset passwords for other services.

Turn on multifactor authentication or passkeys

Multifactor authentication adds another security check when someone tries to sign in to your account. Enable it for your email and financial services whenever available. Choose a passkey or authenticator app when supported. Passkeys can provide stronger protection against phishing than traditional passwords. Keep in mind that these protections cannot prevent every attack. The ConnectWise incident involved compromised application credentials rather than someone entering an employee's password.

Check which apps have access to your accounts

You may have granted third-party applications permission to access your Google or Microsoft account without thinking much about it. Review those connections periodically. Remove permissions for unfamiliar services or applications you no longer need. For personal Microsoft accounts, visit account.microsoft.com. For Google accounts, review your connected apps through myaccount.google.com. Look for unfamiliar sign-ins while you're there. If something seems suspicious, secure the account and revoke any sessions you don't recognize. For work accounts, contact your IT department before changing business application permissions.

Watch for suspicious breach notifications

Cybercriminals often use major security incidents to create convincing phishing messages. You might receive an email claiming your bank was hacked and asking you to verify your password. Another message could direct you to a fake account recovery page. Avoid clicking unexpected links or opening unfamiliar attachments. Instead, visit the company's official website or open its app directly to check for alerts. Never share verification codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly, even if the person claims to work for your bank.

Keep your devices updated and use antivirus protection

Install security updates on your computer and phone. These updates frequently address vulnerabilities criminals could exploit. Strong antivirus software with real-time protection can also help identify malicious downloads and suspicious programs. Some security tools offer additional protection against phishing websites. However, antivirus software on your personal computer cannot prevent criminals from compromising a company's cloud systems. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Monitor your accounts for unusual activity

Check your financial accounts regularly and enable transaction alerts. These notifications can help you spot unauthorized activity quickly. Review your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or credit inquiries. You can request free reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If your Social Security number has been exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze is free and can make it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts using your identity. A freeze will not prevent fraud involving accounts that are already open, so continue monitoring those accounts.

VISA, MASTERCARD AND JPMORGAN CUSTOMER DATA LEAKED

Know what to do if your information is exposed

If a company notifies you about a breach, find out exactly what information was compromised. Then take action based on the type of data involved.

Change exposed passwords immediately. Update any other accounts where you reused the same password.

Update any other accounts where you reused the same password. Secure your email account. Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules or recovery information. Sign out of suspicious sessions.

Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules or recovery information. Sign out of suspicious sessions. Contact your bank if financial information was exposed. Ask whether your accounts need additional protection.

Ask whether your accounts need additional protection. Consider a credit freeze . This can help protect against fraudulent new credit accounts if sensitive identity information was stolen.

This can help protect against fraudulent new credit accounts if sensitive identity information was stolen. Watch for follow-up scams. Criminals may use stolen details to make fake security alerts more convincing.

Criminals may use stolen details to make fake security alerts more convincing. Report identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan if someone has misused your personal information.

You can also report suspected internet crime to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/.

Kurt's key takeaways

A backup service is supposed to help protect a company's information. In the ConnectWise attack, hackers abused that trusted connection to gain access to customer systems. That's especially concerning because employees could have followed every security recommendation and still been exposed through a service their company depended on. The speed of these AI-powered attacks also worries me. Three hours gives security teams very little time to stop criminals who know exactly where they're going. I think companies need to take a much harder look at the outside applications they trust and how quickly they can detect unauthorized access. For you, the best approach is to secure your own accounts and pay attention when a company reports a breach. You shouldn't have to become a cybersecurity expert to feel confident that businesses are protecting your information.

World.title: Trump to confront Newsom over plan to spare 548 death row inmates, including notorious child killers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX — President Donald Trump will confront California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his sweeping plan to spare 548 death row inmates from execution, including a man who murdered nine members of his own family, the killer of 12-year-old Polly Klaas and the man convicted of torturing 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez to death.

Trump is expected to appear alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel at the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Monday afternoon to condemn the Democratic governor's proposed commutations, the White House confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Families of murder victims are expected to attend the event, where their stories will be highlighted as the Trump administration challenges Newsom's effort to replace every California death sentence with life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

NEWSOM'S BID TO EMPTY CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW COLLIDES WITH VOTERS' REPEATED REJECTION OF ABOLITION

"Governor Newsom is failing the victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these barbaric child killers and serial killers. These murderers raped, tortured and terrorized innocent victims. Governor Newsom must stop playing politics with public safety," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intended to commute all 548 California death sentences to life imprisonment without parole, arguing that capital punishment is incompatible with the state's values.

Asked by Fox News Digital about the proposed commutations, Newsom's office did not directly address the individual murder cases highlighted by the White House. Instead, the governor's office referred Fox News Digital to his previously published letter defending the decision.

"California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that," Newsom wrote. "But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment."

Newsom also acknowledged that some victims' families strongly oppose his decision, while his office pointed to other survivors who support eliminating capital punishment.

The White House provided Fox News Digital with a list of 20 notorious convicted killers who would benefit from Newsom's proposed clemency, detailing crimes involving murdered children, sexual violence, torture and serial killings.

NEWSOM ORDERS CALIFORNIA’S MOST REVILED KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW – 10 OF THE WORST WHO COULD BENEFIT

Among them is Marcus Wesson, who was convicted of murdering nine members of his family in Fresno, including children and grandchildren. Wesson was also convicted of rape and sexual abuse involving his daughters and nieces, whom he subjected to years of abuse within a cult-like family structure.

Richard Allen Davis was sentenced to death for kidnapping and murdering 12-year-old Polly Klaas, who was abducted from a sleepover at her Petaluma home in 1993. The case shocked the nation and helped galvanize support for California's three-strikes sentencing law.

The White House also highlighted Isauro Aguirre, convicted of the torture and murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez in Los Angeles County. Gabriel suffered prolonged abuse before his death, a case that drew national outrage and later became the subject of a documentary series examining the violence he endured and failures to protect him.

Other offenders identified by the White House include Charles Ng, convicted of 11 murders involving captivity, torture and sexual violence, and Randy Kraft, the so-called "Scorecard Killer," convicted of murdering 16 men in crimes involving sexual assault and mutilation.

Chester Turner, convicted of murdering 14 women in Los Angeles, and Cary Stayner, convicted of four murders near Yosemite National Park, were also named.

Some of the cases involved the slaughter of entire families. Ramon Salcido was convicted of killing seven people during a Sonoma County rampage, including his wife and two young daughters, while former school administrator Vincent Brothers was convicted of murdering his wife, three children and mother-in-law in Bakersfield.

The White House's intervention comes as Newsom faces mounting opposition from California prosecutors and victims' advocates who argue that his sweeping clemency plan disregards the verdicts of juries and the suffering of families who spent years pursuing justice.

CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

Although the condemned inmates would remain behind bars for life without the possibility of parole, the commutations would permanently remove the prospect of execution, regardless of the wishes of families who continue to seek that outcome.

"I was just sickened, frankly, for the crime victims in California who were slapped in the face by our governor," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow previously told Fox News Digital.

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer previously accused Newsom of extending "mercy for the wolves … while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep."

The proposed commutations have not yet taken effect. Under California law, 382 requires a recommendation from the state Supreme Court because the inmates have multiple felony convictions. Newsom's administration has said it will not proceed with any of the commutations until the court acts.

The legal battle intensified last week when a coalition of California prosecutors and victims' advocates asked the state Supreme Court to halt the plan, arguing that Newsom failed to provide victims and their families an opportunity to be heard before pursuing the sweeping clemency action.

The court has invited additional briefs through Tuesday, Nov. 24, as it considers the governor's request. Newsom has asked the justices to act before his term ends in January.

California voters rejected efforts to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. The state has not carried out an execution since 2006, and Newsom imposed a formal moratorium on capital punishment shortly after taking office in 2019.

Trump has taken the opposite approach, directing the Justice Department on his first day back in office to prioritize seeking and implementing lawful death sentences. In April, the department announced additional measures to strengthen federal capital punishment procedures, including reinstating its previous lethal injection protocol and expanding available execution methods.

Representatives from the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration, U.S. Marshals Service, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Federal Bureau of Prisons are also expected to attend Monday's event.



Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano contributed to this reporting.

World.title: Marilyn Monroe's 1950s stuffing recipe fetched $16,000 at auction — and holds clue to Joe DiMaggio marriage
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Thanksgiving recipe of Marilyn Monroe's was just as fabulous as she was and offers a glimpse into a lesser-known side of the Hollywood star.

Her handwritten stuffing recipe is a far cry from the boxed bread-and-herb side many families serve on Thanksgiving, loaded with 18 ingredients including sourdough, ground beef, poultry livers or hearts, hard-boiled eggs, raisins, Parmesan and nuts.

Written in pencil on both sides of a sheet of City Title Insurance Company stationery, the recipe was cataloged by Julien's Auctions as circa 1954. It sold for $16,000 at the auction house's June 2026 sale, more than five times its estimate.

JESSIE JAMES DECKER SHARES 'SECRET SAUCE' BEHIND FAMILY'S FOOD, FAITH, TRADITIONS

The recipe is attributed to Monroe because it is written entirely in her hand, according to Julien's Auctions, and came from the estate of her acting coach, Lee Strasberg, who inherited her personal effects.

"Something as simple as a handwritten recipe helps humanize Marilyn and reminds us that behind one of the most recognizable faces in Hollywood history was a woman who enjoyed many of the same ordinary pleasures as everyone else," Scott Fortner, a lifelong Monroe scholar and collector who is often consulted on authenticating her personal effects, told Fox News Digital.

"I think it offers a wonderful glimpse into another side of Marilyn Monroe, beyond the glamorous movie star and Hollywood sex symbol," he added, noting that she had "a genuine interest in cooking and domestic life."

She reportedly enjoyed cooking and entertaining, especially during her later marriage to playwright Arthur Miller when the couple had a farm in Connecticut.

'FOOD BABE' DECLARES WAR ON THE 'HOLIDAY DEATH AISLE' AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING

"Her personal library also included several cookbooks, some with markings and annotations," Fortner said.

The San Francisco address on the stationery and the note "No garlic" have fueled speculation about a connection to baseball legend Joe DiMaggio, who reportedly disliked garlic and with whom Monroe lived in San Francisco after their 1954 marriage.

Fortner said it is possible she made the stuffing for the former Yankees star, but there is no documented evidence of that.

CLASSIC AMERICAN PANTRY STAPLES ARE GETTING A MAJOR PROTEIN- AND FIBER-PACKED MAKEOVER

He said the San Francisco stationery makes it reasonable to think Monroe wrote the recipe during her relationship with Joe DiMaggio, whom she began dating in 1952 and married in January 1954, but the timing remains unclear.

The couple separated in October, so if Monroe wrote it later that year, they would have been apart by Thanksgiving, Fortner noted.

The sourdough, he added, could reflect San Francisco's food culture, but it is also a common stuffing ingredient.

"Just because the recipe was written on stationery from a San Francisco business doesn't necessarily mean it was written while Marilyn was in San Francisco, or even during her relationship with Joe," Fortner told Fox News Digital. "Without knowing exactly when she wrote the recipe, we can only speculate about its connection to Joe or whether she ever prepared the dish for him."

6 VINTAGE RECIPES OF DECADES PAST, FROM OYSTER STUFFING TO HOT DR PEPPER

Regardless, the relic reminds us that Monroe "valued her personal relationships and had a genuine interest in the everyday experiences of life outside the movie studio," Fortner said.

For home cooks hoping to bring a bit of Monroe's kitchen to their own Thanksgiving table, The New York Times published a modern adaptation of the recipe that could feed a crowd.

It yields nearly 20 cups and follows Monroe's handwritten instructions to use sourdough soaked in cold water instead of broth. Her note suggests the stuffing for chicken, turkey or even pheasant.

Below is an adaptation of Monroe's recipe.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Ingredients

1 (10-ounce) loaf sourdough bread

½ pound chicken or turkey livers or hearts

½ pound ground beef

1 tablespoon cooking oil

4 celery stalks, chopped

1 large onion, chopped

2 cups chopped parsley

2 hard-boiled eggs, chopped

1½ cups raisins

1 cup grated Parmesan

1 ¼ cups chopped walnuts, pine nuts or roasted chestnuts, or a mix

2 teaspoons each dried rosemary, oregano and thyme

3 bay leaves

1 tablespoon salt-free, garlic-free poultry seasoning

1 tablespoon kosher salt, plus more to taste

1 tablespoon black pepper

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

If you don't have poultry seasoning, The New York Times version suggests substituting 1 teaspoon each dried sage and marjoram, plus ½ teaspoon each ground ginger and nutmeg.

Directions

1. Tear the bread into pieces and soak it in a large bowl of cold water for 15 minutes. Drain and squeeze out the excess water, then shred the bread into smaller pieces.

CLICK HERE TO 

2. Boil the livers or hearts in salted water for 8 minutes. Drain and chop finely.

3. Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook, breaking it into small pieces, until browned and cooked through.

4. In a large bowl, combine the bread, livers or hearts, beef, celery, onion, parsley, eggs, raisins, cheese and nuts. Mix the rosemary, oregano, thyme, bay leaves, poultry seasoning, salt and pepper together, then stir them into the stuffing.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

5. To serve as dressing, divide the mixture among shallow baking dishes, using about 2 quarts per 9-inch-square dish. Bake at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for about 1 hour, until browned and a food thermometer inserted in the center registers 165 degrees Fahrenheit.

World.title: Democratic National Committee sets broad rules for the party’s 2028 presidential debates
World.content:
The Democratic National Committee will hold 12 debates next year and in 2028 for candidates seeking the party’s presidential nomination, the party announced, as it sets rules of the road for what’s expected to be a crowded campaign for the White House.

The Monday morning announcement from the DNC lays out a process that hews closely to the rules under which Democrats ran in 2020, the last time the party had an open primary.

Each debate may be split across two nights, with no more than 20 candidates qualifying in total — an implicit acknowledgement of the dozens of Democrats from all corners of the party who are openly musing about running for president. And the party will determine who makes the debate stage through criteria like polling and grassroots fundraising figures.

Exact dates and media partners for the first two debates will be announced in January.

The biggest rules change compared to past campaigns is that the party will require presidential candidates to sign a pledge denouncing “dark money spending in our primary” used to boost a candidate or cut down a Democratic rival.

It’s a relatively symbolic pledge — it doesn’t have the teeth to actually stop that kind of outside spending, but it will try to attach a political cost to it, all while uniting Democratic candidates behind the party’s frustration with rampant outside spending in federal elections.

Candidates will also have to adhere to a series of other promises, as always. That includes agreeing to follow the DNC’s new nominating calendar. Candidates who compete in states that are trying to jump ahead of the party’s approved early-primary order face being stripped of delegates won in every early-nominating state, and the DNC made that punishment harder to undo than in past years.

Minyon Moore, a longtime DNC senior adviser and veteran party strategist, will lead the DNC’s Debate Planning Committee alongside Roger Lau, the party’s executive director. The DNC added that the committee also includes people who staffed past presidential campaigns including those of Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Amy Klobuchar, Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama.

“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement. “The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House.”

The June start to the debate calendar puts the Democrats in line with their 2020 schedule, when NBC News hosted the first debates in Miami alongside MSNBC and Telemundo. Those events sparked the first in-person clashes among the sprawling field of Democratic hopefuls, with two 10-person debates on back-to-back days. Then, the vast majority of the announced Democratic candidates qualified for the stage.

Like in 2020, the DNC plans to randomize the two-night debate stages “in a manner that will ensure parity across both nights.”

The announcement also includes additional details about some of the more technical rules governing the nominating contest.

Under the party’s new anti-dark money pledge, candidates have to agree to a blanket denunciation of political nonprofits or super PACs that spend for or against candidates in the primary race, and they must specifically denounce new outside spending that pops up on their behalf.

A DNC official told NBC that the pledge has been endorsed by a handful of elected Democrats, including Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Andy Kim, of Massachusetts and New Jersey respectively, as well as Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Candidates must also agree not to enter into any joint fundraising agreement with local party organizations unless they’re the party’s official nominee, a measure aimed at ensuring the Democratic Party apparatus remains neutral across different levels.

World.title: Rough weather expected to hit both coasts, may disrupt Thanksgiving travel
World.content:
Strong storms, serious flooding and powerful winds could dampen Thanksgiving travel plans and celebrations in parts of the Northeast and California, forecasters said.

A spinning winter cyclone over the urban Northeast on Thanksgiving Day could create 50 mph wind gusts, boost coastal flooding, and produce “bursts of heavy rain and embedded thunderstorms,” the National Weather Service said.

It described the storm as likely to quickly spool up and move fast due to “rapid cyclogenesis,” a term associated with rain-heavy storms known as bomb cyclones. The storms take place when air rises, barometric pressure drops, and wind spirals.

New York City Emergency Management is warning residents to stay tuned to weather alerts and forecasts this week.

“Keep an eye on Thursday,” it said on X. “The forecast shows a storm that could bring strong winds, rain, and coastal flooding to the city on Thanksgiving Day, with gusts of 40 to 45 mph possible and 1 to 2 inches of rain.”

It’s not clear how the weather might affect the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. New York City regulations state the parade’s hallmark balloons can’t fly if there are sustained winds of greater than 23 mph or gusts above 34 mph.

Heavy rain, coastal flooding could hit East Coast

National Weather Service hazardous weather outlooks for Wednesday and Thursday predict possible widespread and potentially heavy rain, strong winds, coastal flooding, and high surf from southeast Virginia to waters off New Haven, Connecticut.

The National Weather Service warns of winds 40 mph and stronger buffeting the Interstate 95 corridor in the Northeast midweek.

“Confidence is increasing” that the system will produce serious weather after developing off the Southeast coast Wednesday and rapidly moving north, it said.

Federal forecasters said the cyclone will spin and strengthen with the help of unusually warm Atlantic waters.

The weather service added in a forecast discussion, “Coastal flooding issues, beach erosion, and dangerously rough seas appear likely, especially from the Mid-Atlantic up into the New England coast.”

King tides and flooding in California

Tuesday’s full moon will help pull seawater ashore on both U.S. coasts, with California officials preparing for the highest tides of the year and associated coastal flooding that could be exacerbated by an incoming Pacific storm.

Coastal flood watches and advisories based on the year’s highest tides Tuesday through Thursday were in effect from Portland, Oregon to the U.S.-Mexico border.

The weather service said the winter-pattern Pacific storm will move over land Tuesday in the Pacific Northwest and Northern California, with federal forecasters in San Francisco expecting 1 to 2 inches of rain through Wednesday along with occasional 45 mph wind gusts.

The Sierra Nevada mountain range will get fresh snow and “difficult travel,” the weather service office in Reno, Nevada, said.

The West Coast storm is likely to be followed up by another, federal forecasters said, with those based in the San Francisco Bay Area saying it could strike Friday or over the weekend.

Busy travel week

Thanksgiving week’s departure and arrival days often vie for the title of the busiest travel day in America, with Transportation Safety Administration data showing Nov. 30, 2025, with the most daily airport security screenings, more than 3.1 million, for the year.

Slightly fewer travelers are expected on highways and in the air during the typically busy Thanksgiving travel period, the American Automobile Association said.

A postpandemic streak of an increasing number of travelers during Thanksgiving week each year is likely to come to an end as slightly fewer people, 81.5 million, leave home for holiday trips compared to 81.6 million last year, the AAA said in a statement.

The week’s travelers are contending with higher prices for gas and airfare, with roundtrip tickets up 17% over Thanksgiving 2025, and the average price at $800, AAA said.

Gas station price app GasBuddy projects the national average for a gallon of gas to be $3.62 on Thursday, a likely record high for the date but also reflective of prices falling rapidly — by at least .50 cents — so far this month.

World.title: Crowd evacuated from U.S. rapper Don Toliver’s concert after ‘unknown substance’ released
World.content:
MANCHESTER, England — Thousands of people attending the concert of U.S. rapper Don Toliver were evacuated from a major British arena on Sunday evening, police said, after an “unknown substance” was released into the crowd.

About 12,000 concert goers were evacuated by emergency workers just after 10 p.m. local time (5 p.m. ET) from Toliver’s show at the Co-op Live venue in the northern English city of Manchester.

The North West Ambulance Service declared a major incident and​ said the substance was “believed to ​be tear gas” and was understood to ⁠have been released toward the ​end of the show.

“We deployed several emergency crews, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene,” it said in a statement, adding that one person had been hospitalized.

“More than 50 people have been assessed by our clinicians, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms. Decontamination is being carried out as a precaution,” the ambulance service said.

People in the crowd were suffering effects “from an unknown substance,” Greater Manchester police said in its latest statement on Monday. “Enquiries are underway into what the substance is and what caused the incident,” police added.

The venue, in the center of the busy city, was hosting Grammy Award-nominated R&B rapper-singer Toliver, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, as part of his Nitrous tour.

Don Toliver performing in Thermal, Calif. in April. Greg Doherty / Getty for REVOLVE

The Houston based rapper is best known for hits “No idea” and “After Party,” and features on the soundtrack to the new “Grand Theft Auto VI” blockbuster game. Toliver has yet to publicly comment on the incident but is due to perform in London on Monday and Tuesday as part of his tour.

Manchester was left shaken in 2017 after a bombing at a nearby venue during an Ariana Grande concert left 22 people dead and made global headlines.

“We understand the concern that this incident will have raised,” Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said Monday. “We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about.”

“Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital,” Parker added.

Concert goer Joey Howe, 22, told BBC Radio Manchester the lights came on and Toliver appeared to have been “rushed off stage.”

“I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue,” Howe said. He said people were “choking” and there was a “horrible smell” in the arena.

“It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see,” he added.

Authorities respond to an emergency incident during a concert by rapper Don Toliver at Co-op Live on Sunday. Ryan Jenkinson / Getty

The venue, which opened in 2024, is due to host U.S. singer Phoebe Bridgers on Thursday.

It said in a statement on X that it was “working closely with Greater Manchester Police to identify the cause and action appropriately. Our priority remains the safety and security of all visitors to Co-op Live, and we will provide more information once we have an update.”

World.title: NFL Week 11: A Travis Kelce game years in the making, and Dak Prescott keeps dealing
World.content:
Week 11 of the NFL season featured a throwback performance by Travis Kelce, a nail-biter in New York, and the second start for Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza.

Here’s everything you need to know from Sunday.

A vintage day for Mahomes and Kelce

The Kansas City Chiefs rolled over the Arizona Cardinals, cruising to a 34-7 victory. Tight end Travis Kelce caught two touchdowns — his first regular season game with at least two receiving scores since 2022. Kelce hasn’t caught more than five touchdowns in a season since 2022, and he’s now up to four this year with seven games to go.

Patrick Mahomes is also on a tear. After a three-touchdown performance against the Cardinals, Mahomes has thrown for 13 scores with zero interceptions over the last four games, during which Kansas City has a 3-1 record.

Patrick Mahomes during the first quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday. Jamie Squire / Getty

It should be another classic on Thanksgiving when Mahomes, Kelce and the Chiefs take on Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills, who beat the Miami Dolphins 26-9 on Sunday.

The Giants keep finding a way

New York improved to 6-3-1 after holding on for a 23-18 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars. That’s the best win for head coach John Harbaugh in his first season with the Giants, taking down a team that was 16-3 in its last 19 regular season games.

There was controversy late, as what appeared to be a touchdown catch by Jaguars receiver Parker Washington was instead ruled incomplete. Jacksonville also opted for a field goal from inside the 10 while trailing 23-15 with under four minutes to go. The Jags never saw the ball again.

New York was outgained on offense, but its defense forced two turnovers to overcome an anemic passing attack. The Giants remained in the driver’s seat to win the NFC East.

Eagles get their first win since September

It’s been a long fall for Philadelphia, which went two whole months between wins before a 19-16 victory over their cross-state rival the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 11. Eagles quarterback Joe Milton did just enough for the win, ending their seven-game losing streak.

Aaron Rodgers, meanwhile, struggled again. Rodgers averaged only 5.2 yards per attempt, and was sacked five times in the loss. The Steelers have now dropped two straight after a four-game win streak. Rodgers has avoided big mistakes, but in turn has failed to consistently make big plays. His current average yards per passing attempt is a career-low mark.

More heartbreak for the Ravens

After a 4-1 start, Baltimore has lost six straight games. And for the second straight week, a late turnover ruined a potential comeback.

World.title: It was the NFL’s toughest test. Then the 49ers made it look easy.
World.content:
During breaks in Sunday’s matchup against Minnesota, San Francisco 49ers players retreated to their sideline in Mexico City and were handed breathing masks connected to oxygen tanks.

Facing the blitz-happy, havoc-inducing Vikings has had the effect of leaving opponents breathless all season. But even playing at 7,352 feet of elevation, San Francisco’s players barely looked to be breathing hard while blunting the NFL’s most dangerous defense.

In its 35-10 win in Estadio Azteca, San Francisco took apart vaunted Minnesota while showing why the 49ers (9-1) remain a leading Super Bowl contender 11 weeks into the season.

Under the charge of coordinator Brian Flores, Minnesota had blitzed on more than three-quarters of their downs; no other team had done it even half the time. Not coincidentally, the Vikings had allowed the league’s fewest points and its second-fewest yards, while becoming the NFL’s most difficult problem to solve.

Until Sunday — when the Vikings ran into the league’s toughest team.

The 35 points were the most Minnesota (7-3) had allowed all season; its one sack tied for its fewest; its zero takeaways are the fewest. No other offense had enjoyed such success against them to this point, not even Detroit, Green Bay and Chicago, the NFC North rivals who also boast explosive offenses.

The performance was so one-sided that 49ers coach and offensive play caller Kyle Shanahan was asked whether this is the best team he has led in his 10 seasons in San Francisco.

“No, but it’s still early,” Shanahan said. “We got to earn that and we’re halfway through the year. We’ve done some good things but it’s still to be determined. (A season) is 7 months long. We know how we’ve been so far but we’re halfway there and we got a long way to go.”

The mood was also light enough that tight end George Kittle, after catching two touchdowns, wore a lucha libre mask to his postgame press availability.

“Did I distract you at all?” Kittle said to his teammate on the dais. Quarterback Brock Purdy shook his head.

Little distracted Purdy while completing 21 of his 26 passes for 255 yards and three touchdowns and taking away Minnesota’s greatest strength — its ability to speed up quarterbacks by sending waves of pressure.

Rather than be rattled, Purdy completed his first eight passes against Vikings blitzes for two touchdowns. When one rushing defender leaped to hit Purdy or at least deflect his pass, the quarterback calmly pump-faked, dipped down and found a receiver for a 7-yard gain instead of 7-yard loss. On another play, he leaped into the air behind his blockers before firing an accurate strike.

“We never recommend the jump pass,” Shanahan said. “But when he pulls it off and it works, then we congratulate him.”

The scariest thing for the rest of the NFL is that if Purdy could play cool and collected against pressure like that, the rest of his opponents will be tame by comparison. Indeed, all season, Purdy ranks first among all quarterbacks in both yards per attempt and passing touchdowns when facing a blitz, per ESPN.

“Best player in the game right now,” 49ers receiver Mike Evans said. “He’s super dialed-in. The way he prepares, the way he competes, he’s tough. I always thought he was underrated.”

No receiver was targeted more than seven times, but the mixture of passes, runs and misdirections by Shanahan kept the Vikings from keying onto any of the nine players who caught a pass Sunday. Purdy’s passer rating wasn’t only the highest allowed by the Vikings this season — it was also the highest QBR allowed by Minnesota in the regular season since ESPN began tracking the statistic 20 years ago.

Entering the week, the matchup between Shanahan and Flores was more than simply an exceptional appetizer to the league’s slate of Thanksgiving week matchups. It was no exaggeration to describe the showdown of the NFL’s most-disruptive defense and its second-highest-scoring offense as one that might be repeated in two months’ time during the NFC Championship. In each of three previous matchups between a Flores defense and Shanahan offense, Flores had won the game while allowing just 17 points.

On Sunday, that script flipped.

By late in the second quarter, the 49ers’ offense had already scored 21 points. San Francisco widened its lead further, to 28-10, when Ji’Ayir Brown intercepted Minnesota’s Kirk Cousins and ran it back for a touchdown. It wasn’t even halftime and the Vikings had already allowed more points, and trailed by more points, than they had all season.

“Our game plan was so good,” Kittle told ESPN. “It was really just trying to take advantage of how much they pressure us. Try to get guys in those little gaps. ... And then, when you look out there and you see Mike Evans, Keenan Allen, Christian McCaffery, Deebo Samuel, it really makes my heart happy.”

When Vikings star receiver Justin Jefferson fumbled on the opening drive of the second half, the game was effectively over and so was any doubt about the best team, so far, in the NFC. That wasn’t solely because of their offensive performance, either. After allowing 40 points last week against Dallas, the 49ers’ defense forced two turnovers, including the pick-six, and held Minnesota to 1-of-3 on fourth-down attempts.

The Vikings had allowed opponents to travel an average of just 25.2 yards per drive this season, second-fewest in the league. And those drives turned into scores just 26% of the time, a league-best rate.

San Francisco, though, found little resistance. Its first three touchdown drives traveled 72, 67 and 65 yards, respectively. Its final scoring drive, in the fourth quarter, chewed up 7 minutes of time while traveling 98 yards. It was 4-for-4 scoring once inside the red zone.

It was tempting to pin the performance on their preparation, after spending several days last week practicing at the Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, Colorado, to acclimate to Mexico City’s elevation. But San Francisco has looked like a team to beat since Week 1, too, when it convincingly took out the Super Bowl contender Los Angeles Rams in Australia.

San Francisco’s control was so secure that it removed Purdy and played backup quarterback Mac Jones with 5 minutes still to play in the fourth quarter.

“I think their quarterback’s really good,” Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell, a former NFL quarterback himself, said. “And I think they got a bunch of really good players.”
