World.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship off Libya in latest expansion of the war
World.content:
Ukraine has taken its fight against Russia to the shores of North Africa, claiming to have sunk a warship off the coast of Libya in its latest bold expansion of the war.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Ukrainian naval drones had been used in the attack in the Mediterranean a day earlier, which came after Moscow said another of its ships was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea.

Zelenskyy shared footage of the attacks in a post on X, showing drones approaching several vessels followed by massive fire balls.

He said his forces deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones to sink the Russian corvette, Merkury, and hit a transport ship, the Angara, in an “exemplary Ukrainian operation.”

Ukraine’s Security Service, SBU, said the attacks took place near the Libyan port of Benghazi, some 1,500 miles from the established front lines of the conflict.

It said the corvette “regularly escorted enemy naval convoys” and in particular guarded the Angara cargo ship that was used to move weapons. “Both vessels were legitimate military targets for Ukraine, as they worked directly for Russia’s military capabilities,” the SBU said in a statement on Telegram.

A screengrab from a video shared by Zelenskyy shows a Ukrainian attack on the Russian corvette Merkury, off the coast of Libya. Volodymyr Zelenskyy / via X

Ukrainian uncrewed boats were delivered to a designated location and launched into the water from a so-called “mother ship,” the SBU said, reaching their targets despite “enemy’s attempts to destroy the Ukrainian drones from the air.” It said the Ka-27 multi-purpose helicopter was on board the corvette and was also sunk.

“The Defence Forces of Ukraine have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea,” the SBU added.

Ukraine noted that the ship was one of Russia’s newest, commissioned only in 2023.

Moscow has noted Zelenskyy’s “statement on this matter,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday when asked about the attacks. He deferred to Russia’s defense ministry, which was yet to comment.

It’s the latest example of Kyiv launching daring, surprise attacks to hit back against the Kremlin.

But the weekend attack caused fallout in Libya, where local authorities expressed outrage and the United Nations called for an independent probe.

The eastern Libya-based government said Sunday that an explosion took place aboard a Russian vessel docked at the Benghazi Naval Base. It said the vessel was en route back to Russia and had stopped at the port to refuel and take on supplies.

A comprehensive investigation into the attack will be launched, it said, in coordination with Russian authorities.

World.title: Plastic surgeon sentenced to death for of killing lawyer in Florida
World.content:
A judge in Florida sentenced a plastic surgeon to death for killing an attorney in a law office bathroom and then dumping his body in a trash bin in the Everglades, where it was never found.

Dr. Tomasz Kosowski killed attorney Steven Cozzi in the bathroom of Cozzi's law office in March 2023, moments after both participated in a conference call about a lengthy, acrimonious legal battle over medical billing, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said Kosowski took the call from a Toyota pickup truck outside the office and that he had supplies to commit the killing, including trash bags, a syringe containing a paralyzing drug and a wagon to haul the corpse out. CBS affiliate WTSP-TV reported that prosecutors unpacked a black duffel that they referred to as Kosowski's "murder bag" — containing items like passports, a crowbar, brass knuckles, a track phone and a mask.

Investigators used cellphone records and surveillance video to track Kosowski to a remote area west of Miami on the Tamiami Trail, also known as U.S. Highway 41. That's where they believe Kosowski tossed the body into a Dumpster that was eventually emptied by a garbage truck. The driver noticed an unusually "vile" smell at the stop, authorities said.

Trash from the route is typically hauled to a Collier County landfill, but authorities who searched the property for Cozzi's body said the facility routinely compacts its trash, making recovery efforts nearly impossible. In addition, investigators said, Cozzi's blood and DNA were found in the law office bathroom and in the garage at Kosowski's home.

Kosowski was convicted in September, following a trial in which he represented himself and presented no defense beyond making a closing argument in which he said prosecutors had not proved their case.

Pinellas Circuit Judge Joseph Bulone was tasked with deciding whether to sentence Kosowski to death or to life in prison without the possibility of release.

Kosowski declined to present any mitigating evidence on his own behalf, but a special counsel appointed by the court highlighted his lack of criminal history and his medical work. A graduate of Dartmouth College medical school, Kosowski specialized in reconstructive breast surgery.

This photo provided by the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office shows Dr. Tomasz Kosowski, who was arrested on a first-degree murder charge, March 25, 2023, by Largo Police, in Florida. / AP

The judge acknowledged in court that there were several mitigating factors, but said none outweighed the aggravating factors - most importantly, that the crime was committed in a "cold, calculating and premeditated manner, without any pretense of moral or legal justification."

"The court concludes that the defendant, under the laws of the State of Florida, has forfeited his right to live," Bulone said.

Investigators said that when they arrested Kosowski, he had $280,000 in cash, masks, duct tape, firearms, a ballistic vest with "EMS" written on it, law enforcement patches and a vial of succinylcholine, which is a paralyzing drug. A search of his home turned up about 200 guns, according to court documents.

Cozzi, meanwhile, seemingly disappeared without a trace. His keys, wallet and cellphone remained on his law office desk and a work file was open on his computer. His husband never heard from him.

Steve Cozzi St. Petersburg Bar Association

The missing lawyer represented a Dunedin, Florida-based medical practice that Kosowski alleged had shorted him thousands of dollars in billings and damaged his reputation as a doctor.

Bulone appointed the public defender's office to represent Kosowski in his appeals.

Kosowski's neighbors previously told WTSP-TV that he was a nice guy and said he was very conversational when he went to community functions. They said they were shocked by the news.

Michael Montgomery, who identified himself as Cozzi's husband, posted a message on Facebook in 2023, saying Cozzi was "stolen from us."

"Today, our greatest fears were realized," he wrote. "My husband and best friend was stolen from us."

World.title: Pro golfer, chef arrested for 111 pounds of alleged drugs in luggage
World.content:
Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency Sunday said it had arrested a South African professional golfer with 50.4 kilograms (111 pounds) of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at Lagos airport.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said 37-year-old Henlo Grobler was arrested on October 11 after arriving from South Africa.

The agency said Grobler and his alleged Kenyan accomplice, a 25-year-old chef named Faiza Njambi Abubakar, swapped luggage tags to conceal ownership of the cannabis. Officials said the golfer traveled in business class while his accomplice flew economy.

While Grobler carried bags tagged in the Kenyan woman's name, she collected two bags bearing his tags and left the airport.

The bags found with Grobler contained 46 parcels of a "strong strain of cannabis," the NDLEA said.

Grobler told investigators he was recruited by a South African associate and was promised $280 upon successful delivery of the drugs.

Abubakar, who was arrested on October 15 as she prepared to board a flight to Kenya, told investigators she had been offered $8,000 for her role in the operation.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said pro golfer Henlo Grobler was arrested on October 11 after arriving from South Africa. His alleged Kenyan accomplice, Faiza Njambi Abubakar, swapped luggage tags to conceal ownership of the consignments. National Drug Law Enforcement Agency

"Both suspects identified each other during an identification parade," NDLEA spokesman Femi Babafemi said in a statement.

The agency said tracking devices were installed on the luggage and Grobler's mobile phone, allowing the syndicate to monitor its couriers and consignments.

Similar devices were also found in bags abandoned by an American professional basketball player arrested at the same airport on November 11 with 34 kilogrammes of cannabis. Officials said the player, DaMonte Greene, claimed he was visiting Nigeria to "build networks for his basketball career" but examination of his mobile phone showed information suggesting his "knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."

PGA South Africa lists a player by the name of Henlo Grobler.

Nigeria is considered a trafficking and production hub for drugs destined for other countries, but researchers say the contraband also finds its way into local markets.

Recent discoveries of industrial-scale methamphetamine production laboratories have raised concerns among authorities that Mexican cartels are establishing links in Nigeria to produce and ship the drug abroad.

World.title: Search on for lioness seen roaming Istanbul's outskirts
World.content:
Istanbul — Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials said Monday.

A resident spotted the animal Sunday evening in Uskumrukoy, an upscale neighborhood on the northern edge of Istanbul's European side, surrounded by forests. The lioness was later captured on security camera footage.

"The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive," the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement posted on social media.

Turkish gendarmerie officers block a road as police and animal welfare teams search for a lioness spotted roaming in the Sariyer district of Istanbul, Turkey, on Nov. 23, 2026. Ahmet Faruk Sarikoc / IHA via AP

Grainy images published by the Demiroren News Agency showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched an investigation focused on identifying its owner.

The National Parks Directorate said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search, which was focused on the wooded area.

An aerial view shows police and emergency teams searching an area in the Sariyer district of Istanbul, Turkey, following a report that a lioness had been spotted, on Nov. 23, 2026. Cem Tekkesinoglu / Anadolu via Getty Images

Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search.

"I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it," he said in comments reported by the Cumhuriyet newspaper. "While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie (police)."

Residents were warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighborhood.

Turkey has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia. In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

World.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine sank Russian warship off Libya's coast
World.content:
Kyiv, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind an attack on a Russian warship off Libya on Sunday, claiming Ukrainian naval drones sank the vessel. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.

Zelenskyy said Monday in a social media post that Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones in the operation, which sank a Russian corvette. The Ukrainian leader described the ship as one of Russia's newest vessels commissioned in 2023 during Russia's invasion.

"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," he wrote. He added that a Ka-27 military helicopter was destroyed in the attack.

A satellite image shows a capsized Russian corvette and the northern area of the port after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base, which Libya's eastern-based government said was caused by a suspected drone attack, in Benghazi, Libya, on Nov. 22, 2026. The vessel later sank, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Vantor / Handout via REUTERS

"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara off Libya on Sunday. Zelenskyy said Moscow had used the vessel to transport weapons. The Angara has been under U.S. and international sanctions for illegally transporting weapons for Russia.

Another Russia-linked cargo ship, the Sparta II, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, was struck by drones Saturday in international waters in the Gulf of Finland, causing a fire on board. Kyiv has not confirmed or denied any role in that attack, but Finland's military said it was likely a Ukrainian strike. The Sparta is also under U.S. sanctions for illicit transportation of military hardware.

Russian, Estonian and Finnish vessels helped put out the fire and all crew members were rescued from the Sparta, and a Russian ship then started towing it away Sunday, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, and other Ukrainian defense forces that took part in the strikes off Libya's coast, which he called "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."

Zelenskyy said he received detailed briefings on Sunday and Monday and that "the targets we set were achieved."

The Kremlin made no immediate comment, but said the Russian defense ministry would provide information later about the attack on the ship off Libya's coast.

The operation, conducted some 1,500 miles from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spider's Web in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft on bases across Russia.

The latest strike by sea drones severely damaged the Russian navy corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw fire at the base early Sunday. Civil defense rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Qaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

The U.N. mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the latest attack and called for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation."

"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) wrote on social media.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West. They used the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.

The SBU described the latest operation as "unique." It said the drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target. Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.

"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

Russia hammered Ukrainian cities with another deadly round of airstrikes overnight, meanwhile.

Regional authorities said 17 people were killed as a result of Russian attacks on Kyiv and the southern Zaporizhzhia region, including one child. Dozens more have been injured.

World.title: When disaster strikes, Medicaid work rules add barriers
World.content:
PO'IPŪ, Hawai'i — A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool's concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean.

On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to about 1,800 nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a sharp decline in visitors. The number of Medicaid applications submitted by island residents jumped by about 50% in the following month, according to the Hawaiʻi Department of Human Services.

In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Trump signed last year, has put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January.

In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies on a federal law that allows the president to issue a disaster or emergency declaration and authorizes federal assistance, but any declaration can take months or may not come at all.

Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it's unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn't offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees.

Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel's hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn't hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities.

Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, was laid off by the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort after it sustained significant damage from Hurricane Lowell. Her family is getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News

Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to delay enforcing the work requirements until next July, but states are still expected to implement eligibility checks by Jan. 1.

"It would be devastating if suddenly 40,000 or 50,000 people didn't have their Medicaid benefits," he said. "It could affect our rural hospitals, our nurse practitioners, our doctors, so timeliness is key."

Hawaiʻi officials said they will keep people who don't meet the work requirements enrolled until July.

A month after Hurricane Lowell in September 2026, sand still covered the grounds of the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort. Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News

At least 34 states, plus Washington, D.C., plan to adopt the optional hardship exemptions to those work requirements. So far, four states — Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio — do not plan to adopt the exemptions, according to KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. All four were issued disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding this summer.

CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster told KFF Health News in a statement that states can request a longer duration for a hardship exemption if they can prove that barriers to demonstrating work requirements persist in disaster areas.

Tom Cotter, CEO of Health Response Alliance, a nonprofit focused on improving healthcare access in disasters, said that when people lose coverage they end up using emergency rooms and charitable clinics, among the few places that will treat patients regardless of their ability to pay.

"All of these are really stretched thin during an emergency because their patient load goes way up," he said. "That makes it even more expensive for the healthcare system that is being otherwise also burdened for the disaster."

With additional work requirements, "it is going to slow the economic recovery of any particular community," Cotter said. "It's going to require people to be thinking about how they're paying for healthcare when they have a lot of other things to worry about."

Nebraska work requirements begin

Once the president declares a disaster or emergency, the short-term hardship exception applies for the full month the disaster took place. Eligibility can apply retroactively after a disaster declaration, and enrollees can be reimbursed for expenses from previous months.

Nebraska implemented Medicaid work requirements early, in May, offering states a preview of how the hardship declaration might provide relief. For Nebraskans, that relief was delayed.

It took three months for Mr. Trump to declare a federal disaster for March and April wildfires. For severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding that occurred in May, he didn't declare a federal disaster until August.

Six Nebraskans impacted by the disasters lost coverage because they did not comply with work requirements. In October, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services reported it was reprocessing their eligibility now that they qualify for a hardship exemption.

Sarah Maresh, director of the Health Care Access program at the nonprofit advocacy group Nebraska Appleseed, said the early rollout of the Medicaid work requirements has been marred by uncertainty.

"This is part of the confusion that comes with the Medicaid work requirements, because it applies differently depending on your situation," she said. "I think it'll be very challenging for new applicants."

Local economies and businesses can take years to recover after a natural disaster. About 90% of businesses fail within two years after being struck by disaster, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration. Housing shortages can hamper business recovery as employees repair their homes or are displaced to areas farther from work. Three years after the 2023 Maui wildfires that killed over 100 people, recovery is ongoing, with most storefronts still shuttered in what was once a bustling area.

After CMS published rules governing the exceptions to the work requirements, several Democratic states sued the agency. Their lawsuit cited the narrow time frame for securing natural disaster exceptions. The complaint argued that the lack of guidance burdens state Medicaid agencies determining eligibility.

In its response filing, CMS wrote that the restrictions ensure the exemption applies only when a disaster affects Medicaid enrollees' ability to comply with work requirements.

Disaster delays, denials

In Mr. Trump's second term, he has denied nearly a quarter of disaster and emergency declaration requests as of mid-November, a denial rate higher than that of any other presidential administration in more than two decades, KFF Health News found. While decision wait times have increased across the country, they're more acute in states with Democratic governors. Those states experienced both significantly higher denial rates and longer decision times than states with Republican governors, according to 2026 analyses from The Associated Press and Politico's E&E News.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied any politicization in Mr. Trump's decisions on disaster relief. She wrote that his response to requests from states ensures appropriate use of taxpayer money and that federal funds are used to "supplement — not substitute" states' obligations to respond to disasters.

The presidential major disaster declaration for Kauaʻi was the state's sixth disaster or emergency declaration this year. As of November, Hawaiʻi had received more disaster and emergency declarations than any other state in 2026. The president's disaster declaration for a 6.0-magnitude earthquake that damaged over 300 homes on Hawaiʻi Island took about three months.

Local economies and businesses can take years to recover after a natural disaster. Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News

Other states have waited longer for disaster declarations. New Mexico, where the Democratic Party controls the governor's office and majorities in both legislative chambers, had one of the longest wait times for a decision — nine months for a presidential disaster declaration for severe storms and flooding in September 2025. Illinois, which also has a Democratic trifecta, waited over seven months and was denied. The state has yet to secure any major disaster declarations during Mr. Trump's second term, despite several attempts.

Some who lost their jobs and don't qualify for Medicaid have few resources to help them.

Oscar Cardova worked at The Terrace Hanalei, a restaurant on Kauaʻi's North Shore that was significantly damaged in the hurricane. When the restaurant closed, he lost his employer-provided health insurance. Although he has a work permit visa from Peru, he was denied Medicaid because of his immigration status.

Cardova and his wife, Yesenia, live in their van. Yesenia has astigmatism and, without insurance, she will need to pay for glasses out-of-pocket, Cardova said. The cost is expected to be about $500.

The couple planned to work for two more years in the U.S. before returning to Peru. A month after the hurricane, they were still struggling to find work. In search of more job opportunities, they considered moving to Honolulu.

"Right now, we're just surviving," Cardova said. "We're waiting to see what happens before making other decisions, because we can't keep living like this."

Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? Click here to contact KFF Health News.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Army plans to carry out detonation at Iowa plant on Wednesday
World.content:
The U.S. Army says it plans to move forward with the detonation of several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced," the military said in a post on social media Sunday night.

The Army had earlier said in a court filing that it planned to carry out the detonation by Tuesday.

The detonation is being planned despite a federal court order that paused it indefinitely, which the Army said it does not need to follow because of the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

In federal court records filed late Saturday, the Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.

On Friday, a federal court suspended the U.S. Army's plan to detonate the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.

The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.

The military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said.

A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In its filing on Saturday, the government had warned that it must conduct the controlled explosion by Tuesday because the temperature is expected to drop below 30 degrees in the next several days. It says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop. It did not immediately explain if the forecast or other factors had changed to make a move to Wednesday safer.

"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. "The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion."

In response to the Army's filing, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed a motion Sunday seeking to supplement their emergency request to block the planned detonation.

The filing includes three expert and local government declarations challenging the Army's assessment of the risk of delaying the detonation, as well as concerns about public notice and potential health and environmental impacts.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration, saying "this emergency is of the Army's own making."

"The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.

Iowa's new Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek said in a statement Sunday that he is "concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army's planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army."

"I also believe we need a full investigation into why this stockpile of lead azide, which has been at IAAAP for decades, was allowed to degrade into this critical state, why safer methods of disposal were not pursued, what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at the IAAAP and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again," he said. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning."

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

World.title: Tom Jackson, former Broncos star and sports broadcaster, dies at 75
World.content:
Former football star and famed broadcaster Tom Jackson has died, his family and ESPN announced Sunday.

Jackson rose to prominence as a Denver Broncos player and went on to build a career as a beloved NFL analyst for ESPN, becoming a mainstay of the network's Sunday football programs for three decades, including its "Sunday NFL Countdown" show. He was 75.

Jimmy Pitaro, the chairman of ESPN, praised Jackson in a statement released by the network after his death. In it, Pitaro called Jackson "one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN's history," who "brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans."

"Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make NFL Primetime an iconic part of our football weekends," Pitaro said. "Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him. His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure."

Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wish that his death not be announced until the start of the network's "Sunday NFL Countdown" show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman.

"Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom's was frequent and unmistakable," Berman said at the start of the show. "Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too."

Former NFL player Randy Gradishar, right, and his presenter form Denver Broncos teammate Tom Jackson pose with his bust during an induction ceremony at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, in Canton, Ohio, Saturday, Aug. 3, 2024. AP Photo/David Dermer, File

Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was the inspirational leader of Denver's first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team's second Super Bowl appearance. He was a two-time Associated Press All-Pro and three-time Pro Bowler.

Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on "Sunday NFL Countdown" and "NFL Primetime."

Before the internet and NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, "NFL Primetime" was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interplay between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other's sentences.

"I can remember coming from games and waiting in a rush to get home, to watch 'Primetime' because all I wanted to know was, what were you and Tom Jackson gonna say about one, the team?" ESPN analyst and Hall of Fame wide receiver Randy Moss said to Berman.

Jackson briefly returned to ESPN in 2019 and reunited with Berman to do an online version of "NFL Primetime." He was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

Tom Jackson preparing for a workout with the Denver Broncos on Jan. 22, 1987, in Irvine, California. AP Photo/Ed Andrieski, File

"In my lifetime there was Howard Cosell doing 'Monday Night Football' halftime highlights and then there were Boomer and TJ doing 'Sunday NFL Countdown.' I am not here as a colleague but as one of million who watched, learned from and idolized the two of you," ESPN host Mike Greenberg said during Sunday's show.

ESPN's studio crew wore orange ties in honor of Jackson during the three-hour show.

Berman said Jackson was the last of seven people interviewed for the studio analyst job and that the last person rarely gets the job. But Jackson nailed the interview.

ESPN's NFL studio in Bristol, Connecticut, is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. It is the only named studio on ESPN's campus.

"The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history," the Broncos said in a statement.

"An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos' first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country."

Jackson is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and daughters Taylor and Morgan.

World.title: "I Have a Dream" pages written by Martin Luther King Jr. to go up for auction
World.content: "I Have a Dream" pages to go up for auction Martin Luther King Jr. wrote his famous "I Have a Dream" speech on yellow legal paper in long cursive in blue ink. Those pages have been tucked away until now; they are headed to auction in January. Brian Unger has the story. More

World.title: Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says

toggle caption i Satellite image ©2026 Vantor/via AP

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbor, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.

Russian officials made no immediate comment.

The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

toggle caption i Security Service of Ukraine/via AP

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked near air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.

Sponsor Message

At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.

A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.

Ukraine hits Russian assets from Siberia to Libya, Zelenskyy says

Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."

"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

toggle caption i Security Service of Ukraine/via AP

Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter in the attack, the Ukrainian leader said.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

Sponsor Message

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.

Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.

Libyan officials say two sea drones hit Russian warship

Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.

At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.

toggle caption i Security Service of Ukraine/via AP

The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.

Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.

Russian cargo ship was sanctioned, Ukraine says

Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose corvette Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.

Sponsor Message

The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.

A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.

Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.

"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

World.title: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
World.content:
Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety

toggle caption i Jimena Peck for NPR

EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.

Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.

"I just get in and go," Spalding says.

For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.

"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.

Sponsor Message

The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.

Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.

That was, until she saw what it could do.

"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."

toggle caption i Jimena Peck for NPR

There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.

"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.

It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.

Sponsor Message

Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.

Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.

"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."

Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.

toggle caption i Jimena Peck for NPR

"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."

Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.

"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."

If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.

The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.

"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.

Sponsor Message

But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.

"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."

Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.

toggle caption i Jimena Peck for NPR

The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.

In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.

"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."

Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.

"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.

Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.

"I feel safer riding with this auto system than I do driving or riding with anybody. It's just been flawless," Dimmock said. "I'll get in the car and go somewhere, otherwise, I probably wouldn't."

toggle caption i Jimena Peck for NPR

For Joan Spalding in Colorado, it's more than just a question of convenience. She says FSD is allowing her to live independently in the house that she and her late husband built more than 50 years ago.

Sponsor Message

"I love the solitude of being in that place and being by myself," she said.

Without the mobility that FSD gives her, Spalding said, she would likely have to find another place to live where she wouldn't need to drive.

"I'd have to move," she said. "This way, I think I can drive it for as long as I want to. I don't see any reason why not."

World.title: K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
World.content:
K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it

toggle caption i Sesame Workshop

Parents and caregivers of young children worry the world has become less kind, and they now value empathy in their children over good manners, compassion over confidence.

Those are just a few highlights from a new survey of families' views on kindness from Sesame Workshop, the education nonprofit behind Sesame Street.

"Caregivers see the world as much more unkind to their young children than they did in 2016," says Kim Foulds, vice president of research and evaluation at Sesame Workshop, "but the reason to hope is that parents see their children as more kind, more empathetic, more resilient than they did in 2016."

Sponsor Message

The new "K is for Kind Study 2026" comes 10 years after the original "K is for Kind: A National Survey on Kindness and Kids," and it offers a remarkable glimpse at how families' feelings about kindness have shifted, in some cases dramatically, over a decade defined by the rise of social media and bitter political polarization.

Monday's release also coincides with the debut of Sesame Street's 57th season, which will focus on kindness and compassion in action.

Let's start with that bad news: Compared to survey results from 2016, caregivers today have a much darker view of the world:



About 80% often worry the world is an unkind place for children. That's a nearly 11-percentage-point increase since 2016;

Fifty-four percent say kindness is not a priority for most people, a 10-point increase since 2016; and

On a scale of 1 to 5, caregivers give the average American a 2.8 for kindness.

Taken together, the data shows a worrying shift in the way families perceive the world — as a place with more rough edges that is less attuned to the needs of their young children. To draw these conclusions, Sesame Workshop conducted 2,080 interviews in October with a nationally representative sample of caregivers of children ages 3-8 years old across all 50 states.

Sponsor Message

The good news, Foulds says, is that, while caregivers "are concerned about the division and unkindness they see in the wider world, their experience of their own children is much more immediate and hopeful."

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

This manifests in a few key ways. First, in parents' own values for their children:

Caregivers say they value their child being considerate (68%) over being smart (32%);

They value compassion (56%) over confidence (44%), a big swing of 8 percentage points compared to when the same question was asked in the 2016 survey; and

They value empathy (64%) over manners (36%) — an even bigger swing of 24 points compared to a decade ago.



In short, parents and caregivers say their values are shifting toward kindness. That shift, in turn, is showing up in the behaviors families say they're seeing from their kids.

A whopping 92% of caregivers rate their child highly for kindness, a 5-percentage point increase since 2016;

Some 74% of caregivers rate their child highly for resilience, a 12-point increase;

And 56% gave their child a low anxiety rating, an 8-point improvement over 2016.

And that leads to what Foulds says was one of the most startling — and hopeful — results from the survey: 94% of caregivers said, when their child does something kind, they do it on their own, without encouragement or nudging.

"The child was seeing the opportunity to be kind themselves," Foulds says. "And I thought that was an incredibly beautiful, incredibly powerful finding to see how kindness is showing up in action in young children's lives."

These encouraging numbers come with one grain of salt: It's not unusual for caregivers to have a rosier view of their own children or their own local circumstances than of the wider world. In fact, this is a common phenomenon in education research, for example, where families often give America's schools low marks but high marks to their child's school and their child's teacher.

Sponsor Message

While this phenomenon likely influenced today's results, too, Sesame's twin surveys still offer a remarkable view of how caregivers' own views have shifted over the past decade.

What is kindness? The survey offers answers there, too. Caregivers talk about their children sharing in a way that requires them to give something up, connecting across languages and culture, making room for different abilities and including children who have been left out.

The survey also includes caregiver testimonials.

The parent of a 4-year-old told researchers, "He has a child in his class that is neurodivergent, which is different than him, and he is always helpful, always kind, always says 'Hi' whenever he sees this child for class and tries to be a good friend."

The parent of a 6-year-old told researchers, "My child was friends with an autistic child who is nonverbal. My child figured out a way to communicate with him, even though he could not express himself with words."

In the new survey, 85% of caregivers say it's "extremely important" to promote kindness, which is what Sesame Street's latest season will do when it debuts today on both Netflix and PBS KIDS.

"Each story really focuses on kindness, compassion, big feelings, and it's really designed to inspire children to carry the lessons beyond the screen," Foulds says. "We want the viewing to be the beginning of something, not the beginning and end."

In one scene from the new season, Muppets Elmo and Abby realize their choices have made a playmate feel left out and alone. They feel badly and decide to comfort and include him.

As one of the show's grown-ups reminds them, "One little help is all it takes."

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

World.title: Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year
World.content:
Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year

toggle caption i Apu Gomes/AFP via Getty Images

If you're planning to cook this Thanksgiving, you might not be so thankful for higher food prices.

Grocery costs have risen nearly 22% over the past five years, according to federal data. Wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Trump administration's tariffs and severe weather across the globe have pushed up the price of food.

Still, food-price experts say it's unclear whether you'll be spending more dough this Turkey Day — and, if so, by how much.

The American Farm Bureau Federation estimates that the cost of Thanksgiving will be up more than 6% compared with last year, with staples like cranberries and dinner rolls boosting the overall cost.

The Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute found that drinks like sparkling water and wine have become more expensive but that the average Thanksgiving food bill will come in a little cheaper than last year, due in part to sales and promotions.

Sponsor Message

"But you have to be very disciplined," said Wells Fargo chief agricultural economist Michael Swanson. "You get the turkey at a great price, but then you might throw a bunch of stuff in the cart you didn't look at that carefully and find out you spent more money than you intended to."

Financial worries have pushed some people to shake up their Thanksgiving celebrations. In a recent survey by the website LendingTree, 53% of respondents said inflation was affecting their holiday plans or how much they expected to spend on the meal.

"They're doing everything from changing their food choices to couponing more and even cutting back on guests," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree.

The survey also observed a drop in the percentage of people who said they might host Thanksgiving this year: 51% expect to have company over, down from 59% last year.

Shoppers say they still want to celebrate Thanksgiving, despite the price of groceries.

"It's too high," said Philadelphia resident Andre Andrews, who is retired. "Things are high, so much higher." Nevertheless, Andrews said he plans to smoke a turkey and a roast for the holiday, even though they cost him more than previously. "I can tell you this: I know it was more than it was last year," he said.

Schulz of LendingTree said those cooking on Thanksgiving can save money by sticking to a budget, shopping around for the best price and paring down the menu.

Sponsor Message

"Nobody wants to cut back on something as meaningful as a gathering of family and friends on Thanksgiving because it costs too much," he said, "but that's what a lot of people are facing right now."

World.title: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
World.content:
Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?

Maria Fabrizio for NPR

Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.

"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."

Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.

"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."

Sponsor Message

Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.

"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."

The claim

Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.

For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.

And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.

The evidence

Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.

Sponsor Message

Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."

Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."

Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.

In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.

"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.

Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.

Sponsor Message

"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."

Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.

Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."

The bottom line

In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.

And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."

Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.

"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

World.title: Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.
World.content:
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.

toggle caption i John Minchillo/AP

The death of Fiona, a beloved hippopotamus who captured hearts, has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.

Fiona, 9 years old, died Thursday after ingesting a hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo. The zoo said that the hat was lodged in the hippo's small intestine and surgery was not possible.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a statement .

While deaths are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall, and sometimes are tossed, into animal enclosures.

Sponsor Message

In 2024, 70 U.S. coins were successfully removed from an alligator at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium. And in 2025, a Komodo dragon ate a shoe that was thrown into its habitat at the Memphis Zoo. The shoe was removed and the dragon survived.

Dr. Gabriella Flacke, an associate veterinarian at Zoo Miami, said the zoo's staff have retrieved items such as cellphones from alligators.

"We've had to remove those items both endoscopically, which is basically putting a camera through the mouth and down into the stomach to grab and retrieve those items, or we've in a few cases had to do surgery where they were larger items that couldn't be removed that way," Flacke told NPR.

toggle caption i John Minchillo/AP

Recovering items from an alligator is easier than a hippo, she said. Unlike the alligator, which has a digestive system with one stomach divided into two parts, hippos have a multichambered stomach. This can make retrieving objects, such as the small hat that Fiona ingested, difficult, according to Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.

"It's not necessarily always the shape or size of the object, but it's maybe the twists and turns, metaphorically and physiologically, that things have to go through," Quammen told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Be aware that the animals have specialized dietary needs and requirements that caretakers provide them, Flacke said. She also asked visitors to follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.

"Anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head if you're leaning over and looking at something," she said. "If your child has a toy in its hand and you're walking around, it could just decide to throw the toy, whether it's thinking about that or not."

It's not just dangerous for zoo animals

Both Quammen and Flacke said people should not only be mindful of items that can harm animals at the zoo, but also what could hurt animals in the wild or pets at home.

Animals explore the world by putting things in their mouths, making them naturally curious about items that can be dangerous, Quammen said.

toggle caption i Frank Augstein/AP

To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.

"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen.

World.title: What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse
World.content:
What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse

After two weeks of negotiations, international climate talks fail to reach an agreement. NPR's Rachel Waldholz was in Turkey for the conference.

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended today after negotiations fell apart. NPR's Rachel Waldholz has been at the conference and sent us this report.

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: I'm here in the Antalya Expo Center, which, for the past two weeks, has been packed with some 70,000 people who came to the COP31 climate conference. Now it's almost completely empty. In fact, they're disassembling parts of the venue around me. The climate talks ran two days past their scheduled end. By the time the gavel fell, many negotiators had already left to catch their flights home. Australia climate chief Chris Bowen led the negotiations.

CHRIS BOWEN: I haven't slept for the last three nights, been negotiating all the way through, but more importantly, people on delegations came at it and gave it everything they had.

WALDHOLZ: Delegates came to Antalya with long wish lists, from electrifying more of the global economy to money for developing countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change. Looming over it all is that this is the first summit to squarely face the reality that the planet will miss a key target of the Paris Climate Agreement, reaching warming of 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above pre-Industrial levels. The U.N. says limiting that overshoot requires cutting the use of fossil fuels nearly in half in the next 10 to 15 years. Many countries wanted an agreement explicitly calling for a transition away from coal, oil and natural gas. But big oil-producing countries, like Saudi Arabia, blocked any mention of fossil fuels. Ultimately, the European Union decided no deal was better than the deal on the table. Darragh O'Brien is Ireland's environment minister.

DARRAGH O'BRIEN: We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.

WALDHOLZ: Many negotiators left the expo center dragging their suitcases on the way to the airport. They'll pick up negotiations next year at the next climate summit in Ethiopia. I'm Rachel Waldholz in Antalya, Turkey.

(SOUNDBITE OF SOFTLY'S "FLORA")
