World.title: Canadians fed up with long hold times want telcos to answer calls within 10 minutes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Frank Brown spent almost an hour on hold with Rogers last June, while simultaneously trying to get help through the company's online chat.

The Aurora, Ont., man was trying to find out why a $25 charge had appeared on his mother's account, which he manages.

After more than 40 minutes, he says he gave up on the chat because it wasn't helping. He soon abandoned the call, too.

Two days later, he tried calling Rogers again. This time he couldn't even get into the queue. A recorded message told him the system was overloaded and too busy to take his call.

"It isn't customer service if you can't talk to anybody," Brown said.

"Access to a human representative should not be treated as an additional premium service."

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

For the last few months, Brown's been on a mission to get the federal government to take the issue seriously, launching a petition urging Ottawa to force telecom providers to connect with a human agent within 10 minutes.

"There is no measurable customer service standard in this industry," said Brown. "We need to make sure consumers are protected."

WATCH | The man behind the 10-minute petition: This man started a petition to force telcos to answer customer calls within 10 minutes | Go Public | Duration closed caption 2:09 An Ontario man has started a parliamentary petition calling on the government to implement a law that would require telecommunication companies to answer phone calls with a human agent within 10 minutes.

Brown isn't alone in his frustration.

Long wait times, dropped calls, unhelpful agents and automated systems have sent customers in circles — frustrations Go Public and CBC Marketplace have documented across the country.

Complaints to the Commission for Complaints for Telecom-television Services (CCTS) were up 79 per cent in 2025-2026 over the previous year — ranging from billing and contract disputes to cancellation issues — but the telecom mediator has no mandate to specifically address customer service complaints, such as long wait times. That leaves customers with no independent avenue to complain about the very service they're struggling to access.

And customer service has deteriorated dramatically, according to Mohammed Halabi, whose company MyBillsAreHigh.com helps businesses and individuals save money on telecom and internet costs.

"They've got to be held to account somehow," Halabi said. "The government has to do something."

Mohammed Halabi helps telco customers lower their bills. He says customer service has become 'absolutely horrible' over the last two years. (Michael Cole/CBC)

Go Public asked Rogers, Bell and Telus how they respond to calls for a mandatory 10-minute standard for answering customer calls.

Rogers declined an interview. A spokesperson sent a written statement saying the average wait time to reach a customer service representative was "around 7 minutes" this year — that figure does not include people on hold who give up after not getting through, like Brown. Rogers said a "very small percentage" of callers hang up before reaching a customer service rep and that the company is continuing to improve "the customer experience."

Telus and Bell both wrote that the "vast majority" of customer calls are answered within minutes.

Neither would specify what percentage of callers hang up after failing to reach a human agent — like Rogers, those customers are not included in their wait-time averages.

A growing chorus of complaints

After Brown filed a complaint with the CCTS, Rogers credited the $25 charge to his mother's account in July, calling it a "goodwill gesture." The company told Go Public it understood Brown had a "frustrating experience."

Since then, he's had to make several more calls to his telecom provider about other issues. Rogers says on average, Brown spent about four minutes getting routed to a customer service rep — but he says his concerns stand.

He initially launched a petition on Change.org, a petition platform, asking Canadians to support his call for better response times. So far, over 1,200 have signed.

Some have left comments describing two-hour waits, calling the delays "disgusting" and saying they felt "held hostage" on the phone.

Frank Brown spent nearly an hour on hold trying to resolve an issue with his mother's bill. (Submitted by Frank Brown)

Go Public has also received plenty of complaints from customers. Most emails are about Rogers, but some customers have also described difficulties getting through to Bell and Telus.

"It should not be this hard [to close an account]," wrote one person. "What in the world is going on with this company?"

"We have documented 18 separate call attempts totalling over 10.5 hours attempting to resolve this issue," wrote another.

"They keep laying people off, but cannot answer their phone," wrote another.

Customer service 'absolutely horrible'

Halabi says telecom customer service has become "absolutely horrible" over the last two years.

During that time, all three major telcos have laid off or offered buyouts to segments of their Canadian workforces. According to Unifor telecommunications director Roch LeBlanc, roughly 20,000 telecommunications jobs have been lost due to automation and offshoring in the last 10 to 15 years.

"It's just gotten so bad," Halabi said. "It's a constant circus."

He also believes telecom companies are increasingly trying to push artificial intelligence over the use of human agents — technology that can frustrate customers when it misunderstands what callers are saying or directs them to the wrong department.

"All of this is creating a sense of anxiety, especially for senior citizens."

Spain's new 3-minute law

Before retiring two years ago, Brown spent eight years as president of a company that employed dozens of people. For years, he says, he personally responded to every consumer review because he wanted customers to know "the person at the top" cared about their business.

"I hate the hypocrisy of Rogers courting me on TV — as if me giving them my business is very much appreciated — and then hearing ‘your call is important to us' while waiting forever for them to answer the phone," he told Go Public.

Brown believes telecom companies should be held to a measurable customer-service standard, as is the case in Spain.

Spain passed legislation last December requiring companies with more than 250 employees to ensure that when customers request a human agent, they can reach one within three minutes in 95 per cent of cases.

"Three minutes is pretty aggressive," said Brown, which is why he thought a 10-minute standard would be a reasonable starting point here.

"It's the Canadian way, we're nice people."

WATCH | Why telecom complaints are on the rise: Telecom complaints soar as Canadians rail over billing issues | Duration closed caption 2:02 Canada’s telecom watchdog says complaints about cellphone, internet and television services shot up by 17 per cent from 2024 to 2025, with the chief gripe being about unclear or incorrect billing.

Hoping to get action from the federal government, Brown also launched a parliamentary petition , which would compel a written response from the government should it reach 500 signatures by Nov. 26. As of Nov. 19, it was sitting at 425 signatures.

The petition calls on the federal government to direct the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to establish "clear, measurable and enforceable" customer service standards for telecommunications providers.

Specifically, it calls for a "maximum 10-minute telephone hold time" for customers seeking access to a human agent and requests "meaningful and proportional consequences" for providers that persistently fail to meet that standard.

"There is no measurable customer service standard in this industry," said Brown. "As long as we're going to limit competition in the industry, we need to make sure that us consumers are protected."

Brown is also scheduled to discuss his petitions when he appears before the CRTC next week, as it begins hearings on protections for home phone, wireless, TV and internet consumers.

"There's a real feeling that we just have to accept [bad customer service]," he said. "And I decided, no, I'm going to try and do something about it."

World.title: 'Unprecedented': Why this round of Stellantis, Unifor contract talks is like no other
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Back in the spring, Unifor Local 444 president James Stewart warned that this year's contract talks with global carmaker Stellantis would be the toughest round of bargaining ever in the powerful union's long history — even worse than during the 2008 financial crisis.

"I think any other round of negotiations is easy compared to what we're facing now," the Canadian union leader said in late May. "I think this is a much worse position for longevity and making sure we're around long term."

So far, Stewart seems to have been right.

The September deadline for the union's contract passed eight weeks ago without much fanfare.

The more than 6,000 workers Stewart represents at the Stellantis assembly plant in Windsor, Ont., have been repeatedly laid off , as have parts suppliers, with the automaker citing tariffs and lower consumer demand. Contract talks were stalled over Stellantis's plan to sell its plant in Brampton to a defence contractor.

The idled Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant in Ontario is seen on Aug. 19. (REUTERS/Carlos Osorio)

On top of all that, the provincial and federal governments are now involved, trying to make sure that plant has a future building cars — a future they say would help fuel the economy by keeping thousands of people there employed, in addition to the vast supply chain that supports the facility.

"I've been here 30 years — I've never been through a contract negotiation like this," Jeff Edward, an autoworker at the Windsor plant, said recently.

The path forward, for now, seems unclear, with the future of Stellantis's roughly 10,000 employees in Canada — and maybe the future of the industry itself — hanging in the balance.

"This is unique and I would use the word anomalous, like it's an anomaly, and not so much that the union is doing something that's anomalous," said Herman Rosenfeld, a retired Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) staffer who worked in the education department for over a dozen years.

"They're facing a situation which is, if you look at the industry itself in Canada, it's in trouble in lots of ways."

'Unusual' that 'multiple players' involved in talks

Rosenfeld and others identify a common undercurrent today: A man in Washington with an oft-criticized and increasingly unpopular plan to revive American manufacturing by punishing a longtime trade partner he claims has taken advantage of the U.S.

"We don't want this Stellantis plant to be the first plant to close as a result of the disruption created by Donald Trump," says Ken Lewenza, who led the CAW for years before it merged with the Communications, Energy and Paperworkers Union of Canada to form Unifor in 2013.

Ken Lewenza, former president of the Canadian Auto Workers, is shown at his home in Windsor on Nov. 17. 'We don't want this Stellantis plant to be the first plant to close as a result of the disruption created by Donald Trump,' he says. (Emma Loop/CBC)

Lewenza said the current negotiations are "unprecedented," in large part because they involve an existential battle, rather than the typical fight over benefits and wages.

"The reality is there's multiple players involved in these negotiations, which by itself is unusual," he said. "But what we're trying to do is preserve as many jobs as we can in Canada. We're actually trying to preserve the manufacturing footprint of auto plants in Canada [that are] manufacturing vehicles."

Stellantis has cited the trade war as a key driver in its decision to sell Brampton. Another element to consider is the North American industry's retreat from electric vehicles (EVs) that has been fuelled in part by Trump's rollback of green energy initiatives.

A Stellantis employee works on an internal combustion engine at the company's assembly plant in Windsor on May 28. (Ken Amlin/CBC)

Before Stellantis halted retooling on the plant last year, the plan was for the Brampton plant — like the one in Windsor — to be upgraded to support both electric and gas-powered vehicle production.

Stellantis has received at least $220 million in federal funding for the upgrades to its Ontario facilities, as CBC Windsor first reported last year . The automaker has offered to repay $24 million it says it received for Brampton specifically. But Ottawa has said the company breached the funding agreement by closing and seeking to sell the plant, and is on the hook for "hundreds of millions."

Stewart and Unifor did not respond to interview requests for this story. But in a public update Wednesday night, the union said Stellantis has presented its first closure agreement for the Brampton members. The union also reiterated its opposition to the sale, though it continues to say it wants to try to avoid a strike.

Stellantis, in a statement to CBC Windsor, said it is "engaged in discussions with Unifor."

Workers at the Windsor Stellantis plant, shown on May 28, continue to work under the terms of the previous collective agreement until a new pact is in place. (Ken Amlin/CBC)

Beyond Brampton, the union has said it needs firmer production allotments to secure employment in Windsor and at the company's casting plant in Etobicoke in suburban Toronto.

For now, members at those facilities continue to work under the terms of the previous collective agreement. Stellantis said that contract "continues until the union ratifies a new agreement."

Premier, union head urge Ottawa to take action

On Friday, Stellantis's global CEO Antonio Filosa spoke with federal, provincial and union representatives to discuss the Brampton situation.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said after the meeting that Stellantis, a multinational facing financial challenges, identified penalties for Canada's greenhouse gas emissions as a major cost to doing business — in addition to tariffs and zero-emissions vehicle rules in Quebec and British Columbia.

Stellantis also released a statement, saying, "The future of our Canadian operations and our employees remained the focus of today’s second meeting with representatives of the Canadian and Ontario governments and Unifor. We remain committed to continuing constructive discussions."

Ford is urging the federal government to take action, as is Unifor national president Lana Payne.

Payne said Stellantis was "unwavering" in its decision to sell the plant at the start of the discussion.

"And then we talked more about proposals and eventually getting ourselves to a different place, what has to be done here to change this outcome."

Filosa, Ford said, is sending his "right-hand man" to Ontario early next week, and that the parties will keep talking.

World.title: Spying on survivors: Why RCMP watched Wab Kinew's father in the 1960s
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Inside the Manitoba premier's office, Wab Kinew unravels a state secret.

With a mix of wry amusement and serious concern, he flips through censored copies of the RCMP's historic surveillance dossiers, each one marked in pen as "racial intelligence," compiled on Indigenous organizations from the 1960s to the 1980s.

What he learns he calls damning and alarming: the Canadian government spied on his father, the late Anishinaabe leader Tobasonakwut Kinew, in a countrywide infiltration initiative later dubbed the "Native extremism program."

"Finding out that there was surveillance by law enforcement, by national security, for what today we would consider very routine political organizing and activism, it shows you, I would say, the racism of the time," the premier told CBC News in October.

At home in Orillia, Ont., Wab Kinew's uncle Fred Kelly untangles the same tale of espionage and deceit. He too was spied on for lawful democratic activism in the '60s, though it's hardly a surprise. He strongly suspected it.

"I had no actual proof that I was being spied upon, but I knew it," said Kelly, also known as Kiizhebowse Makwa, a distinguished Anishinaabe elder, spiritual leader and former grand chief of Grand Council Treaty #3 in northwestern Ontario.

WATCH | Fred Kelly reacts to being spied on by the RCMP: Anishinaabe elder gets proof of long-suspected RCMP spying | Duration closed caption 1:10 Fred Kelly, who spent his life fighting for justice, peaceful coexistence and human rights, reacts to proof the RCMP placed him under surveillance and labelled him an "agitator" because of his peaceful political work.

CBC News provided these documents to the family for the first time during a years-long investigation into Canada's Cold War-era program to spy on Indigenous leaders and activists, which the RCMP created and which CSIS revived in the late 1980s.

The story of this one famous family reveals how many RCMP surveillance targets were residential school survivors who went on to lead legitimate political movements to reclaim their identity. To them, it's no shock the government that openly suppressed First Nations culture in residential schools also tried to suppress their newfound political voice.

As former national chief Georges Erasmus put it in an interview earlier this year, "It is just the next chapter of oppression."

From residential school to resistance

Tobasonakwut Kinew was about seven years old when he was taken to St. Mary’s Indian Residential School in Kenora in northwestern Ontario in the 1940s, where he experienced almost a decade of horrors.

Catholic priests and nuns tried to strip him of his culture by cutting his hair short, changing his name from Tobasonakwut to Peter Kelly and giving him a number, 54. He suffered psychological, physical and sexual abuse.�

Eight-year-old Tobasonakwut standing with his grandfather, Kaagagewannakweb, who came to visit him at St Mary's Residential School in Kenora, Ont., circa 1944-45. (Submitted by Diane Kelly)

Both as a CBC reporter and in his 2015 memoir, Wab Kinew candidly explored his father's residential school experience and how the resulting trauma nearly severed the ties that bind a family together.

"Look at my dad, he had the Indian agent deciding everything about his life in his early years, until he went to residential school when it was a boys' keeper and a priest … Then he left and it was back to the Indian Agent. And then this surveillance," Wab Kinew told CBC News.

"There's a longer history of government and corporate entities monitoring Indigenous families, assigning numbers, assigning qualitative evaluations of them, but seemingly not engaging with them as people."

Fred Kelly's experience was similar. He said he suffered physical and sexual abuse as well, and he too got the Irish surname Kelly at St. Mary’s, where he was taken at five years old.

"My impression of the residential school system was very much a system of incarceration to teach me and to force me to believe that my system, my original system of spirituality, was wrong," he said.

Fred Kelly (left) and Tobasonakwut Kinew (Peter Kelly) in their 20s in an undated photo taken in their community, Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation. (Submitted by Diane Kelly)

The 6,000 pages of formerly secret intelligence files gathered on First Nations leaders by the RCMP Security Service and obtained by CBC News under access to information law reveal another chapter in this story.

As the brothers joined a generation of Indigenous leaders getting organized politically, it was no longer priests and nuns giving them numbers but Mounties — giving them file numbers as perceived subversives.

Fred Kelly entered the national political spotlight in November 1965, when he organized a pivotal protest in Kenora against racial injustice, now hailed as the country's first civil rights march.

Newspapers called Kenora Canada's Alabama and compared the racial tensions to "Bloody Sunday" in Selma, where Alabama state troopers attacked peaceful Black civil rights marchers earlier in 1965.

"Our people did not do these kinds of things. Our people are rather stoic: If that's the way it is, that's what we've got to live with," Kelly recalled.

WATCH | The 1965 Kenora march: Indigenous people demand a better deal in Kenora, Ont. in 1965 | Duration 26:13 As 400 residents march on the streets, CBC Newsmagazine examines the lives of indigenous people in the northern Ontario town. Aired Dec. 7, 1965.

Town council mocked him, saying he'd be lucky if four people showed up. Instead between 400 and 500 Anishinaabeg filled Kenora's streets, marching in a silent and peaceful but proud show of dignity that still inspires First Nations leaders 60 years later.

"We were not looking for love," Kelly said.

"We were looking for justice and equality."

'Known agitators'

The premier's father and uncle, or the "Kelly brothers," soon gained celebrity and notoriety.

The Globe and Mail ran the headline "Indian brothers predict Kenora race riots" after a group of white men attacked them in 1967, and CBC flew them to Toronto to discuss the incident on national television.

The RCMP Security Service, a domestic intelligence agency that became CSIS in 1984, took notice, too. Amid the paranoia of the Cold War, Mounties feared radicals and communists could infiltrate and exploit the First Nations rights movement.

By 1969, Mounties had Winnipeg-based human sources informing on the brothers. One informer meticulously tracked Fred Kelly's movements and politics, depicting him as a potentially violent subversive.

"The source considers him to be a radical and somewhat dangerous person," an intelligence investigator reported.

In a separate report, a Mountie in Winnipeg reported both brothers "have been connected with the 'Red Power' movement." The RCMP labelled them as "known agitators" and tracked their movements across Canada.

Fred Kelly is unsurprised, but he still denounces these reports as "the wrong interpretation of what I was seeking." He draws parallels between how residential school officials carried out their mission and how Mounties did theirs.

"That was probably an order. How they carried that out is something that they have to live with," he said.

"But they did it in much the same way as those Catholic priests believed in what they were doing."

Diane Kelly, Wab Kinew's sister, was stunned and disappointed to see these references to her father and uncle.

"These are the things that we've always suspected, not just as a family, but as Indigenous people," said Diane Kelly, a former grand chief of Grand Council Treaty #3.

Diane Kelly says it's shocking and disappointing but not really surprising to see the contents of the declassified surveillance files. (Brett Forester/CBC)

In the 1970s, her father was helping bring back that grand council, laying the foundation for the resurgence of the very political body she later led, she said.

"How was that terrorism? How was that being an agitator? It's about having pride in who you are and knowing who you are," she said.

By 1971, the Security Service explicitly targeted the legitimate Indigenous movement, writing in a secret, urgent-marked report that "the activities of the National Indian Brotherhood," now the Assembly of First Nations, were "of special interest to us."

"As stressed in previous correspondence forwarded to all divisions, the organized activity of our Canadian Indians are of interest," the report said, calling it "most desirable" if the brotherhood's annual spring conference was infiltrated with "human source coverage."

Singled out as top targets were Fred Kelly and Tobasonakwut Kinew, or Peter Kelly. Their movement, in other words, was compromised.

Jeffrey Copenace, chief of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, where the brothers and premier are from, is outraged.

Chief of the Ojibways of Onigaming Jeff Copenace speaks to reporters following the First Nations Summit at the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Que., in July 2025. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

"These two men should be celebrated along with all of the other Treaty 3 and First Nation leaders that have been trying to attain human rights in Canada," he said.

"To think that these two men had their privacy infiltrated, that there's all kinds of documentation about them that they're not aware of that's just coming to light now, it's a bit sad. It's just a little bit heartbreaking."

In response to the rise of the American Indian Movement and arrival of Red Power activism, the RCMP Security Service intensified the surveillance and expanded the dragnet by formally establishing a full-time "Red Power desk" in Ottawa in 1973.

Here, intelligence officers tapped phones and paid informers to infiltrate groups like the National Indian Brotherhood and Dene Nation. The RCMP files name 150 Mounties involved, dozens of organizations monitored, and hundreds of individuals targeted.

"When you hear these actions, it's hard to believe that reconciliation is really a tangible thing in Canada," said Copenace.

What now?

At the Manitoba legislature, Wab Kinew has questions. First, naturally, is "who were these informants?" But that evolves into a call for all-around clarity.

"Was the RCMP paying people? Were people giving this information under duress?" he said.

"Does the way that this information enters the permanent record speak to whether it is credible or not? Were people being induced? Bribed?"

Using informers to infiltrate legitimate movements is far from harmless, said John Carlson, who is Anishinaabe from Red Rock Indian Band in northwestern Ontario and an associate professor of criminology at the University of Ottawa. He argues this countersubversion program had a chilling effect on political activism and free expression.

Associate professor John Carlson teaches his students at the University of Ottawa about the significance of the silent march in Kenora led by Fred Kelly in 1965. (Brett Forester/CBC News)

"That's the legacy. It's purging the movement of what the RCMP, I'm sure, would call subversive ideology and organizational practices," Carlson said.

"But I would call [those practices] relevant to fighting for a society where Indigenous dignity, self-determination and relations, responsibilities and values could also shape this society."

Ultimately Tobasonakwut Kinew and Fred Kelly became political and community leaders, leaving an indelible mark on Canadian history.

Fred Kelly was part of the team that negotiated the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement that led to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Tobasonakwut Kinew personally reconciled with Pope Benedict in 2009, presenting him with an eagle feather and ceremonial pipe. Both brothers were on Parliament Hill in 2008 to witness prime minister Stephen Harper's historic apology for the residential school system.

Tobasonakwut Kinew (Peter Kelly) holds the Assembly of First Nations ceremonial staff on his way to a news conference after Pope Benedict's general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, April 29, 2009. (Pier Paolo Cito/The Associated Press)

As for the spying, RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme issued a statement of regret after CBC News revealed the program's existence in May 2026, but the Assembly of First Nations continues to seek a full apology, access to uncensored files and answers.

Public Safety Minister Gary's Anandasangaree office said in September that he is working with relevant federal departments to support the release of those documents.

For Wab Kinew, the files confirm Canada's intelligence service of the 1960s "was racist," but he believes those organizations today have a more progressive and egalitarian view. On that front, Manitoba's first Anishinaabe premier finds a silver lining in his relationship with the RCMP today.

Mounties still follow him around the country, as they did his father. It's just no longer the secret spy branch. It's the executive protection unit.

World.title: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine was behind attack that sank Russian warship off Libya
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind an attack on a Russian warship off Libya on Sunday, claiming Ukrainian naval drones sank the vessel.

Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X that Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones in the operation, which sank a Russian corvette. The Ukrainian leader described the ship as one of Russia's newest vessels commissioned in 2023 during the invasion.

"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons. He added that a Ka-27 military helicopter was destroyed in the attack.

Zelenskyy thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, and other Ukrainian defense forces that took part in what he described as "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."

Zelenskyy said he received detailed briefings on Sunday and Monday and that "the targets we set were achieved."

The strike by sea drones severely damaged the Russian navy corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw fire at the base early Sunday. Civil defence rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

World.title: More Canadians are using cannabis daily than are drinking alcohol daily: study
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Daily use of cannabis has outstripped daily use of alcohol in Canada, according to a new study, with young Canadians as the main driver — signalling a shift in our habits that experts say has far-reaching implications.

A study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) analyzed survey data from nearly 100,000 Canadians and found that 5.7 per cent of people — roughly 1.8 million Canadians — reported using cannabis every day or nearly every day, compared to 5.2 per cent who reported daily or near daily alcohol use.

Only Canadians over 50 still reported higher rates of daily alcohol use compared to daily cannabis use.

"What we're kind of seeing is this generational shift between these different substances," said André McDonald, a postdoctoral fellow at the Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research at McMaster University in Hamilton and lead author of the study.

"Historically, a lot of public health has focused on cigarette use and alcohol use. But these findings are kind of suggesting that we have to take daily cannabis use pretty seriously."

Researchers looked at the nationally representative 2023 to 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey to measure patterns of daily use of alcohol, cigarettes and cannabis.

When taking all age groups into consideration, the daily rate of cigarette use was the highest of the three at 8.5 per cent. But among adults younger than 35 years old, daily cannabis use was not only higher than daily alcohol use, but also higher than daily cigarette use.

Men aged 25-34 had the highest rate of daily cannabis use of any age group, at nearly 11 per cent. The percentage of women aged 18-24 who reported daily cannabis use was more than 17 times higher than the percentage that reported daily alcohol use.

It's part of an apparent cultural shift that extends beyond Canada. In the U.S., where many states now permit legal or medicinal cannabis, studies have shown that cannabis is outpacing alcohol as the daily drug of choice, with one 2024 study finding that 17.7 million people used cannabis daily or near-daily in the U.S. compared to 14.7 million daily or near-daily drinkers.

A person walks by a cannabis dispensary on Queen Street in Toronto. Among Canadians under 35, the number reporting they used cannabis every day was higher than those reporting they smoked cigarettes or drank alcohol every day. (Cole Burston/The Canadian Press)

Public messaging needs to keep up by apprising Canadians of the risks that come with heavy use, McDonald said.

"If, [for] the younger generations, this is becoming their preference, we could see this becoming a long-term trend," McDonald said. "It's very possible that … as they become older, these patterns are going to become middle-aged patterns."

Researchers noted that the study is limited by its use of self-reported data and the fact that the survey didn't look at how many times a day Canadians were using these substances if they reported daily use. It also did not include vaping.

Positive signs in drop of daily alcohol, tobacco

Does this study mean more and more Canadians are lighting up a joint every day as time goes on? Not necessarily — the survey is a snapshot of habits in 2023-2024, meaning the data doesn't show exactly when daily cannabis use overtook daily alcohol use.

About 41 per cent of those who reported daily or near daily cannabis use in the study said they started using cannabis daily after legalization in 2018.

"For cannabis, we saw a bump in the first year or two after legalization and then it's actually flattened — so it's a question of alcohol and smoking tobacco coming down more so than cannabis going up," said David Hammond, a professor in the School of Public Health Sciences at the University of Waterloo, who studies tobacco and cannabis harm reduction and was not involved in the study.

In Canada, the smoking of cigarettes has been declining for decades due to public health campaigning to highlight the serious cancer and health risks. Drinking has also been going down , with recent studies and polls highlighting that younger generations are drinking less than previous generations.

WATCH | 2025 report looked at alcohol consumption drop in B.C.: New report shows British Columbians are drinking less alcohol | Duration closed caption 2:57 A new report shows British Columbians seem to be drinking less alcohol than they have in 20 years. And Statistics Canada data is showing declining alcohol sales across Canada. Our medical columnist, Dr. Melissa Lem, is someone who might be happy to hear this news.

The shift has some positive indications for public health in Canada.

Broadly speaking, daily cannabis use isn't associated with nearly as many negative health outcomes as daily alcohol and cigarette use is, Hammond said, and certainly not the "same levels of mortality."

"About half of all long-term tobacco smokers will die, and alcohol has a range of direct health effects [including] impaired driving and social disorders, so it's actually not much of a competition. Alcohol and tobacco take the trophy in terms of the biggest harms among Canadians."

But while cannabis is seen as a much safer drug in general, health experts caution that the occasional partaking of cannabis products is very different from heavy use — and that there are risks.

The dangers of overuse of cannabis

We don't have as much research on the long-term impacts of cannabis compared to alcohol and cigarettes. But there's strong evidence that too much cannabis use, particularly among young people, can lead to addiction and have serious mental health implications, said Romina Mizrahi, a psychiatrist and director of the McGill Research Centre for Cannabis in Montreal.

For those over 25, the concerns with daily use are largely "changes in their mood and their motivation," she told CBC News.

But for those in their teens and early twenties, overuse of cannabis can increase their risk of psychosis , something Mizrahi said most patients aren't aware of. The risk grows when more potent, high-THC cannabis products are involved.

Apart from age, the study found that income was also connected to high rates of daily cannabis use.

WATCH | Researchers say high-potency THC needs more studying: As high-potency THC demand grows, experts call for more research on cannabis compounds | Duration closed caption 3:10 Experts are warning of the serious health risks of high-potency THC. And a psychiatry professor at Dalhousie University says better education on cannabis compounds can help consumers make informed choices when purchasing cannabis products. As Max Baco reports, THC is only part of the story.

The less money Canadians made, the more likely they were to report daily cannabis use, while Canadians in the highest income bracket (making more than $150,000 per year) reported the lowest rates of daily cannabis use.

Other groups that reported high rates of daily cannabis use included transgender and gender-diverse Canadians, as well as people with mood or anxiety disorders.

Those experiencing the stress that comes with marginalization or income pressures may be more likely to lean on cannabis to deal with it, McDonald said.

But with overuse, what can start out as a treatment for anxiety can end up perpetuating or exacerbating it, Mizrahi said.

"People tend to start using because they feel it can help them with their anxiety and even their mood sometimes. And what happens is when it becomes a regular use, then their anxiety levels start to creep up, and the same with depression and mood symptoms."

The rotating set of health warnings on cannabis products intended for smoking does include a warning that "cannabis can cause psychotic symptoms like severe paranoia," and that this risk is greater in those younger than 25.

But experts say that as Canadians' habits shift, we may need stronger visual warnings, like those on cigarette packaging, and more awareness so that Canadians can make informed choices.

WATCH | Does cannabis play a role in psychosis rates going up?: Researchers suggest link between cannabis use and rise in psychotic disorder diagnoses | Duration closed caption 2:05 New research published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal suggested a sharp rise in the rate of psychotic disorder diagnoses in young people over a nearly 50-year period and researchers suggest cannabis use may play a role.

"The more we talk about this, especially for young people, the more they're going to be aware of it, and maybe they are going to reduce their use," Mizrahi said.

"Daily use is a problem. Daily use is a problem for alcohol, daily use is a problem for tobacco, obviously, and it is a problem for cannabis."

World.title: A gold mine has created a 'little town' in central Newfoundland — and it's about to get bigger
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There's a new town in central Newfoundland and most people don't even know it exists.

It's not incorporated and doesn't have an official name, but its population is greater than that of all the closest communities combined.

This is the Valentine gold mine — the largest in Atlantic Canada — where thousands of people live and work.

"We're very much a little town here. Currently, we're about a thousand employees at the site at one time," said Jason Cyr, the VP of Canadian operations for mine owner Equinox Gold.

"So think about that, it's actually 2,000 because it's ... two weeks on and two weeks off."

The town with no name is driving a big part of the economy in the region, and it's going to get bigger.

Phase 2 construction starts in the new year, and it's expected to bring more long-term jobs in a region that's desperate for them.

The mine is undergoing a $436-million expansion and increasing gold production by about 25 per cent, Cyr said.

Jason Cyr is the manager of Canadian operations for Equinox Gold. (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)

It takes about three hours to reach the Valentine site once you turn off the Trans Canada Highway toward Buchans.

Most of that is over dirt roads, which become a river of mud when it rains and a whirlwind of dust when it doesn't. One section is so twisty, employees call it The Snake.

It's so tough to access, the company has supplied everything workers might need, from a gym to a recreation centre, to a cafeteria that provides 20 different sandwich options every day.

The site even has its own clinic, complete with paramedics and an ambulance.

At the rim of the Leprechaun pit, one of three the company works, giant dump trucks look like dinky cars, far far below. Gray rock covers the land like the surface of the moon.

'Liberate' the gold

This is where the gold journey begins, Cyr says.

"We drill and blast what you've seen out in the open pit. That gets trucked over to the crusher. We crush it from roughly 16 inches down to 4-6 inches in diameter. It goes into a storage stockpile, which then feeds a mill for further pulverization and liberation of the gold particle. Then it goes on to leaching, and then it's refined right here on site to a bar of 85-88 per cent purity," he explained.

From there, he says, Brinks picks up the refined gold and carries it out of the province where it's purified and then made into jewelry and coins.

The crusher at the Valentine gold mine pulverizes the raw ore. (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)

The whole vast operation is run from a control room, operated by Kyle Park.

"If this plant was a body, I'd be the brain," he said. "We control everything from this room, front to back, and try to recover as much gold as we can. Basically, we want to take the rock that comes in from the crusher and begin to turn it into a slurry so we can transport it throughout the system and recover as much as we can. Liberate some gold."

But not everybody is allowed to liberate the gold, Cyr says. Security is tight and background checks are completed, among other measures.

Workers coming home

Cyr says one of the things Equinox is most proud of is its commitment to local hiring. About 94 per cent of employees at the mine are from this province, including Shannon Parsons.

"This is my fifth mine now," he said. "I've worked all over Canada, in Ontario and Nunavut, but it's nice to be back home again. There's a lot of talent that worked out of province, same as myself. So people are looking for the opportunity to come home again."

And Cyr says the jobs people on site do are often very different from what outsiders might imagine.

"I like the vast skill set that mining brings. It's not just what you'd think growing up ... that there's pickaxes and such," he said. "It's the technology. It's the different skill sets from instrumentation to environment, health and safety, accounting, HR, mining, milling, electrical, mechanical. There's a lot of talent all on one site."

The company offers specific training on its equipment for those who are newer to mining. Mike Hann runs a state-of-the-art equipment simulator.

"We're set up to actually allow people to get control familiarization before they actually hit the field," he said. "So anybody who don't have prior experience, they can get used to the controls, which allows them to get comfortable, allows them to get a lot more efficient."

This is a win-win, he explained, as it's safer for the employees and there's less damage on the equipment due to inexperience.

Amanda Jacobs is a second-generation excavator operator who now trains new employees.

"I always liked equipment," she said. "Dad actually worked with Abitibi [paper company] in here, building roads and stuff. He was on an excavator and that got me interested in it, I guess."

A conveyor belt carries the crushed ore into the milling plant at the Valentine gold mine. (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)

And while workers on site make good, dependable salaries, they're not the only ones who benefit from Valentine, Cyr says.

He highlighted the use of local contractors and suppliers for the company's needs — from catering to T-shirts.

"So yeah, there's a lot of spinoff from this little asset we're sitting on here today," he said.

World.title: Montreal Canadiens acquire centre Dylan Larkin from Red Wings in blockbuster trade
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadiens fans serenaded Dylan Larkin with chants of "We Want Larkin !" last month.

On Sunday, they got their wish.

Montreal acquired the 30-year-old centre from the Red Wings in a blockbuster deal, ending a drawn-out saga that began when Detroit's former captain requested a trade in the off-season.

In return, the Canadiens sent the Red Wings a major package that includes forward Kirby Dach, goalie Sam Montembeault and highly touted prospect Michael Hage.

Detroit also received top-10 protected first-round draft picks in 2027 and 2029, a second-round pick in 2027 and a fourth-round pick in 2028.

Along with Larkin , the Canadiens acquired the Red Wings' second-round pick in 2028 — then traded it to the Anaheim Ducks for Detroit's 2027 second-rounder — and their third-round pick in 2027.

The move fills a need that has lingered near the top of Montreal's wish list for more than a year, with Larkin slotting in behind Nick Suzuki to give the Canadiens a legitimate second-line centre.

The speedy six-foot-one, 198-pound forward has two goals and six assists in 10 games this season for 278 goals and 649 points in 818 career games since Detroit drafted him 15th overall in 2014.

Adding Larkin is yet another step as the Canadiens push to become perennial Stanley Cup contenders. His US$8.7 million salary through 2030-31 — in the NHL’s ballooning cap environment — is also manageable on a team that has signed each of its core skaters to long-term deals under $10 million annually.

Detroit Red Wings center Dylan Larkin (71) plays against the Seattle Kraken in the third period of an NHL hockey game, Oct. 9, 2026, in Detroit. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

The Canadiens have spent much of the past year searching for this top-six upgrade.

They reportedly agreed to acquire forward Matthew Knies from the Toronto Maple Leafs at last season's trade deadline, but the deal wasn't completed in time. Montreal was also among the most aggressive suitors for Kirill Marchenko before Toronto landed the Columbus Blue Jackets winger in September, sending Knies as the centrepiece of its package.

Larkin's departure brings closure to a turbulent stretch with the team he grew up cheering for. The Waterford, Mich., native asked out of Detroit after a decade of missing the playoffs, and his relationship with the organization deteriorated further as the season opened.

The Red Wings stripped Larkin of the captaincy before he reported to training camp this fall. He missed Detroit's first two games with an injury and was booed while standing by the bench during player introductions at the team's home opener.

Canadiens fans made their interest known a few days later, chanting "We Want Larkin !" when Detroit visited Montreal on Oct. 10.

"I never would have imagined that in this building and in my career," Larkin said after the Red Wings lost 1-0 in a shootout. "They are passionate fans."

The situation reached a tipping point on Oct. 29 when Larkin informed the Red Wings he would sit out until a trade was completed.

Detroit then suspended Larkin without pay while interim general manager Shawn Horcoff — boxed in by the player’s no-trade protection — waited for a suitable return.

Michigan forward Michael Hage (19) during an NCAA hockey regional game against Minnesota Duluth, Sunday, March 29, 2026 in Albany, N.Y. Michigan won 4-3. (Vera Nieuwenhuis/The Canadian Press)

Larkin forfeited more than $1 million in salary.

He reportedly initially told the Red Wings he would only accept a trade to Florida, Minnesota or Vegas, before expanding his list to 10 American teams — and eventually waiving his full no-movement clause for Montreal.

But the price wasn't cheap, especially with Hage included.

Montembeault fell out of favour in Montreal's crease last season, while the oft-injured Dach — with eight points in 22 games playing bottom-six minutes this season — failed to meet lofty expectations in Montreal.

Hage, drafted 21st overall by the Canadiens in 2024, leads the NCAA with 26 points (five goals, 21 assists) in 13 games in his third year at the University of Michigan.

The 20-year-old from Mississauga, Ont., also had two goals and 13 assists in seven games for Canada at last year's world junior championship.

Many Canadiens fans had pegged Hage as the team’s eventual second-line centre. Instead, it will be Larkin .

World.title: N.L. fisheries minister stayed in Scottish castle, ‘luxury’ shooting lodge on aquaculture giant’s dime
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s NDP says the province’s fisheries minister put himself in a "brutal" conflict of interest when he stayed in a castle, then a "luxury" shooting lodge — all on the dime of an aquaculture company — during a trip to Scotland last June.

Most of Loyola O’Driscoll’s travel to the Aquaculture U.K. conference, including airline tickets and hotel accommodations at the beginning and end of the trip, was paid for by the provincial government.

But after a brief stint at the conference in Glasgow, the minister embarked on a two-night "familiarization" tour of aquaculture sites paid entirely by sea products giant MOWI Scotland.

O’Driscoll’s itinerary for the entire trip, obtained through access to information legislation, shows that on June 16, the minister stayed at the Cameron House, billed on its website as a "luxury Loch Lomond hotel."

The following night, after being ferried to the isolated Isle of Muck, the minister stayed in the Gallanach Lodge, described as a "luxury catered accommodation" with "magical views across the sea to Rum, Canna and Skye."

On the left, the Cameron House, "luxury hotel" located on Loch Lomond. On the right, the Gallanach Lodge, a "luxury catered accommodation" on the Isle of Muck. (Cameron House; Gallanach Lodge)

O'Driscoll's department said it could provide no "value/record" of the travel arrangements, which were made directly by the company.

One night at the Cameron House Loch Lomond, for the same date as the minister stayed but in 2027, would cost at least £429 (about $800), according to the hotel’s website. The Gallanach Lodge’s site shows that a room including breakfast and dinner costs £185 per night (about $350).

‘I had no idea what the accommodations were’

O’Driscoll’s department confirmed that "travel and accommodations and associated expenses" were paid for by MOWI, but stressed that "permission was granted" by Commissioner of Legislative Standards Ann Chafe prior to the trip.

"I had no idea what the accommodations were," O’Driscoll said in an interview, despite the itinerary for his trip clearly listing the names of the hotels at which he stayed.

"We were over there to get more knowledge on the aquaculture industry. I would say personally, before we even went, I called the commissoner of legislative standards to make sure that this is open and transparent and that there would be no issues with what I was doing when I went over there."

In this photo uploaded to Facebook by O'Driscoll's departure, the minister meets with MOWI workers in Scotland. (Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture)

Chafe, whose office oversees MHA ethics, confirmed by email that "approval to accept this sponsored travel was given to the minister following the filing of the full details with this office before leaving to attend the Aquaculture U.K. conference."

Like Chafe, a spokesperson for O’Driscoll’s department said "proper procedures were followed" and that the minister submitted an addendum to his yearly public disclosure statement following his trip, as required by a section of the House of Assembly Act on "accepting extra benefits."

The act states that MHAs may only accept gifts or personal benefits "received as an incident of the protocol or social obligations that normally accompany the duties or responsibilities of office." They may only receive third-party reimbursements for "reasonable travel and associated expenses incurred in performing services that are in the public interest."

For gifts over $500 and for any external travel reimbursement, MHAs must disclose the amount, the source of the gift or money, and a description of the circumstances under which the benefit was received.

Fisheries and Aquaculture Minister Loyola O'Driscoll holds a salmon during a sponsored trip to MOWI fish farms in Scotland. (Department of Fisheries an Aquaculture)

The disclosure addendum O'Driscoll submitted to the commissioner, which can only be viewed in person by visiting Chafe’s office in St. John’s, indicates that the minister received "sponsored/supported" travel to aquaculture sites while in Scotland last June.

However, the document does not give the name of the company that paid for the travel. It also doesn’t provide the value of the travel.

Radio-Canada asked Chafe to provide an estimate for the sponsored travel O’Driscoll received. She did not provide that information.

'I'm sorry, it's brutal'

The provincial New Democrats said regardless of the commissioner’s decision, the minister put himself in a flagrant conflict of interest.

"I’m sorry, it’s brutal," said NDP Leader Jim Dinn, whose last election campaign focused heavily on strengthening ethics rules for provincial politicians.

"We know the controversy around aquaculture in this province, but we also know that government is also the regulator of this industry, making sure that standards are followed," Dinn said. "It's kind of hard to be that regulator when you're accepting these gifts from the very companies you're trying to regulate."

Newfoundland and Labrador NDP Leader Jim Dinn. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)

Perception of conflict, despite commissioner’s decision?

"When they were in opposition, this is the very thing that the PCs railed against," said Dinn, pointing to a controversy involving former Liberal premier Andrew Furey’s 2021 trip to a fishing lodge owned by then-billionaire John Risley.

Risley, present for part of Furey’s stay according to news outlet AllNewfoundlandLabrador, announced a major wind-hydrogen development on Newfoundland’s west coast about half a year later, following a decision by the province to lift a long-time moratorium on onshore wind projects.

The Progressive Conservatives, then in Opposition, pounced on the posh fishing trip and filed a complaint with the legislative standards commissioner. Chafe eventually ruled Furey didn’t break any rules.

"Now we're here in this situation and [the PCs] are doing, basically doing, the same thing that they lambasted the Liberals for," Dinn said.

"It's not only important to do right, but to be perceived as doing right, as well," he said.

Asked directly whether he believed an aquaculture company paying for a fisheries minister’s accommodations at a castle and a shooting lodge could create the perception of a conflict of interest, O’Driscoll said: "I don’t think so."

"When I went to the commissioner of legislative standards that's what my intention was, to make sure it was perceived right, transparent and that there were no concerns to me," he said.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.
