World.title: Cuba and the Unbearable Habit of Waiting for Miracles
World.content:
Life Happening. I refuse to accept that resignation is our only destiny. / 14ymedio

Perhaps my grandparents were right: Not even the US Americans can fix this. We’ll have to fix it ourselves.

By Yunior Garcia Aguilera (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – My grandparents used to repeat two sayings that seemed to sum up all the wisdom of our national pessimism. The first was: “Not even the US Americans can fix this.” The second: “Hope was green, and a goat ate it.” I grew up hearing them without imagining that, several decades later, they would still describe the mood of Cubans with such accuracy.

In Cuba, everything seems to be in free fall except the regime. The economy is sinking, buildings are crumbling, hospitals are collapsing, public services are disappearing, and the country is emptying out. But those in power remain firmly in place, clinging to their privileges, floating as though they had discovered the secret of political weightlessness.

For years, we have repeated that the dictatorship is about to hit rock bottom. Yet the bottom keeps moving farther away. Perhaps because, as the regime falls, it is society that absorbs the blows. The government has managed to survive the failure of absolutely everything it promised to save.

The capture of Nicolas Maduro in January unleashed a new wave of expectations. Many Cubans believed our turn had finally come. Trump fueled those hopes with warnings about the regime’s future and statements suggesting that an outcome was near. But the months passed, and the US strategy focused solely on intensifying economic and energy pressure.

And the negotiations, enthusiastically announced by some and downplayed by others, also seemed like the chronicle of a failure foretold.

Now Trump speaks of resolving the Cuban problem before the end of his term in January 2029. Freedom is once again postponed, like a public works project with no reliable completion date.

Perhaps we should update that cartoon of the ripe fruit that John Quincy Adams imagined falling toward the United States. Two centuries later, the fruit is bruised, indebted, depopulated, and in need of a billion-million-dollar investment to become edible again. It hardly seems like a delicacy Washington is in any great hurry to acquire.

But it would be unfair to place all our frustrations on the United States. We must also look in the mirror.

I left Cuba in November 2021, following the repression against my family and me. I was not willing to spend more than twenty years in prison for attempting to organize a peaceful march. Some compatriots called me a coward. Nor do I intend to portray myself as a hero. I know my fears, my limitations, and my contradictions.

Yet I have seen how opposition activists who did endure years in Castro’s prisons end up being subjected to the same public lynching on social media by people who supposedly share their democratic aspirations.

Those who leave are called cowards. Those who stay are expected to deliver results. Those who are imprisoned are constantly put on a scale to check whether they have really lost weight. Those who are released are scrutinized for some blemish that might discredit their sacrifice. We demand perfect heroes, without fear, without mistakes, without families to protect, and preferably with an unlimited capacity to endure torture.

There is no shortage of Facebook prosecutors. What is missing are citizens willing to assume even a small portion of the risks they demand of others.

And yet, inside Cuba, there are people who continue to resist. Anna Bensi, Alina Barbara Lopez, Yoani Sanchez, Camila Acosta, and many others who defy repression with admirable perseverance. They receive solidarity, especially from religious circles and activists, but that support rarely reaches the same scale in the streets as it does on the internet.

I do not intend to judge those who are afraid. That would be unforgivable hypocrisy. Fear is legitimate. Repression is real. But we need to recognize that no viral post can replace civic organization, and a million insults will not bring down a dictatorship.

Is there still hope? Yes, although it does not come wrapped in Trump’s promises or depend on finding another martyr willing to sacrifice themselves for everyone else.

Hope begins when we stop demanding impossible heroes and learn to protect the imperfect human beings who still dare to stand up. When we manage to disagree without destroying one another, offer support without imposing conditions, and turn outrage into meaningful solidarity.

The July 11, 2021, protests demonstrated that there is one thing the regime fears more than anything else: losing control of the streets. That is why the greatest strength of an organized civil society lies not only in its ability to denounce abuses, but also in its capacity to bring people together, sustain relationships, and mobilize.

The protests against power outages express needs that are as urgent as they are legitimate. But if scattered discontent finds a nationwide, sustained expression capable of moving beyond immediate demands, those in power will have to confront a reality they cannot resolve simply by restoring electricity to a circuit.

The true bottom of a political crisis is not measured by the depth of the economic disaster, but by the limits that organized citizens are capable of imposing on their rulers.

I do not know when this downward spiral will end. I distrust those who insist that freedom is always just around the corner. But I also refuse to accept that resignation is our only destiny.

Perhaps my grandparents were right: Not even the US Americans can fix this. We’ll have to fix it ourselves.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: The War of the Entire Cuban People
World.content:
Cuban president Miguel Diaz Canel in a meeting with top military officials.

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – Cuba has spent nearly 70 years preparing for a military war with the United States, but the truth is that, after the 1960s, that possibility became increasingly remote.

The current US administration has said on more than one occasion that it does not rule out that option, but the reality is that adding yet another armed conflict to the financial burden borne by United States taxpayers would be extremely complicated, to mention only the economic aspect.

Beyond that—which remains a hypothetical scenario—what is actually happening in Cuba is that fear of war is being used to serve the interests of the dictatorship. At the same time, the regime wants Cubans to believe it could withstand a military confrontation, when we all know that would be impossible.

This week, President Miguel Di’z-Canel met with the country’s top military leadership to reiterate the decision to repel any aggression (it would be the height of absurdity if they surrendered at the first opportunity). But far from projecting an image of strength, he looked exhausted.

His words conveyed anything but determination, confidence, courage, or leadership. What we saw was someone badly in need of sleep, someone weakened. Someone repeating the same old rhetoric while seeming almost to beg the United States not to go so far as to invade and to let them live in peace, as he claims the rest of the world advocates—even if that means he can continue enjoying his privileges while the vast majority of Cubans endure hardship.

What we witnessed at the beginning of this year with the capture of Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela demonstrated the enormous military disparity between a superpower and a Third World nation, a gap that would be even greater in a confrontation between Cuba and the United States.

Perhaps the dictatorship’s only advantage in such a scenario would be its extensive infiltration of US government institutions with spies, an effort that has been underway for decades and has proven highly effective. But even if military secrets could not be adequately protected, everything would ultimately be decided on the battlefield. And there, it would be the classic fight between a lion and a monkey—with the monkey tied to a post.

The tyranny’s position is clear: it seeks to impress those who still believe in it and intimidate everyone else, attempting to prevent these threats from triggering another social uprising, which would actually be the perfect formula for change.

To that end, every so often they display their obsolete weapons, which must give US military intelligence a good laugh, while here only the ignorant could believe they would withstand an assault.

Since Fidel Castro’s time, the island’s strategy has been based on establishing pockets of resistance throughout the country, under what was officially called the “War of the Entire People.”

But there is one enormous difference between the Fidel Castro era and today, and it is the key to understanding how different the situation would be now: the vast majority of Cubans do not support their leaders.

I know there are no reliable statistics to substantiate this. That would require the referendum we have been demanding for years, which the dictatorship refuses to hold. But it is what I see every day: countless people tired of being used in this political confrontation while watching their own dreams, and those of their children and grandchildren, continually postponed, just as the dreams of their parents and grandparents were buried.

There is a weariness that makes no noise, that is not proclaimed in public squares or featured in headlines. Instead, it settles on the shoulders of someone returning home late, in the hands of someone counting coins before making a purchase, in the eyes of someone who has learned not to promise their children too much. It is the exhaustion of feeling used.

For years, far too many people have been called upon to defend flags that offered them no shelter, slogans that put no food on their tables, promises that evaporated as soon as the march ended or the ballot boxes closed. They were asked for patience, sacrifice, and loyalty. They were told of a bright future, an imminent victory, a higher cause. And they gave their days, their enthusiasm, even their resentments, while watching the present slip through their fingers.

They had been promised that education would open doors, that honest work would allow them to build a home, that perseverance would be rewarded. But many of those doors remain closed. Owning a home has become a distant aspiration. Young people pack their bags not out of a thirst for adventure, but because they feel that staying means giving up. Parents watch silently as their children inherit not only a surname and a history, but also frustrations and the obligation to start over somewhere else.

That is why the frustration keeps growing. Not necessarily because people have abandoned their ideals, but because they are beginning to distinguish between ideas and those who exploit them. They no longer want to be a crowd, fuel for someone else’s cause, or an argument to be used. They do not want their suffering invoked in speeches by people who live far removed from its consequences. They do not want to keep sacrificing the present in exchange for a future that is always postponed.

The truth is that the real “War of the Entire People” is the struggle for survival. What people want is something simpler and, for that very reason, more profound: to live.

To live without having to justify their children’s hunger. To work without feeling that every effort disappears into a labyrinth. To grow old knowing that their grandchildren will have more opportunities than they did, not fewer. To reclaim the right to dream without asking permission, without waiting for another promise, without turning every hope into an act of faith.

Perhaps the time has come to listen to that exhaustion. Because when a society stops believing in those who summon it to action, it does not always abandon its dreams. Sometimes, at long last, it begins to demand that they be fulfilled. And that is the real terror sweeping through the corridors of the Central Committee.

Read more from Cuba here at Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba’s Benchmark Hospital That Lost Its Greatness
World.content:
Photo of the exterior of the Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital, taken from the hospital’s archives.

By Kamil Kenders

HAVANA TIMES – Some buildings are part of a city’s landscape, while others are also part of its memory. Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital belongs to both categories.

Its tower, visible from different points along Havana’s Malecon, was for many years an image associated with the development of Cuban medicine. For thousands of people, that building represented something more than a hospital: it offered the possibility of receiving specialized care, obtaining a diagnosis for a complicated condition, or undergoing treatment that was not available at just any other institution in the country.

Inaugurated on December 3, 1982, Hermanos Ameijeiras was conceived as a national referral center. Its facilities, equipment, specialists, and the diversity of services it offered placed it among Cuba’s most prestigious hospitals.

Highly complex medical procedures, research, and professional training programs were carried out there. For decades, its name inspired confidence. For many Cubans, being referred to Ameijeiras meant reaching one of the best possible places to receive medical care. But the years have passed, and that image of excellence seems to have become trapped in memory.

Today, speaking of Hermanos Ameijeiras also means speaking of shortages, deterioration, limited services, and difficulties that ultimately affect both patients and their families.

The reality behind its doors is far removed from the institution that was once a source of pride. It is not simply a matter of the physical deterioration of certain areas. It goes much deeper. The scarcity of material resources, lack of supplies, difficulties keeping equipment operational, and loss of medical professionals have gradually weakened the capacity of an institution that needs precisely the opposite: resources, technology, and specialized personnel.

Many healthcare professionals have emigrated in search of better living and working conditions. Those who remain in the country try to practice their profession under increasingly difficult circumstances. And those who continue caring for patients must confront a reality in which they do not always have what they need to do their jobs. Because a doctor may possess all the knowledge in the world, but without the necessary medications, reagents, instruments, or equipment, their ability to provide adequate care is inevitably limited.

According to accounts I have heard, difficulties performing certain clinical tests because of a lack of reagents have become another obstacle for patients at this hospital. Sometimes, even when a patient manages to obtain an appointment or see a specialist, completing the necessary diagnostic tests remains an unresolved problem.

A CT scan can be crucial in determining how a disease is progressing. An MRI can provide essential information for establishing a diagnosis. These are not optional machines or luxuries reserved for those who can afford them. They are fundamental tools of modern medicine. Yet breakdowns and a lack of resources to maintain and repair this equipment have ended up compromising essential services.

In July 2026, Associated Press published a report on the state of healthcare in Cuba that specifically included Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital. A patient with a history of cancer had been waiting seven months for a CT scan because the hospital’s machine was broken. Her story was a painful illustration of what it means to lack access to technology that can be decisive for a person’s life.

But some situations do not need to appear in a news report to reveal just how far the deterioration has gone. Not long ago, I witnessed a scene that I still find difficult to forget.

One of the hospital corridors. The cart with two blue tanks is used to transport water to the upper floors.

Family members accompanying hospitalized patients had to go down to the hospital basement to fetch water because the supply was not adequately reaching the upper floors. While patients remained hospitalized, their relatives had to take responsibility for obtaining something as basic as water. I am not talking about a bottle of drinking water out of personal preference or some additional comfort. I am talking about a basic necessity in any healthcare institution, especially in a place where there are sick people, some with mobility difficulties and others completely dependent on those caring for them.

I stopped to think about what it means for a family to have a loved one hospitalized and, on top of worrying about their health, have to go down to the basement to fetch water. How many other things must these family members manage on their own? How many needs end up becoming family responsibilities because the hospital cannot guarantee even the most basic conditions?

It is difficult not to feel disappointed. Because one can understand that a country is going through economic difficulties, that there are supply problems, or that certain resources are hard to obtain. But it is also impossible not to wonder how an institution of such importance has come to depend on such makeshift solutions for basic aspects of its operation.

And what is most troubling is that we are not talking about a small municipal hospital, a secondary facility, or a center that never had substantial resources. We are talking about Hermanos Ameijeiras.

That hospital which was once a national benchmark, which received patients from across the country, and which for years concentrated some of Cuba’s most specialized medical services.

I think about those who arrive there seeking answers about a serious illness. About those waiting for a diagnostic test that cannot be performed because the equipment is broken. About those who need laboratory tests and discover there are no reagents. About the family members who walk the corridors, climb up and down stairs, and end up taking care of needs that the institution itself should guarantee.

I also think about the doctors and other healthcare workers who remain there, trying to keep what still functions going, often under conditions that do not match the enormous responsibility resting on their shoulders.

Because the deterioration of a hospital is not measured solely by its walls, elevators, or facilities. It is measured, above all, by what it can no longer offer those who need its services.

And perhaps that is the saddest part of this story: the hospital’s name still carries the prestige of what it once was, but the everyday reality of many patients no longer seems to live up to that reputation.

The building is still standing. Its tower continues to dominate part of Havana’s skyline. It still bears the name “Hermanos Ameijeiras” and preserves the memory of an era when it represented the most advanced achievements of Cuban medicine.

But a hospital cannot live off its history. It cannot make diagnoses with memories of its former specialists, perform CT scans with broken equipment, or guarantee medical care by relying solely on the prestige of its name.

A hospital needs doctors, nurses, technicians, medications, reagents, water, electricity, and functioning technology. Above all, it needs to be able to care for its patients.

Hermanos Ameijeiras is still there. But I fear that, for many Cubans, its greatness is beginning to belong to the past. And that is much more than the deterioration of a building.

Read more from the diary of Kamil Kenders here on Havana Times.

World.title: Police Inaction Accelerates the Depopulation of Rural Cuba
World.content:
Photograph taken on April 1, 2025, of a farmer on his property in Cárdenas, Cuba. Julio, a 71-year-old Cuban farmer, decided to sell all his cows last year, fed up with vandals who would steal them at night to then sell the meat on the black market. File photo: EFE/ Ernesto Mastrascusa

By Amado Viera

HAVANA TIMES – It was not until late August, after a gang of cattle rustlers kidnapped a family on their farm, that the police in Guantanamo took notice of the wave of violence sweeping through the countryside of this eastern Cuban province. It took two weeks and an extensive operation to capture the 13 members of the gang responsible for the crime, some of whom resisted arrest with weapons.

Their behavior was predictable after months of growing accustomed to terrorizing vast rural areas of the province. At least a dozen families had been forced to abandon their farms for fear of violence.

The mass kidnapping in Palmarito del Guaso attracted attention because among the victims was a 10-year-old girl who was held captive along with her family while the thieves looted the farm. The outrage sparked by this abuse forced the police to launch an active search for the criminals. In the weeks that followed, the Palmarito gang and other criminals were captured in operations carried out throughout the province and neighboring Santiago de Cuba.

But shortly afterward, robberies and assaults were once again reported in the same areas. “There are mountainous areas of Guantanamo where people hardly plant crops or raise animals anymore because there are so many loafers waiting for a chance to steal whatever they can,” explained Yonimiller Horrutiniel, a Guantanamo native from the municipality of Niceto Perez.

The situation he describes is not limited to eastern Cuba. Nearly 500 kilometers to the west, in Camagüey province, the owners of the farm where he works decided to sell the property to “avoid trouble.”

That was the expression the owner used when he informed Yonimiller of his decision. Since the beginning of the year, thieves had stolen seven head of cattle and a myriad of other, less valuable belongings. But the incident that marked the point of no return was the theft of a horse to which the owner was particularly attached. The victim himself tracked down the animal and notified the authorities so they could arrest the thieves. But by the time they did so—a week later—the criminals had already slaughtered the horse.

Cities Come First

The farm where Yonimiller worked is located in Siete Palmas, a rural community southwest of the city of Camagüey. Because of its distance from the provincial capital, the community had its own police post for decades.

These neighborhood police posts form the foundation of Cuba’s public security system. Staffed by an officer and several agents, their responsibilities include compiling what is known as the “criminal potential” registry, a list of residents with criminal records or behavior suggesting a propensity to commit crimes. Traditionally, they have been an effective tool for preventing crime and identifying perpetrators.

Years ago, as part of a process of closing local police posts, the one in Siete Palmas was dismantled and converted into housing. To compensate, the police sent patrols through the community and surrounding areas for a time, but these visits gradually became less frequent. By the time the fuel crisis reached its peak this year, such patrols had long since become a thing of the past.

“We’d also have to see how they would manage to get here, considering the terrible condition of the roads. Modern patrol cars are only good for driving around town,” said Emilio Acevedo, a resident of the area.

When planning new purchases of police vehicles, the Ministry of the Interior has for years favored sedan models from brands such as Geely, Peugeot, and Hyundai, which are well suited to cities but impractical in rural areas. This reveals its priorities regarding public order: maintaining it in urban centers is considered more important than doing so in the countryside. To understand why, one need only ask where most anti-government protests have taken place in recent years.

More Crime Despite Harsh Sentences

In 2025, more than 90% of those tried in Cuban courts for stealing and slaughtering cattle and other large livestock were sentenced to prison. A report on the subject by the People’s Supreme Court adds that another 7.5% of defendants received fines, while barely 3% were found not guilty.

Such a high conviction rate is virtually unparalleled in contemporary legal systems. Nor is the severity of the sentences: according to the Ministry of Justice’s own statistics, judges’ decisions tend to be characterized by their “exemplary nature,” meaning that they impose the harshest penalties provided for in the Penal Code.

Despite the government’s punitive approach, reports of livestock theft and slaughter have continued to multiply. These cases represent only the “tip of the iceberg,” since “there are other crimes that aren’t even reported,” Felix Duarte Ortega, president of the National Association of Small Farmers (ANAP), pointed out a few months ago.

At an assembly of the organization held in the western province of Mayabeque, participants told him that many farmers find it burdensome to travel into town to report everything that happens on their farms. As a solution, the leader recommended “forming more farmers’ patrols.”

These groups attempt to make up for the absence of police in rural areas. Provinces such as Santiago de Cuba and Camagüey stand out for the number of farmers’ patrol units they have organized to confront cattle rustlers.

In September, ANAP’s leadership in Camagüey announced that it already had 25 such groups, with approximately 330 members in total. At first glance, that might seem like an impressive number, but in reality it falls far short of the province’s security needs. Covering 15,000 square kilometers, Camagüey is increasingly feeling the absence of the police, to the point that many farmers are beginning to wonder what purpose reporting a crime even serves.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Bolsonaro "clinically stable" in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction
World.content:
Bolsonaro “clinically stable” in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 04:17 UTC Full article

Bolsonaro walking in the hospital corridor, connected to an IV line.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction, is “clinically stable”, the DF Star hospital in Brasília said on Sunday. Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, under house arrest.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction, is “clinically stable”, the DF Star hospital in Brasília, where he was admitted on Friday, said on Sunday. Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, under house arrest.

According to the hospital bulletin, the former president is continuing “clinical treatment, fasting and nutritional support”, and there is no forecast yet for his discharge. His wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, wrote on Instagram that he “spent the night without pain” and had been able to walk, and asked for prayers so that he “does not need to undergo a more invasive procedure”. His son Carlos, however, said on X on Saturday that his father had spent the previous night vomiting and in pain, and warned that he could face “the tenth surgery in less than eight years”.

The symptoms began on Friday morning with abdominal distension, and his doctor decided to take him to hospital as his condition worsened. Since he was stabbed in the abdomen during the 2018 election campaign, Bolsonaro has suffered recurrent episodes of intestinal obstruction and has undergone several operations.

Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes authorised three of his sons to visit him during his hospital stay, banning phones, cameras and other recording devices. The Supreme Court will vote between December 4 and 15 on the constitutionality of a law that reduces the sentences of the former president and others convicted in the coup plot.

His eldest son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, had promised to pardon him if he won the election, but lost the October run-off to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and left Brazil for the United States after becoming the target of a money laundering investigation, according to AFP and O Globo. Flávio denies the allegations and says he is the victim of political persecution.

World.title: COP31 ends without a major climate deal amid divisions over fossil fuels
World.content:
COP31 ends without a major climate deal amid divisions over fossil fuels

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 04:12 UTC Full article

COP31 President Murat Kurum (L) and Australian minister Chris Bowen at the summit in Antalya.

The UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya ended on Sunday without a major political agreement, after deep divisions between countries over fossil fuels and finance for the poorest. It is the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen summit that the main declaration of one of these conferences has collapsed in this way.

The UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya ended on Sunday without a major political agreement, after deep divisions between countries over fossil fuels and finance for the poorest. It is the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen summit that the main declaration of one of these conferences has collapsed in this way.

Negotiations, due to end on Friday, ran into Sunday, making COP31 the longest UN climate conference in history, according to the BBC. The final draft, presented in the early hours, did not mention “fossil fuels”, the main cause of global warming, and referred only indirectly to the commitment made at COP28 in 2023 to “transition away” from them in energy systems. An earlier draft mentioned them six times, which was unacceptable to oil-producing countries.

The European Union, Pacific island states and others rejected the text. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels,” said the EU's representative, Irish minister Darragh O'Brien. Panama and the Marshall Islands also criticised its lack of ambition. At the other end, Saudi Arabia's delegate, Mohammad Ayoub, said Arab countries had negotiated “in good faith” and noted that they account for only a small share of historical emissions, while Russia warned that moving away from fossil fuels too quickly would cause “fuel poverty”.

Developing countries also objected to the absence of concrete figures to deliver on the commitment, agreed last year at COP30 in Brazil, to triple finance for adaptation to climate change. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed,” said Mohamed Adow of the African think tank Power Shift Africa.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, at his last climate summit before stepping down, said he was “deeply disappointed” and accused “powerful fossil fuel interests” of following “a page from Big Tobacco's playbook”. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose government led the negotiations, blamed the failure on “difficult geopolitical times”. Australian minister Chris Bowen, president of the negotiations, spoke of “unbridgeable red lines”.

There was some progress, including on a “just transition mechanism” to support workers and communities affected by the energy shift, and more than 80 countries backed Turkey's proposed target for electricity to meet 35% of global energy use by 2035. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on reforming a consensus-based process that “fell short” on Sunday. The next summit, COP32, will be held in Ethiopia in November 2027.

With current policies, the planet is heading for warming of about 2.8C by 2100, according to the UN, well above the 1.5C limit set in Paris in 2015, which will be exceeded in the next few years.

World.title: Colombia's government asks X to suspend Petro's account after he calls for the president to resign
World.content:
Colombia's government asks X to suspend Petro's account after he calls for the president to resign

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 04:06 UTC Full article

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella (L) and former President Gustavo Petro (R).

The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the social network X on Sunday to suspend the account of former President Gustavo Petro, after he called on the public to demand the president's resignation.

The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the social network X on Sunday to suspend the account of former President Gustavo Petro, after he called on the public to demand the president's resignation. Petro, who does not recognise De la Espriella's election victory, called the request censorship.

“That social network cannot become the main tool for spreading an anti-democratic and destabilising plan, threatening and attacking the institutions of the Colombian state,” the Ministry of Information and Communications Technologies said in a statement. The ministry argues that the former president's posts violate X's rules on incitement to violence, and asked that account be taken of the reach of his account, which has 9.1 million followers, and of the role social media played in the 2021 protests. It also recalled that the Council of State ordered Petro in late October to remove posts accusing the national registrar of fraud.

The trigger was a message Petro posted on Saturday. “I ask the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo's resignation now,” he wrote, alongside a video of his speech on Thursday in Cali, during marches called by the opposition. “It is massive, peaceful popular mobilisation that will bring about a change of the current illegitimate government,” he said. The former president alleges electoral fraud, although election observers defended the work of the National Registry.

Petro responded that Minister Alexandra Falla was violating the Constitution: “She is asking for nothing less than the censorship of my communication with the people.” Senator Iván Cepeda, of the Historic Pact, called the request “despotic”. “We will continue advancing the mobilisation, the preparation of the National Strike and civil disobedience,” he wrote. De la Espriella had warned on Thursday: “I will never accept that he attacks democracy, promotes a coup or seeks to destroy Colombia.”

The request also drew criticism from independent analysts. “The message does not violate X's terms of service. A suspension for that would be a total overreach by the platform and a violation of the former president's rights,” said lawyer Carlos Cortés, a former Twitter employee. Political scientist Andrés Celis, a critic of Petro's government, said the administration's campaign “will end up empowering” the former president.

The clash comes amid an escalation between the two leaders, who are trading serious accusations that each denies. De la Espriella asked on Thursday that the United States investigate his predecessor, while Petro insists the current government is “illegitimate”. Regional elections are due in 2027 and presidential elections in 2030.

World.title: Prosecutors: Argentina's top shrimp exporter dumped waste at sea through a hidden system
World.content:
Prosecutors: Argentina's top shrimp exporter dumped waste at sea through a hidden system

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 04:02 UTC Full article

The Golfo Nuevo, next to Puerto Madryn, is one of the main breeding grounds of the southern right whale.

Two former managers of Conarpesa, Argentina's largest exporter of wild shrimp, have faced a new trial in Chubut province since this month over the discharge of fishing industry waste into the Golfo Nuevo, next to Puerto Madryn, through a hidden connection that prosecutors say the company set up.

Two former managers of Conarpesa, Argentina's largest exporter of wild shrimp, have faced a new trial in Chubut province since this month over the discharge of fishing industry waste into the Golfo Nuevo, next to Puerto Madryn, one of the main breeding grounds of the southern right whale, through a hidden connection that prosecutors say the company set up. Conarpesa denies the discharges came from its plant.

The defendants are the company's then environmental manager and the manager of its effluent treatment plant. Both were acquitted at a first trial in 2023 by a judge who found that procedural guarantees had been violated, although prosecutor Alex Williams had sought prison sentences of more than three years. Prosecutors appealed, and Chubut's Superior Court of Justice overturned the ruling in June and ordered a new trial before another judge.

The investigation began in February 2023 with a video by a local resident showing an orange stream flowing into the sea. Investigators found an undeclared connection near the company's premises, and tests concluded that the samples were consistent with “a raw liquid from the shrimp-processing fishing industry”, with more than 1,500 milligrams of organic matter per litre, against a legal limit of 50. Prosecutors also presented messages from the former manager's phone which, in their view, show the defendants knew of the connection. Conarpesa maintained during the proceedings that it was unaware of its existence.

Founded in 1977 and chaired by Spanish businessman Fernando Álvarez Castellano, Conarpesa is partly owned by Galicia-based Worldwide Fishing Company, has 25 vessels and runs four plants on the Patagonian coast.

The company is also named in another investigation opened this month in Puerto Madryn into possible discharges in 2016, along with Red Chamber, Estrella Patagónica and Congeladores Patagónicos. The case spent almost ten years in the federal courts before they declared themselves incompetent and passed it to the province, whose prosecutors now have six months to bring charges or seek dismissal.

The Golfo Nuevo hosts more than a thousand southern right whales every year, according to El País, and is one of Patagonia's main tourist destinations. Fishing is one of the region's economic drivers, and crustaceans are Argentina's second-largest export to Spain, according to Spanish trade statistics.

World.title: Argentina's lawyer in Hamburg: if Sea Lion goes ahead, "those rights are lost forever"
World.content:
Argentina's lawyer in Hamburg: if Sea Lion goes ahead, “those rights are lost forever”

22nd Sunday, November 2026 - 13:10 UTC Full article

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, part of Argentina's legal team, during the hearings before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg.

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, one of the lawyers representing Argentina before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, has argued that if the United Kingdom begins extracting oil at the Sea Lion project north of the Falklands, Argentina's rights over those resources “are lost forever”. The tribunal will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina's request to suspend the project.

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, one of the lawyers representing Argentina before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, has argued that if the United Kingdom begins extracting oil at the Sea Lion project north of the Falklands, Argentina's rights over those resources “are lost forever”. The tribunal will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina's request to suspend the project.

“States have the right to decide when, how and under what conditions they will exploit non-renewable resources,” Kohen said in an interview with Infobae. “Drilling and oil extraction cause an irreversible physical change to the continental shelf and its non-renewable resources. Once produced, there is no going back.”

Kohen, a native of Rosario based in Geneva, a professor of international law and secretary-general of the Institut de Droit International, previously represented Argentina before the same tribunal in 2012, when it unanimously ordered Ghana to release the frigate Libertad, held at the request of a creditor fund. In this case he is part of the team led by Argentina's agent, Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal.

According to the jurist, the United Kingdom centred its defence on sovereignty over the islands so that the tribunal would conclude it lacks jurisdiction, since it can only rule on matters under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Argentina, he said, limited itself to seeking to preserve its rights over the disputed continental shelf “while the dispute remains unresolved”.

At the November 10 and 11 hearings, the British delegation, led by Attorney General Ellie Reeves, argued that the tribunal has no jurisdiction over sovereignty issues and that suspending Sea Lion would “kill” it, with “devastating” consequences for the islanders. British lawyers estimated the loss for Rockhopper at about US$1 billion, and the chief executive of its Israeli partner, Navitas, warned in writing that even the briefest suspension would be “terminal” for the project. “Economic damage can be compensated; the modification of the continental shelf is irreversible,” Kohen replied.

The jurist also challenged the 2013 referendum invoked by Reeves as an expression of the islanders' self-determination, which he had described during the hearing as a “self-satisfaction referendum”. “It was a referendum that was neither organised nor supervised by the United Nations,” he said. In that vote, 99.8% of voters backed the islands remaining a British Overseas Territory. The United Kingdom maintains that the islanders have the right to decide their future and to develop their natural resources.

For Kohen, whatever the outcome, the case has already forced London “to justify itself before an international tribunal”. “The only way Argentina had to stop the United Kingdom from moving ahead with hydrocarbon exploitation was to turn to international jurisdiction,” he said.

World.title: Falklands: Public Accounts Committee to scrutinize several contracts and projects
World.content:
Falklands: Public Accounts Committee to scrutinize several contracts and projects

22nd Sunday, November 2026 - 13:09 UTC Full article

The contracts under scrutiny include the FIGAS hangar and the contract with construction firm RSK.(Pic FITV)

The Falkland Islands Public Accounts Committee (PAC) announced this week, as part of its remit, its routine 2026/27 programme of oversight and scrutiny of a number of government projects and contracts.

The Falkland Islands Public Accounts Committee (PAC) announced this week, as part of its remit, its routine 2026/27 programme of oversight and scrutiny of a number of government projects and contracts.

Over the next two months the programme covers two construction projects and three government contracts: the FIGAS hangar, FIGAS being the Islands government's air service; the contract with construction firm RSK; the lease contract for five cranes; the project for the installation of a new port; and the contract with Ramboll, the firm that advises and assists in planning the Islands' various infrastructure development projects.

The PAC's role is to provide external oversight of budget execution and of the legality of disbursements under current regulations.

The cases to be examined were selected by PAC staff, and the committee will also set the terms of reference for each before assigning them to an individual or team.

The PAC invites members of the public to contact that individual or team to assist with the scrutiny of the various cases if they believe they hold relevant information, which can be done in confidence. Those interested in joining as reviewers are likewise invited to contact the PAC.

PAC Executive Secretary Bernie Goodwin said the “function of the PAC is to ensure that the disbursements made by the Islands government are carried out properly, also drawing on the experience and skills of all members of the community.”

He added: “There are great benefits in including every possible area of information, not only within Government itself. We also hope to hear the views of any member of the public who feels able to contact or write to us, whether in confidence or publicly.”

World.title: Danstar to follow international maritime law: will seek clearance only for Punta Arenas departure and Stanley arrival
World.content:
Danstar to follow international maritime law: will seek clearance only for Punta Arenas departure and Stanley arrival

22nd Sunday, November 2026 - 13:07 UTC Full article

The flyer announcing the arrival of the SSL Chile representatives.

Pablo Pacheco, owner and general manager of the shipping company Easter Island Logistics, told the Chilean press that the cargo vessel Danstar “will strictly follow international maritime law” on its inaugural voyage between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, scheduled for December, which has prompted reports in Argentine media about an alleged request to cross Argentine waters.

Pablo Pacheco, owner and general manager of the shipping company Easter Island Logistics, told the Chilean press that the cargo vessel Danstar “will strictly follow international maritime law” on its inaugural voyage between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, scheduled for December, which has prompted reports in Argentine media about an alleged request to cross Argentine waters.

“We are only going to request clearance for departure from Punta Arenas and arrival at Stanley,” Pacheco said, stressing that “this procedure is the one that corresponds under international regulations and the bilateral treaties in force.”

The Danstar, which sails under the Chilean flag and is currently undergoing technical maintenance at the ASMAR shipyards in Punta Arenas, is scheduled to begin commercial operations around mid-December 2026.

On this route — roughly 900 kilometres and two and a half days' sailing — the company will reactivate a direct maritime connection between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, suspended for more than a decade.

The shipping line also reiterated that the cargo carried is for exclusively civilian and humanitarian purposes, consisting of perishable foodstuffs, fruit, vegetables, liquefied gas and construction materials to supply the archipelago's residents, distancing itself entirely from any logistical operation linked to the hydrocarbons industry in the area.

In the Islands, meanwhile, the Falkland Islands Development Corporation, which reports to the Islands government and has conducted all the negotiations for restoring the commercial link with southern Chile, announced that it welcomed Jaime and Javier of Sea Shipping Line (SSL) this Saturday. They will remain in the Islands for a week, until November 28.

“The team will be available to provide support on supply matters and on loading and dispatch arrangements for the new Punta Arenas/Stanley supply line operated by Naviera Easter Island,” the Development Corporation said in a statement.

As part of their visit, Jaime and Javier will give a presentation on SSL Chile's services, covering who they are and what they offer, with an opportunity to meet them and put questions to them.

The presentation takes place on Monday November 23, from 4.30pm to 6.30pm, in the Events Room at the Harbour Lights cinema. Traders, business owners and the general public are invited to attend.

For further information, contact communications@fidc.co.fk

World.title: Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised in Brasília with abdominal pain
World.content:
Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised in Brasília with abdominal pain

21st Saturday, November 2026 - 06:25 UTC Full article

Jair Bolsonaro surrounded by security officers.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to hospital in Brasília on Friday after suffering abdominal pain and distension, according to a statement from the medical centre where he remains. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, under house arrest on health grounds.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to hospital in Brasília on Friday after suffering abdominal pain and distension, according to a statement from the medical centre where he remains. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, under house arrest on health grounds.

Doctors carried out a series of tests to determine the cause of his symptoms, the hospital said. News of his admission was first given on X by his son Carlos Bolsonaro, elected senator in October's elections, who spoke of “intense abdominal pain”.

Bolsonaro, who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022, was convicted by the Supreme Federal Court in September 2025 and has been serving his sentence since that year. He was granted house arrest at his home in Brasília on humanitarian grounds. Since 2018, when he was stabbed in the abdomen at a campaign event, he has undergone several surgeries and been hospitalised on numerous occasions.

His eldest son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, lost the October 25 presidential run-off to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, did not concede defeat and left Brazil via the Argentine border bound for the United States. From 2027, four members of the Bolsonaro family will hold seats in Brazil's Congress.

World.title: The history of Mexico’s corridos and the controversy over censorship
World.content:
Talking about music and the effect it has on humans is complex. Music shapes brains and communities: it forges neural connections, helps regulate emotion and offers a language for belonging.

The corrido — Mexico’s narrative ballad — embodies all those powers. It has been a walking newspaper, a moral pamphlet, a protest song, and, increasingly, a contested cultural weapon.

So why does the Mexican state practice a veiled censorship of this genre today, and what does the corrido tell us about modern Mexico?

Jugglers and corridos

To find the corrido’s origin, we must look to medieval jugglers. Before newspapers and radio, itinerant narrators moved from town to town, recounting events and epics with a vihuela, a precursor to the guitar.

That practice evolved into the Spanish romancero of the 15th and 16th centuries: eight-syllable verses delivering current events in a direct, emotional tone. Some scholars trace a specific Andalusian strain — marked by a “correntío” or accelerated rhythm — as a key progenitor.

Arriving in New Spain, the romancero did not remain pure. It fused with Indigenous oral forms and Afrodescendant rhythms, folding pre-Hispanic narrative techniques into a hybrid vernacular that became uniquely Mexican. In Northern Mexico, a further infusion came from German, Swiss and Austro-Hungarian immigrants who introduced polkas, mazurkas, redovas, the violin and the accordion.

The guitar, bajo sexto, accordion, and polka and waltz-derived meters together formed the musical DNA that allowed Spanish-inflected corridos to evolve into the Northern Mexican styles now among the genre’s most recognizable variants.

The 19th-century corridos

Under Porfirio Díaz, European refinement was idealized. As a result, the corrido became a popular countervoice. In a mostly illiterate society, corridos functioned as both information and entertainment — often carrying clear moral lessons. They narrated land disputes, banditry, and local injustices in compact, episodic verses that crystallized communal memory.

The “Corrido of Heraclio Bernal” (circa 1870–1880) exemplifies this. Bernal — cast as a bandit and a kind of proto-Robin Hood who opposed Díaz’s order — was immortalized in song as a brave, authentic figure unafraid of death.

Contemporary corridos were pamphlets set to music: instruments of social critique and folk memory.

Revolutionary corridos (1910–1920)

During the Mexican Revolution, the corrido flourished. Thousands of ballads recounted the deeds and deaths of Emiliano Zapata, Pancho Villa, Francisco I. Madero, Venustiano Carranza and countless local actors. Corridos appeared in newspapers and on loose broadsheets advertised as “new corridos,” and for many they were a primary source of news.

But the songs did more than report events: they authorized new imaginaries. Much as muralists refigured the nation — elevating peasants and laborers into civic icons — the corrido became the musical narrative of rural life, a sonic repository of popular values.

“La Adelita,” “Valentina,” the “Corrido de la Toma de Zacatecas,” and an adapted “La Cucaracha” (used to lampoon President Victoriano Huerta) entered a shared cultural lexicon that helped legitimate postrevolutionary ideologies.

1930 to 1960

El Pablote - Francisco El Charro Avitia - Primer Corrido de Narcotrafico "Narcocorrido" 2da version

Watch this video on YouTube

After the Revolution, Mexico experienced a profound transformation in its political, social and demographic landscape. Urban centers — especially Mexico City — began to attract large numbers of newcomers lured by promises of modernity and a better future, fueling rapid city growth and social change.

At the same time, rural Mexico acquired a romantic-epic image, with inhabitants stereotyped as “rough, direct, uncivilized, but kind-hearted.” This dual narrative — that of proud countryside and modern city — would shape Mexico’s cultural landscape for decades.

In both music and cinema, rural people were portrayed as humble yet proud, embodying virtues that contrasted with urban sophistication but also contributed to a shared national identity. To legitimize this collective vision, the Mexican state deployed culture as a tool of consolidation: Literature, cinema, theater and especially radio were used to craft and disseminate a unified image of Mexico.

Corridos, alongside genres such as huapango, banda, sones and rancheras, transitioned from local, fiery oral traditions into part of a broader, state-backed cultural repertoire — an effort to forge a common cultural fabric across regional boundaries.

This period also marks the emergence of the first narcocorridos, even as they continued to contain cautionary messages. The earliest recorded narcocorrido, “El Pablote” (1931), tells of Pablo González, known as “The Morphine King,” and functions primarily as a warning, emphasizing the tragic, often deadly consequences of criminal life rather than glorifying the outlaw.

Unlike the narcocorridos of later years, which would celebrate criminal figures and their deeds, these early songs served to dissuade people from following such dangerous paths. As radio and cinema standardized and disseminated these songs, local variations and rough edges of regional narratives were smoothed, turning them into a national storytelling tradition — yet still rooted in the social realities of marginalized communities.

1960 to 1980

By the late 1950s, many regarded the corrido as folklore in decline — a nostalgic but dated taste of Mexican peasantry gone by. Themes shifted toward migration, identity and the reality of drug trafficking.

The late 1980s brought a pivotal rupture in the figure of Chalino Sánchez. His unpolished delivery and raw narrative aesthetic cut through studio gloss; he popularized the practice of composing commissioned corridos for criminal figures and, crucially, normalized a celebratory tone toward illicit actors. That normalization carried risks — several singers and composers of the time paid with their lives.

Infamously, Sánchez is said to have been handed a note before performing his final song, informing him that he would be executed at the conclusion of his concert. A video of him receiving and reading the note, before launching into a spirited final performance, has become an important part of Mexican folklore. Regardless of the contents of the note, Sánchez was shot and killed immediately after leaving the stage.

2008 and the ‘altered corrido’

President Felipe Calderón’s militarized offensive against cartels in the late 2000s altered the cultural ecology. Corridos evolved from chronicling social life to entering criminal ecosystems.

New singers — sometimes commissioned by cartels, sometimes seeking notoriety — produced explicit songs that described organizational structures, operations and personalities. In some regions, corridos functioned as targeted messages among rival groups or as status instruments within criminal networks.

Chalino Sánchez - Alma Enamorada (En Vivo) Video Oficial con Letras

Watch this video on YouTube

Mainstream radio and public venues — conscious of safety and reputation — began to restrict such songs. The state framed these restrictions as public safety measures: Songs that normalize criminality can arguably promote recruitment or confer legitimacy on violent actors.

Yet the evidence for direct causality is weak. Cultural products shape imaginaries but do not by themselves produce armed actors. What bans often achieve is displacement: corridos migrate to pirate radio, local stations and online platforms where they can become more clandestine and, in some cases, operational.

New media and corridos

Digital platforms have proven more permissive than traditional broadcasters. Streaming, social networks and video sites have decentralized control, allowing subgenres to proliferate and cross borders. Corridos tumbados — a hybrid of trap, hip-hop cadence, autotune and corrido storytelling — illustrates the genre’s current elasticity. It speaks to urban youth experiences of identity, marginalization and aspiration.

The growth of this genre, and major singers such as Natanael Cano, Junior H, Fuerza Regida and Peso Pluma, reflects Mexico’s continuing appetite for corridos — more specifically, narcocorridos.

Peso Pluma’s appearance on “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” in 2024 represented the moment at which the genre became mainstream among not only Northern Mexicans but also younger Mexican-Americans on the other side of the border.

Made in Mexico: Corridos

Watch this video on YouTube

Beyond the obvious parallels to urban music genres in the United States, their success underscores a deeper truth: In a country of nearly 130 million, stark economic inequality (INEGI figures show only about 1.2 percent in the upper class while 56.6 percent fall into lower brackets) makes narratives of rapid ascent and alternative forms of capital especially resonant.

Do corridos cause violence?

The government’s justification for restricting corrido broadcasts is straightforward: Songs that glorify crime can normalize and celebrate violence. Cultural expressions do shape worldviews. But violence has multiple and deeper causes — poverty, impunity, institutional weakness and the lucrative rewards of illegal markets. To treat songs as primary causal agents is naive.

Moreover, suppression can backfire. Making content forbidden can enhance its allure and shift it into darker channels where it accrues different kinds of power.

Luis R Conriquez, Neton Vega - Si No Quieres No [Video Oficial]

Watch this video on YouTube

Why are narcorridos being censored?

The state’s veiled censorship is partly symbolic. Controlling the airwaves is a visible way to contest narratives that valorize criminal actors. But censorship addresses a symptom, not the structural conditions that make criminal economies attractive.

A more effective public strategy would combine cultural measures — support for alternative narratives, protection for artists and journalists, media literacy — with robust action on inequality, corruption and impunity.

The continuing importance of the corrido

The corrido endures because it is a living archive. It records who people were, whom they admired, whom they feared and whom they aspired to become. Attempts to erase the genre will not silence the stories; they will only change their modes of circulation and, perhaps, their social meanings. If policymakers seek to blunt the corrosive effects of glamorization, they must address both symbolic and structural realities. Otherwise, the corrido will continue to sing Mexico’s contradictions — unaltered in form, but perhaps louder in the shadows.

The corrido’s long road — from medieval jugglers to global streams — reminds us that music is both history and argument. It is a conversation about memory, identity and legitimacy. Censoring verses is a poor substitute for fixing the conditions that give those verses their force.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico’s tourism sector rushes to ensure cultural heritage remains compatible with 32-ounce margaritas
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUADALAJARA, Jalisco — Following new government data showing that 36.3% of foreign visitors now travel to Mexico primarily for its culture rather than its beaches, tourism officials confirmed Tuesday that the hospitality sector is working quickly to make millennia of heritage compatible with a 32-ounce blended margarita.

The figures, announced during the opening ceremony of the inaugural ITB Americas trade show in Guadalajara, revealed that cultural tourism now more than doubles the 15% to 16% share of visitors seeking traditional coastal vacations. To meet the shifting demand, hotel operators and tour planners across the country have unveiled a new “Conscious Cuervo” initiative designed to pair pre-Hispanic history, contemporary art and regional gastronomy with an uninterrupted supply of salted-rim cocktails.

“Travelers today want a deep, meaningful connection to Mexico’s living traditions, provided it is accompanied by crushed ice and a tiny paper parasol,” said Rodrigo Villalobos, a hospitality consultant attending the Guadalajara conference. “Our data shows that visitors are thrilled to explore a 16th-century convent or a neighborhood artisan market, as long as there is a frozen margarita waiting at the exit.”

Under the updated guidelines, several museums and archaeological zones are piloting “interpretive refreshment stations,” where audio guides automatically pause every 15 minutes to direct guests toward the nearest mixology cart. Meanwhile, culinary operators in Oaxaca and Mexico City reported high satisfaction scores after introducing “heritage flights,” allowing visitors to sample three distinct varieties of ancestral mezcal alongside a pitcher of strawberry margaritas large enough to require two hands.

Tourism analysts noted that the trend reflects a broader global shift in which travelers increasingly view cultural enrichment as an essential vacation component, ranking just ahead of pool access and slightly behind happy hour.

“I came to Mexico specifically for the architecture and the history, and learning about the Zapotec civilization while holding a yard-long plastic cup really brought the ruins to life,” said a visitor from Chicago before boarding a tour bus to a local weaving cooperative. “Honestly, it is nice to engage with the real country without having to give up blended tequila.”
