World.title: The two shipwrecked Spaniards who changed the history of Yucatán
World.content:
On Feb. 18, 1519, Hernán Cortés departed from Cuba on the great adventure that would end with the destruction of the Mexica Empire. By March, his small fleet sailed along the Yucatán coast, shores still uncharted by any Spaniard.

While on the island of Cozumel, he heard of a “bearded man” who lived some distance away. Excited that this sounded like a fellow Spaniard, he found villagers willing to take a message to this mysterious person.

Although the original letter has been lost, it was copied at the time, and we can be reasonably confident of its content:

“Noble sirs: Those of the island have assured me that there are in the country five or six men with beards and resembling us in all things. They are unable to give or tell me other indications, but from these I conjecture and hold certain that you are Spaniards. I and these gentlemen who go with me to settle and discover these lands urge that within six days from receiving this you come to us, without making further delay or excuse. If you shall come we will make due acknowledgment, and reward the good offices which this armada shall receive from you. I send a brigantine that you may come in it, and two boats for safety.”

A strange encounter off Cozumel

Unsure if the messengers would return, if the man they spoke of was still alive, or if he had even existed, Cortés continued his journey.

By chance, a leaking ship forced his return to Cozumel, and while repairs were underway, native canoes arrived from the mainland. Bernal Díaz del Castillo left a firsthand account of this encounter in his book, “The True History of the Conquest of New Spain.”

The canoes were greeted by a group of conquistadores out hunting, and one of their new arrivals stepped forward to greet them. The visitor was not immediately recognized as Spanish, for, as Díaz del Castillo writes, “they could not distinguish him from an Indian as he was naturally brown and he had his hair shorn like an Indian slave, and carried a paddle on his shoulder, he wore one old sandal and the other was tied to his belt, he had on a ragged old coat, and a worse loincloth with which he covered his nakedness.”

The man identified himself by shouting “God and Holy Mary and Seville!” in Spanish, and was immediately brought to Cortés.

The story of Gerónimo de Aguilar

Here, he introduced himself as Gerónimo de Aguilar.

Back in 1511, he had been aboard the Spanish caravel Santa María de la Barca, which had sunk in a storm while sailing from Darién to Santo Domingo. A dozen or so people had escaped the sinking vessel by clambering into a small boat. Without a sail, and with only minimal food and water, they drifted for 13 days on the open sea. The survivors had finally been washed ashore along the Yucatán coast, where they were captured by a Maya chief identified as Waymil.

Aguilar described how some of the survivors were immediately sacrificed and eaten by their captors, while he and a few others were caged “to be fattened” for the next festival.

This part of the story is doubtful, for while Maya society certainly made human sacrifices, there is no evidence of cannibalism. Similarly, no details are offered as to how Aguilar, along with a fellow prisoner, Gonzalo Guerrero, escaped from captivity. The most likely explanation is that they were passed on from their initial captors as a gift to a greater chieftain.

Two paths in captivity

The two survivors were separated and forced into slavery. Gerónimo de Aguilar was a religious man who refused all temptations to take a Maya wife, and he impressed Cortés by producing a worn prayer book that he had protected all those years. He saw Cortés as his long-awaited savior and happily joined the expedition as guide and translator.

Aguilar explained that his late arrival in Cozumel was due to trying to contact Gonzalo Guerrero. However, Guerrero, who lived some distance away, had declined to join him as he was “married and had three sons, and that his face was tattooed and his ears and lower lip were pierced.”

Aguilar served Cortés well and, after the conquest, settled in Mexico City, where he was granted land and slaves. He died in the city in 1531. He should not, it must be noted, be confused with Francisco de Aguilar, who later wrote “Brief Record of the Conquest of New Spain,” in which he also gave a passing mention of Cortés encountering a marooned Spaniard while on Cozumel.

A new attempt at conquest

A decade after Cortés had subdued the Mexica, the Maya remained stubbornly independent, but eventually Spain once again set her eyes on this world of dry scrub and thorny forests.

With this, our story switches from Hernán Cortés to Francisco de Montejo.

At this point, Montejo was in his 50s and had spent much of his adult life in the Americas. He had sailed with Cortés, for which he had been rewarded with mines and haciendas. Having been granted a charter by Charles V to “explore, conquer and colonize the islands of Cozumel and the Yucatán,” he reached Cozumel in September 1527. From there the party crossed the channel to the mainland, where they established a small settlement.

The Yucatán, however, would not be an easy conquest, and sickness, the lack of water and natives on the defensive saw the colony collapse. This was the start of a protracted struggle that would bring the Spaniards numerous setbacks, and it would be 170 years before the last independent Maya state finally fell.

The renegade Spaniard

When Montejo heard of a renegade Spaniard living with the Maya, he correctly assumed this was Gonzalo Guerrero, with whom Aguilar had been shipwrecked 16 years earlier.

While Gerónimo de Aguilar had been a priest, Guerrero was a soldier with experience from Spain’s numerous wars against the Moors and in Italy. Unlike the pious Aguilar, Guerrero had been more willing to make the best of his situation.

After 16 years with the Maya people, he was not only still alive but had used his military experience to reach a position of authority in his adopted home.

Frustrated at their lack of progress, and anxious to seek local expertise, Montejo sent Guerrero a letter reminding him of his Christian faith, and offering his friendship and a complete pardon if he would join them. Guerrero replied by writing on the back of the letter that he could not leave his lord because he was enslaved, “even though I am married and have a wife and children. I remember God, and you, Sir, and the Spaniards have a good friend in me.”

Historical accounts and condemnation

The use of the word “slave” has been questioned, as Guerrero seems to have achieved a high military rank, but there is no reason he could not have gained promotion while remaining the property of his lord.

For an account of this part of the story, we rely on the writings of Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés. After spending much of his life in the Americas, Oviedo returned to Spain, where he wrote “La Natural Historia de las Indias” in 1526 and “Historia General de las Indias,” which was published in 1535.

Oviedo was an eyewitness to much of what he recorded and is considered a “good” historian for conducting careful interviews with other veterans of the American campaigns. Where the facts can be checked, his work appears accurate, with none of the wandering into fantasy that marks many other travel accounts of this age.

Where Oviedo is at fault is not in his recounting of events, but in offering judgment on other people’s actions. He was obsessed with Guerrero’s physical transformation and his adoption of Maya culture, writing, “This Gonzalo, the sailor, had already been converted into an Indian and was much worse than an Indian. He was married to an Indian woman. His ears and tongue were disfigured by sacrifice, and his body decorated and painted like that of an Indian; and he had a wife and children.”

A warrior’s final battle and legacy

Oviedo attributes Guerrero’s reluctance to join his fellow Spaniards to shame about his appearance and what he had become. He does not consider that the man might have had genuine affection toward his wife and children.

Oviedo also felt the need to explain how a “primitive” people such as those of the Yucatán could have proved so resistant to Spanish arms. The answer, he felt, could only be that they had help, and the villain was obviously that lost soul Gonzalo Guerrero. Oviedo credited Guerrero with coordinating Maya resistance to Montejo in 1528 and being behind the ambush of Alonso de Dávila’s forces in 1531.

On Aug. 14, 1536, Andrés de Cereceda, governor of troublesome provinces in modern Honduras, wrote to Spain, informing the king that a party of 50 war canoes had arrived to support the uprising of the local people. They had paddled up the Ulúa River to Ticamaya, where there had been a fierce battle. During the fighting, a heavily tattooed white man had been killed by a shot from an arquebus. This was almost certainly Gonzalo Guerrero.

Oviedo wrote of Guerrero as a traitor, but that viewpoint has changed over the years. Today Guerrero is celebrated as a freedom fighter and father of the mestizo population. He has been the hero of historical novels, most notably Eugenio Aguirre’s bestseller “Gonzalo Guerrero,” and there is an impressive bronze statue of him and his family in the Yucatán resort town of Akumal. Whether a hero of the Maya or a traitor to the Spanish, he certainly appears to have been a brave and honorable man.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: ‘He woke us up’: The man who changed the map of Mexico (Part I)
World.content:
In my family, we called him Super Carlos. Together with the Wixárika people and his team of dedicated attorneys, he changed the map of Mexico.

Carlos Chávez Reyes, who died in October at the age of 72, was a pioneer in Mexico’s Indigenous rights movement. Working alongside the leadership of the Wixárika — the Indigenous group also known as the Huichols — and a team of attorneys, researchers and technicians, he led the recovery of 65,000 hectares of stolen land, according to his son Cristian — and trained a generation, Indigenous and not, to carry on the work. The effort also recovered land in the disputed borderlands between Jalisco and Nayarit — territory lost to ranchers backed by the government in Tepic, which prompted the Nayarit governor to declare Chávez persona non grata and suggest he was Subcomandante Marcos.

“Carlos Chávez educated us. He woke us up when we were terrified — when we had no knowledge, no wisdom to defend ourselves,” said Maurilio Haiwiye Ramírez, general coordinator of the Wixárika Regional Council. When Carlos arrived, he added, “there was no one who could speak on our behalf.”

Chávez was one of a generation who chose to drop out of the system and look to Nature — and, increasingly, to those who lived closest to it — for answers.

As UC-Berkeley geographer Diana Negrín tells it, Carlos belonged to a first generation of “huicholeros de corazón” (“Huichol supporters of the heart”) who came to the sierra as collaborators rather than researchers or bureaucrats. Among them were Rocío Echevarría and Diana Negrín’s own parents, Juan and Yvonne.

The late 1970s were a hinge for the Wixárika communities. “The first roads had been built, and the logging companies were coming in with a vengeance,” explained Diana.

In 1977, at the age of 23, Chávez met Eulalia González Ávalos, his beloved Lala; together the two had five sons, each of whom carries on his legacy. Tunuary and Cristian, his twin sons, have gone on to earn degrees in environmental science, deepening and broadening the territorial defense that their father began.

Carlos and Lala launched a natural medicine project in the countryside outside of Guadalajara, exploring the healing properties of plants and treating people for miles around. His search for plant medicines led him to the Wixárika, and to the mara’akate (shamans).

Rocío Echeverria, a registered nurse who ran the health center in San Andrés Cohamiata for six years before founding Casa Huichol, remembers those days fondly, having logged many miles with Carlos.

“Those were crazy, crazy times,” she recalled. In their first journeys, the highways to Wixárika territories had not yet been built, so reaching the communities meant a plane and then days on foot. There they accompanied the people to other dimensions, sitting around Tatewari, Grandfather Fire, through long nights of music, dance, sacrifice and vision.

They walked with local medicine men and women through the Western Sierra Madre, learning the Wixárika pharmacopeia. But the most important medicine did not grow in the Sierra Madre. Hikuri, the Wixárika word for peyote, is gathered in their annual pilgrimages to Wirikuta, one of the five most sacred sites in their millennial cosmology.

In those journeys, Carlos and Rocío observed the terrible poverty of the people, a bare subsistence that left them vulnerable to hunger and common illnesses that could quickly turn deadly with the lack of care. And as Carlos himself told the story to this reporter on a long-ago journey to the Sierra in his trusty grey Toyota pickup truck, the people told him repeatedly that what they really needed was their land — the best land, taken by neighboring ranchers to harvest timber, graze cattle and, in the worst cases, grow marijuana and poppies for the cartels.

They needed an advocate, not an herbalist. In his travels, he met Juan Negrín, another pioneering figure who came to the same conclusions. Juan, roughly a decade older, had already built the organizations through which Chávez learned institutional work, and the two joined forces. In 1990, he helped found the Asociación Jalisciense de Apoyo a Grupos Indígenas (AJAGI), which would become the legal and technical backbone of the Wixárika land struggle for the next three decades.

Paul Liffman, an anthropologist who served as an expert witness in a number of AJAGI’s land cases over two decades, remembers Carlos describing the realization himself. He had begun believing healing came through medicine. “But then he understood that for people to be healthy, they first had to eat well. And to eat well, they needed maize. And to have maize, they needed land.” The illness and the landlessness were the same problem.

Under a blanket in the back of a pickup

The danger was not abstract. Yvonne Negrín, Juan’s widow, learned that a $25,000 bounty had been placed on her husband’s life. “Every time my husband went to the sierras, I didn’t know if he would come back.”

A decade later, as the Wixárika community of Bancos de San Hipólito in Durango planned an amparo against illegal logging, Maurilio Haiwiye Ramírez was hiding Chávez under a blanket in the back of a pickup so the ranchers who controlled the road through San Juan Peyotán would not see him.

“We hid him because we didn’t want the mestizos who were against us to know,” Ramírez said. Meetings were held at night for the same reason: “So no one could find out.”

The danger was not abstract to me, either. In the winter of 2010, as I rode with Carlos through the night toward Bancos de San Hipólito, he told me plainly that the road ahead ran through territory controlled by narcos, and that if I wanted to get out and run now, he would understand.

He said it wryly, the way a man says something he has said before, to other passengers, on other nights. “Vamonos,” I said. He put the truck in gear and drove.

Five little boys and a washboard

What held was Lala. Yvonne Negrín remembers driving past the couple’s place in the countryside and seeing her at a washbasin, “scrubbing diapers on a washboard for five little boys,” the clothesline so full she never forgot it. Tunuary described parents who never let their children see the strain — not when Lala was ill, not when Carlos was. “They decided to resolve it themselves, so that we could grow up without having to resolve their affairs.”

The children kept codes and false names; Carlos saved each of them in his phone under someone else’s name, and the habit outlasted the danger. What healed the family, Tunuary said, was Wirikuta. He dropped out of school at 15 and asked his mother to let him go to the desert. She put him on a train.

A seat at the Zapatista table

In 1996, when the Zapatista army and the Mexican government sat down in Chiapas to negotiate the terms of constitutional recognition for Indigenous rights, Carlos Chávez and the lawyer Ángeles Arcos, of AJAGI, were named advisors to the dialogue tables held in San Andrés Sakamchén de los Pobres. The Zapatista uprising two years earlier — an armed rebellion in the south of the country that captured the attention of Mexico and the international community and placed Indigenous rights at the center of the national agenda — had turned the negotiation into a national event, and the list of advisors was published in the national press.

“Without a doubt, the Indigenous movement was never the same after the Zapatista uprising,” Arcos said. “It put the question of constitutional recognition of the collective rights of the pueblos at the center of the federal agenda.”

What the Wixáritari brought to those tables were territorial claims argued under AJAGI’s most powerful weapon: Convention 169, the International Labour Organization treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples’ rights, which Mexico had ratified in 1990. What they took away was something less tangible: the Wixárika delegations traveled to Chiapas and spent time with the Zapatistas, and Arcos remembers it as a period of mutual enrichment.

“The Wixáritari occupied a very important place in the demands the Indigenous movement put to the Mexican government,” she said. “Their territorial struggle was iconic, and the EZ (Zapatistas) also showed them new forms of struggle.”

‘He didn’t want to be indispensable’

What made Chávez effective was not only conviction but method. Agustín del Castillo, who has covered agrarian conflicts for top Guadalajara media outlets for 38 years, argues that his contribution was strategic rather than moral. “He gave the struggle a component of intelligence, of a sense of strategy,” del Castillo said. “Many can fight. Fighting with intelligence, with strategy — that’s the merit I attribute to Carlos.”

What distinguished Chávez, del Castillo said, was that he deliberately made himself unnecessary.

“He didn’t want to be indispensable. He wanted the communities to take their own destiny in hand.” By the time of Wirikuta, del Castillo said, “I no longer saw him in the leading role he had in the ’90s. I saw him as an accompanist” — and that, he insists, was the triumph of the model rather than its failure.

What Liffman remembers is a seemingly fearless man who was “as much a moral as an intellectual example” — and he doubts the communities would have trusted him otherwise.

The communities describe something more concrete. Ramón González López, a community member from Tuxpan de Bolaños, remembers the workshops on Convention 169 and the agrarian law. “That was what opened our eyes,” he said. “We realized we had many rights — and many obligations, too.”

The money was modest and came from far away. Outi Hakkarainen, a Finnish researcher who met Chávez in 1995 while studying civil society in Jalisco, spent two decades channeling funding to AJAGI — much of it from a student union at the University of Turku.

“Our money was not much,” she said, “but it was essential for this work,” because it could be directed at what most donors avoided: litigation over land tenure.

She was candid that the finances were chaotic. “We understood that his way of working was chaotic too, but we couldn’t change it.” What she never doubted was that the funds went where they were meant to.

Lalo Guzmán, who worked alongside Chávez for years in the Wirikuta Defense Front and has defended the desert for decades, rejects the accusations that have circulated about the money. He is a witness, he said, that the family never enriched itself — that everything Carlos raised went into the struggle, sometimes at the cost of his own household.

“That will sound bad to others,” Guzmán said. “To me it speaks well of him.”

Quetzal Prado, a lawyer who joined AJAGI in December 2012, described an organization built around a division of labor: a technical team, a legal team, and Chávez holding the political and strategic vision.

“You present him with a problem and he was very good at understanding the whole broad picture of it — not just the present moment, but how we can project it into the future.” She recalled leaving meetings and having Chávez decode them afterward: “No, this person told us such-and-such, because what he actually means is this.”

Raymundo Vázquez Sánchez, an agrarian lawyer from San Sebastián Teponahuaxtlán, described the years before AJAGI as stalled. Petitions went nowhere, and the community had no legal footing.

What Carlos left behind, he said, was a generation that could argue its own case.

Next week, Part II: ‘They don’t see with their eyes’ — Carlos Chávez’s last 15 years, from the fight for Wirikuta to the fire that sustained him.

Tracy L. Barnett is an independent journalist and founder of The Esperanza Project. She worked with Carlos Chávez on the Wirikuta Defense Front’s communications team for two years, and loved him and his family like her own. She counts him, as do countless others, as a mentor and a guide.

World.title: From the archive: A comprehensive guide to Mexican hangover cures
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in December 2024 — explores the distinctive approaches taken by Mexicans when it comes to curing a hangover.

If you’ve been in Mexico for any amount of time, you’ve no doubt noticed something: Mexicans do not shy away from drinking.

When I first arrived, this was a shock to me, though I knew “in theory” to expect it.

My own family leaned puritanical when it came to any mind-altering substances; drinking, even a little, was never not considered deviant. There was hardly ever alcohol on the table, and once when I found cigarettes in my mom’s purse, I almost fainted, pearls tightly clutched.

Fast forward to the beginning of my first year in Mexico. I remember staring open-mouthed as the study abroad program director ordered a beer with his lunch. What?! As far as I knew, one beer could get you fall-down drunk and into all sorts of trouble.

Learning to drink, the Mexican way

Ah, such innocent times. As the year wore on, I loosened up a bit. I started having a little beer at parties, not knowing any better when it came to quality. I loved a good paloma on a night out. I was into wine for a while too when living in Querétaro, where nearby Tequisquiapan was an up-and-coming producer. And straight tequila and mezcal, I’ve loved from the first sips.

But as all of us who are old enough know, learning to “hold our liquor” takes time and practice. After sleeping a few times with one foot on the ground to keep the room from spinning or rushing to the bathroom when our bodies have had enough, most people are incredibly motivated to prevent the sick feelings that come after too much and that can last hours to days.

It speaks to the tastiness and inhibition-shedding qualities of alcohol that we don’t just give it up after a nasty experience, doesn’t it?

Instead, we try to game the system of our body’s response. Is this the part where I need to say that Mexico News Daily does not condone drinking excessively? Well, we don’t, I guess.

Anyway. Because most Mexicans really like to drink and do not have the kinds of puritanical views of it that some to the north do, hangover cures are an important aspect of cultural knowledge.

And besides, they can even be an extension of the fun!

So without further ado, let’s take a look at some of Mexico’s favorite remedies.

First, plan ahead

Before you start out on your imbibing, plan what you’re going to drink. If it’s a fancy affair, have some fancy drinks. “Entre más fino, menos cruda,” one friend told me (the fancier it is, the less of a hangover it will cause).

The exception to this, apparently, is red wine, no matter how fancy it is. Most of my friends here have told me that it’s a surefire way to wind up with a hangover the next day.

Mezcal, on the other hand, has a reputation for not causing hangovers at all. I have a feeling that I don’t actually believe that, but honestly I can’t remember, so take from it what you will.

Not mixing the type of alcohol you have in one sitting is also considered a good strategy. If it’s beer, stick to beer; if it’s tequila, stick to tequila. You get the idea.

And finally, drinking lots of water is a good idea all the time, but especially if you’re drinking lots of other stuff as well. I don’t drink a lot personally, but if I have more than one of something, I’ll make sure to have a big glass of water in the middle. So far, it’s proven a good strategy.

Shoot, I got carried away and didn’t prepare at all

Well, my friends, you’re not alone. Luckily, plenty of other people have been in your shoes and shared their hard-won lessons. Especially luckily, most of them involve food!

Let’s have a look at the traditional cures:

A michelada

Now, if you ask me, curing a hangover with even a little alcohol is not a good idea. But it’s not just beer, and Mexicans really have a lot of faith in it. From this article on the famous michelada: “Apart from the flavor, we argue that Clamato contains electrolytes that can rehydrate us, vitamin C from the lime juice that can strengthen our immune system, antioxidants from the tomato that can help maintain our youthfulness, and the capsaicin from the chili that can help keep us alert. While these claims haven’t been scientifically proven, we feel that our health improves every time we drink it.”

I mean, I guess, but I’d still personally classify it as one of the grossest drinks I’ve tried. Bleh.

Suero

Now this, I can get a bit more behind. “Suero” can mean a lot of things, but it’s basically electrolytes. This could be in the form of Gatorade or Powerade, but it could also be a simple marinero: mineral water with salt and lime. That’s something I drink anyway because I like it, so I’m going to go ahead and count some free health points for myself.

Alka-Seltzer Boost

I haven’t personally tried this one, but I have a friend who swears by it. When you’re feeling like death, though, anything’s worth a try!

Hearty, spicy food

Through the power of corn and chiles, you will come back to life! And if you don’t, you’ll at least get some good, sturdy food in your stomach. Chilaquiles are an incredibly popular choice, as is a nice, spicy pozole.

Seafood is also a popular choice, especially if you choose a nice shrimp cocktail, which actually has some of the same ingredients as a michelada. Maybe they’re on to something!

In the end, the best cure might actually be the memory of a past experience. But in case you get caught up and forget, we’ve got your back!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum in China, Rodríguez at the mic and a kingpin behind bars
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent most of the week in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. That left Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez running the mañaneras from Monday on. The Minnesota Vikings, meanwhile, were pumping thin air into a chamber in the Midwest to prepare for Sunday night’s kickoff in Mexico City.

It was a relatively calm week at home while the president was abroad. That changed Friday night, when Mexican special forces captured an alleged drug kingpin on the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted list, sparking violence in Sinaloa.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Nov. 16? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum touches down in Shenzhen

Sheinbaum left Mexico City’s airport at 11 p.m. on Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana. She then boarded China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen. It was another commercial flight, in keeping with the austerity symbolism started by her predecessor. She arrived at 11:30 a.m. Monday local time and went straight to the Tequila Coyote’s restaurant to meet Mexicans living in China, whom she called “extraordinary.” The economy-class journey also struck a chord online: Bloomberg reported that a hashtag about her arrival was seen 10 million times on Weibo.

Sheinbaum pitches Plan México at APEC

In a 13-minute speech at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday, Sheinbaum told more than 2,000 business and political representatives that Mexico “guarantees conditions for investment.” She said the government and private companies expect to invest US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030. She also described the plan as having a “humanist vision.”

Mexico News Daily noted that foreign direct investment hit a record of almost $35 billion in the first half of 2026, though growth was only 2.1%. Insecurity, USMCA uncertainty and the recent judicial reform are seen as deterrents. On Thursday, she gave a four-minute address at the Leaders’ Meeting, calling this “a decisive moment for humanity.” Mexico will host APEC in 2028.

Meetings with Xi, Carney, Trump and more

Sheinbaum told Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday that her visit marks “a new era” in bilateral ties, focused on science, technology, clean energy and health. Neither side’s readout mentioned Mexico’s new tariffs on Chinese goods. She also revealed she had asked Xi for a panda for Chapultepec Zoo.

She also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that day, and both reaffirmed support for renewing the USMCA. Carney said bilateral trade is up 18% this year.

On Wednesday came the one many were watching: a roughly 20-minute meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, her first formal in-person talks with him. Sheinbaum said trade negotiations are “very far along” but gave no timeline for a deal. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said 56 technical meetings have been held. Trump’s recent tariff threat over the migrant caravan went unmentioned, and the two agreed to meet again at next month’s G20 summit at Mar-a-Lago.

She also met leaders from Vietnam, Australia, Singapore and Peru, plus the IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva. At her closing press conference, Sheinbaum called the trip “very productive and very successful” but said Mexico has no plans for a free trade agreement with China.

Rodríguez takes the mañanera podium

With the president away, Interior Minister Rodríguez led this week’s morning press conferences. On Monday, the mañanera featured World Bank data showing that Mexico’s monetary poverty rate fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025, with 17.3 million fewer people in poverty projected by the end of 2026. Officials also touted a CB Global Data poll putting Sheinbaum’s approval at 69.8%, the highest in Latin America.

Sheinbaum joined Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday’s mañanera by video link, and on Thursday, Rodríguez praised her boss’s “composure” and “firmness, without confrontation or subservience.”

Mexico ranks fourth in APEC tech exports

An APEC report showed that Mexico ranks fourth among APEC economies in the share of exports that are medium- and high-tech goods, at 70.6%. Only Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea rank higher. Mexico sits ahead of China (61.6%), the United States (46.5%) and Canada (31.7%). APEC projects regional growth of 3.4% this year and 3.1% in 2027.

Revolution Day parade

Hours after landing from China, Sheinbaum presided over the parade marking the 116th anniversary of the Mexican Revolution. She invoked the 1917 Constitution and defended democratic freedoms. She also accused political opponents and foreign interests of trying to weaken her administration and delegitimize the 2027 midterms. Pageant floats and military contingents then rolled through the Zócalo and down Paseo de la Reforma.

What’s going on with the peso?

The peso sank past 19 per dollar on Thursday, hitting 19.04, its weakest level in 17 months. Bloomberg tied the move to Banxico’s dovish stance, after a 25-basis-point cut to 6.25%, and expectations of another Fed hike in December. That would narrow the interest-rate gap that supports the carry trade. The peso is down about 5.5% this year.

The November MND Peso Index™ offers some context. It found the peso 4.2% undervalued at 18.67 per dollar, versus a 0.7% undervaluation in October. The swing was driven almost entirely by depreciation.

Mexico and US lose measles-free status

The Pan American Health Organization revoked the measles-free status of Mexico, the United States and Bolivia after 12 months of continuous transmission. Canada lost its status a year earlier. Mexico has recorded 20,601 cases over 2025 and 2026, but only 14 are currently active, down from a February peak of 1,314. The government aims to end the outbreak in the second half of 2027 and regain recognition in 2028.

Migrant caravan trudges north

A caravan of about 1,500 migrants left Tapachula last Tuesday, and Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if it isn’t stopped. By Tuesday, it had shrunk to 781 people in Mapastepec, Chiapas, as migration officials urged people to go home. On Thursday, Rodríguez responded to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s remarks by saying Mexico “will continue detaining” people involved in smuggling.

Former Iguala mayor sentenced

José Luis Abarca, Iguala’s mayor during the 2014 Ayotzinapa tragedy, was sentenced to 60 years on Nov. 10 by a federal judge in Tamaulipas. He and 25 co-defendants, including the police chief, were convicted of six counts of aggravated homicide and attempted murder. Those charges stem from the attack on a bus carrying the Los Avispones soccer team. Abarca is already serving 20- and 92-year sentences. His lawyer argued police control had been ceded to then-Gov. Ángel Aguirre.

‘El Chapo Isidro’ captured in Sinaloa

Friday night’s big news came from Sinaloa. Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” and two other leaders of his organization.

The FBI lists Meza Flores on its Top 10 Most Wanted list and had offered up to US $5 million for information leading to his arrest. Agents came under fire from gunmen using explosives during the raid in Guasave, according to the Defense Ministry. Violence erupted afterward, with civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game and vehicles burning on a highway near Los Mochis. The Mexican government said U.S. intelligence helped, giving few details. The three were flown to Mexico City.

Looking ahead

The aftermath in Sinaloa is the story to watch, as violence following the capture may not end quickly. On trade, Sheinbaum and Trump are due to meet again at the G20 in Florida next month. Sheinbaum has said talks are “very far along,” but no deal date has been set, and the U.S. has still not agreed to any tariff reductions for Mexican automobiles, steel or aluminum. Financial markets, meanwhile, will be watching the Fed’s December meeting and Banxico’s decision on Dec. 17 for clues about whether the peso’s slide continues. Back at the Estadio Azteca, the Vikings and 49ers will find out Sunday whether their different altitude strategies paid off.

PERU · EARTHQUAKE

A truck driver hit by falling rocks is the only known death from the magnitude 6.7 earthquake that struck Peru’s central Andes on Friday 20 November 2026. The Geophysical Institute of Peru (IGP), the national quake monitor, is still logging aftershocks, two of them near magnitude 5.

The quake hit at 7:09 in the evening, Peru time, the same clock time as on the US East Coast, about 30 km north-west of the town of Junín. The shaking was felt as far away as Lima, the capital.

Key Facts Who Indeci, Peru’s civil-defence agency, confirms one death, a truck driver killed by falling rocks.

What A magnitude 6.7 quake, about 130 km deep, shook Peru’s central Andes.

When Friday 20 November 2026, 7:09 p.m. Peru time; aftershocks continue.

Peru’s central Andes are counting damage and listening for aftershocks after a deep quake that killed one driver and cracked more than a hundred homes.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Peru earthquake Email address Follow

IGP chief Hernando Tavera said the quake came from deformation inside the Nazca plate, the slab of ocean floor that slides under South America, and put its depth at about 130 km. On 18 July 2026 a much weaker but shallow quake in Chupaca, also in Junín, which the IGP first measured at magnitude 5.1, killed five people, Indeci reported, and the agency pointed to the shallow depth and homes built of adobe, or sun-dried mud brick.

Indeci, the National Institute of Civil Defence, said on Saturday 21 November that its chief, Brigadier General Luis Enrique Vásquez Guerrero, had sent a rapid-response team to Junín and ordered 500 donated food baskets moved by road with the UN World Food Programme. Asked over the weekend whether a bigger quake could follow, Tavera said nobody can know what will happen tomorrow, but that the aftershocks should be part of a return to calm.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 53.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The dead man was at the wheel of a tanker truck when rocks from a slide set off by the quake fell on it at Mati Chico, on the boundary of the Huánuco districts of San Rafael and Ambo, according to preliminary inquiries. He was taken to a health post in Ambo and then to the Hermilio Valdizán regional hospital in Huánuco, where the health ministry’s emergency centre confirmed his death.

Junín’s regional government, adding up reports from district mayors, counted 10 injured, 105 homes affected and 22 uninhabitable on 22 November, plus two damaged schools and six damaged health facilities. Indeci’s emergency centre counts one dead, 15 injured and 853 damnificados, people who lost their homes or belongings, in its 22 November update, and both bodies call their numbers preliminary.

In San Pedro de Cajas, 23 homes are affected and five are unfit to live in, while Palca counts 36 affected and seven unfit. Elio Zevallos, mayor of the Junín district, said 40 homes have cracked walls, most of them in Ulcumayo, where “the quake was quite strong” and “the houses suffered more structural damage.”

In Huancayo, the largest city of the Junín region, residents reported cracks in walls and some falling plaster, according to the regional authorities. People in Satipo and Chanchamayo, also in Junín, left buildings and gathered in public spaces as a precaution.

The damage is concentrated in highland farming districts, and the capital’s services came through largely intact. Indeci said crews cleared slide debris from roads in Huánuco, Junín and Lima, the airports kept operating, and power was fully restored at the Zapallal substation.

Schools with visible damage are cordoned off until safety inspections are done, the Education Ministry said through Indeci. For families and travellers with plans in the Andes, that means school closures and occasional road work are likelier than any wider disruption.

Tavera said that “neither we nor anyone has control over nature” and urged households to rehearse an evacuation drill. The regional government says its figures will change as more districts file reports.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was Lima damaged by the Junín quake?

Lima felt the shaking, but Indeci says its airports and urban transit kept running. The damage listed so far is in the highland regions.

Could a bigger quake follow?

IGP’s chief says nobody can predict that and calls the aftershocks part of a return to calm. He urges every family to practise an evacuation drill.

Who counts the damage?

Indeci’s national emergency centre consolidates reports from regional and district authorities. Its figures can change as new reports arrive.

World.title: LatAm and Africa Prediction Markets, Week of 23 Nov
World.content:
Inflation bets moved most this week in South Africa and Brazil, while bets on a US strike on Colombia and an early Venezuelan election faded.

File photo: the Hillbrow skyline in Johannesburg, where South Africa’s inflation rose to 5.2% in October.

Prediction Markets: Latin America and Africa

Traders on Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction exchange, now give 59.9% to South Africa ending 2026 with inflation of 4.7–5.0%, up from 38.0% a week earlier. Our daily readings show the jump on 20 and 21 November, after Statistics South Africa reported on Wednesday 18 November that October inflation rose to 5.2% from 4.5%, though no source says what moved traders.

It matters to US readers because inflation steers central bank interest rates, and rates drive the bonds, currencies and US-listed shares of emerging markets. This report covers 15 to 23 November across Latin America and Africa, and every price is a bet, not a poll.

Key Facts South Africa inflation. The 4.7–5.0% bracket for 2026 rose from 38.0% to 59.9% on Polymarket.

Inflation bets moved most this week in South Africa and Brazil, while bets on a US strike on Colombia and an early Venezuelan election faded.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction markets are exchanges where people buy and sell contracts on future events, and a price of 60 cents means traders give that outcome roughly a 60% chance. We read all prices below on Monday 23 November 2026 at 05:30 Eastern Time (ET), which is 10:30 UTC, and “a week earlier” refers to our snapshot taken 6 to 8 days before.

Volume means all money traded on a market since it opened, unless we say 24 hours or one week. Polymarket is a crypto-based exchange, while Kalshi is a US exchange regulated in the United States by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

In Plain English Bracket: a band of possible values, such as inflation of 4.7–5.0%. Each bracket is its own contract, so prices need not add up to 100%. Statistics South Africa and IBGE: the official statistics offices of South Africa and Brazil. Copom: the committee of Brazil’s central bank that sets its benchmark rate, the Selic. Thinly traded: under US$50,000 behind a market, so a few traders can move the price.

The Week’s Biggest Moves

South Africa: inflation bets climb toward 5%

Polymarket’s market on South Africa’s consumer inflation for the 12 months to December 2026 (US$156,849 in total, US$390 in the last 24 hours) now puts 59.9% on 4.7–5.0%, up 21.9 points. The bracket above 5.0% stands at 26.4%, and 4.4–4.7% fell from 21.5% to 9.8%.

Statistics South Africa, the national statistics office, said on Wednesday 18 November that consumer prices rose 5.2% in October from 4.5% in September, the highest since May 2024 (SAnews, the government news agency, 18 November 2026). Annual fuel inflation reached 42.9%, up from 27.9%, and transport added 2.1 percentage points to the headline rate.

The market resolves on the December reading, due on Wednesday 20 January 2027 under the market’s rules. October’s 5.2% already sits above the 4.7–5.0% bracket, and Governor Lesetja Kganyago said on Thursday 19 November that “[h]igh inflation prints, over 5%, are expected to persist into early next year”, so we cannot say why traders favour the lower bracket.

Our earlier report on South Africa’s high-inflation odds tracks the same market.

Brazil: bettors lean toward 5% inflation

Polymarket’s market on Brazil’s 2026 inflation, measured by the IPCA price index (US$258,410 in total, US$3,417 in 24 hours), gives 67.8% to 5.00–5.49%, up 19.0 points from 48.8%. The 4.50–4.99% bracket stands at 13.8% and 5.50–5.99% at 13.8%.

IBGE, Brazil’s statistics office, said on Thursday 12 November that the IPCA rose 0.14% in October, bringing 12-month inflation to 4.63% and 4.10% for the year to date (Agência Gov, the federal news service, 12 November 2026). By our arithmetic, reaching 5.00% by December needs prices to rise roughly 0.9% over November and December combined.

That release came before our snapshot window, and we found no named source linking this week’s move to a new event. Our report on economists’ recession warnings covers the growth backdrop.

Venezuela: oil bets rise, election-date bets fall

Polymarket’s market on Venezuelan crude output (US$190,560 in total) gives 40.5% to the 1.2 million barrels a day line, up from 21.5%, while the 1.3 million line fell from 13.5% to 6.0%. The rules say the market resolves Yes if output reaches the listed level in any month of 2026 in the Monthly Oil Market Report of OPEC, the oil producers’ group, using secondary sources.

We found no reported trigger for either move, and the next test is the next monthly report of OPEC, the oil producers’ group. Our report on Venezuela’s 84 oil and gas agreements gives the policy background.

In the market on when Venezuela’s next presidential election is scheduled (US$685,699 in total), a date set by 31 March 2027 fell from 28.0% to 16.5%. A date by 30 June 2027 stands at 41.0%, by 31 December 2027 at 52.0% and by 31 December 2026 at 11.0%.

Acting president Delcy Rodríguez promised elections on Thursday 29 October but named no date, according to Emol, a Chilean newspaper. The market resolves only when a date is officially scheduled, not when the vote happens, and our report on an ex-mayor demanding a date has the local debate.

Colombia and the US: strike bets fade

Polymarket’s market on a US strike on Colombia by 31 December (US$2.38 million in total) fell from 17.5% to 4.5%. We found no report of a new US strike threat or of a specific de-escalation in November, so we give no trigger.

Smaller moves

Maduro’s prison term: traders give “no prison time” 60.5%, down from 67.5%, and 60 years or more 22.5%, on US$1.12 million in total. Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela’s ousted president, has a US trial set for 1 June 2027 before Judge Alvin Hellerstein in New York, according to JURIST, a US legal news site (July 2026).

Latin America

Brazil’s year-end central bank decision looks settled to traders. Polymarket’s market on Copom’s December decision (US$150,557 in total, US$73,095 in the week) gives no change 86.5%, a quarter-point rise 4.9% and a quarter-point cut 2.4%.

Mexico’s central bank, Banxico, is thinly traded for December at US$34,244, with no change at 97.4% and a quarter-point cut at 2.5%. Brazil’s January and March decisions each hold under US$22,000 in total, so we do not read them.

Venezuela has the region’s busiest markets. Polymarket gives opposition leader María Corina Machado 69.5% to win the next presidential election (US$74,553 in total) and Delcy Rodríguez 11.5%.

The market on who leads Venezuela at the end of 2026 has drawn about US$101 million in total and about US$0.7 million this week. Its rules name whoever “officially holds” the post of head of state, and it prices Nicolás Maduro at 90.8% and Rodríguez at 8.5%.

A separate de facto leader market gives Rodríguez 97.5%, and we have not checked why the two differ. Cuba has some of the region’s busiest markets.

Traders give 6.5% to US military action against Cuba by 31 December (US$7.78 million in total) and 7.9% to President Miguel Díaz-Canel leaving power (US$2.36 million), and a US–Cuba diplomatic meeting by 30 November stands at 43.5% on thinly traded US$41,641.

Africa

African markets are thinner than Latin American ones, so a few orders can move them. South Africa’s inflation market is the busiest, and Statistics South Africa’s December reading will settle it.

Governor Lesetja Kganyago said on Thursday 19 November that South Africa’s central bank, the South African Reserve Bank, held its repo rate, the main lending rate, at 7.25%. “After two policy adjustments this year, and with a moderately restrictive policy stance, we decided to pause for now,” he said, and four of seven committee members backed the hold while three wanted a quarter-point rise (SAnews, 19 November 2026).

In Nigeria, Polymarket gives President Bola Tinubu 69.0% and Peter Obi, the 2023 Labour Party candidate, 26.0% to win the presidential election (US$163,984 in total). The vote is set for Saturday 16 January 2027 by the electoral commission, INEC, according to Guardian Nigeria, a Lagos newspaper.

In Mali, traders give 18.0% to military leader Assimi Goïta being out of office by 30 June 2027 on US$65,441, and 4.2% by 31 December. For Sudan, a civil war ceasefire by 31 December 2026 stands at 8.0% on US$119,665.

Decisions Ahead

Two tracked markets end within 14 days, and several data releases will test the prices. Times are UTC with US Eastern in brackets, and forecasts come from RT’s economic calendar, a financial data service.

What It Means for US Readers

Higher inflation in South Africa and Brazil would make interest-rate cuts harder, which matters to US investors holding emerging-market bonds, currencies and US-listed shares. Mexico’s mid-month reading on Tuesday and Brazil’s IPCA-15 on Thursday are the next checks.

Venezuela and Cuba are the markets most tied to US policy, which is why US readers follow them. Treat each price as a snapshot of where traders stand on Monday 23 November, not a forecast.

What Is Not Known

A price cannot tell us why traders bought, and a one-week move on a market with a few hundred thousand dollars can come from a handful of large orders. We found no clear trigger for the South Africa, Brazil, Venezuela oil, Venezuela election date, Colombia, El Salvador and Mexico moves, and we do not invent one.

We have not read the full resolution rules of every market, and rules decide payouts. Check the platform before relying on any single price.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are prediction markets saying about South Africa’s inflation?

Polymarket gives 59.9% to South Africa ending 2026 with inflation of 4.7–5.0%, up from 38.0% a week earlier. The market holds US$156,849 in total.

Is a prediction market price a forecast?

No. It is the price of a bet, so 59.9% means traders pay about 59.9 cents for a contract that pays US$1 if the outcome happens. Thin markets can be moved by a few traders.

Do traders expect a Venezuelan election soon?

Polymarket gives 16.5% to an election date being set by 31 March 2027 and 41.0% by 30 June 2027. The market asks only whether a date is announced, not whether the vote happens.

Who leads Nigeria’s presidential market?

Polymarket gives President Bola Tinubu 69.0% and Peter Obi 26.0%. The market holds US$163,984 in total, and the vote is due on Saturday 16 January 2027.

Which market had the most money this week?

Polymarket’s market on who leads Venezuela at the end of 2026, with about US$0.7 million traded in the week and about US$101 million in total.

World.title: Nigeria Sets US$11M Stablecoin Capital Floor
World.content:
Nigeria is telling dollar stablecoin firms to open a local company, hold local capital and answer to its central bank, or stay out of the market.

Nigerian five-naira banknotes issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria. File photo, August 2025. (Photo: FAdelabu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

NIGERIA · MARKETS

Nigeria’s central bank has told the makers of dollar stablecoins to open a local company or stay out of the country. Under rules released on Thursday 5 November 2026, an issuer that wants Nigerians to hold a dollar-linked token must run a Nigerian company with ₦15 billion (about US$11 million) of paid-up capital, the money its owners have actually put in.

A stablecoin is a digital token built to hold the value of one currency, most often the US dollar. The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), which runs the country’s payments system, sets its highest bar for tokens tied to a foreign currency.

Key Facts Who The Central Bank of Nigeria, the country’s banking regulator, issued the rules.

What Issuers of dollar-linked tokens need a Nigerian licence and paid-up capital of about US$11 million.

Where Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country; naira-token issuers need a lower floor of about US$7 million.

When Existing operators have 180 days from the start date to apply for a licence.

As of 23 November 2026, 11:00 GMT

The Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria, dated November 2026, say they were issued under a 2026 Presidential Executive Order on Virtual Assets Coordination. They state the aim plainly: to “preserve the effectiveness of the Bank’s monetary policy instruments and its capacity to monitor and manage capital flows and foreign exchange dynamics.”

The naira has swung between about ₦1,345 and ₦1,385 per US dollar since 18 November, according to market data. That is the backdrop for a rule that generally bars dollar tokens from being used to price or settle debts owed in naira.

The CBN closes the offshore route in its own words: “There is no offshore issuer exemption from incorporation, licensing or capital.” A foreign licence cannot stand in for a Nigerian one, and tokens that rely mainly on code rather than full reserves, known as algorithmic stablecoins, are prohibited.A dollar issuer, which the rules call a Class 2 issuer (naira issuers are Class 1), must also keep operating liquidity of at least US$10 million, held apart from its capital. Every issuer must also hold a reserve buffer of 2% above the face value of tokens in circulation, and the CBN must approve any release of it.

Capital must sit as cash in a CBN account or as Nigerian government securities pledged to the central bank through a legal claim known as a lien. Together with the liquidity, a dollar issuer would tie up at least about US$21 million in Nigeria to hold a licence.

Issuers of naira tokens face a lower floor of ₦10 billion (about US$7 million at about ₦1,365 per US dollar on 23 November), and their tokens must be fully backed by naira reserves. No issuer may pay interest or yield to holders.

Operators already working in Nigeria must register with the CBN within 30 days of the start date and report to it within 60 days. They must file a full licence application within 180 days, or stop until they are licensed.

Nathaniel Luz, president of the Africa Stablecoin Network, an industry group, called the rules “one of the finest and clearest pieces of regulation we have seen in Nigeria.” He welcomed the way the rules divide duties between the CBN and the Securities and Exchange Commission, the capital-markets regulator.’Laolu Samuel-Biyi, co-founder of the crypto exchange Busha, struck a warning note in a LinkedIn post.

Without proportionate rules, he wrote, “we risk building an excellent regulatory framework with no participants.”Rume Ophi of the Virtual Asset Service Providers Association, a body for crypto firms, expects big foreign issuers to comply. “They need to come and establish in Nigeria,” he said.

For US companies, Nigerian users turn from a free add-on into a regulated market.A US stablecoin firm must now choose between a Nigerian subsidiary with locked capital and cutting off Nigerian customers.

The exact start date is set in the CBN’s issuing circular, and the registration and licensing clocks run from it. The CBN says it may issue further guidance, circulars and directions to apply the rules.

Do the Rules Apply to US Stablecoin Companies?

Yes, if their tokens reach people in Nigeria. A foreign licence does not replace a Nigerian one, so they need a locally incorporated company with a Class 2 licence.

Can Nigerians Still Hold Dollar Stablecoins Today?

Existing operators may keep serving customers at their current scale while they apply for a licence. After the transition, dollar tokens may be offered only through a licensed Class 2 issuer.

Honduras’ health ministry (Sesal) confirmed a new measles case in La Ceiba, a Caribbean port city, on Sunday 22 November 2026. The patient is a 28-year-old man treated at the Hospital General de Atlántida, and he is stable.

Health teams have visited 188 homes and vaccinated 229 people so far, the ministry said. A vaccination post is open at the Uniplaza shopping centre in La Ceiba.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Finishes Runner-Up at ATP Finals in Turin
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić fell just short of the ATP Finals doubles title Sunday, losing 3-6, 7-6 (2), 10-6 to France’s Théo Arribagé and Albano Olivetti in Turin. Arévalo and Pavić took the opening set 6-3 but could not hold off the French pair, who won the second-set tiebreak 7-2 and carried that momentum into the deciding match tiebreak at Inalpi Arena, played in place of a full third set.

Arribagé and Olivetti won 10 consecutive points across the two tiebreaks to turn the match around, then closed out the decider 10-6 to claim their seventh title of the season. The defeat ended Arévalo and Pavić’s run at the season-ending tournament, which brings together eight of the year’s leading doubles teams. It was their second appearance together in the ATP Finals title match. They also finished as runners-up in 2024.

The fourth-seeded pair arrived at Sunday’s final unbeaten in Turin, including a group-stage victory over Arribagé and Olivetti. Arévalo and Pavić had reached the final with a hard-fought semifinal win over American Christian Harrison and Britain’s Neal Skupski. They came through that match 7-6 (10), 6-7 (7), 10-7.

The final also marked the end of Arévalo and Pavić’s three-year partnership. Together, they won nine tour-level titles, including the 2024 French Open and four ATP Masters 1000 tournaments. Their 2026 season included a title at Queen’s Club in London and a run to the Wimbledon final. They also reached the finals of the Masters 1000 events in Monte Carlo and Canada.

For Arribagé and Olivetti, the win capped their first appearance together at the ATP Finals. The French pair began playing together in October 2025. In the singles final, Carlos Alcaraz beat Alexander Zverev to win his first ATP Finals title.

World.title: US Helicopters Support Costa Rica Crackdown on Illegal Gold Mining
World.content:
Costa Rican police have found about 2,000 sacks of sediment and 50 processing pools on Cerro Conchuditas, a hill near the Nicaraguan border, during an air and ground operation against illegal gold mining that is being supported by helicopters from a United States government aviation program.

The Ministry of Public Security reported the findings on Saturday, two days after officers moved into the area in Cutris, a district of San Carlos in the northern part of Alajuela province. Officers remain on the hill to guard the sites, seize equipment and detain anyone found working them, the ministry said.

Alongside the sacks and pools, police reported finding 20 makeshift shelters, six tents, seven drums, 30 jerrycans, 10 hoses, an electric generator and a water pump. They also recovered rotary hammers, shovels, wheelbarrows and gasoline.

The operation brings together the Public Force, the Border Police, the Migration Police and the Intelligence and National Security Directorate (DIS). Air support comes from helicopters belonging to the US government’s Aviation Program, which works in coordination with the Air Surveillance Service (SVA), the ministry’s air wing.

The ministry did not say how many aircraft are taking part or describe the role, if any, of US personnel. The SVA received four UH-1ST helicopters from the United States in 2019 under a training and maintenance program run through the State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs.

Security Minister Gerald Campos traveled to the site on Thursday to direct the deployment, joined by the heads of the Public Force and the DIS. Much of the terrain is difficult to reach on foot, which is why the ministry combined ground patrols with flights.

Gerald Camacho, director general of the Border Police, said patrols along the border corridor run throughout the year and concentrate on the areas where illegal mining takes place. He described the current deployment as a special reinforcement operation carried out at this time of year.

Today, police said officers had moved on to nearby Cerro Fortuna, in Crucitas, where they found several extraction points in use and detained three men. The three, who police said were in the country irregularly, were referred to the San Carlos prosecutor’s office on suspicion of illegal mining. Officers seized three sacks of sediment, carpets used to wash the material and digging tools.

Ministry figures put the number of people arrested in connection with these operations at 528 so far in 2026. Of those, 239 were held over their migration status, 194 on suspicion of violating the Mining Code, 17 in drug-related cases and six under the Arms and Explosives Law.

Cerro Conchuditas lies close to the San Juan River, which marks the border with Nicaragua, and has become one of the main points for extracting and processing gold-bearing material taken from the Crucitas area. The ministry has said since 2024 that organized crime is present in the zone.

The environmental stakes are a central part of the dispute. Police have previously reported that sediment from the hill is processed with mercury or cyanide to separate the gold, and in May the Public Force said it had seized 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of cyanide and 115 kilograms (254 pounds) of activated carbon from a camp on the same hill, along with 25 active pools. Both substances can contaminate soil and the streams that drain toward the San Juan.

Campos used the visit to call on the Legislative Assembly to approve a government bill on mining in the area. He said the legal tools now available limit what police can achieve and described the work as exhausting for officers without producing lasting results.

The executive branch’s proposal, submitted in 2024, would authorize gold exploration and open-pit extraction in Cutris and remains under discussion in the legislature. The Broad Front and the National Liberation Party oppose it, arguing that reopening Crucitas to gold mining would cause environmental damage of its own.

The ministry said officers will stay on Cerro Conchuditas and in Crucitas to find further processing sites and seize materials.

World.title: Alcaraz Saves Three Set Points to Beat Zverev for First ATP Finals Title
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz defeated world No. 1 Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6 (7) on Sunday in Turin, Italy, to win his first ATP Finals title, closing the tennis season with a 14-match winning streak. The Spaniard saved three set points in the second-set tiebreak before finishing off Zverev at Inalpi Arena. The victory gave Alcaraz his third consecutive tournament title after wins in Vienna and Paris.

It also made him the fourth man to win all four Grand Slam tournaments and the season-ending championship, joining Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic. For Alcaraz, the championship was a step further than he managed a year ago, when he lost to Jannik Sinner in the ATP Finals title match. The season-ending tournament brings together the top eight players of the year.

The 23-year-old took control early against Zverev, who had reached the final without dropping a set or losing his serve. Alcaraz broke the German’s serve three times in the opening set, while Zverev struggled with errors. Zverev recovered from a break down in the second set and forced a tiebreak. He led 6-3, giving himself three chances to send the match to a deciding set, but Alcaraz fought back and eventually closed out the final 9-7 in the tiebreak.

Alcaraz had also needed a comeback to reach Sunday’s match. Playing with his left thigh strapped, he defeated American Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (1) in Saturday’s semifinals after advancing through the group stage unbeaten. Zverev reached the final by beating Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (0), 6-4. He was seeking his third ATP Finals title after winning the event in 2018 and 2021.

The defeat brought an end to a season in which Zverev won his first two Grand Slam titles, at the French Open and US Open, and rose to No. 1 in the world. Alcaraz’s late-season run followed an absence of more than four months because of a wrist injury. He returned at the US Open and went on to finish the year with titles in Vienna, Paris and Turin.

World.title: Get Paid by SINPE Móvil in Costa Rica? You Must Register the Number by Jan. 18
World.content:
If you take payments by SINPE Móvil for a rental, a tour, freelance work or any other business in Costa Rica, you now have a date. By Jan. 18, 2027, you will have to tell the tax authority which phone numbers you use to get paid. The rule was made official on Nov. 20, when the resolution was published in the official gazette, La Gaceta. Miguel Ángel Solís Sánchez, director general of the tax administration, signed it on Nov. 9. It puts into practice a decree issued in October.

This is not a new tax, and nothing is charged on your transfers. You are only reporting which numbers receive business income, so the tax authority can match the money arriving on your phone with what you declare. You have to register if you are signed up as a taxpayer, as a person or a company, and customers pay you by SINPE Móvil. You can list more than one number. That includes a number belonging to an employee or a partner if your customers send payments to it.

You do not have to register a number you use only for personal transfers, such as sending money to family or splitting a bill with friends. If you never collect business payments by SINPE Móvil, you leave the field blank. The numbers go into your file in the Single Tax Registry, known as the RUT. A new field will appear in the economic activities section of the registration and update forms. You can fill it in online through the TRIBU-CR tax platform or in person at a tax office.

If you are already registered as a taxpayer, you get 12 months to comply, and the resolution says that period cannot be extended. There is one open question. As written, the 12 months appear to run from the Nov. 20 publication date, not from Jan. 18, which would put the deadline in November 2027. The Finance Ministry has not clarified the point, so the safe reading is the earlier date.

If you sign up as a new taxpayer after the rule takes effect, you give the numbers as part of the normal registration. After that, you have to update your file whenever you add a number, replace one or stop using one for payments. Skipping it can be expensive. The penalty comes from Article 83 of the Tax Code and equals 2% of your gross income from the previous tax year. It cannot be lower than three base salaries, about 1.39 million colones ($3,108), or higher than 100 base salaries, about 46.2 million colones ($103,593).

If the tax authority does not know your income, the fine is set at 10 base salaries, about 4.62 million colones ($10,359). Those amounts use the 2026 base salary of 462,200 colones and will change if that figure does. A missing number does not trigger an automatic fine. The tax administration says each case will be weighed on its circumstances, and any penalty has to go through a formal process in which you can defend yourself. The law also allows a reduced fine if you correct the omission.

There is nothing to file yet, because the field will not be available until the rule takes effect. In the meantime, make a list of every number your customers pay, and consider moving business payments to a line you use for nothing else. A number that handles both personal and business transfers becomes part of your tax file once you register it.

It is also worth comparing your SINPE Móvil income with what you reported on your last income tax return, and talking to an accountant if the two do not match. SINPE Móvil has become the most common way to pay in Costa Rica, and the registry gives the tax authority a direct way to compare those payments with declared income.

World.title: Flights to Costa Rica Could Cost 20% More as Tourism Board Blames Fuel for Seat Cuts
World.content:
Airfares on most routes into Costa Rica are projected to rise by more than 20%, and the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) expects prices to keep climbing through 2027 as airlines reduce the number of seats they fly here. The institute attributes the reduction to swings in oil prices during the year and to operational adjustments by the airlines.

It estimates that Costa Rica could close 2026 with 15% fewer airline seats from the United States, its largest source of visitors. ICT Executive President Marcos Vargas presented a study on the possible cuts to tourism business leaders on Oct. 23. The figures first surfaced through the tourism chambers that attended.

Hans Pfister, president of the National Chamber of Ecotourism and Sustainable Tourism (Canaeco), said the reduction at Juan Santamaría International Airport near San José could reach 21% between October 2026 and August 2027. Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), put the cut at Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia at 3%.

The collapse of Spirit Airlines alone removed about 95,000 seats from the market after the carrier declared bankruptcy and shut down. American Airlines and JetBlue have also reduced some routes, according to the institute. The ICT said route changes do not necessarily point to a general decline in tourism, because airlines make those decisions based on how profitable each route is and on other commercial opportunities.

Fewer seats could lower arrivals by air, it said, but the real effect will depend on how full the remaining flights are. Since Nov. 15, the institute has been running promotion and outreach with airlines that serve the US market to offset the projected reduction. It acknowledged that its options are limited by the airlines’ own commercial decisions.

Arrival figures already show the pressure as tourist arrivals by air fell 1.9% in October compared with the same month last year, the third monthly decline in a row. Juan Santamaría, which handles nearly two of every three tourists arriving by air, has now recorded seven straight months of year-over-year declines.

The United States accounted for 51.3% of air arrivals in October. A total of 65,071 US visitors arrived that month, down 3.6% from October 2025 and the third consecutive monthly drop for that market. The cuts come as the dollar trades at record lows against the colón, which raises the cost of a stay for visitors paying in dollars. Some capacity is still being added, including JetBlue’s move to daily flights from New York to both main airports.

Fewer seats on the main US routes generally mean less choice of dates and fewer late bargains in the busiest weeks of the year. The ICT has not published route-by-route fare projections, and monthly arrival data through the high season will show how far the reductions reach.

World.title: Improved Road to Costa Rica’s Barva Volcano Opens to Drivers
World.content:
Those heading to Barva Volcano now have a newly paved road to the entrance of Braulio Carrillo National Park, following the completion of a project in the mountains of Heredia. The upgraded road through Sacramento de Barva was inaugurated on Friday. The work covered approximately 3.7 kilometers (2.3 miles) between Sacramento and the park entrance.

Crews paved the road with concrete and improved drainage along the route. The changes are intended to make the trip easier for residents and visitors, particularly during the rainy season. President Laura Fernández attended the inauguration alongside local and government officials. The project cost approximately ₡2.2 billion and was financed mainly by the Rural Development Institute, with a contribution from the Municipality of Barva.

The route also serves communities in the area, including Sacramento and San José de la Montaña. Barva Mayor Alejandra Arce said the work addressed a need for residents, especially when heavy rain affects travel. Construction disrupted access to the volcano earlier this year. For part of the work, the Barva sector opened only on weekends, and visitors had to walk from Sacramento to the park entrance.

The project has also drawn environmental concerns. Earlier this year, the citizens’ group CONCEVERDE questioned the road’s potential effects on wildlife and water resources and called for information about environmental approvals and measures to protect animals. Barva Volcano is one of two visitor sectors of Braulio Carrillo National Park. Its attractions include high-elevation forest, a crater lake and four trails: Cacho Venado, Laguna Barva, Copey and Mirador Vara Blanca.

The National System of Conservation Areas, known as SINAC, lists the park’s hours as 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. daily, including holidays. Its published entrance fee is ₡1,130 for Costa Rican citizens and residents over 13 and $13.56 for nonresidents over 13. Visitors can check current conditions and reserve through SINAC’s online services at https://serviciosenlinea.sinac.go.cr/. Because weather, access and park rules can change, travelers should confirm the latest information before setting out.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Two Most Active Volcanoes Are Quieter but Their Craters Stay Restricted
World.content:
Poás and Rincón de la Vieja produced nearly all of Costa Rica’s volcanic eruptions in the first 10 months of 2026, and both are now less active, according to the Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (Ovsicori) at the National University. Neither has returned to normal visiting conditions.

Rincón de la Vieja, in Guanacaste, was the busier of the two. Ovsicori volcanologist Geoffroy Avard said it registered hundreds of eruptions during the year. The activity began between March and April, rose sharply from July and stayed high for several months. Several of those eruptions were strong enough to produce lahars, which are flows of water and volcanic sediment that run down the slopes and into nearby river channels. The observatory raised its alert for the volcano to the level it calls Precaución for several months.

On Oct. 30, with no significant changes detected in the volcano’s deep activity, Ovsicori lowered the alert one step to Advertencia. The observatory stressed that the lower level does not mean the danger has passed. Eruptions can still occur without warning, including ones able to send lahars downslope, and it recorded 12 small eruptions between Nov. 9 and Nov. 13.

Poás, in Alajuela, was less active than in 2025. Avard said its strongest eruptions came in July and August, when some threw material almost to the crater rim, but he described them as isolated events. Activity was concentrated in the rainy season and has declined since. The crater lake at Poás rose for part of the year and has recently begun to fall. Avard said scientists have seen no drastic change linked to the drop and will keep assessing whether it could affect activity in the coming months. Ovsicori also identified two landslides inside the crater, which did not alter the overall downward trend.

Turrialba and Arenal had no eruptions in the period. Turrialba’s activity is decreasing very slowly, with landslides seen inside its crater, while Arenal remains calm after several years of gradual decline. For visitors, the restrictions introduced earlier in the year are still in place. Poás Volcano National Park is open but has admitted about half as many people since Aug. 28, with 1,064 visitors a day, mandatory helmets, two open trails and 20 minutes per group at the crater lookout.

At Rincón de la Vieja National Park, the trail to the active crater remains closed. The Las Pailas sector, with its mud pots and steam vents well below the summit, is open Tuesday through Sunday. Five areas of Upala and Liberia near the volcano have been under a yellow alert since Oct. 1.

Both parks sell entry online, and volcano parks can change their rules with little notice. The current list of closed trails and visitor limits covers the other major parks. Ovsicori keeps both volcanoes under constant monitoring.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Unfreezes Millions for Police and Courts in 2027 Budget
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Judiciary, which includes the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ), will be able to spend about 29,844 million colones ($66.9 million) in 2027 without first seeking approval from a legislative committee, after the Constitutional Chamber ordered lawmakers to strip the conditions from next year’s national budget bill.

In a second resolution the same day, the court ordered the Legislative Assembly to reverse an 8,048 million colones ($18 million) cut to public university funding. Together, the two rulings affect roughly 37,900 million colones ($85 million) in the 2027 budget.

Magistrate Ingrid Hess, who drafted the university ruling, said in remarks published last evening that the Assembly exceeded its powers when its budget committee reduced the funds by motion. She said the Constitution protects higher education through university autonomy, academic freedom and guaranteed funding, and that lawmakers may only act as arbiters when the Executive and the universities disagree.

In this case there was no disagreement, Hess said. The money covers payments to universities that the government postponed in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic and later agreed with university rectors to repay in installments. The Executive had included the installment in its draft 2027 budget before the Assembly’s budget committee approved a motion moving it to cover employer contributions to the teachers’ pension fund, Jupema.

The rulings were voted on Friday and respond to consultations filed by the Supreme Court and by a group of lawmakers. According to the court’s findings as reported on Friday, the decisions address procedural defects and do not rule on the merits of the spending choices.

The Judiciary ruling, drafted by Magistrate Anamari Garro, found substantial defects in four budget execution rules. Rule 9 tied the release of about 29,844 million colones, or 5.6% of the Judiciary’s budget, to approval by the legislature’s special committee on public income and spending. Other rules blocked ordinary transfers between budget lines and restricted the filling of vacant positions.

The court found that the Judiciary was not consulted while the bill was drafted or debated, as the Constitution requires for legislation that affects its operations, and that the rules were introduced through the budget process even though their content belongs in ordinary law. Supreme Court President Patricia Vargas said the ruling confirms warnings the Judiciary had raised publicly with the Assembly and the Executive.

She said the branch is not seeking more money but wants to use funds already approved for it, and that those resources are needed to serve the public and to fight crime and organized crime. She added that all branches had committed at a recent meeting of the heads of state powers to comply with the court’s decisions.
