Michael Soto, acting director of the OIJ, said the ruling would let the agency use its funds and vacant posts in 2027, rather than giving it additional money. OIJ planning and operations chief Omar Brenes said this week that the agency had halted purchases of ballistic helmets, weapons and ammunition because of Finance Ministry cuts, leaving agents short of rounds for firearms training.

The pressure on the OIJ comes as a recent national report warned that organized crime has become Costa Rica’s third economy, and as Santa Cruz, home to Tamarindo, leads Guanacaste in homicides.

The university cut had drawn thousands of marchers into San José in October. National Rectors’ Council (Conare) President Jorge Herrera said the ruling confirms the universities’ position, and the council said in a statement that budget decisions in this area affect society beyond the campuses.

The Assembly must now remove the challenged provisions before it gives the budget final approval. The Constitution requires the national budget to be approved before Nov. 30, and ruling-party caucus chief Nogui Acosta has cited Nov. 29 as the last day for a second-debate vote. His caucus said it would wait for the full written ruling before deciding how to proceed. If lawmakers do not act, the challenged provisions are treated as excluded from the budget.

Frente Amplio lawmaker María Eugenia Román said she plans a motion to restore the university funds in the text, which would require 38 votes. The same 8,048 million colones cut also appears in this year’s second extraordinary budget, which faces a Nov. 24 vote and is not covered by the ruling.

President Laura Fernández said on Friday, before the rulings were announced, that her government would comply with any decision from the court. The rulings come amid a broader squeeze on public spending that has hit courts, police and schools, and they leave lawmakers about a week to settle how Costa Rica will fund its courts, police investigators and universities next year.

World.title: San Pedro man accused of burglary receives 24 pages of evidence and 2 CDs ahead of April trial
World.content:
San Pedro man accused of burglary receives 24 pages of evidence and 2 CDs ahead of April trial

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A San Pedro man who remains behind bars on a burglary charge has received full disclosure of the prosecution’s evidence as his case moves closer to trial in April 2027.

Mervin Ramirez appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, November 17, before Magistrate Tehra Brown, who ordinarily presides over matters in San Pedro.

During the proceedings in Court #4, Ramirez was provided with 24 pages of documentary evidence and two CDs containing additional material relating to the burglary allegation.

Magistrate Brown instructed Ramirez to ensure that the CDs could be opened and viewed. She advised him that if either disc was defective, he should notify personnel at the Belize Central Prison, who would inform the Belize City Magistrate’s Court so replacement copies could be provided.

Although the case originated in the San Pedro Magistrate’s Court, it was heard in Belize City because Magistrate Brown was conducting court proceedings there that day.

Ramirez remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison. The Magistrate indicated that he could be brought back before the court in early January 2027 for bail consideration.

His burglary trial is scheduled to commence in the San Pedro Magistrate’s Court in April 2027.

World.title: Man fined $805 for 1.1 grams of crack cocaine after telling court he would not waste its time
World.content:
Man fined $805 for 1.1 grams of crack cocaine after telling court he would not waste its time

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 41-year-old Belize City man has been fined $805 after pleading guilty to possession of 1.1 grams of crack cocaine, telling a Magistrate that he did not want to waste the court’s time and promising that he would not return.

Marvin McFoy appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he admitted to possessing the controlled drug.

During his arraignment, McFoy told the Magistrate, “I nuh wah waste yuh time or the court time so I wah plea guilty.”

He further explained that he was not a cocaine user but had gotten caught up in an unfortunate situation, telling the court, “I nuh use cocaine but dah just wah incident happen mek I get caught up.”

McFoy concluded his remarks by assuring the Magistrate, “Yuh nuh wah see me back here again.”

The court heard that McFoy had no previous convictions for drug-related offenses. Taking his guilty plea and circumstances into consideration, the Magistrate imposed a non-custodial sentence of $800 plus $5 in court costs.

McFoy was given until February 15, 2027, to pay the fine or face six months’ imprisonment in default.

World.title: Ladyville man fined $305 for piece of crack so small it didn’t even show on a scale
World.content:
Ladyville man fined $305 for piece of crack so small it didn’t even show on a scale

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 29-year-old Ladyville resident has been fined $305 after pleading guilty to possession of a quantity of crack cocaine so small that its weight could not be determined.

Dalwin Hernandez, an employee of a bodywork business on Marage Road, appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, November 16, where he admitted to possessing the illegal substance.

Police say Hernandez was detained around 11:00 p.m. on Friday, November 13, while officers were conducting mobile patrol along Marage Road in Ladyville.

According to police, two officers noticed Hernandez, who was wearing a blue T-shirt and brown pants, leaving a yard known to police for drug activity.

Officers reportedly became suspicious when Hernandez began hurriedly reaching into his pockets as they approached him. A subsequent search uncovered a small, stone-like substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

The quantity was recorded as undetermined because it was reportedly too small to register a weight on the scale.

Hernandez pleaded guilty and was fined $300 plus $5 in court costs. He was given until January 15, 2027, to pay the fine or face three months’ imprisonment in default.

World.title: Woman accused of unlawful sexual intercourse with 15-year-old boy makes second court appearance; case adjourned to January
World.content:
Woman accused of unlawful sexual intercourse with 15-year-old boy makes second court appearance; case adjourned to January

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 37-year-old Sandhill woman accused of having sexual intercourse with a 15-year-old boy has made her second appearance in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where her case was adjourned until January 2027.

Sherise Shelmadine Moralez, a cook by profession, appeared in Court #3 on Monday, November 16, in the absence of the Chief Magistrate. She remains free on $10,000 High Court bail while the criminal proceedings continue.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Moralez was initially arraigned on August 25 on two counts of unlawful sexual intercourse involving a 15-year-old boy.

Police allege that the incidents occurred on July 30, 2026, at Moralez’s residence in Sandhill, where she allegedly had sexual intercourse with the minor on two occasions that day.

The allegations were reported to Ladyville police on August 6 when the boy, accompanied by his mother, made a formal complaint. Moralez was subsequently detained and questioned by investigators, during which she denied the allegations.

Following her initial arraignment, Moralez was denied bail and remanded to the Belize Central Prison. However, as BBN subsequently reported, attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington successfully secured her release on September 3 before High Court Justice Derick F. Sylvester.

Bail was granted in the sum of $10,000 with two sureties of $5,000 each. Her conditions prohibit her from leaving Belize without permission from a High Court judge or interfering directly or indirectly with the complainant or prosecution witnesses.

Moralez is expected to return to the Magistrate’s Court in early January 2027 as the case continues.

World.title: Man charged with possession of 5.9 grams of crack cocaine remanded after failing to post $2,000 bail
World.content:
Man charged with possession of 5.9 grams of crack cocaine remanded after failing to post $2,000 bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 42-year-old Belize City resident accused of possessing 5.9 grams of crack cocaine has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after he was unable to post bail following his arraignment.

Anthony Francis Belezaire, a washman of Flamboyant Street, appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in Court #8 on Friday, November 20, where he pleaded not guilty to a drug-related charge.

According to the allegations, Belezaire was found in possession of 5.9 grams of suspected crack cocaine on Thursday, November 19.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted Belezaire bail of $2,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

As part of his bail conditions, Belezaire must report to the Mahogany Street Police Station every Friday between 6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.

However, Belezaire was unable to secure a surety and post bail, resulting in his remand to the Belize Central Prison until he can meet the requirements.

He is scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on February 2, 2027.

World.title: Man fined $610 for crack cocaine and smoking pipe, but old unpaid $105 fine lands him in prison
World.content:
Man fined $610 for crack cocaine and smoking pipe, but old unpaid $105 fine lands him in prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 40-year-old Belize City construction worker who pleaded guilty to possession of crack cocaine and a smoking pipe has been fined $610, but ended up behind bars after failing to pay an outstanding $105 fine from a previous drug conviction.

Rugro Manzanero, an unemployed resident of Mile 2 on the Philip Goldson Highway, appeared before a Magistrate in Court #8 on Friday, November 20, where he pleaded guilty to possession of 0.3 grams of crack cocaine and possession of utensils used for smoking a controlled drug.

Police say Manzanero was detained around 9:24 a.m. on Thursday, November 19, during a patrol along Cran Street in Belize City.

Police reportedly noticed Manzanero, who was wearing a pink shirt and shorts, entering an alley. As officers approached, she allegedly observed him placing something beneath a piece of wood in a backyard.

A search of Manzanero revealed nothing illegal on his person, but officers subsequently checked beneath the wood and discovered two pieces of suspected crack cocaine along with a two-inch silver metal smoking pipe.

Manzanero was taken to the Queen Street Police Station and charged.

For his guilty pleas, the Magistrate fined him $350 plus $5 in court costs for possession of crack cocaine and $250 plus $5 in court costs for possession of the smoking pipe, bringing his total fines to $610.

He was given until February 26, 2027, to pay, with a default sentence of two months’ imprisonment on each charge.

However, court records revealed that Manzanero still owed $105 from an earlier drug conviction on August 28, 2026, involving an offense committed eight days earlier.

That fine had been due since September 30, and when Manzanero was unable to settle the outstanding amount before the end of the court day, he was escorted to the Belize Central Prison.

World.title: Fisherman busted with 17 grams of weed in his groin says he was taking his smoke to sea
World.content:
Fisherman busted with 17 grams of weed in his groin says he was taking his smoke to sea

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 36-year-old Belize City fisherman who told a Magistrate that he was simply preparing to take his personal supply of marijuana to sea has been fined $155 after police discovered 17 grams of cannabis concealed in his groin area.

Wayne Patrick Herrera, a resident of the Saint Martin de Porres area, appeared unrepresented in Court #8 of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 20, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug.

Police say Herrera was detained around 2:42 a.m. on Wednesday, November 18, during an operation on Nutmeg Street. Officers conducting mobile patrol noticed him standing in a yard with several other individuals and approached to conduct a search.

During the search, police reportedly discovered a transparent plastic bag containing cannabis concealed in the front groin area of Herrera’s clothing.

In court, Herrera explained that he had recently obtained his Social Security card and was preparing to head out to sea for work when police arrived. He said he had purchased the marijuana for personal use and had no idea it exceeded the permitted quantity.

Herrera told the Magistrate that he was not particularly concerned when officers arrived because he believed he had nothing illegal on him apart from his personal supply of marijuana.

Under Belize’s Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act, 2017, possession of up to 10 grams of cannabis is decriminalized in qualifying circumstances. Herrera’s 17 grams exceeded that threshold by seven grams.

For his guilty plea, Herrera was fined $150 plus $5 in court costs, payable by January 29, 2027, or two months’ imprisonment in default.

However, court records also revealed that Herrera owed $405 from a previous drug conviction dating back to February 2026. He was ordered to settle that outstanding amount immediately or face an additional seven months in prison.

World.title: Man fined $1,260 for holding knife to girlfriend’s neck and damaging her property, but old unpaid fines land him in prison
World.content:
Man fined $1,260 for holding knife to girlfriend’s neck and damaging her property, but old unpaid fines land him in prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 37-year-old Belize City construction worker who admitted to threatening his common-law wife with a knife and damaging her belongings has been fined $1,260 and ordered to pay $400 in restitution, but ended up behind bars after being unable to settle outstanding court fines.

Jimmy Junior Parham, a resident of Raccoon Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to aggravated assault with a knife and damage to property following a domestic dispute with his common-law partner of three months.

According to police, the incident occurred on Monday, November 16, when Parham allegedly returned home under the influence of alcohol and began insulting the woman. She reported that he subsequently retrieved a six-inch knife from the kitchen, placed it against her neck and threatened her, saying, “I wah do this to you.”

The woman further alleged that when she attempted to leave the residence later that afternoon, Parham removed the battery from her vehicle to prevent her from driving away. As his behaviour escalated, she reportedly left the house with her granddaughter.

When she returned, the woman discovered that her TCL television, valued at $300, had been damaged, along with a camera valued at $100.

During his arraignment, Parham admitted damaging the items but claimed the damage was accidental and occurred while he was doing sheetrock work. He told the court that he had apologized to the woman.

The Magistrate fined Parham $1,000 plus $5 in court costs for aggravated assault and $250 plus $5 in court costs for damage to property. He was also ordered to pay Oregon $400 in restitution for the damaged items.

Parham was given until April 30, 2027, to pay the new fines, with a default sentence of four months’ imprisonment on each count.

However, despite receiving non-custodial sentences for the new convictions, Parham was taken into custody after failing to settle outstanding fines from previous court matters before the end of the day.

World.title: ‘Bad apples’
World.content:
St Ann North Eastern Member of Parliament Matthew Samuda (centre) speaks during the funeral for Kenise Dunn, with St Ann’s Bay Mayor Michael Belnavis and Lime Hall Division Councillor Genevor Gordon-Bailey.

MEMBER of Parliament for St Ann North Eastern Matthew Samuda has expressed anger over what he described as a lack of empathy and respectful communication towards the family of Kenise Dunn following her death.

He noted that, while Jamaica has some of the best doctors and nurses, there are “bad apples” in the health system whose treatment of patients and relatives must not be tolerated.

Speaking at Dunn’s funeral at Exchange Seventh-day Adventist Church in St Ann on Sunday, Samuda said his concern was not to judge the medical treatment she received, but the way patients in pain and their relatives are treated by hospital staff.

He said the family’s grief had been made worse by what he described as a lack of care and consideration, adding that no family should have to endure such an experience while dealing with the death of a loved one.

“Now, Mayor Belnavis would have spoken to the fact that, yes, the matter is under investigation, but one thing is clear — a family is hurting and that hurt was made worse because of the lack of empathy, lack of care, and the decency of respectful communication, and that gives me concern, real concern. And I don’t want this to be mistaken because Jamaica has, in all things — whether you talk about sports or music and even in health care — you have some of the best doctors and best nurses in the world in this country, but you do have bad apples,” he said.

“And this is not an assault on those who work in that sector; this is, I want to be very clear, an acknowledgement that there are those in the system who are not showing their humanity in how they speak to people, how they treat those who visit the hospitals. And, certainly, I am deeply concerned,” he added.

Samuda, who said he was “admittedly angry”, made it clear that he was not qualified to determine whether the medical care provided to Dunn was appropriate. Instead, he said health-care workers must show compassion to people experiencing physical pain, and communicate with their relatives in a respectful manner.

Dunn, who died at age 33, passed away on August 14, five days after giving birth, according to previous reports. Her death prompted concern from relatives, who called for answers about the circumstances surrounding her treatment at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital.

Her uncle, Kirk Hall, had previously told the Jamaica Observer that Dunn was admitted to the hospital on July 29, while eight months pregnant. He said she had been experiencing severe stomach pain and difficulty passing stool. Hall also said she underwent emergency surgery and that doctors reportedly found a tumour in her colon and a ruptured bowel.

Following her death, the hospital said an internal investigation was underway, while the North East Regional Health Authority said a comprehensive investigation and clinical review had been launched into the circumstances surrounding her death.

At Sunday’s funeral, St Ann’s Bay mayor and chairman of the St Ann Municipal Corporation Michael Belnavis pledged that the investigation would be thorough.

“When this happened… it was really a traumatic experience for all of them. I was there, and I’m here to tell you publicly that no stone will be unturned… and there will be full investigation into the situation that caused her demise,” Belnavis said.

Samuda also welcomed changes to the hospital’s management, saying further changes were expected. He said Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton had tabled a report examining the hospital’s operations in Parliament on Tuesday.

He said the wider health system must ensure that families are not left feeling mistreated when they are already dealing with loss. He also pointed to increased staffing and improved pay for doctors and nurses, arguing that these developments should be matched by respectful treatment of patients and relatives.

“We’re putting the system on notice that what took place should never happen. The communication after, and the way the family feels, no family should feel like that again, and that is why I’m happy with the fact that there have already been management changes at the hospital and that there are more to come,” he said.

World.title: Downswell urges young Reggae Boyz to bounce back against Uzbekistan
World.content:
Wendell Downswell

Jamaica’s Under-17 head coach Wendell Downswell says his technical staff has been working on both the mental and tactical aspects of the team’s game as they seek to revive their FIFA Under-17 World Cup campaign against Uzbekistan on Monday.

The young Reggae Boyz suffered a humiliating 6-0 defeat against European champions Italy in their opening Group E encounter last week, leaving them with little room for error as they chase a place in the next round.

However, Downswell believes the heavy defeat has provided valuable lessons for his players and is confident they can respond positively in their remaining group matches.

“As a staff, we have learnt many things, a number of lessons from the encounter. We were up against one of the European giants, back-to-back champions of their confederation at this age group,” Downswell told the Jamaica Observer.

“Despite the humiliating defeat, the staff has been working assiduously from a mental and tactical standpoint with the players to gain six or four points as a means of our goal to advance to the next round,” he added.

Jamaica will need a strong response against Uzbekistan to keep their qualification hopes alive with a final group game set to be played against Ivory Coast.

Downswell, though, insists that the atmosphere within the Jamaican camp remains positive despite the setback against the Italians.

“As a Jamaican delegation, we are very optimistic and looking forward to the challenges that lie ahead. The spirit in the camp is high. One Jamaica,” he noted.

The encounter against Uzbekistan therefore represents an important opportunity for Downswell’s young charges to demonstrate their resilience and show that the opening defeat has not derailed their ambitions at the tournament.

With their hopes of progressing still alive, Jamaica will be looking for a much-improved performance as they attempt to get their World Cup campaign back on track.

World.title: IShowSpeed tests himself against Usain Bolt in new video
World.content:
The trend continued on the Jamaica leg of his Caribbean tour in April, where he participated in a relay at the National Stadium.

This meeting with Bolt, however, he describes as a lifelong dream

“This episode is so important to me. Like, my name literally has Speed in it. Obviously, I take every episode I do very seriously. But this one, I’m taking it more to the heart. I’m training so I can impress Usain Bolt, the GOAT,” he said.

He added, “My whole life I’ve been waiting for this moment. I still picture that little boy on his…on his mom’s computer, at my mom’s house, watching Usain Bolt run, watching his highlights, watching his sprints…So, I got to make that little boy happy,” he shared.

Boldon and Bolt were both present for the one-man race, in which Speed attempted to beat his training time of 10.72, passing on encouragement and guidance.

The sprinting sensation ribbed Speed even as he gave advice.

“You guys think track and field, easy,” Bolt joked, but admitted that he was genuinely impressed with the efforts from the youngster

“[He has] competitive mindset that’s why he’s pissed,” Bolt shared after one failed attempt ending in a time of 10.50.

“I think overall, he might be disappointed. But if you ask any track person, it’s impressive,” Bolt added.

When questioned on whether Speed was in Bolt’s league, the sprinter responded: “No, no, no. That’s a different story,” with a laugh.

For Speed, who eventually hit 10.35, his excitement at being guided by Bolt was immense

“This is a very exciting day for me, man. It’s like I was playing baseball with my dad, you know, like the classic,” the streamer said.

Speed expressed excitement for the journey, acknowledging Bolden’s caution that the work will be extremely difficult.

World.title: Opposition senator questions Government’s commitment to accountability
World.content:
In this video grab Opposition Senator Kisha Anderson makes her contribution to the debate on the asset tax in the legislature.

Opposition Senator Kisha Anderson has accused the Government of practicing accountability “only when it is convenient, when the questions are comfortable or when the answers are favourable”.

Anderson made the accusation Friday, during her contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Nation Debate in the Senate.

“Every Jamaican has the right to ask, ‘Weh di money deh?’, and every government has a responsibility to provide an honest answer and to account for its decisions, expenditure and performance,” said Anderson. She noted that while elections give governments the authority to govern, “what they do not give governments is the authority to operate without scrutiny”.

“The Jamaican people do not surrender their right to ask questions when they cast their ballots. Neither do they relinquish their right to know how their taxes are being spent, whether public commitments are being honoured, or whether the decisions taken in their name are improving their lives,” Anderson remarked.

She argued that accountability is not a foreign concept that Jamaica must now discover, the country having demonstrated, through experience, what can be achieved if it is taken seriously. The JMMB Director pointed to 2013 when the public debt stood at 147 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) and the steps taken, with the involvement of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and bipartisan support in the Parliament, to turn the situation around.

About the state of affairs in 2013, Anderson said, “I will not debate how we got there, as I know we all know that since independence both political parties have held state power.

“So in 2013 Jamaica had been to the IMF before, we had signed past agreements, but this time something had to be different. In May of that year when the IMF approved the 4-year Extended Fund Facility for Jamaica, it came with accountability – clear targets, strict reporting requirements and consequences for failing to meet our commitments”.

Anderson highlighted that requirements for public disclosure allowed Jamaicans to know whether their government was doing what it had promised, “And importantly, we strengthened accountability through legislation”. In this regard, she pointed to the reinforcement of the fiscal rules in 2014, establishing the framework for reducing public debt to 60 per cent of GDP by 2025/26.

Said Anderson: “The IMF programme changed the terms of accountability in effect from ‘trust us’ to ‘show us’ and accountability did not stop there. As a responsible Jamaican collective, we were mature enough under the leadership of Dr Peter Phillips at the Ministry of Finance to establish the Economic Programme Oversight Committee (EPOC)”.

Anderson told her fellow lawmakers that EPOC was part of the then Government’s commitment to transparency, led by the independent private sector. She noted that it brought together representatives from business, trade unions, civil society and the State with a straightforward mandate to monitor whether the Government was meeting its targets and report its findings to the Jamaican people, plainly and regularly.

“Every quarter, EPOC reported publicly on performance relative to target and any risks that existed. EPOC engaged with the Jamaican people and in one such engagement with residents in Swallowfield, (now) Government Senator Keith Duncan said, ‘To have oversight means that you hold the Government, any Government, to do what dem supposed to do.’

“Any Government; EPOC was not a partisan instrument. It began under one administration and continued under the next,” Anderson highlighted.

She reminded that in 2016, Prime Minister Andrew Holness re-established EPOC and told its members that it was “‘very important that the Government be kept on its toes.’”

She cited that even after the IMF arrangements ended, the Government signed a memorandum of understanding to keep EPOC in place because Jamaica had recognised the value of independent oversight.

The Opposition lawmaker also noted that EPOC’s responsibility for monitoring Jamaica’s fiscal rules passed to a permanent statutory body in 2024 with the establishment of the Independent Fiscal Commission. She said temporary oversight became part of Jamaica’s permanent institutional framework, demonstrating how accountability can turn commitments into measurable results.

Anderson also pointed to other examples of accountability, highlighting that a company listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange that raisees money from the Jamaican public must publish its unaudited results within 45 days of each quarter.

“It must file audited accounts within 60 or 90 days of its financial year-end, and a full annual report, including management’s explanation of the numbers, within 120 days.

“If a company expects to be late, it must explain why and indicate when its reports will be submitted. And if it fails to report, trading in its shares can be suspended until it complies. The Exchange exercises this power and publishes monthly regulatory reports identifying companies that are late,” said Anderson.

“Should a Government that spends hundreds of billions of the people’s dollars be held to a lower standard?” she asked.

She added that, “If these reporting standards and consequences are good enough for the shareholders of a listed company, surely they should be good enough for the shareholders of Jamaica: its citizens, the Jamaican people”.

World.title: JPL matches postponed over unpaid referee fees
World.content:
FIFA referee Daneon Parchment (right) looks on as Montego Bay United’s Demario Phillips receives treatment in a Jamaica Premier League game against Harbour View at the Montego Bay Sports Complex on September 23, 2024 during the 2024-25 season. (Photo: Paul Reid)

All Jamaica Premier League (JPL) matches scheduled for this weekend have been postponed amid an ongoing dispute over unpaid referee fees, with negotiations continuing between the league’s organisers and the referees’ association.

According to sources, the referees’ association is still owed millions of dollars.

Discussions are ongoing and the parties are hoping to reach an amicable agreement that would settle the outstanding balance, establish payment dates and allow referees to return to the pitch.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Fragile cash
World.content:
A vendor displays torn $100 and $500 bills to the Jamaica Observer.

Vendors, cab drivers, bus conductors, and other Jamaicans whose livelihoods depend heavily on cash transactions say they are taking losses as some of the country’s most frequently circulated banknotes succumb to tearing and fading, prompting concerns about their durability.

The Bank of Jamaica (BOJ), acknowledging the problem, says it is exploring ways to make the notes more resilient.

“It’s too easy to tear, man; soon as you draw them so they split… I’m not comfortable with them,” long-time Coronation Market vendor Nadine Campbell told the Jamaica Observer.

“I have [so] much in my drawer, about $5,000 [worth of] $100, $50, all of them, I just throw them down,” Campbell added.

The polymer notes now in circulation were introduced in 2023, replacing cotton-based $50, $100, $500, $1,000, and $5,000 denominations, incorporating new designs and enhanced security features. The roll-out also saw the introduction of an entirely new $2,000 denomination.

At the time, then Finance Minister Dr Nigel Clarke said the upgraded notes have the latest in material technology for greater durability, which reduces the frequency of replacement. That would have a positive impact on the BOJ’s annual spend of about $1.4 billion every year to print banknotes.

Additionally, the new notes have specific markers to facilitate ease of use by visually impaired people.

However, Jamaicans who engage in cash-heavy transactions daily are now doubtful about the notes’ longevity.

“If there’s a little tear, nobody wants it, [and] it washes out easily,” shared a vendor who identified herself as Denneshia.

“It is easy to slide out of your pocket; I don’t like them. But we have to use them because… we have to use them,” she added.

Andrew, who loads taxis plying the Price Rite/Whitehall route, had several $50 and $100 bills with microtears along the edges in his hand when the Sunday Observer spoke to him in Half-Way-Tree.

“They are quick to tear and, as you get a tear on it, it rips off completely,” he said.

In June 2026 the central bank, in an interview with the Observer, had maintained that the new notes far outlast the old cotton-based currency

— up to three years compared to 1.5 years.

When contacted for this story, the BOJ declined to comment on the complaints. However, it did admit that the lower denomination notes, including $50, $100 and $500 bills, are coming back to the bank damaged more frequently than higher denomination notes.

Almost a quarter, around 22 per cent, of the notes in these denominations that it processes are deemed unfit for recirculation.

But anecdotal evidence suggests the number could be higher, as a familiar refrain among vendors and customers with whom the Sunday Observer spoke is that they don’t return the most damaged notes.

Some, like a cab driver who identified himself as Prince, showed the newspaper their stash of damaged notes.

This is not good, look at this,” Prince said, flipping through a wad of torn bills, mostly $50 and $100 notes.

Similarly, more than half of the vendors and customers who spoke to the Sunday Observer said they have damaged bills collecting dust at home.

One vendor, who identified herself as Grace, said she had taken the torn notes to a bank to have them replaced. But that effort failed as the bank refused to take them.

“When I bring it to the bank, they told me to go and find the other piece if there’s another piece to find, but they’re not changing it,” Grace said.

That, she insisted, was opposite to her experience with the former cotton-based notes. “We always could bring them to the bank as long as they have on the serial number,” Grace explained.

She said the serial numbers are visible on the damaged $500, and $1,000 bills she had, but she has since thrown them away “because we don’t know what to do with them”.

A vegetable vendor, Gem, who said she has been selling in Half-Way-Tree for more than 15 years, told the Sunday Observer she has her own collection of damaged notes.

“As you quint [blink] they tear,” she said. “The amount that I’ve gotten I have to carry them and put down at my house, because sometimes how people ginnal you and give you, you don’t even notice. Some of them you can use a piece of tape and it’s good to go, but others…”

“Maybe one day when I am broke and don’t have any money I can draw back for them and carry them to the bank,” Gem added, laughing.

A driver who travels through Spanish Town, Frankie, maintained: “Once they have a rip, that’s it; they don’t have any value unless you take them back to the bank.”

Despite the complaints, the bills seem almost impossible to rip. Jamaica Observer reporters who tried various methods to tear a $100 bill found that it merely bent and wrinkled.

When the Sunday Observer contacted De La Rue, the British company that manufacturers the notes, an employee explained that it would be very difficult to comment without knowing the state of the notes beforehand, including how old they were and how they had been used.

However, the employee said: “If you have to work really hard to destroy the notes and then you are seeing some that are damaged, it suggests that the notes have two very different histories.”

The BOJ has blamed rough handling, including stapling and graffiti, for the state of some of the bills.

It also said in June, that while replacement rates have dropped across all denominations, it is working with the manufacturer to “identify ways to further improve durability, particularly for the lower denominations”.

The Sunday Observer then asked De La Rue whether any changes have been signed off on with BOJ regarding the notes; if so, when are they due to begin production, and whether Jamaicans could expect any tangible changes, for example, a different feel or thickness. However, the manufacturer said it was not able to comment on any conversations it had with any central bank.

In the meantime, Jamaicans who use the lower denominations the most say it’s costing them money.

“It is a loss for me, because when a passenger gives me a torn note I have to just fold it up and put it somewhere; I can’t even pass it on,” said Prince.

Another issue that several bus conductors and drivers on the Spanish Town to Kingston route pointed out was that the notes tend to stick together when they get damp or moist, leading them to give away more bills than they intend.

They explained that this regularly causes conflicts between commuters and conductors.

Similar concerns were shared by a Coronation Market vendor who identified herself as Dimples.

“It is nice, but when it is wet it can be a little tedious because it sticks together… it poses a problem because suppose a shopper comes, and they come thinking it’s one note and… pass it on to me, and I give you the change, and you go to someone else thinking you have the other money, which you don’t; it’s gonna cause a problem… there’s a little friction, and we don’t really want that,” she said.

Regular consumers had fewer issues with the currency, though they still shared complaints about it tearing.

One customer in Coronation Market was complaining about the very issue when the Sunday Observer visited.

Displaying her $500 bill with a small piece missing from the edge, she said: “I don’t have a problem with the money, but there are times when you come and you will give someone, say, $1,000 or $2,000, and they tend to give you back money that is torn. And then now when you try to spend it, nobody will take it, and that is where I have a problem,” she said.

Another customer explained that she loves the fact that the notes can stand up to water, especially with accidental washing.

“So when you check the pocket now after the clothes dry, you find the money, and it’s still all right. It’s not crushed up… So you can use it again. The only problem with it, when it tears, you have a problem, because nobody want to take it from you. But I think it was a good switch. I appreciate it,” she explained.

World.title: Safety sells Jamaica
World.content:
CHANG... my job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach

WHITEHOUSE, Westmoreland — Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang has declared that Jamaica’s continued success in tourism depends heavily on maintaining a safe environment for both visitors and residents, insisting that the country’s natural attractions mean little if people are afraid to enjoy them.

“Safety is part of the product. The most beautiful beach in the world means nothing if people are afraid to walk on it. My job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach,” Chang said to applause last Thursday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitated Sandals South Coast in Westmoreland.

The hotel, which reopened to guests on Wednesday after sustaining extensive damage during the passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, was restored over a compressed 10-month period by a combined team of Jamaican and American architects.

Chang said the Government’s investments in national security, coupled with the efforts of the security forces, were helping to create an environment in which tourists could move beyond hotel compounds and experience the wider Jamaican community without fear.

He said the ultimate goal was for visitors to feel comfortable travelling to nearby communities, visiting beaches and local attractions, and interacting with residents.

“[We want guests to] begin to feel free to go on the road and walk, take a taxi, go down to Whitehouse, go down to the beach, down to the fishing beach, buy some fried fish, and jump on any taxi and come back to the hotel without feeling fear,” he said.

“We have made significant progress, and as the ministry responded, with the support of the prime minister, we have made the investment in our security, and our police have responded,” Chang added.

He stressed, however, that safeguarding the tourism industry also means protecting the thousands of Jamaicans employed in the sector, particularly in the communities where they live.

The minister said hotel workers sometimes face criminal pressure as they return home at weekends, despite the industry’s move away from paying salaries in cash.

“Our security forces have delivered a sharp reduction in murder, and we will not ease up. We will keep strengthening policing in our resort areas and the communities where hotel workers live,” Chang assured.

He acknowledged that unemployment and other social challenges continued to contribute to criminal activity, adding that the police were also having to contend with domestic violence and less serious offences that could escalate into deadly confrontations.

Pointing to the impact of increased investment in policing, Chang highlighted an 82.14 per cent reduction in homicides in Westmoreland, which he said had previously recorded more than 100 and, at one stage, over 140 murders annually.

“Today, we have 25 for the year,” he said, while commending the work of the police leadership, including head of the Westmoreland division, Senior Superintendent Othneil Dobson.

Despite the significant decline in murders, Chang cautioned that domestic and interpersonal violence remained a troubling source of killings across the country, requiring more targeted interventions alongside conventional crime-fighting measures.

Describing the trend as “an unfortunate part of the social scene today”, he said the Government was developing a range of interventions involving communities, schools, and the police to address the problem and encourage behavioural change.

He said the police had established the Community Security and Safety Branch, while the Government intended to roll out a major anti-violence programme aimed at encouraging people to report domestic disputes before they turned fatal.

“We intend to embark on a major programme

— anti-violence

— to provide an opportunity for domestic disputes to be reported to the police early, and to avoid the fatal outcome,” Chang said.

He also disclosed that the Government had established approximately 20 domestic violence centres, with men accounting for about 30 per cent of those seeking assistance.

“Not sure what it’s saying

— men reporting threats of violence

— but we are getting responses, and we intend to expand those centres and ultimately begin to get the kind of behavioural change we want in that sector,” the minister added.

World.title: A separate Grammy category for dancehall?
World.content:
Since the nominations in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced on November 16, there has been some uproar across social media platforms by fans and some members of the entertainment fraternity alike about the non-inclusion of some notable albums by dancehall artistes.

Some of the albums include God and Time by Vybz Kartel, Eminence by Beenie Man, Heights of Fire by Capleton, Forever Reign by Masicka, NPT by Alkaline.

Some have even suggested a bias towards dancehall artistes.

The 2027 reggae Grammy nominees are Too Too Bad by Buju Banton, The Art of Acceptance by Protoje, Supernova by Runkus, Exile by Chronixx, Brightside by Ziggy Marley, and Lottery by Shaggy.

There has been a call for a separate category for dancehall artistes, while others have argued that renaming the category to Best Reggae/Dancehall Album would suffice.

A few months ago, the JUNO Awards (Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys) announced the renaming of its Reggae Recording of the Year category to Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year for the 2027 staging.

The reality, some say, is that there are not sufficient releases each year by dancehall artistes to argue for a separate dancehall category in the Grammys. The Best Reggae Album category, instituted in 1985, was allegedly on the chopping block a few years ago due to the low number of submissions. This year, the number improved to 119, compared to 73 last year.

Recording artiste, producer, and music executive Ce’Cile, who is a registered member of the Recording Academy, says the Grammys aren’t obligated to do anything to drown out the noise created each year after the nominations are announced.

“They [Grammys] are not obligated to do anything. They gave us a category, and it would be nice to have an additional dancehall category, but there are many other genres that are still not a part of the Grammys,” Ce’Cile told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

She also argued that there hasn’t been the same enthusiasm and support for local award shows.

“The Grammys can do what they want to do. How many of us within the industry are voting members? We don’t even support our local award shows.”

Well-known entertainment attorney and music business consultant Lloyd Stanbury doesn’t support renaming the Best Reggae Album category. Instead, he supports the idea for a separate category for dancehall.

“The dancehall music genre, although born out of the reggae music genre, has evolved and grown to establish itself globally as yet another distinct music genre coming out of Jamaica. Dancehall music has earned and deserves its own standalone category in the Grammys. What is needed is more membership representation in the Recording Academy of both reggae and dancehall creatives to lobby and advocate for change.

“I think we will see more qualified submissions from both reggae and dancehall when Jamaican music creatives take their activities as serious business, inform themselves, and create support teams with qualified personnel,” the respected music industry insider told the Observer.

Music producer, artiste manager, publicist and podcast host Ralston Barrett, who has more than 30 years of experience in the industry and has represented Grammy-nominated and Billboard-charting acts, concurs with Stanbury that a separate dancehall category is needed.

“I think dancehall is more vibrant than reggae right now, so I expected to see more dancehall artistes nominated. To me, it’s a slap in the face to dancehall music. Buju Banton is the only nominee I’d put squarely in the dancehall camp. Some people would include Shaggy, but his music blends dancehall, reggae, and other genres. I was hoping to see Masicka, Vybz Kartel, and Alkaline among the nominees, and I would have liked to see Capleton nominated too,” said Barrett.

Barrett continued: “I’d like to see two separate Grammy categories: Best Reggae Album and Best Dancehall Album. Right now, I don’t think we have the numbers to make a strong case for that, though. Our industry needs to get more organised and united, do more to strengthen both genres, and encourage more eligible Jamaican music professionals to join the Recording Academy as voting members. Putting dancehall by itself could encourage more submissions. A category of our own would give artistes even more reason to submit.

“We also need more dancehall artistes making strong albums. Once the album is done, you still have to market it, network, and get people to hear it. When an artiste wins, people are quick to curse the artiste or the team. Give them credit for putting in the work. And where are our own award shows in Jamaica? We should be honouring our music and the people who make it right here at home,” he charged.

Music executive, Grammy-nominated producer, and former chair of the Grammy reggae committee Cristy Barber poured cold water on the assertion that no dancehall artistes were nominated this year.

“Although some of the predictions that were spoken about were not among the six nominees this year, there are three deejays nominated — Buju, Shaggy and Runkus — this year. So there is a dancehall presence. Hard-core, crossover, however you see it, they are still dancehall. So, renaming the category probably won’t change the problem some have with the title just being reggae. But the Academy looks at the category as all-inclusive — reggae and dancehall,” Barber reasoned.

Dancehall artistes who have won the Best Reggae Album award over the years include Shabba Ranks, Beenie Man, Sean Paul, Buju Banton, and Shaggy.

World.title: Belgium’s De Wever visits the king (again) with no budget deal in sight
World.content:
De Wever, a Flemish nationalist politician who was previously mayor of northern powerhouse Antwerp, sought to overcome differences Monday morning but a two-hour meeting failed to result in an agreement.

“There is no deal,” Economy Minister David Clarinval of the French-speaking center-right Reformist Movement told reporters when exiting the negotiations.

Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke, deputy prime minister from the Dutch-speaking socialists, did not answer reporters’ questions.

De Wever’s meeting with the king started shortly after 11:30 a.m. De Wever previously offered his resignation at the start of November, but the king gave the prime minister more time to find agreement among his coalition partners. Monday’s trip is the third visit by De Wever to the palace in less than a month.

If De Wever abandons attempts to clinch a deal between his government parties, Belgium is on track for a snap election.

World.title: UK appoints energy boss to drive reindustrialization
World.content:
LONDON — Great British Energy Chair Jürgen Maier has been appointed the government’s new northern economy and reindustrialisation commissioner, in a move aimed at attracting private investment and accelerating growth across the North.

The appointment was announced by First Secretary of State Louise Haigh during her keynote address to the CBI annual conference Monday, where she set out plans for a stronger partnership with business to drive reindustrialization.

The former Siemens UK boss, who has led the publicly owned clean investment company Great British Energy since 2024, will be based at No. 10 North and will report to the Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds.

Announcing Maier’s appointment, Haigh said the role of the private sector was “essential” to creating good jobs in Britain’s industrial heartlands.

As northern economy and reindustrialization commissioner, Maier will be tasked with implementing the government’s reindustrialization agenda and using his “extensive expertise to link with business and leverage private capital,” Haigh added.

World.title: EU opens antitrust probe into Coca-Cola bottler
World.content:
Brussels is also looking into claims that the U.K.-based bottler refused to let retailers negotiate a single supply deal covering several countries, forcing them to strike separate deals country by country.

“People across Europe enjoy soft drinks every day. But they should not have to pay more simply because they live in one EU country rather than another,” EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said in a statement.

Coca-Cola Europacific Partners is a distinct, publicly listed company that bottles and sells Coca-Cola drinks under licence from The Coca-Cola Company, which owns a 17% share in the firm.

The case comes as the Commission prepares new rules on so-called territorial supply constraints, the practice of big brands stopping retailers from buying goods in one EU country to resell in another.

Brussels has already targeted the practice under its antitrust rules. It fined Mondelez €337.5 million in 2024 for restricting cross-border sales of its snacks, and raided Ferrero in April.

The Commission raided CCEP’s offices in several countries in March 2025. The company could face a fine of up to 10% of its global annual turnover if the case is proven. There is no deadline for the investigation to finish.

World.title: How industrial cooperation strengthens Europe’s defense readiness
World.content:
Europe’s defense industrial sector is evolving as governments, manufacturers and suppliers work together to strengthen production capacity, technical expertise and long-term resilience. Across the continent, collaboration between European and North American industry is helping expand manufacturing networks, support highly skilled jobs and develop the capabilities needed to sustain critical defense programs over time.

As policymakers focus on readiness, industrial resilience and security, cooperation across borders is becoming increasingly important. Advanced manufacturing, engineering expertise and long-term investment depend on extensive networks of suppliers and technology partners working together to support shared objectives.

One example of this cooperation can be seen in the Patriot program, led by Raytheon, an RTX business. Patriot brings together a broad network of industrial partners across Europe and supports collaboration among companies that contribute specialized expertise and capabilities from across the continent.

Maintaining and producing Patriot technology in Germany through this partnership is an excellent contribution to support Germany and NATO partners while strengthening industrial capabilities across Europe.”

Developing, delivering and deploying truly integrated air and missile defense systems depends on Europe’s aerospace and defense engineers, suppliers and production facilities. Technological interoperability and availability among European and NATO partners rely on shared engineering standards, coordinated production processes and aligned sustainment pathways.

With the support of 24 European suppliers, Raytheon is not doing this alone. A cornerstone of this expansion is COMLOG, Raytheon’s joint venture with MBDA Deutschland, which will begin production in Germany by 2027. This initiative will boost output, increase in-region sustainment capacity and further anchor production within Europe and expedite deliveries on both sides of the Atlantic.

“Maintaining and producing Patriot technology in Germany through this partnership is an excellent contribution to support Germany and NATO partners while strengthening industrial capabilities across Europe,” explains Jürgen Koneczny, Vice President Program Patriot at MBDA Deutschland GmbH and Managing Director of COMLOG GmbH. “This collaboration strengthens industrial and military capabilities in Europe, creates jobs in Germany and strengthens supply chains that benefit European partner nations.”

Expanding industrial capacity and strengthening supply-chain resilience are becoming increasingly important priorities across Europe. Bayern Chemie, a key German supplier supporting the Patriot program, plays an essential role in building manufacturing capacity and diversifying sources of critical components.

“Our partnership with RTX’s Raytheon is a strong example of how U.S. and German industrial cooperation can accelerate innovation, deepen co-production and reinforce the technological strength of the Western defense industrial base,” says Dr. Wolfgang Rieck, Managing Director of Bayern Chemie GmbH. “By bringing together complementary expertise, advanced technologies and shared industrial capabilities, we are well positioned to support evolving defense and security requirements across Europe and for customers worldwide.”

Europe’s defense readiness depends on the ability to sustain critical systems throughout their operational life.”

Beyond production, European governments are increasingly focusing on sustainment, the maintenance and modernization capacity that keeps systems operational over decades. In the Netherlands, Fokker Techniek provides specialized maintenance, repair and overhaul support for Patriot units. In Poland, Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne (WZE) delivers electronics modernization and testing capabilities that help improve readiness and expand national industrial expertise.

“Europe’s defense readiness depends on the ability to sustain critical systems throughout their operational life,” says Roland van Dijk, CEO of Fokker Techniek. “Through our partnership with Raytheon, Fokker Techniek brings decades of Dutch MRO expertise to help ensure long-term readiness, reliability and availability. Together, we are strengthening the resilience of Europe’s defense industrial base while supporting the security and operational readiness of The Netherlands, NATO and its allies.”

For WZE, participation in the Patriot program represents both industrial growth and strategic value:

“Our cooperation with Raytheon represents an important opportunity for Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne to further develop its technological and industrial capabilities. Through our participation in an international supply chain, we have strengthened specialized expertise, contributed to the growth of Poland’s defense industrial base and supported the development of modern capabilities for Poland and allied nations. This collaboration demonstrates the value of long-term industrial partnerships in fostering innovation, strengthening industrial resilience and enhancing collective security across the Alliance,” says Damian Gorzelany, WZE President.

Today, 24 European partners support Patriot-related work, making the system an increasingly co-produced and co-maintained asset built in Europe for Europe.”

Together, these partnerships reflect a broader shift in Europe – a move toward more distributed production, resilient supply chain and deeper industrial cooperation among allies. With 21,000 employees across 65 locations and 13,500 suppliers in Europe, RTX is woven into this ecosystem. Today, 24 European partners support Patriot-related work, making the system an increasingly co-produced and co-maintained asset built in Europe for Europe.

For companies across Europe, these collaborations are about more than production. They help sustain specialized expertise, create high-value employment opportunities and reinforce the interconnected industrial ecosystem that supports security, innovation and economic growth across the region.

World.title: Ukraine sank Russian warship off Libya, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
The operation used seven Ukrainian-made sea drones and also hit the cargo ship MV Angara, which Kyiv accuses Moscow of using to carry weapons.

Moscow has not yet commented. The U.N. mission in Libya called for an independent investigation.

In March, Russia accused Ukraine of launching sea drones from Libya against the Arctic Metagaz, a sanctioned LNG tanker that was hit around 240 kilometers north of the Libyan port of Sirte and left damaged and drifting in the Mediterranean.

The Libyan strikes occurred a day after a drone hit the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. Finland’s defense forces said Ukraine was likely behind that attack.

“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X on Saturday. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Overnight, Russia launched 153 drones at Ukraine, the air force said. In the Kharkiv region, eight people were injured when drones hit a kindergarten and a hotel, regional officials said.

World.title: Badenoch and Farage: The battle for business
World.content:
It’s business as usual as party leaders head to the annual CBI conference – all except for Andy Burnham, who is sending his first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, instead.

A punchy move, when a PM or chancellor usually attends. So, can Haigh succeed in her pitch to private sector bosses for more public control? And can the Conservative and Reform UK leaders use Burnham’s absence to their advantage?

Among the attendees will be a certain Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy, who will be speaking to the head of the CBI, Rain Newton-Smith.

Ms Newton-Smith will tell the conference, “Brexit was a wrong turn for our country” – music to the ears of Burnham as he tries to sell the country the idea of closer ties with the European Union.

**A message from TikTok: Did you know TikTok contributed at least £10 billion to the UK economy in 2025? The platform supported 153,000 jobs, turning online discovery into real-world growth, from high streets to bookshops, new research from Public First and EY shows.**

World.title: France gets an EU budget win — but wants more
World.content:
Over the weekend, European Council President António Costa unveiled a new budget in which he managed to slash the money pot by €44 billion. The main winner? French President Emmanuel Macron.

Today on the show, Ian Wishart and Nick Vinocur discuss how Costa’s plan hands Macron a key win ahead of a meeting of EU leaders this Thursday, as well as why the French are still super unhappy with how the budget proposal looks now.

Also on the podcast: Kinga Gál, co-president of the far-right Patriots group in the European Parliament, wants to reshape Brussels in the 2029 EU election.

And finally, the U.K. and the EU may be trying to rekindle ties, but as with any toxic couple, things last week got a little messy.
