World.title: “Faire des milliardaires les méchants de l’histoire” : à Paris, les gauches occidentales tâchent de faire front commun
World.content:
“On voit une idée jugée radicale il y a dix ans faire son chemin et être de plus en plus perçue, comme on dit en Québécois, comme du gros bon sens”, a-t-elle confié à POLITICO en marge de l’événement.

Internationale de la taxation

Comme tous les participants interrogés par POLITICO, Trottier nourrit l’espoir qu’un front mondial voit le jour.

“Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, Steve Bannon... ils organisent tous leurs mouvements de droite et oligarchiques au-delà des frontières, et se rassemblent autour d’une vision commune de ce qu’ils veulent accomplir. Si nous voulons les combattre, nous devons nous unir autour de notre propre vision”, estime ainsi Pramila Jayapal.

Si la question fiscale reste le point de départ, le public du jour s’accorde à dresser un tableau plus large, dans lequel les milliardaires, par le pouvoir que leur confère leur fortune, représenteraient une menace directe pour la démocratie et son bon fonctionnement.

Aux Etats-Unis, la victoire des démocrates aux midterms peut leur permettre d’imposer le sujet de la taxation des ultrariches au niveau fédéral. “On a gagné ce débat, poursuit Jayapal. Même si des propositions diverses existent, avec trois ou quatre propositions de loi, elles visent toutes à taxer la fortune. Reste la question du comment, combien et sur quelle période.”

Son collègue Ro Khanna, élu de Californie — où Gabriel Zucman a été l’artisan d’un référendum visant à instaurer un prélèvement exceptionnel de 5% sur le patrimoine des milliardaires, finalement rejeté début novembre — prévoit de déposer “dès la première semaine” de la mandature un Tax Billionnaires Act cosigné avec le sénateur Bernie Sanders, indique-t-il à POLITICO. Une façon d’“ouvrir la voie sur la taxation et de prouver au monde que c’est possible”, selon Khanna.

World.title: Mercedes, BMW hit by 24-hour strikes as German pay dispute widens
World.content:
Workers in Germany’s metal and electrical industries walked out this week after three rounds of pay talks ended without a deal. IG Metall called on more than 23,000 workers at 19 sites in northern Germany to take part in a 24-hour strike.

 

Further walkouts are expected in Berlin and the union's central district, which covers Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland, and Thuringia.

The latest "warning strikes" follow nationwide walkouts on Friday that drew 151,000 workers, according to IG Metall. Audi’s main plant in Ingolstadt and three BMW plants in Bavaria were among the sites hit.

Three rounds of negotiations for around 130,000 employees in northern Germany have so far been unsuccessful.

IG Metall is seeking a 5% pay rise over one year for 3.7 million workers, including those in the automotive sector. Employers have offered a one-off payment in July 2027 worth 1% of gross annual pay, and a 1.3% pay rise from July 2028. The union said the offer would leave workers worse off after inflation.

Strikes began at several factories on Sunday evening as night shifts started, including at Mercedes-Benz plants in Bremen and Hamburg.

Tagesschau, the news service of German public broadcaster ARD, reported that production lines at Mercedes-Benz’s Hamburg plant have been idle since 10pm on Sunday.

"So far, the plant is completely sealed off and no one has been allowed in to work," an IG Metall representative told the news service on Monday morning. "Only plant security is present, and otherwise nothing is happening here."

Wind turbine maker Siemens Gamesa in Cuxhaven is also impacted.

The union also called on workers at the Meyer Werft shipyard in Papenburg to walk out on Monday, NDR reported.

Volkswagen, which owns Audi, is seeking a two-year pay freeze and more flexible working hours in separate talks with IG Metall covering about 120,000 employees, according to Reuters.

BMW previously sought to cut nearly 8,000 jobs through voluntary severance, according to Münchner Merkur.

Mercedes-Benz is seeking €800 million in annual savings in Germany, Handelsblatt reported. Longer working hours without extra pay and cuts to benefits were among the options under discussion, German public broadcaster SWR reported. Mercedes-Benz has also said it would suspend investment in Germany.

Euronews contacted BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen for comment.

World.title: Exclusive: China-backed hackers suspected behind ongoing EU Commission cyberattack
World.content:
The European Commission suspects that a large-scale cyberattack, still spreading through its IT systems, is the work of a China-backed network of threat actors, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter.

 

"Panda" is the codename circulating inside the Commission for the suspected perpetrators. In the cybersecurity community, the animal name is used to loosely tie threat actors to their state sponsors, in this case China.

On 22 October, the Commission's IT department detected a malicious actor in its internal networks. A month after the attack began, the EU executive has yet to fully contain the breach and was forced to take the EU Academy website offline on Saturday.

The EU Academy is an online platform offering professional development and specialised learning to young people.

"The incident is still under investigation. Public access to the platform has been disabled and measures to contain, mitigate and limit the impact of the incident have been taken, including the implementation of preventive, detective and corrective controls," reads the EU Academy's website.

The Commission has confirmed a leak of names and email addresses and is warning users of possible follow-ups from the attacker, such as phishing campaigns based on their personal data.

That is the first major consequence of the incident. For other IT systems, EU cyber experts have not confirmed data theft affecting Commission staff, though several internal apps were taken offline as a precaution and some remain unavailable.

According to the current threat assessment, the China-linked actor was not targeting specific systems or individuals, which would have called for a less visible attack. Instead, it wanted to test more broadly how far it could compromise the Commission's IT networks.

Suspicion of a link to Chinese security services rests on the sophistication of the attack and on the use of ARTEX, a Chinese-developed cybersecurity tool that uses AI to detect vulnerabilities that hackers can then exploit.

Leading cybersecurity firms like Microsoft and CrowdStrike have attributed to the China-linked groups Storm-0940 and Panda Vapor attacks using ARTEX for AI-driven global espionage campaigns targeting hundreds of organisations globally.

The Commission has been hit by two other cyberattacks this year: one on the cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu website and one on its mobile infrastructure in January.

Both are also deemed to stem from China's cyber threat landscape, but from different groups, and neither was ever formally attributed.

The Chinese government has consistently denied sponsoring, directing or supporting hacking groups accused of conducting cyberattacks on foreign governments and institutions.

Since the hack became public last week, the main trade union of Commission staff has vehemently criticised management of the incident, notably for leaving civil servants to learn about it from the press.

A Commission official rejected that criticism, stressing that public communication is not foreseen in such cases because it would tip off the malicious actor that mitigation measures are under way.

Secrecy also prevents the spread of panic, which makes life harder for the security experts trying to contain the incident, Euronews understands.

World.title: EU military chief warns of escalating hybrid threats as Europe races to strengthen defences
World.content:
Europe faces an escalating wave of hybrid threats, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, and must urgently accelerate its military preparedness to confront them, the EU's most senior military official has warned.

 

General Seán Clancy, chairman of the EU Military Committee, told Euronews on Monday that the proliferation of asymmetric attacks was his greatest security concern, pointing to incidents in Poland, Denmark and Germany.

"The main concern is the spread and escalation of hybrid threats," he said in an interview with Europe Today. "We've seen this particularly over the past six to twelve months, from the Baltics to the Black Sea."

His warning follows another weekend of Russian attacks on Ukraine and comes as European governments grapple with growing concerns about sabotage, drone incursions and other forms of hybrid warfare.

Clancy said the threats were designed to destabilise not just Ukraine but European democracies more broadly.

"That's why readiness and preparedness are at the centre of the EU's strategy," he said. "The sooner member states can act collectively in a crisis, the better our chances of containing it."

Military chiefs meet

Europe's military chiefs will meet in Brussels on Wednesday to assess the continent's defence readiness, with Ukraine and the Coalition of the Willing high on the agenda.

Clancy acknowledged that enormous challenges remained, particularly in building up weapons stockpiles, industrial production capacity and the ability to sustain military operations over time.

"We're in a better position than we were. But we need to move faster and accelerate our preparedness," he said.

"Europe is stepping up. It's leaning in. We're closing the gaps."

However, Europe remains heavily dependent on the United States for critical military capabilities, including air defence, air-to-air refuelling and other strategic support.

Clancy dismissed fears that Washington's ongoing review of its military presence in Europe would undermine the continent's security, insisting that any transition would be managed jointly.

The transatlantic partnership, he said, was "without equivocation, our most important relationship, and it will remain so, now and into the future."

Asked whether Europe could defend itself against Russia without American support, Clancy expressed confidence in its armed forces.

"We are ready to defend and secure Europe," he said, while stressing that NATO remained ultimately responsible for the continent's collective defence.

World.title: Donald Trump urges Nvidia to rehire former CEO Jensen Huang
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has called on Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO.

 

Trump's appeal adds to growing calls for Huang's return, including a petition with more than 200,000 signatures that Elon Musk has signed.

Huang, who co-founded the AI chip giant in 1993, is due to answer lawmakers' questions in Congress on 1 December.

"I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the company, and also, for the U.S.A.," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.

Trump has stepped up his support over the past week for Huang's return.

Last Monday, he said he "would not mind" seeing Huang reinstated. On Friday, he told reporters at the White House that he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance".

Huang resigned on 12 November after it emerged that he had two extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations and US authorities said they have not reached a conclusion.

Musk and other tech leaders back a return

The "Stand with Jensen" petition, an open letter to Nvidia's board, had more than 206,000 signatures as of Monday morning, according to its website. More than 10,000 signatories claim to be current Nvidia employees.

The letter asked the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts". It also highlighted that Nvidia and Huang have not endorsed it.

"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on 13 November.

Tobi Lütke, CEO of e-commerce platform Shopify, and Tim Sweeney, CEO of Fortnite developer Epic Games, have also signed it.

Huang said on 17 November that he would be "honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO" if the board judged that best for the company, its staff, its shareholders, and America.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on 15 November that Nvidia needed "a dramatic shake-up" and a CEO from outside the company.

However, in an interview with CBS on Sunday, he stated: "I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now".

Thus far, Nvidia's board does not plan to bring him back. Chair Harvey Jones told analysts during the company's earnings call last Tuesday that the board had "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".

Colette Kress, Nvidia's finance chief, has taken over as interim CEO during the search for a permanent replacement. An outside law firm is currently undertaking an investigation.

Nvidia's shares closed around $125.5 on Friday, representing a 48% collapse since their intraday all-time high price of roughly $243.3 on 6 October.

They lost over 20% just last week, their seventh weekly decline in a row and the longest losing streak since 2008.

The slide continued despite Nvidia beating earnings forecasts last Tuesday.

Friday's 14% drop followed a Reuters report, citing two people briefed on the matter, that the Securities and Exchange Commission, the US markets regulator, was examining possible accounting issues at Nvidia.

Questions in Congress

Huang will answer questions from three House committees behind closed doors on 1 December: Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

The committees are looking into the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese businesses.

The session will be a transcribed interview and will not be open to the public.

Huang's public testimony will come before the Senate Banking Committee, according to the office of its chair, Republican Senator Tim Scott. No date has been set, though Scott had originally asked for 3 December.

Two Nvidia shareholders, the investment firms Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management, have asked the board to keep Huang's return open and to hold off on a permanent CEO until all the facts are known.

World.title: Iran vows 'every means' to counter US blockade of Hormuz after Trump threat
World.content:
Iran's foreign ministry condemned the US naval blockade as "military aggression" on Monday and said Tehran would use "every means" to counter it, a day after US President Donald Trump threatened to sink Iranian tankers attempting to breach it.

 

Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, speaking at his weekly press briefing, described the blockade as a violation of the UN Charter and an "act of crime," adding that Tehran considered itself entitled to use any means to defend itself.

"We will certainly not tolerate this situation and will use every means to counter US aggression," Baghaei said.

On Sunday, Trump warned that Iranian ships attempting to break the blockade would be sent to the "bottom of the sea."

Asked about the possibility by a Fox News reporter, he said: "I hope they do it; they'll all go down to the bottom of the sea, just like the rest of their navy."

Convoy uncertainty

Media outlets and figures close to the IRGC have called in recent days for a convoy of Iranian oil tankers to be dispatched to break the blockade, with some threatening that Gulf oil facilities would be targeted if the vessels came under attack. Iranian officials have said they have no concrete plan to do so.

IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency published an article on Sunday acknowledging the wave of reports, and said no competent or official authority in the armed forces, the Supreme National Security Council or the government had announced such a plan.

Tasnim said the reports stemmed entirely from proposals put forward by individuals in the media and on social media.

The news agency added that "Iran's plans to break the blockade are certainly being drawn up," but that no one outside the circle of security and military decision-makers had knowledge of them.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed on Sunday at least one incident involving an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, saying military forces had been involved in the encounter.

No further details were released about the identity of the forces involved or whether the tanker had been attempting to circumvent the blockade. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) had not commented on the incident as of Monday.

Also at Monday's briefing, Baghaei was asked how Tehran might respond to reported US planning for a possible attack on Iran.

"The best scenario is for them to get the hell out of the region," he said, adding that IRGC Air Force commander Majid Mousavi would deliver Iran's response to any potential attack "in a neat and elegant package."

Mousavi said on Sunday that IRGC aerospace capabilities had grown since the previous round of conflict and that "the field is ours and we determine the battlefield."

A boat floats as commercial vessels appear anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP) AP Photo

IRGC deputy commander-in-chief Major General Mostafa Izadi said Iran's missile range had been significantly upgraded and that any threat would draw an immediate response "without geographical limitations."

Azizi, chairman of parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated the same position, saying Iran had determined it would face no geographical limitations in any future confrontation.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf cited remarks by Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei about the need to end the current situation, saying "sustainable deterrence" was the way out of the crisis.

"We must remove the shadow of war from ourselves," Ghalibaf said. Iran needed to fulfil "the directive of the Supreme Leader" Khamenei, he added.

What will it take to reopen Hormuz?

Baghaei elaborated on remarks by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who said the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within two hours of the other side fulfilling its commitments.

Baghaei said the comment was meant to signal Iran's readiness to act quickly, not to minimise the complexity of a potential agreement.

Tehran's conditions, he said, include lifting US sanctions, ending the naval blockade and implementing commitments Washington accepted under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.

Trump has described the Islamabad memorandum as a waste of time and declared it null and void, and has characterised ongoing negotiations with Iran as "a load of nonsense".

Diplomatic efforts are continuing despite the standoff. Qatar's prime minister is expected to meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday, with Doha serving as a key mediator between Tehran and Washington.

World.title: Can AI help detect breast cancer faster? Major new trial will find out
World.content:
Researchers in the United Kingdom will test whether artificial intelligence tools can help improve breast cancer detection, in the world’s largest study of its kind.

 

Early breast cancer detection can save lives, but diagnosis can be a time-consuming process. Currently in the UK, at least two radiologists review every mammogram, or breast x-ray, but very few — less than 1% — of these scans actually show signs of cancer.

In the trial, known as EDITH, radiologists will use an AI-assisted tool to help detect cancers that are too small to see or feel. The goal is to give specialists more time to diagnose and care for women with cancer, while reducing the time they spend reviewing mammograms with no signs of disease.

“If successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery,” said Yvette Cooper, the UK’s health and social care secretary. The UK government is backing the trial with £10 million (about €12 million).

The study will enroll about 660,000 women aged 50 to 71 who are due for a routine breast cancer screening, which is offered every three years in the UK. Women can opt out if they do not want to take part in the trial.

Women will be split into three groups: the first group will undergo a standard breast cancer screening, with two radiologists reviewing the x-rays. In the second group, a radiologist and the AI tool will both review the mammograms to see if the AI tool catches any signs of cancer the radiologist may have missed.

In the third group, the AI tool will take the first look at an x-ray and determine whether the likelihood of cancer is high or low. If it is low, one radiologist will review the images, but if it is high, two radiologists will check the images and decide whether to refer the patient for additional testing.

The AI tool could “help experts review images more efficiently,” said Fiona Gilbert, a radiology professor at the University of Cambridge and one of the study’s lead researchers. She is also studying whether AI can help identify women at higher risk of developing breast cancer.

Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one radiologist, according to the trial announcement, and the AI-assisted tool will only be integrated into routine breast cancer screening if the study shows it is as safe and effective as the existing screening programme.

Currently, around 2.1 million women in the UK undergo breast screening each year, preventing around 1,300 deaths.

Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in the European Union, with an estimated 360,000 women diagnosed in 2024, EU data shows. That accounts for 29% of all cancer diagnoses in women.

World.title: 'We should not be okay with a handover of society to AI', warns Meta's AI boss
World.content:
The world is entering the era of superintelligence, and the AI industry must prioritise safety and human control rather than allowing an unconstrained handover to machines, Meta’s AI chief has warned.

 

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s Chief AI Officer, made the warning in a post on social media platform X on Sunday in light of rival Anthropic’s announcement on Friday that one of their mathematicians had used their Claude AI model to solve the famous Riemann Hypothesis mathematical problem.

The hypothesis suggests that the seemingly random appearance of prime numbers actually follows a hidden, strict pattern. Solving the problem could eventually have enormous real-world consequences, by giving certainty to the way prime numbers are distributed, computer systems, for example, can run more quickly and leaner.

It comes at a time when global debate over AI has reached fever pitch, with concerns among the public over the risks AI poses not only to jobs and the economy but also to security and human rights.

Young people in 20 countries took to the streets on Friday to protest the cost of living, with the lack of AI regulation and fears over autonomous weapons following talks over killer robots also among concerns.

The AI chief said he sees the discovery as “marking the beginning of a significant change” and argued that “nothing humanity has ever accomplished compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might and strength”.

It’s for this reason Meta’s AI chief is concerned that the intelligence of AI models may outpace humans, raising questions of what the future holds.

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” said Wang.

“It is equally hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1,000-times smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”

Wang criticised the “lazy thinking within the AI industry” that advanced AI capable of surpassing human intelligence across all domains is “inevitable” and cannot be stopped.

“We should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI,” warned Wang.

“We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment.”

Wang concluded saying while he believes it is possible, it means “the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the ‘default path’ in front of us”.

The latest in a series of warnings

His warning echoes similar statements made by other leading AI research labs.

On Friday, Google DeepMind researchers including Tim Genewein warned that artificial general superintelligence could soon be within reach, opening the door for recursive self-improving AI models.

On Sunday OpenAI publicly urged rival AI labs to agree on shared safety limits until better monitoring and control tools exist, amid Anthropic’s claim of solving the Riemann Hypothesis.

In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for “pacing the frontier”, to slow down the development of advanced AI models to give time for sufficient safety guardrails to be put in place.

His call was welcomed by some leaders such as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen who reiterated his call to slow down development and establish global rules.

However, US President Donald Trump has taken a different approach. At the end of September, he convened a summit with America’s biggest AI firms and made an agreement that the companies can police themselves.

Last week in China, America’s approach to AI safety was at loggerheads with the Chinese premier Xi Jinping, who called for global action to keep “AI under human control”.

Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney also warned last week that global governance on AI is an “enormous risk”.

World.title: From COP31 Antalya to Copenhagen: UN climate summits where no agreement was reached
World.content:
The COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya have ended without a final deal. The EU and other countries rejected a cover decision because it did not cover how to quite fossil fuels or fund climate action in developing countries.

 

As the COP process depends almost 200 countries reaching a consensus, it is far from easy, especially with geopolitical tensions as they are.

Since the first United Nations' Conference of the Parties (COP) in 1995, many summits have seen fierce arguments when countries failed to find common ground.

Here we take a look back at previous COP summits where tensions ran high.

2000: COP6, The Hague

At COP6 in 2000, held in The Hague, the negotiations were suspended. Talks resumed months later in Bonn, where the secretariat of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change is based.

The summit took place at a time when the United States was locked in an extremely tight presidential election. Negotiators did not know whether the next leader of the world's largest economy would be George W. Bush, who was sceptical of climate policies, or Al Gore, who would later share the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate advocacy.

Ironically, Bush's election victory, and his subsequent rejection of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, encouraged other countries at the resumed Bonn talks to push ahead with plans to implement the protocol.

However, France's former chief negotiator Paul Watkinson criticised the summit, saying it ended in "chaos".

2009: COP15, Copenhagen

Expectations rose after the election of US President Barack Obama. But COP15 failed to deliver the binding global climate agreement many countries had hoped for.

Deep divisions between developed and developing countries, especially disputes between Washington and Beijing, blocked a deal on mandatory cuts in emissions.

In the end, the conference only agreed to "take note" of the non-binding Copenhagen Accord. The accord included a goal of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 2 degrees and a pledge by rich countries to provide 100 billion dollars a year in climate finance by 2020.

2012: COP18, Doha

Countries agreed a second commitment period under the Kyoto Protocol. But major emitters such as the United States, Russia and Canada did not take part.

Critics of the deal argued that the targets were not ambitious enough and that the arrangement covered an ever-shrinking share of global emissions.

2019: COP25, Madrid

Talks in Madrid overran their scheduled finish time by more than 40 hours, as they did this year at the summit in Antalya.

At COP25, countries failed to agree rules to govern international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

The summit's final text disappointed the countries most vulnerable to climate change and environmental groups, because it did not include a significant increase in emissions reduction pledges.

2022: COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt

Countries agreed to establish a historic "loss and damage" fund to support those most affected by climate change.

But negotiators were unable to strengthen commitments to phase down the use of fossil fuels. Many governments and climate activists criticised the outcome, arguing that there had been insufficient progress on cutting emissions.

2024: COP29, Baku, Azerbaijan

At COP29 rows over climate finance for developing countries pushed the negotiations beyond their planned end date.

Negotiators struggled to bridge differences over the scale of financial commitments between rich and poor nations.

The summit eventually produced an agreement, avoiding a complete breakdown. But many developing countries judged the outcome to be inadequate.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.

“This is part of a process of basically closing down all independent media that might risk reaching followers of the ruling party,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb of Human Rights Watch.

“The whole tactic of the Erdogan government has been to use court orders. The court orders are so problematic in themselves, so overreaching, so disproportionate, that this has nothing really to do with the legal process. This is all about a political crackdown.”

Turkey talks green at Cop31 while cracking down on activists

Sinclair-Webb noted that television remains the primary news source for most Turks, making both networks and individual journalists who question government policies prime targets.

Four journalist have been detained or placed under house arrest for reporting on the investment scandal.

Authorities accuse Sozcu TV of ties to followers of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for masterminding a failed 2016 coup. Four of its executives and officials have been detained. Halk TV faces separate corruption allegations.

Both broadcasters strongly deny the charges.

Investment scandal

The closing of the channels comes amid fallout from the collapse of more than 100 investment funds, which wiped out $20 billion, stranded more than 500,000 investors and triggered a stock market crash.

The scandal has implicated numerous figures linked to Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party).

According to recent polls, 80 percent of Turks are closely following the scandal, with a similar majority blaming the government.

On Thursday, protesters demonstrated outside the Capital Markets Board, the country's financial regulator, in Ankara.

Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next

Around 500 people are under investigation and more than 100 suspects have been jailed. Erdogan vowed this week that no one would escape justice and promised to expedite repayments to affected investors.

Political analyst Sezin Oney said the government is scrambling to control the public narrative as its reputation among its own voter base unravels.

“Up to now, AK Party and government circles were able to project to their base the idea that the opposition [is involved in] all sorts of corruption. So all of a sudden, that facade, that rhetoric has collapsed. Now it’s the government circles who are massively corrupt."

Debate moves online

Atilla Yesilada, a Turkey analyst at New York-based consultancy firm Global Source Partners, warned that the scandal has exposed deep flaws in financial oversight, threatening severe economic and political fallout for Erdogan.

“Turkey is heading for a recession because the institutional structure has completely collapsed,” Yesilada said. “In a free market economy, you really need regulatory boards to do their work which clearly, as we see in this instance, they don't. In fact, they enable or incentivise thieves [and make] their jobs easier."

Yesilada added that Erdogan lacks a clear path to resolve the crisis, as opposition figures release new allegations implicating AK Party associates daily.

Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy

Following the state takeover of another broadcaster last year, the loss of Sozcu TV and Halk TV marks a grim turning point for Turkish media, Oney said. However, she questioned whether the government can successfully suppress public discourse.

“It’s the end of the road for TV journalism, you don’t have any oppositional voice or oppositional debate. But people talk, people think, one way or another. Because Turkey was a thinking and talking nation before, it's very difficult to stop [that]. It is just [being done now] on social media.”

The government has accelerated efforts to police online dissent, shutting down hundreds of critical social media accounts, although new ones are emerging just as rapidly.

Meanwhile Koza TV, a previously fringe station, has seen its ratings surge after becoming a new outlet for independent reporting on the scandal – although mounting regulatory fines make its future uncertain.

World.title: German police respond to multiple school bomb threats
World.content:
Police in Germany are responding to bomb threats against a series of schools, but say that at present they don't believe them to be credible. Danish authorities are reporting a similar series of apparent hoaxes.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

What did police say about the bomb threats?

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release . "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."

Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.

Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."

Various disruptive incidents targeting Europe in recent weeks

This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Europe.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

This is a developing story, more to follow...

World.title: 'I've Lost Her Forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract
World.content:
For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.

For over 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.

But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.

Netflix contract sparks AI dispute

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.

The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.

They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

Katrin Fröhlich, who has dubbed the German voice of Cameron Diaz for over 30 years, is worried about the future of the voiceover industry Image: Nicole Kubelka/Geisler-Fotopress/picture alliance

"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."

"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.

Union says deal offers legal safeguards

The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.

Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.

"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.

Is AI killing creative jobs? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.

"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."

He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.

Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.

"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

Matti Klemm is the voice of children's character Benjamin Blümchen Image: RTL+/dpa/picture alliance

Voice actor plans legal challenge

Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon character Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."

He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.

The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

Matti Klemm wants to find out exactly how Netflix has used his voice to train its AI and is suing the company Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"

Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.

Industry fears growing AI impact

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.

Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.

"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.

Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.

"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.

But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: 'On the verge of collapse': Germany's budget cuts threaten anti-racism and democracy work
World.content:
Numerous grassroots initiatives in Germany are facing funding cuts. Affected organizations are sounding the alarm, pointing to growing challenges posed by far-right extremism.

Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts toward the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.

The"Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.

The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.

Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation , a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat. "In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.

Politically-disillusioned youth? Far from it! To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lasting damage to democracy in Germany?

According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.

The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany. The in parts far-right extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Amadeu Antonio Foundation board member Tahera Ameer.

The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.

During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, according to him.

But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS) , the nationwideOFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims , CLAIM.

The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.

Games with purpose — more than entertainment To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD: 'Program to secure power by the Left'

The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."

If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.

In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.

A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."

However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.

German influencer fights extremism on TikTok To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How is democratic civil society prioritized?

"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."

Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color. "The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered, if someone needs support."

For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Lina Mitschke lamented.

The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: What is crawling on Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch'?
World.content:
A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

'The Night Watch Lives' study is conducted in collaboration with a major restoration and research project called 'Operation Night Watch' Image: Niels de Vries/Artis/dpa/picture alliance

Putting microbes in the spotlight

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

A study in progress

At the opening of the exhibition on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the upcoming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds. That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

Microbiologist Eline van Bloois will be taking samples from the original painting once a month, over a period of six months Image: Niels de Vries/ARTIS

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."

The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form spores that are inactive, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

When art and science meet

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch'."

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

World.title: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
World.content:
Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge.

Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.

In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman, and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.

As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.

To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.

Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.

How does the Early Start Pension work?

Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager aged six to 18.

Beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.

Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.

Parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.

Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.

"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.

What are the German government's pension, labor reforms? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.

"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he said.

The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.

It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens."

What does the government say?

The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.

Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.

Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.

But Germany's plan differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.

The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.

What Germans young and old think about the pension system To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can the scheme encourage long-term investing?

Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.

"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them."

Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.

"If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions."

In the meantime, he says, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.

Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the plan, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.

Yet Geyer says the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.

"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he said.

What else should be done to stabilize the pension system?

Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.

To address the challenge, he calls for a moderate increase in pension contributions, a broader contributor base that includes groups such as the self-employed, and policies aimed at attracting more qualified workers to the labor market.

Börsch-Supan, who specializes in the economics of aging, says the government's primary goal should be to stabilize the pay-as-you-go statutory pension system.

"A transition to a fully funded pension system would actually be desirable, but it would initially place a heavy double burden on the younger generation, because they would have to save for themselves while also paying contributions for their parents," he explained.

The expert also suggests other measures like restoring the sustainability factor, which is designed to link annual pension hikes to demographic shifts, and linking the retirement age to life expectancy.

World.title: NATO Parliamentary Assembly convenes amid Russian airspace violations
World.content:
Skip next section Wadephul: 'We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory'

11/23/2026 November 23, 2026 Wadephul: 'We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory'

Following the most recent violations of Polish airspace by Russian weapons, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has emphasized NATO's determination to defend itself.

"We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory," he said on Monday as the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continued in Berlin.

Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin, he added: "Don't be deceived: we may be a defensive alliance but we are prepared to defend our countries and our alliance."

According to Polish state prosecutors, the three objects which crashed in southeastern Poland on Friday were Russian CH-101 cruise missiles.

Wadephul said he was in close contact with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and assured Warsaw of his full solidarity.

Later, at approximately midday local time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte is expected to address the assembly before heading to an official reception with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the afternoon.
