World.title: Street plays to promote co-existence between humans and wildlife organised in Kotagiri
World.content:
Street plays to promote peaceful co-existence between humans and wildlife were organised in Kotagiri and Kattabettu forest ranges in the Nilgiris forest divisions recently.

The street plays were organised by Keystone Foundation in collaboration with the Forest Department. The two-day human-wildlife interaction awareness programme included street plays performed by Aayudham Foundation, Coimbatore, which ‘presented a series of engaging street plays to raise awareness among local communities about reducing negative interactions between humans and wildlife,’ a press release stated.

The performances focused on the importance of peaceful coexistence with wildlife, particularly species such as sloth bears, leopards, tigers and elephants and practices that can be adopted by human communities to minimise negative interactions with wildlife. Key themes of the plays included understanding wildlife behaviour, avoiding encounters with wild animals, responsible waste disposal and the role of improper waste management in attracting wildlife towards human settlements.

Through interactive and culturally engaging performances, the street plays highlighted how everyday human activities can influence wildlife movement and contribute to human–wildlife conflict. The programme also encouraged villagers to adopt responsible practices, remain alert and work collectively towards creating safer environments for both people and wildlife, the release added.

A total of six street plays were conducted across the two forest ranges. Through the medium of street theatre, the initiative aimed to strengthen community awareness, encourage responsible behaviour and promote harmonious coexistence between local communities and wildlife, it added.

World.title: Bangladesh garment makers eye 15% wage hike, far short of workers' demand
World.content:
Bangladesh’s garment manufacturers could propose a roughly 15% ​increase in the minimum monthly wage at talks with authorities on Monday (September 23, 2026), industry ⁠leaders said, far short of workers’ demands for more than double their pay.

Also Read: Fresh unrest in Bangladesh as garment workers protest, block highways for higher wages

Since early November, unrest over wages has led to shutdowns and violence in the world’s second-largest garment exporter, which employs over 4 million ‌workers and provides supplies for major global retailers including H&M, Gap and Walmart. The protests over pay are testing the cost advantage of an industry that ‌generates more than 80% of the country’s export earnings.

Workers are demanding a rise in ‌the ⁠minimum monthly wage to 30,000 taka ($242) from 12,500 taka, citing soaring food, housing and ⁠transport costs.

Industry leaders, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the issue, said an increase of more than 15% would be unsustainable as the sector grapples with rising costs and weak ​global demand.

Also Read: Bangladesh agrees new garment pay scale from December amid protests

“Even then, many small factories ‌could struggle to cope with the increase,” one of the industry leaders said.

The industry has suffered significant losses from the unrest.

A survey by the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association found that disruptions over 18 days caused losses of about $428 million in 317 ‌factories, while international buyers shifted orders worth roughly $254 million to other countries amid concerns ​over production disruptions.

There was no immediate comment from the Labour Minister or workers’ representatives.

Higher production costs, rising utility tariffs and intense competition from rival apparel-producing countries ⁠limit manufacturers’ ability to absorb a substantially larger wage increase, industry leaders said.

Protests that began earlier this month forced hundreds of factories to close and led to clashes between workers and police, who ‌used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse demonstrators.

Labour unrest continued on Monday, forcing dozens of garment factories to shut down in Ashulia and Gazipur, two major apparel manufacturing hubs on the outskirts of Dhaka.

Factory owners have warned that unrest could further disrupt production and export shipments during a crucial period for overseas orders, while labour representatives said workers are unlikely to accept an increase significantly below their demands.

Several global labour rights groups, trade unions and brand coalitions ‌have backed Bangladeshi workers’ demands for higher wages.

Also Read: ‘Garment workers unrest narrows Tarique Rahman’s window for India visit’

The Action, Collaboration, Transformation (ACT) initiative, a global wage-bargaining initiative bringing together apparel brands ​and trade unions, called on November 19 for an urgent and meaningful increase in Bangladesh’s minimum garment wage, citing living costs, inflation, productivity and economic ⁠conditions.

In a joint statement, ACT expressed concern over reports of violence and retaliation linked to the ⁠wage-setting process and urged all parties to respect workers’ rights to freedom of association, peaceful assembly and social dialogue.

It also called on the government-appointed wage board to reach ‌a negotiated agreement that moves pay closer to a living-wage level.

ACT’s brand members, which include H&M Group, Inditex, C&A, Primark, Next and PVH Corp, said they would work ​with suppliers to ensure statutory and negotiated wage increases are reflected in purchasing prices.

World.title: Dhanraj murder case: Court convicts three accused, acquits 17 others
World.content:
The Taliparamba Additional Sessions Court has convicted the first three accused in the murder of CPI(M) worker C.V. Dhanraj, while acquitting the remaining 17 accused, giving them the benefit of the doubt. The accused from fourth to the twentieth were acquitted by the court.

Dhanraj, a former CPI(M) branch secretary in Ezhimala and DYFI leader was hacked to death on the night of July 11, 2016. The attack took place in front of his mother and wife at his residence in Kunnaru Karanthat, Ramanthali.

The testimony of Dhanraj’s mother proved crucial in the case. The court described the murder as brutal and said there would be no leniency in sentencing, adding that the maximum punishment would be imposed. The sentencing arguments will be heard later, with the final sentence to pronounce the day after tomorrow.

The three convicted accused include the first accused T.P Biju, second accused M. Vipin and third accused M. Vaishak. The verdict was delivered by Additional Sessions court Judge K.N. Prasanth. The court found the prosecution had established their involvement in the murder. The court acquitted accused Nos. 4 to 20 because it found the testimony of the first prosecution witness, Prajeesh, unreliable.

Accepting the defence argument, the court noted that Mr. Prajeesh was an active CPI(M) worker and an employee of an institution controlled by the party. His testimony also contained inconsistencies with the statement of other witnesses.

However, the court fully accepted the testimony of Dhanraj’s mother. Although she was unable to identify some of the accused, the court observed that this was natural given her mental condition at the time of the incident.

The court rejected the defence arguments that the prosecution had failed to establish the motive for the murder and that witnesses had identified the accused based on the media reports. Instead, it accepted the prosecution’s contention that the witnesses had seen the accused under the electric lights at the house.

During the hearing, the judge strongly criticised the defence’s arguments and questioned its attempt to portray the case as a political murder. Pointing to a photograph of Dhanraj lying injured, the judge noted that he had suffered 37 cuts. The judge remarked that one strike would have been enough to kill someone and questioned why so many blows were inflicted. The judge also said that Dharnraj had not died by accidently striking himself with a sword and that the incident was neither theft not robbery.

“This is not a political case. This is the work of a gang of criminals. This is not a case involving a protest, it is a case of a person being hacked to death,” the Judge told the defence.

The court further clarified that the case could not be classified as the rarest of rare and that the death penalty would not be imposed. However, it stressed that there would be no leniency in sentencing and that the maximum punishment would be awarded.

World.title: Low Power Distance Measuring Equipment installed at Tiruchi international airport
World.content:
A Low Power Distance Measuring Equipment (LP-DME) has been commissioned at the Tiruchi international airport in a significant step towards enhancing air navigation safety and landing precision.

Manufactured in South Korea, the 100 watt LP-DME is collocated with the Instrument Landing System to provide pilots with continuous and real-time distance information to the runway threshold supporting safe and precise approaches. The LP-DME equipment for Runway 27 has been installed at a cost of ₹73 lakh.

Compliant with the International Civil Aviation Organisation Annex 10 standards, the system offers high measurement accuracy and can handle up to 200 aircraft simultaneously. Equipped with dual transponders, monitors and redundant power supplies, it ensures high operational reliability. Following successful flight inspection and calibration by the Airports Authority of India Flight Inspection Unit and regulatory approvals, the facility had been commissioned for operational use.

The LP-DME equipment was commissioned by the Officiating Airport Director of Tiruchi International Airport G. Gopalakrishnan on Monday. Senior officials of the Communication Navigation System, Air Traffic Management, and Operations department were present.

The commissioning of the LP-DME equipment is a significant step towards enhancing air navigation safety and landing precision. This addition reinforces Airport Authority of India’s commitment to modernising airport infrastructure and enhancing the safety, efficiency, and reliability of flight operations at the Tiruchi international airport, said Mr. Gopalakrishnan in a press release.

The non-metro Tiruchi international airport, equipped with navigational facilities including the Instrument Landing System, handles more overseas flights than domestic services every day. Overseas flights by different airlines were being operated to Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Colombo, Abu Dhabi, Jaffna, Muscat, Sharjah, and Dubai. Domestic services are operated to Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru from here.

World.title: Bilawal calls for restoring supremacy of Parliament and trust in judiciary, electoral system
World.content:
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Monday called for restoring the supremacy of the Parliament as well as trust in the judiciary and the electoral system.

He made the remarks while addressing an event to mark the launch of the Sindh Youth Card.

“To restore the trust of Pakistan’s youth, if any reset is to take place, it must be a democratic reset,” the party leader said.

“If a democratic reset happens, then the people’s stake will remain, and through that reset, we must restore the supremacy of our Parliament. We must restore confidence in our judiciary, and the election system we have, we must restore trust in it now.”

Bilawal’s remarks come as the debate over a “system reset” in the country has intensified over the past few months. In July, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi stirred a political storm by calling for the creation of new administrative units, arguing that the current system of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

Last week, in a hard-hitting speech, the PPP chairman had asserted that the governance system had not collapsed, but was rather “made to collapse”.

“Every child in this country hates corruption. The youth [of Pakistan] want to see a country where there is no corruption. They want it, and we also want to join together and build such a Pakistan,” he said.

According to Bilawal, to achieve that objective, two things need to be done: first is to use modern digital technology, whether it is Youth Card or Kissan Card, and build systems in a way that shuts down avenues for corruption.

“Along with that, we have to build a system that functions without discrimination,” he added. “Instead of taking revenge, [the system] works to fix our situation.”

Bilawal stressed that the restoration of trust would have to be a “joint effort” — to restore the opposition’s trust in the government, the government’s trust in the opposition, and the public’s trust in the country’s system, its parliament, judiciary, media and the accountability system.

He said if such conditions were created, Pakistan could achieve unity for the first time.

More to follow

World.title: Naqvi calls on PM Shehbaz as debate on new provinces gains steam
World.content:
ISLAMABAD/LAHORE: Amid growing debate on the issue of creation of new provinces, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

According to an official handout from the Prime Minister Office (PMO), the interior minister met the prime minister in Islamabad and briefed him on the law and order situation in the country.

The two also discussed the prevailing situation in the country, the statement said.

Earlier in the day, Naqvi had met with Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain at his residence in Lahore. The debate over the creation of new provinces and devolution of powers came under discussion during the meeting.

The meeting came amid an ongoing political debate over the creation of new provinces, with several political leaders pushing for a nationwide referendum to settle the matter.

It was sparked by Naqvi’s July remarks, wherein he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

In Monday’s meeting, the two leaders discussed the overall political situation, measures to maintain law and order and the need to transfer power to the grassroots level, according to a statement issued by the interior ministry after the meeting.

During the discussion, Shujaat said the question of creating new provinces was directly linked to public convenience, good governance, administrative efficiency and the country’s future.

“Strengthening existing administrative units and making them more empowered can also be an effective way to address governance-related challenges. The biggest stakeholders of Pakistan are its ordinary people,” Shujaat was quoted as saying, adding that decisions should be made in accordance with the aspirations of the people.

“If we do not take steps in the right direction today, tomorrow will not forgive us,” he remarked.

Naqvi said it was imperative to take all decisions in accordance with the wishes of the people of Pakistan. The interior minister also briefed the PML-Q leader on the government’s counterterrorism and peacekeeping measures in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain and Punjab Minister for Industries Chaudhry Shafay Hussain were also present at the meeting.

The meeting comes as Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry insisted last week that a referendum on the formation of new provinces “will happen” amid the debate on new provinces.

In his remarks on Friday, Chaudhry had maintained that the PML-N would undertake “every last effort” to convince the PPP.

“A referendum is neither non-constitutional nor undemocratic; the public’s opinion can be sought on any important matter,” he had said.

Chaudhry’s remarks came after PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari delivered a no-holds-barred speech earlier last week that covered the question of new provinces.

Bilawal had expressed his opposition to the creation of provinces and the idea of holding a referendum for such a move in his speech. He cautioned that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces, particularly in Sindh, could lead to bloodshed.

World.title: Pakistan has Portugal's 'full support' for GSP+ status, visiting FM says during delegation-level talks in Islamabad
World.content:
Pakistan has Portugal’s “full support” for the European Union’s (EU) GSP+ status, Portuguese Minister of State and Foreign Affairs Paulo Rangel said on Monday during Pakistan-Portugal delegation-level talks held in Islamabad.

Pakistan’s current GSP+ status is set to expire in 2027, after which Islamabad will seek a renewal.

GSP+ status is a special incentive awarded to developing countries to “pursue sustainable development and good governance” in exchange for cutting import duties to zero on two-thirds of the tariff lines of its exports.

The status was granted to Pakistan in 2014, resulting in a 108 per cent increase in Pakistani textile exports to the EU due to concessional tariffs.

In October 2023, the European Parliament unanimously voted to extend the GSP+ status for another four years until 2027 for developing countries, including Pakistan.

The upcoming GSP+ monitoring mission will scrutinise Pakistan’s record on 32 international conventions tied to the trade scheme. Maintaining GSP+ status is critical for Pakistan to keep export costs low.

Rangel, in his remarks, stressed that both Pakistan and the EU would mutually benefit from cooperation, adding that “we should not hesitate on developing these bilateral platforms”.

The Pakistani delegation was led by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar.

In his remarks, DPM Dar said, “Our focus is on strengthening our political ties, expanding bilateral trade and promoting investment.”

He proposed that the two countries regularly convene the Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum to help Pakistani and Portuguese companies “identify trading partners and explore joint venture opportunities”.

He also suggested that the two delegations identify proposals for progress and review implementation through bilateral political consultations.

The two ministers also agreed to set up a Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC) between Pakistan and Portugal. Dar said the JMC would help promote business, trade and investment between the two countries by identifying the “hurdles” for consideration.

Dar added that he and his Portuguese counterpart agreed that parliamentary exchanges between the two countries should be considered as well.

Rangel said this was the first visit to Pakistan by a Portuguese delegation in 19 years.

“We look forward to enhancing our bilateral relationship in the economic area,” he said. He elaborated that a JMC would help “boost the economic dynamics of our relationship”.

Rangel praised Pakistan for its role as a “peace-building actor at a global level” as well as its efforts in Middle East diplomacy and the Palestine issue.

The visiting dignitary said that Portugal had a lot to learn from Pakistan, as it enters the United Nations Security Council.

The Portuguese FM added, “We really want to keep this bilateral political dialogue very intense during the two years that we will be holding a mandate in the Security Council of the United Nations because we know how attached Pakistan is to multilateralism, to the Charter of the United Nations, and to building peace and prosperity across the world”.

Referring to Pakistan’s mediation efforts in the US-Iran conflict, Rangel said: “Without your mediation, we are fully aware that things would have been much more difficult than they are.”

He also acknowledged the Pakistani diaspora in Portugal, describing it as “a quite dynamic and well-integrated community”.

Concluding his remarks, the Portuguese FM described his visit to Pakistan as “very fruitful and very positive”.

According to a separate FO statement , DPM Dar and Rangel signed an agreement on the mutual exemption of visa requirements for holders of diplomatic passports between the two countries.

“The agreement will facilitate high-level engagement, diplomatic exchanges and further strengthen the longstanding and friendly relations between Pakistan and Portugal,” FO said.

Pakistan ‘important economic player’ in EU

Later in the day, addressing a joint press stakeout, Rangel underscored Pakistan’s position as an “important economic player” in the European Union, reiterating Lisbon’s support for the country’s relationship with the bloc.

“We have to do everything that we can to [ensure] that we can even become closer and closer,” he said.

At the outset of the press conference, Dar said the two sides had also explored avenues for improving shipping and logistics for exporters in both countries.

Speaking about visa exemption for diplomatic passport holders, Dar hoped that the exemption could be extended to official and regular passports as well.

Dar announced that the two sides will be signing a Memorandum of Understanding on investment protection between Pakistan’s Board of Investment and the Portuguese Trade & Investment Agency (AICEP).

“Together, these arrangements will provide a stronger foundation for closer bilateral engagement and expanded business and investment ties,” he said, adding that the two sides also reviewed progress on the protocol to amend the convention on double taxation.

We agreed to work towards the early conclusion of the other agreements and MoUs under discussion as of today, he added.

Dar also thanked his counterpart for lending support to Pakistan’s GSP+ status.

“The scheme remains a cornerstone of Pakistan-EU economic cooperation. It supports trade, employment and sustainable development in Pakistan,” Dar said, reiterating commitment to implementing relevant international conventions and continued engagement with the EU.

Dar added that the two leaders had discussed expanding legal pathways for migration.

“I invited Portugal to consider our proposed labour mobility partnership. I also flagged the opportunities that Portugal’s Green Path Mechanism could offer to skilled Pakistani workers to meet its requirement of recruitment.”

Dar said that the two countries had discussed ways to expand people-to-people ties as well as research partnerships, cultural exchanges, parliamentary exchanges and tourism.

Here, he welcomed a partnership between FC Porto, a Portugal-based football club, and the Sialkot Football Academy for a training programme.

“We propose building on this partnership through coaching exchanges, youth tournaments, training camps, and cooperation in sports science, and with closer links between clubs and academies in football and other sports,” Dar said.

Dar also congratulated Portugal on its election to the UN Security Council for the 2027-28 term.

Dar added that the discussion with his counterpart also included Pakistan’s “unwavering support” for the Palestinian people as well as the country’s commitment to a peaceful resolution of the dispute in Jammu and Kashmir.

“On Afghanistan, I stressed that Afghan territory must not be used for terrorist activities against any country, particularly Pakistan,” he said.

On India, DPM Dar reiterated the country’s stance on the Indus Waters Treaty and stressed that India’s unilateral decision to hold the treaty in abeyance constitutes a “material breach of international law and a dangerous attempt to weaponise shared water resources”.

Concluding his address, Dar hoped that the two countries can build on their “long-standing friendship [..] to shape a forward-looking partnership”.

Rangel, in his address, described Monday’s engagement as a “landmark” in Pakistan-Portugal relations, expressing “full trust” in the economic dimension of the two countries’ relationship.

He also acknowledged Pakistan’s mediatory role in the US-Iran war.

“Everybody knows in the world the role that your government, your prime minister, and especially the DPM had in this conflict in the Middle East. Things are not fantastic there; they are difficult. But the truth is that they would be much worse without Pakistani mediation and systematic [outreach] to try to bring all sides and all stakeholders to a very reasonable position.”

He also lauded Pakistan’s tripartite defence pact with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia — the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement — as well as the R4+E4 framework with the UK, France, Germany, and Italy.

Rangel stressed the need for expanding ties in culture and economy and invited DPM Dar to visit Lisbon.

Rangel-Dar meeting

Separately, Rangel reaffirmed his country’s commitment to further strengthening bilateral relations with Pakistan, a statement by the Foreign Office (FO) said.

Rangel made these remarks during a meeting with DPM Dar at the FO in Islamabad, where the Portuguese minister arrived on Sunday on a two-day visit.

In today’s meeting, Rangel and Dar reviewed the “longstanding and friendly relations between Pakistan and Portugal as the two countries mark 77 years of diplomatic relations”, the FO statement said.

It added that DPM Dar stressed the importance of enhanced diplomatic engagement, parliamentary exchanges and regular consultations through existing bilateral mechanisms.

For his part, Rangel reaffirmed Portugal’s commitment to further strengthening bilateral ties, thanked Pakistan for its support at the United Nations and appreciated the contribution of the Pakistani diaspora in Portugal to promoting closer ties between the two countries, the statement said.

“Both leaders also exchanged views on regional developments and discussed cooperation at the UN and within the European Union framework,” it said.

Moreover, Rangel appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability”, the statement said, adding that the two leaders also emphasised the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and effective multilateralism in addressing shared challenges.

During his time in Pakistan, Rangel is also scheduled to hold delegation-level talks with DPM Dar. He is accompanied by a business delegation for the inaugural Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum.

The FO earlier said the visit would also feature a Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum, and companies from both countries would hold business-to-business meetings to explore commercial partnerships and investment opportunities in agri-food, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, information technology and textiles.

Following his arrival on Sunday, Rangel praised Pakistan’s peace efforts in recent months during the US-Israeli war on Iran.

“The world needs you. We have been seeing in the very recent months that the role of Pakistan is decisive for global peace, so we count on you to help all the peoples of the world, reaching peace and prosperity,” he said while speaking to state-run Pakistan TV.

World.title: Asif says process for referendum on new provinces likely to move forward early next year
World.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has said discussions on a possible referendum to create new provinces are expected to take a “definitive shape” by the end of this year, with the process likely to move forward early next year.

Speaking on ARY News programme ‘Sawal Yeh Hai’ on Sunday, Asif said the matter would not take long to reach a conclusion, though he refrained from giving a specific date.

Asked whether the PML-N and the federal government had reached a principled decision on holding a referendum, and what its timeline and outline would be, he said: “Perhaps by the year-end, all this debate and discussion that is taking place will take some definitive shape. What shape it will take, I cannot say, but it won’t take long. I can certainly say that it is not going to take two to four months.”

He said the date could be a few days earlier or later, but the process was expected to move forward soon.

“God willing, but it would not be appropriate for me to give a date. I cannot provide a definitive timeline, but, based on my understanding, the inevitability of this is becoming clearer day by day,” he said.

Asked how the referendum question would be framed, given opposition from one province and the fact that previous referendums had been held under dictatorships, Asif said everyone had the right to express reservations.

“You cannot deny someone that right if they have reservations about the entire matter and are expressing them. That is a fundamental part of a democratic society,” he said.

He said a joint document would be prepared with input from all stakeholders to ensure that the proposal was acceptable to everyone.

“It will be a joint document in which all the stakeholders will have their input. Rather than producing a document that falls prey to disagreement, my own view is that the efforts and back-and-forth meetings currently taking place will produce something that is acceptable to all,” he added.

Asked whether the government would seek consensus on the referendum question to bring the PPP on board, Asif said that was precisely the intention.

He said the question would outline the purpose and objectives of the proposed exercise, requiring people to respond with a yes or no. These objectives, he added, would also be defined through consensus.

Regarding the constitutional requirements for holding a referendum, he said the Constitution provided for such an exercise but also laid down the procedure for constitutional amendments, which could not be bypassed.

“There is room for a referendum in the Constitution; there is no doubt about that. However, the procedure for a constitutional amendment is also laid down in it, and no one can deviate from that procedure,” he said.

The defence minister said the proposed changes could have far-reaching positive consequences, noting that Pakistan had previously altered its administrative map through the creation of One Unit and the subsequent establishment of provinces.

He expressed confidence that the joint preparation of a document would address reservations and prevent major disagreements.

“I think politics is the art of the possible, and this will definitely be made possible, God willing,” he added.

Asif had made similar remarks a few days earlier, saying he believed that a consensus was being developed on the creation of new provinces and that the process was moving towards culmination.

Speaking on Geo News, he had said the new year would bring a new system and that reaching consensus could lead to a progressive change in the country’s political landscape. He had also advocated a robust local government system, saying smaller administrative units would help improve public service delivery.

The remarks come amid a debate over the proposed creation of new provinces, with Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry insisting last week that a referendum on the matter “will happen”.

The issue gained renewed attention after PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari opposed the creation of new provinces and the proposed referendum in a speech on Tuesday, warning that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces, particularly Sindh, could lead to bloodshed.

The federal government, however, maintains that a referendum is a legal and constitutional means of gauging public opinion on the creation of new provinces.

Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

World.title: 7 killed, 2 injured as stone-laden truck overturns onto mini-truck in Bahawalpur
World.content:
LAHORE: Seven people were killed and two others were injured when a stone-laden truck hit a mini-truck and overturned onto it in Bahawalpur’s Uch Sharif early on Monday morning, an official and Rescue 1122 said.

Bahawalpur District Police Officer (DPO) Rana Abdul Wahab told Dawn that the mini-truck, travelling from Dera Ghazi Khan to Khairpur Tamewali, was carrying 16 people and stopped along a highway due to fog.

“The driver was cleaning the windscreen of the stationary vehicle when another truck, laden with stones, hit it and turned over onto it,” the DPO said.

According to the official, the driver of the stone-laden truck, which was also travelling from Dera Ghazi Khan, had lost control of the vehicle.

Passengers in the mini-truck were left trapped, he said.

A Rescue 1122 statement said the passengers were trapped under the truck and the stones, and an excavator was used to clear the stones.

The DPO said police and rescue personnel were able to rescue nine people while seven died because of injuries.

According to Rescue 1122, two people have been injured among those rescued.

DPO Wahab said the driver of the stone-laden truck had fled the scene after the accident. “However, police have identified him and registered a case at Dhoorkot police station. Raids are being conducted to arrest the suspect,” the DPO said.

Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz expressed “deep grief and sorrow” over the loss of lives in the accident, Associated Press of Pakistan reported.

In a message, the CM extended her “heartfelt condolences and sympathies to the bereaved families,” praying for their strength and patience to bear the “irreparable” loss.

CM Maryam also sought a detailed report on the accident and directed relevant authorities to provide the necessary details, according to APP.

Earlier this month, a collision between a passenger bus and truck claimed the lives of 11 people and left 33 others injured near Pakpattan.

On Oct 21, ten people were killed and 44 others injured when a passenger bus overturned after hitting a road divider on the Indus Highway in Rajanpur district’s Rojhan tehsil.

On Oct 19, a road accident on Multan’s Bosan Road claimed the lives of five men in their 20s after their speeding Toyota Corolla hit a road divider before crashing into the wall of a nearby plot and catching fire.

World.title: Bangladesh vows to arrest Hasina if she returns from India
World.content:
Bangladesh will arrest and jail former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina if she returns from India, a senior government minister said, as her plans to come home in December fuel political tension and renewed street violence.

Dhaka is instead seeking Hasina’s extradition from India, where she has lived since fleeing Bangladesh in 2024, and expects New Delhi to comply with an existing extradition treaty, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters.

India’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh’s request to extradite Hasina.

Hasina faces a death sentence in Bangladesh and her Awami League party is banned following the 2024 uprising that ended her long rule. The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

Hasina fled Dhaka in August 2024 as protests demanding her resignation swept the country. She has since sought a new passport and identity card ahead of a planned return in December, requests the government has rejected.

“As soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested. And she will be taken to jail, and the law will take its course,” Obaed said in an interview on Sunday.

“We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict, and the law will take its course. She (Hasina) will have to face the music.” The standoff has brought Hasina’s Awami League supporters out on the streets. The party this month announced a week of protests and rallies in support of Hasina’s return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of arson targeting vehicles in at least 28 districts over the past 10 days, with several police officers and civilians injured, according to local media.

Obaed called the violence a survival tactic by Hasina’s “politically bankrupt political party.” Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury, a senior Awami League official, said the current political establishment was responsible for the violence.

The minister said there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back, adding that Dhaka wanted balanced ties with New Delhi that did not compromise Bangladesh’s “dignity, self-respect and interests.” “India needs to decide what kind of foreign policy they need to adopt for Bangladesh,” Obaed said.

Rohingya verdict

Dhaka is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on neighbouring Myanmar over the return of Rohingya refugees after the UN’s highest court ruled that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Muslim minority in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

Myanmar has criticised the ruling by the International Court of Justice, saying Rohingya would only be able to return “when situations permit”.

“Now, this verdict gives us, Bangladesh, the strength, the Rohingya community the strength to fight,” Obaed said, adding that they deserved to return “with dignity and safety”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in Bangladesh after repeated repatriation attempts failed. Their return has been complicated by Myanmar’s civil war and the Arakan Army militia’s control of nearly all of Rakhine State, which is home for most Rohingya.

Obaed called for greater international pressure on Myanmar and the Arakan Army.

“Bangladesh did not create this crisis. Myanmar created this crisis, so Myanmar has to end it,” she said.

World.title: Residents protest as work continues at Karachi's Nehr-i-Khayyam despite SHC order
World.content:
KARACHI: Residents of Clifton on Sunday expressed concerns that construction and development activities at Nehr-i-Khayyam were continuing despite recent clear directions from the Sindh High Court (SHC) to halt them.

The residents of the area held their weekly protest, marching from Do Talwar towards the under-construction site of a 46-storey building and the Nehr-i-Khayyam site under the banners of “Save Clifton” and “Liveable Clifton”.

They were protesting against the “unchecked transformation of residential neighbourhoods, violations of building regulations and the destruction of public spaces”.

They called upon the authorities to enforce building and zoning regulations, investigate the approval of high-rise buildings in residential streets and protect residential neighbourhoods by stopping “unauthorised commercial conversions and developments that compromise residents’ safety, access, infrastructure and quality of life”.

The residents also demanded the protection of public spaces and an end to the commercialisation and encroachment of parks, green belts and amenity plots. They further called for the restoration of civic infrastructure and greater transparency and accountability, with officials held responsible for violations.

Speaking to the media, Sohail Osman Ali said the “cancer” of high-rise buildings was spreading in the area, describing the trend as “madness”.

Expressing concern over the construction of a 46-storey building, another protester, Shiraz Qureshi, told the media that the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA) had allowed the construction of a high-rise building in a residential area with narrow streets and inadequate resources to accommodate such a project.

He also alleged that the government was only interested in the commercialisation of Clifton Block 5.

He said that despite the high court’s orders, construction work at Nehr-i-Khayyam was continuing round the clock.

Rasha Tarek, a protester and member of the Karachi Residents’ Community (District South), said that “unregulated” high-rise projects in the area were threatening natural ventilation pathways that carry cooling sea breezes inland, potentially trapping heat and compromising the city’s environmental liveability.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

World.title: India to give $1.62bn economic package to flood-hit Nepal
World.content:
India will give Nepal an economic package worth 240 billion Nepalese rupees ($1.62bn), Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Monday, after talks with his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah in New Delhi.

Shah is in the Indian capital for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since coming to power in March, and in the aftermath of the devastating Himalayan flood in August that killed some 1,500 people, with another 5,200 missing and presumed dead.

“Today, to give fresh impetus to Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development, we are announcing a development cooperation package worth 24,000 crore (240 billion) Nepalese rupees,” Modi said, addressing the media after the talks, with Shah standing beside him.

“Our commitment will be to help affected families get their lives back on track, create new opportunities and further strengthen Nepal’s capacity to deal with future disasters,” Modi said.

Shah thanked India for consistently acting as a first responder for Nepal “in times of natural disasters and difficult hours”.

“I warmly welcome Indian investors to Nepal to partner in the economic prosperity of our two countries in the coming days,” he said, and invited Modi to visit the Himalayan nation.

The two countries signed agreements to boost their economic relationship and Modi and Shah jointly opened a train link connecting the two countries.

The August 26 flood, caused by a glacier collapse on Nepal’s border with China, sent a mass of mud and rock crashing into the Trishuli river.

The resulting flood washed away villages, snapped highways, bridges and power lines, and buried homes in the mud in the impoverished country that is wedged between Asian giants India and China.

Nepal and India enjoy longstanding cultural, economic and people-to-people ties with an open border allowing hundreds of thousands of Nepalis to live and work in India.

New Delhi was the first to respond after the August flood, sending several plane-loads of aid to restore communication links that were severed in the mountains.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
