World.title: Gunman in slay of former Miss-Philippines Earth nabbed
World.content:
Lullete Jane Ramilo-De Guzman, Miss Philippines-Earth 2013 runner up. Photo: Facebook/Ofelia Dela Cruz

CITY OF ILAGAN, Isabela— A 30-year-old man suspected of killing beauty queen and teacher Lullete Jane Ramilo was arrested in Cainta, Rizal, on Monday morning, nearly nine months after the fatal shooting.

The suspect, a resident of Cabagan, Isabela, was arrested at Felix Avenue in Barangay San Isidro at 11:10 a.m., Isabela police director Police Col. Manuel Bringas said.

Bringas said the suspect had been hiding in San Vicente, Apalit, Pampanga, before his arrest.

Article continues after this 

READ: Suspect in killing of Isabela ex-beauty queen charged with murder

He was wanted for allegedly shooting Ramilo inside her car in front of her house in Cabaritan village on the evening of Feb. 14. Ramilo, 32, was the third runner-up in the 2013 Miss Philippines Earth pageant.

Intelligence tracker teams served the suspect a warrant of arrest for murder issued by Judge Leif John Robino. The court did not recommend bail.

He was turned over to the San Manuel police for temporary custody while waiting for his court commitment.

Ramilo’s partner, Clifford Dela Cruz, described her as a responsible, sweet and caring mother to their children.

Article continues after this 

In an earlier Facebook post, Dela Cruz said Ramilo had stood up for parents afraid to speak out, opposed bullying in school and challenged authorities when others were intimidated.

“Now, her voice has been silenced, silenced by those who were offended by the truth she carried. But her courage will never be silenced. Her fight will never be forgotten,” he said. /dp

World.title: Maguindanao massacre survivor urged to speak up after 17 years
World.content:
Rep. Esmael “Toto” Mangudadatu speaks during a gathering with families of the victims of the 2009 Maguindanao massacre and members of the media in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur, on Monday, Nov. 23. Photo by Amiel Cagayan

BULUAN, Maguindanao del Sur — Maguindanao del Sur Rep. Esmael “Toto” Mangudadatu has urged a “survivor” of the 2009 Maguindanao massacre to finally speak about his ordeal, saying it is time “to bring out the truth after 17 years of silence.”

At a gathering with the victims’ families on Nov. 23 here, Mangudadatu, who declined to identify the survivor, said he had kept the matter to himself for years but decided to make the appeal now rather than wait until the 20th anniversary of the massacre.

He said he was unsure whether either of them would still be alive by then.

Article continues after this 

READ: Closure, full justice still elusive 17 years after Maguindanao massacre

The lawmaker recalled that whenever they crossed paths, particularly in Cotabato, they would simply bow their heads, seemingly unable to face the painful memories of the massacre.

He appealed to the survivor to share what happened to him.

Mangudadatu said only he and the survivor knew the full story, which had remained untold for nearly two decades.

He said breaking the silence could help ease the emotional burden they had carried over the years and contribute to the continuing search for truth and justice for the victims.

Article continues after this 

“What we are fighting for is not just one life, but many lives. We want to make sure that what happened will never happen again,” he said.

READ: Maguindanao massacre: PTFOMS vows to pursue arrest of remaining accused

Article continues after this 

The lawmaker expressed support for the continuing calls of the families of the massacre victims for justice. He said they could seek updates from their lawyers on the status of the cases and the demands of the victims’ families.

Seventeen years after the Nov. 23, 2009 massacre, the families of the victims continue to seek accountability for one of the country’s deadliest election-related killings.

Fifty-eight people, including 32 journalists and media workers, were brutally killed in a secluded, hilly spot in Ampatuan town. The members of the press were in the convoy to cover the filing of Mangudadatu’s certificate of candidacy for governor, which he won.

World.title: Palace declares holidays in 3 towns for local celebrations
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has declared special non-working days in three municipalities to allow residents to celebrate their respective founding anniversaries and local occasions.

Proclamation No. 1524, series of 2026, declares Dec. 4 (Friday) a special non-working day in Vintar, Ilocos Norte.

The declaration aims to provide the people of Vintar with the opportunity to fully participate in and celebrate the municipality’s special occasion.

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, Proclamation No. 1525, series of 2026, declares Dec. 11 (Friday) a special non-working day in San Jose, Batangas, as the town marks its 260th founding anniversary.

LIST: 2026 regular holidays, special non-working days

The proclamation recognizes the significance of the occasion and allows residents to take part in activities commemorating the municipality’s history and heritage.

Under Proclamation No. 1526, series of 2026, Nov. 20 (Friday) was also declared a special non-working day in Hinoba-an, Negros Occidental, to mark its founding anniversary.

The three proclamations were signed by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto on behalf of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Nov. 12.

Article continues after this 

LIST: Holidays, special non-working days for 2027

Under Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) rules, the “no work, no pay” principle applies to employees who do not work on special non-working days, unless a company policy, practice or collective bargaining agreement provides otherwise.

Article continues after this 

Employees who work on these days are entitled to 130% of their daily wage for the first eight hours. If the special non-working day also falls on an employee’s rest day, the rate increases to 150 percent. /dp

World.title: Manila Water’s lake system boosts water security for El Niño and beyond
World.content:
Nearing completion: The 200-MLD East Bay Phase 2 Water Treatment Plant will further expand Manila Water’s use of Laguna de Bay as a viable raw water source. Once operational, East Bay Phase 2 will bring Laguna de Bay system’s combined treatment capacity to 350 MLD, supporting reliable 24/7 water service amid varying weather conditions. —Photo from Manila Water

MANILA, Philippines — As weather patterns become increasingly unpredictable, water security depends not only on having enough supply today, but also on developing diverse and resilient sources that can withstand the challenges of tomorrow.

Manila Water continues to expand its Laguna de Bay water supply system as a key component of its long-term strategy to sustain reliable, 24/7 water service across the East Zone. By drawing from Laguna de Bay, the company gains greater operational flexibility and reduces its reliance on the Angat-Ipo-La Mesa system, particularly during prolonged dry periods and lower water allocations.

The Laguna de Bay system currently includes the Cardona Water Treatment Plant and the East Bay Phase 1 Water Treatment Plant, with the upcoming East Bay Phase 2 Water Supply System Project set to provide a significant additional supply.

Article continues after this 

READ: Manila Water urges customers to prepare wisely for strong El Niño

Located in Cardona, Rizal, the Cardona Water Treatment Plant was Manila Water’s first major facility to tap the central part of Laguna Lake as an additional raw water source. The plant can provide up to 100 million liters per day (MLD), helping meet the requirements of communities in Rizal and supporting the stability of the broader East Zone distribution network.

Further strengthening the system is the 50-MLD East Bay Phase 1 Water Treatment Plant, which draws raw water from the eastern flank of the lake. The facility serves growing communities in Rizal and provides Manila Water with additional flexibility in managing supply across its service area. It features an eight-million-liter reservoir and a multi-stage treatment process using dissolved air flotation, granular activated carbon filtration, and reverse osmosis technologies.

The 100-MLD Cardona Water Treatment Plant taps the central portion of Laguna Lake as an additional raw water source, supporting Manila Water’s water-security strategy. —Photo from Manila Water

Manila Water is also nearing the completion of the East Bay Phase 2 Water Supply System Project. Designed to add up to 200 MLD, the project includes a new water treatment plant and intake facility in Barangay Kabulusan, Pakil, Laguna, as well as transmission infrastructure that will carry treated water across the lake and connect it to the company’s distribution network.

Once East Bay Phase 2 becomes operational, Manila Water’s Laguna de Bay facilities will have a combined treatment capacity of up to 350 MLD. The additional supply will reinforce water availability for customers in Pasig, Pateros, Taguig, and parts of Rizal Province, while supporting future demand growth across the East Zone.

Article continues after this 

“Water security means having a diversified and resilient supply system that can respond to changing conditions. Through the Cardona and East Bay facilities, Laguna de Bay has become an important part of our efforts to sustain 24/7 water service, especially as we prepare for stronger El Niño episodes and other weather-related challenges,” Manila Water Communication Affairs Department Head Dittie Galang said.

READ: Manila Water readies 33 reservoirs for prolonged El Niño

Article continues after this 

These investments reflect Manila Water’s continuing shift toward a more diversified water supply portfolio. Alongside its other water sources and infrastructure projects, the Laguna Lake system gives the company greater flexibility to balance available supply, manage periods of reduced availability from traditional sources, and respond to the needs of growing communities.

Beyond preparing for the next El Niño, Manila Water is building a water supply system that can adapt to varying weather conditions over the long term. Through continued investments in augmenting sources such as Laguna de Bay, the company reinforces its commitment to water security and dependable 24/7 water service for its customers.

World.title: Mark Villar seeks to penalize malicious use of AI, deepfakes
World.content:
Sen. Mark Villar —Photo from his office

MANILA, Philippines — A bill seeking to regulate deepfakes and other forms of AI-generated or manipulated media and hold perpetrators and digital platforms accountable was filed in the Senate on Monday.Sen. Mark Villar filed Senate Bill No. 2620, or the proposed “Kontra Malisyosong AI Act,” which seeks to address the misuse of a person’s face, voice, likeness and other personal attributes to create misleading or harmful content.In the bill’s explanatory note, Villar cited the Department of Information and Communications Technology’s (DICT) warning that cybercriminals use deepfakes for online scams, phishing, ransomware and other illicit activities.The note also identified the use of deepfakes to impersonate relatives, public officials and business executives, as well as to facilitate harassment, defamation and the unauthorized distribution of sexually explicit content.It further noted that while the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 penalize certain violations involving personal information and computer-related crimes, neither directly addresses deepfakes and their distinct harmful effects.The proposed measure requires AI-generated or manipulated content intended for distribution to carry clear disclosures identifying it as artificially created or altered.It also requires prior written or digital consent for the creation, production or distribution of deepfakes depicting actual individuals when these are reasonably likely to cause harm, deceive, harass, intimidate, distress or exploit them.Digital platforms operating in the Philippines would also be required to establish reporting mechanisms and remove or disable access to reported violating content within 24 hours of receiving a complaint from the person depicted or impersonated, or their parent or guardian if the victim is a child.Victims may also seek the removal of offending content, including duplicates and reuploads, claim damages and obtain court orders to prevent further distribution.Under the proposed measure, individuals who fail to comply with disclosure requirements or deliberately remove, alter or tamper with mandatory disclosures may face fines ranging from P200,000 to P300,000.Those who maliciously create, produce or distribute deepfakes without the required consent may face imprisonment of two to four years and fines ranging from P250,000 to P500,000, or both.If the victim is a child, the penalty increases to imprisonment of eight to 12 years and fines ranging from P500,000 to P1 million.Digital platforms that fail to remove violating content within the prescribed 24-hour period may also face fines of P200,000 for the first offense and P300,000 for subsequent offenses.“Habang patuloy na umuunlad ang artificial intelligence, dapat din nating palakasin ang ating mga pananggalang laban sa mga gumagamit nito sa panloloko at pananamantala,” Villar said.(As artificial intelligence continues to advance, we must also strengthen our safeguards against those who use it to deceive and exploit others.)Villar said the measure is not intended to hinder technological advancement but to ensure that AI innovation is accompanied by accountability and respect for individual rights.“Hindi natin layuning hadlangan ang pag-unlad ng artificial intelligence. Ang nais natin ay matiyak na responsable ang paggamit nito at hindi napipinsala ang ating mga kababayan. Dapat makinabang ang lahat sa makabagong teknolohiya nang hindi isinasakripisyo ang kanilang seguridad, dignidad, at mga karapatan,” he said.(We do not intend to hinder the development of artificial intelligence. What we seek is to ensure that it is used responsibly and does not harm our fellow Filipinos. Everyone should benefit from technological advancements without sacrificing their security, dignity, and rights.) –/ms

World.title: Department execs urged to provide docs for Senate budget hearing
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Monday, Nov. 23, directed department secretaries to provide senators with documents and data to expedite deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.

He made the statement in response to Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, who called for executive officials to cooperate with the chamber, saying “the power of the purse is with Congress.”

“We beg the indulgence of the secretaries to furnish the senators with the data that they need to expedite the analysis. It’s really important to expedite our discussion on the budget,” Gatchalian said.

Article continues after this 

Cayetano called on the Senate to put department secretaries and government agencies on notice, stressing that executive officials should be prepared to answer lawmakers’ questions and provide requested documents during budget deliberations.

READ: Lacson flags P241-B ‘ayuda’ in 2027 budget

“I don’t want to be asking questions tonight only for the discussion to be deferred because they are not prepared or unavailable,” he said.The minority leader emphasized that the opposition was not an adversary of the administration, saying lawmakers could work with the executive branch if officials could sufficiently explain and justify their policies and budget proposals.

“We are not the enemy. We’re called opposition because we oppose certain policies, but if you can convince us, then we are on the same side. Even the majority,” he said.

Cayetano also urged departments to ensure their attached agencies are available and responsive to senators’ requests for information. /ms

World.title: Inside the Shadow Networks Helping Min Aung Hlaing Consolidate Power
World.content:
With the help of a Russian-trained military network led by a key aide-de-camp, a team of old spooks and the military’s security and intelligence apparatus, junta boss Min Aung Hlaing now runs Myanmar with an extraordinary degree of personal authority.

Diplomats, Naypyitaw insiders and regional security specialists say the regime’s system of governance has shifted from institutionalized military junta rule toward a highly personalistic system centered on Min Aung Hlaing.

While formal cabinet ministries, the diplomatic corps and conventional military command structures remain intact on paper, The Irrawaddy has learned that substantive authority is increasingly concentrated within a narrow circle of trusted military, intelligence and informal advisers. Sources said Min Aung Hlaing has consolidated personal control since the 2021 coup, while creating three primary networks that have sidelined formal institutions and now exercise substantial influence over state and military policy.

From institutionalized junta to personalistic rule

Historically, successive Myanmar military regimes—notably the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and the State Peace and Development Council (SPDC)—operated through a degree of collective leadership among senior generals and powerful regional commanders. Since the February 2021 coup, however, sources close to the military say Min Aung Hlaing has systematically dismantled those consultative norms, concentrating executive, legislative and operational authority in his own hands.

According to insiders familiar with decision-making in Naypyitaw, major political, economic and battlefield directives now originate directly from the Commander-in-Chief’s Office rather than through cabinet deliberations or collective military council meetings. They said internal mechanisms for debate and peer review among senior generals have steadily hollowed out, leaving top brass with little room to challenge or shape core regime strategy.

At the same time, cabinet ministers and senior bureaucrats have been subordinated to the role of administrative implementers tasked with executing orders rather than formulating policy, according to people familiar with the regime’s current governance in Naypyitaw.

Within this centralized structure, access to the junta chief depends heavily on personal trust, household proximity and demonstrated loyalty, which frequently outweigh seniority or formal military rank. Insiders note that Min Aung Hlaing routinely prioritizes his own strategic instincts and the counsel of trusted informal circles over professional or technocratic assessments. They said that rather than governing through the military’s established institutional machinery, Min Aung Hlaing increasingly relies on bespoke personal networks, reducing formal state organs to instruments of execution.

Who has his ear? The three circles of influence

Sources within and close to the regime point to three distinct yet overlapping circles that exercise disproportionate sway over Min Aung Hlaing’s thinking across defense technology, foreign outreach and internal security.

Influence Circle Key Figures & Entities Primary Domain Mechanism of Influence Circle 1: Technical & Russian-Trained Network Lt-Col Kyaw Zaw Ye, aide-de-camp, DSA Intakes 46 & 47 graduates Defense procurement, drone warfare, Russia ties, strategic messaging Proximity to the leadership’s household; technical specialization bypassing general staff Circle 2: Former Intelligence Network Thein Swe, Hla Min; Paragon Institute Informal political advice, discreet foreign outreach (especially China) Reactivation of legacy Khin Nyunt-era intelligence networks; track-two diplomacy Circle 3: Security-Intelligence Core Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA) Regime security, internal surveillance, political & battlefield intelligence Direct institutional control over intelligence filtering; constant personal access

Circle 1: Kyaw Zaw Ye and the Russian-trained military network

One of the most striking shifts inside Min Aung Hlaing’s inner circle is the ascent of younger, technically specialized officers educated in Russia—particularly graduates of Defense Services Academy (DSA) Intakes 46 and 47. Some 21 personnel from the two intakes form a key part of the inner circle. Multiple sources told The Irrawaddy that Lieutenant Colonel Kyaw Zaw Ye, a DSA Intake 47 graduate, has emerged as an influential figure with direct access to the junta chief. He was appointed as Min Aung Hlaing’s aide-de-camp last year. Trained in Russia, Kyaw Zaw Ye belongs to a cohort of officers versed in Russian defense hardware, procurement pipelines and emerging military technologies.

Insiders say Kyaw Zaw Ye’s clout stems less from his mid-level rank than from close personal ties to Min Aung Hlaing and the leadership’s immediate household, giving him direct channels to the top that bypass senior commanders. The Irrawaddy has learned that this network plays an active role in bilateral defense dealings with Moscow, specialized arms acquisitions, and efforts to source and deploy unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) to counter resistance forces. Sources also link Kyaw Zaw Ye to military propaganda and strategic communications, reflecting the regime’s push to overhaul its information operations. By elevating Russian-educated technical officers through personal access, Min Aung Hlaing has cultivated an alternative source of military-strategic advice that routinely sidesteps conventional general staff hierarchies, people familiar with the matter said.

Circle 2: Thein Swe and the former military intelligence network

Facing severe diplomatic isolation and institutional deficits after 2021, the regime has turned to veteran operatives from Myanmar’s dismantled military intelligence apparatus—specifically figures formerly aligned with ousted prime minister and spy chief General Khin Nyunt. Both Thein Swe and Hla Min, prominent intelligence officers in the former military intelligence establishment under the previous regime, were arrested during the 2004 purge of Khin Nyunt’s faction and later released. Following the 2021 coup, they quietly returned to advise and assist Min Aung Hlaing’s regime.

The Irrawaddy has learned that the Paragon Institute, a policy and research platform run by Thein Swe and Hla Min, serves as an informal hub for former operatives. In 2024, they travelled to China ahead of Min Aung Hlaing’s trip to meet with organizations that promote Chinese foreign policy and work for policy research projects commissioned by major Chinese government departments.

Sources familiar with the group’s activities indicate operational overlap between Paragon-linked figures and the Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA), particularly in managing discreet international contacts and backchannel outreach to key regional powers, most notably China. Through Thein Swe and platforms like the Paragon Institute, sources said, Min Aung Hlaing has effectively reactivated legacy intelligence networks to conduct sensitive political groundwork and foreign engagement beyond the constraints of formal diplomacy.

Circle 3: OCMSA and the security-intelligence apparatus

While informal advisers provide specialized channels, the OCMSA serves as the regime’s primary institutional pillar of control. Although the agency is now led by Lieutenant General Kyaw Ko Htike, its former chief—current Commander-in-Chief of Defense Services General Ye Win Oo—is widely regarded by insiders as Min Aung Hlaing’s closest confidant and principal gatekeeper, with a steady rise through the military hierarchy that reflects decades of close personal and professional alignment with the junta chief.

Since February 2021, the OCMSA’s reach has expanded dramatically. Sources say the agency oversees surveillance of resistance networks, monitors civilian political actors, vets state officials and conducts intensive counterintelligence policing inside the military itself to preempt defections and internal dissent. They said OCMSA has operated not merely as a counterintelligence service, but as the primary informational filter shaping Min Aung Hlaing’s political and strategic decisions.

The sidelining of ministers and formal institutions

As power has consolidated around these three circles, formal state institutions and cabinet ministries have seen their policymaking authority sharply curtailed. Sources in Naypyitaw say senior ministers and economic officials have repeatedly seen their warnings—particularly regarding foreign exchange controls, trade restrictions and diplomatic isolation—overruled whenever they clash with Min Aung Hlaing’s immediate political or security priorities.

Consequently, key ministries have been hollowed out of strategic influence. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been largely reduced to handling protocol and consular affairs and defending the regime in multilateral forums, while substantive negotiations take place through intelligence and military channels. Economic ministries, meanwhile, operate primarily as enforcement arms for ad hoc directives rather than architects of coherent macroeconomic policy. Even within the armed forces, operational decision-making has become heavily centralized, limiting the autonomy of regional commanders and traditional staff departments while elevating security and procurement insiders.

While formal ministries no longer shape major strategic decisions, insiders note they remain useful to the regime for bureaucratic execution, day-to-day administration and projecting the outward appearance of state continuity.

Min Aung Hlaing’s reliance on the three circles described above has taken its toll on the country, analysts and diplomats said.

On the economic front, he has failed to listen to experts. Instead, he relies on advisers with military backgrounds, leading to misguided decisions and restrictive measures that have further undermined the economy.

As a result, Myanmar’s economic crisis has reached an extremely critical, if not its worst, point, sources said.

In foreign relations, Min Aung Hlaing appears to be counterbalancing China by leaning toward the United States, while also moving noticeably closer to Russia. He appears to be openly snubbing China, failing to recognize that antagonizing Beijing serves neither his own interests nor Myanmar’s efforts to resolve its ongoing crisis, some diplomats said.

His foreign trips have also failed to deliver tangible results. Despite reaching agreements and making commitments with international partners, few have translated into concrete action.

This likely reflects the limited capacity of those advising him, who appear to lack the understanding and expertise needed to turn diplomatic agreements into practical outcomes that serve the country’s interests, insiders said.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Workers Have a Weapon Against Junta Abuses – Here’s How to Use It
World.content:
Representatives of the International Labor Organization (ILO) Workers’ Group for Asia-Pacific and Arab States met on the sidelines of the Governing Body’s 358th Session on Nov. 14 to discuss the junta’s demand that Myanmar migrant workers remit 25 percent of their salaries through official channels.

Among those attending the Geneva meet was Phyo Sandar Soe, Assistant General Secretary of the Confederation of Trade Unions Myanmar (CTUM), who represented Myanmar’s labor movement.

In addition to the remittance issue, participants discussed strengthening trade unions, challenges facing workers across the region, and the hardships confronting Myanmar migrant workers in the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific.

The ILO adopted its strongest constitutional enforcement measure (Article 33) against Myanmar in June 2025 following mass arrests of labor leaders and the dismantling of independent unions. At the latest meeting, member states were urged to enforce Article 33 measures demanding an end to violence, forced labor and conscription, and the restoration of union freedoms. The article also gives countries UN backing to impose trade sanctions while opening a UN channel for workers and unions to submit complaints of junta abuses, including passport extortion, forced remittance rules, and conscription threats.

Myanmar’s regime responded by dismissing the enforcement decision and rejecting the ILO’s monitoring mechanism.

Phyo Sandar Soe spoke to The Irrawaddy about the meeting, the junta’s labor policies, and recent developments at the ILO.

What were the key issues raised at the meeting?

The regime’s remittance rule is not only affecting workers in Thailand and Malaysia but worldwide.

We told ILO regional directors for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East that Myanmar migrant workers are facing serious rights violations and requested an emergency meeting on the issue. The ILO agreed to convene a meeting with experts in attendance.

Junta labor minister Maung Myint has dismissed the ILO’s concerns about migrant workers as exaggerated and misleading. What is your response?

Looking at his social media posts, it’s clear that despite holding the post of labor minister he has no desire to defend workers.

His comments reflect a dictatorship’s mindset. They don’t care how much suffering is endured by workers. Their repression never stops even as people sink deeper into misery.

A labor ministry is supposed to protect the grassroots, the working class of the country. The situation is quite the opposite in Myanmar, which is a shame for the country.

Normally, a country that sends out migrant workers asks the receiving countries to protect its citizens. But in this case, Thailand had to ask the ILO to help protect Myanmar migrant workers. That is deeply embarrassing. The generals should reflect on their own position.

Has the situation for both migrant and domestic workers worsened under the new labor minister?

The regime faces a severe shortage of foreign currency and needs money to fund its military and purchase weapons. So, it has imposed import-license restrictions, tightened access to foreign currency, and is now milking even more from migrant workers through exchange-rate controls and remittance requirements. Regime leaders do not see migrant workers as fellow Myanmar citizens – which is not strange given that they are already killing their own people. What we are seeing is an attempt to squeeze more money from workers to finance further repression.

What decisions were made on Myanmar during the 358th session of the ILO Governing Body in Geneva on Nov. 17?

A follow-up decision on the Article 33 resolution for Myanmar was adopted by the Governing Body. It calls for an immediate end to violence, arbitrary arrests of labor leaders, and forced military recruitment. It also demands the unconditional release of political prisoners, the repeal of laws and orders restricting freedom of association, safe access for ILO missions to Myanmar, and the establishment of a mechanism to monitor labor-rights violations.

The decision further urges member states to review their relations with Myanmar authorities and calls on governments not to forcibly return refugees to Myanmar.

We will urge the ILO to enforce these by January 2027. The ILO Director-General is expected to present an update on Myanmar and progress in implementing the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry at the 359th session of the Governing Body in March 2027.

What message do you have for Myanmar workers inside and outside the country?

Some people think ILO mechanisms achieve nothing, but a mechanism is only effective if people use it. A knife becomes sharp only when properly sharpened. The same is true of international mechanisms: the more workers make use of them, the more effective they become in protecting Myanmar workers.

Many ask why the international community fails to act despite widely publicized abuses. The reason is simple: without complaints from victims and affected workers, cases cannot move forward.

So, if workers want action and accountability, they need to file complaints and use these mechanisms. I encourage workers to make full use of them.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Says Combating Graft in Military Draft Process
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar said Sunday it has taken legal action against dozens of people, including local officials, accused of extortion and illegal detention of men seeking to avoid compulsory military service.

The statement from Myanmar’s Defense Ministry, published in state media, was a rare acknowledgement of official corruption and abuse of the conscription process in the war-torn nation.

Myanmar’s military is fighting various pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority factions in a civil war sparked by a 2021 coup that ousted the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi.

In February 2024, the military activated a conscription law, aiming to bolster its ranks. The move prompted tens of thousands of young people to leave the country to avoid forced recruitment.

On Sunday, Myanmar’s Defense Ministry said authorities had taken unspecified legal actions against 102 offenders in “financial extortion” cases and 97 others accused of unauthorized “forcible conscription”, as of the end of October.

“These forcible detentions and unauthorized collections of funds constitute unlawful acts committed by unscrupulous individuals,” the ministry said.

It said some “have impersonated officials to forcibly detain individuals, extort money, and unlawfully enlist them as public military service personnel.”

Local administrators have also collected “monthly payments under the pretext of supporting” conscripted soldiers from their areas, and illegally accepted money to “pay for substitutes on behalf of those evading service”.

The ministry said its central committee on military service conscription would continue to “prosecute offenders to reduce and eradicate the forcible conscription of travelers, nighttime arrests, paid substitution in conscription, and the unauthorized collection of funds”.

‘Afraid to speak out’

Many young people in Myanmar avoid being on the streets late at night, fearing the military or other armed groups may arbitrarily detain them or abduct them for conscription.

Local media have reported cases of young men being pulled off the streets in Yangon and other cities and taken away to undergo military training.

Authorities have previously denied the reports.

One man said Sunday that his brother-in-law was sitting in front of his own house in Yangon several months ago when a group of unidentified people grabbed him and took him away in a car.

The family later learned the detained man was at a military training base in the city of Pakokku, about 500 km north of Yangon, said the source, declining to be named due to security concerns.

“We paid a bribe [of around US$2,000] to some authorities to get him out… but he has not been released yet,” said the relative.

A Myanmar MP said some youth from his southern state, Mon, have been detained by the army and were released after bribes were paid to some officers.

Their relatives “were too afraid of the army to speak out,” said the lawmaker, who also requested anonymity.

He said he did not know the sum of the bribes.

The conscription law allows the military to draft men aged 18-35 and women aged 18-27 to serve at least two years.

World.title: Rights Groups Demand Action Against Myanmar Junta After Historic Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
Rights groups are urging governments to step up diplomatic pressure, impose fresh sanctions and isolate the military regime following Thursday’s landmark International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017.

It was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Rights advocates say the historic ruling must now translate into concrete measures to hold the regime accountable, rather than remain a symbolic legal victory.

“This is a big blow for [regime leader] Min Aung Hlaing at a time when he is trying to persuade the world to normalize relations,” Tun Khin, president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), told The Irrawaddy.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, as well as ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine State.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, although the court has no independent enforcement mechanism.

If Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling’s orders, the UN Security Council can act to enforce them, according to Article 94.2 of the UN Charter.

Tun Khin said his organization had called on the UK to organize a meeting of the UN Security Council. Though regime allies Russia and China would likely veto any resolution, they would be forced to explain such a move. London has called for a meeting.

“We hope it will result in new sanctions,” Tun Khin said.

Tun Khin expressed concern that the return of the Rohingya is still impossible due to the policies of both the Myanmar military regime and the ethnic Arakan Army (AA), an anti-regime armed group that controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships.

Lucky Karim, executive director of the group Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, said that as an initial step following the ICJ ruling, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member countries should stop engaging with the Myanmar regime.

She noted that this year nine countries have hosted self-appointed president Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw the 2017 atrocities as military chief. She urged all countries to stop welcoming him. Despite the bilateral engagements, Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from ASEAN’s top-level summits.

“I think the regional states should apply the same rule [as ASEAN] and take a pause for now. Stop hosting him and rolling out the red carpet and engaging him,” Lucky Karim said.

The ICJ decision was welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (HRW), along with foreign ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Turkey, as well as Myanmar’s civilian National Unity Government (NUG).

As immediate actions, London ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché from the UK and issued an urgent call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

More than 190 local rights groups welcomed the ICJ ruling.

The regime rejected the verdict. Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for the military-appointed government, said on Friday: “The truth is we were wrongly accused.”

Emphasizing the fact that the verdict was not unanimous, she said, “Not all the judges voted for it, so it’s not a fair judgment.”

The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Meanwhile, the AA said it would act in the best interests of the state following the landmark ruling.

“We need to wait for the regime’s report to the Court. For example, will the regime deny it, or will they say they can’t pay compensation?” Rakhine politician Pe Than told The Irrawaddy.

Backed by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Gambia brought the case in 2019, alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the Genocide Convention. It took seven years to reach a final verdict in the case.

The Myanmar regime has continued to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across the country since the 2021 coup.

Since seizing power, the regime has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners. The group said the regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, while millions of young people have fled abroad amid forced conscription, security fears, inflation, widespread crime, job scarcity and escalating conflict.

The NUG reaffirmed its commitment to justice, citizenship, and human rights norms for the Rohingya in a statement Thursday.

It said communities across Myanmar continue to face airstrikes, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and forced displacement, while hospitals, schools, monasteries and churches have also come under attack.

“The pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by action to end the military junta’s continuing violence against civilians throughout Myanmar,” it said.

Tun Khin said the ICJ judgment is good news for everyone in Myanmar. “Now they [the regime] are officially responsible for genocide and facing renewed international pressure instead,” he said.

World.title: U.S. Sanctions Two More Myanmar Regime-Allied Scam Warlords
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two more top leaders of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) on Thursday, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

Commander-in-chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One join four other senior leaders of the regime-allied militia on the U.S. sanctions list.

Saw Steel, Saw Sein Win, San Aung and Sai Kyaw Hla were added last November as part of Washington’s crackdown on the multibillion-dollar border scam industry targeting Americans.

Also sanctioned Thursday was Cambodian national Zhao Hui and two of his scam-linked firms.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.”

Thursday’s order was the U.S. latest action targeting Myanmar individuals in a crackdown on online scam compounds in Southeast Asia that defrauded an estimated $7.2 billion from Americans in 2025 alone.

The sanctions freeze any U.S.-based assets held by targets and make it illegal for Americans to do business or financial transactions with them.

Saw Shwe Wah took over protection of scam operations in DKBA-held Sone See Myaing, Kyauk Khet, Waw Lay, and Phaya Thonezu in December 2025 after replacing the blacklisted Saw Steel as DKBA’s commander-in-chief.

At least seven scam major compounds were under DKBA protection in 2025. However, staged regime raids on KK Park, Shwe Kokko, and Myawaddy in October and November last year forced a mass relocation to the DKBA’s Sone See Myaing headquarters, while others reportedly dispersed inland to villages under the group’s control.

“Shwe Wah has full oversight. The online scams are operating under his protection since he holds the highest position of the group,” a source familiar with DKBA administration told The Irrawaddy.

“Smaller scam sites are now scattered across DKBA territory. Despite their size they still have concrete buildings.”

He confirmed that DKBA-protected scam operations are concentrated in its Sone See Myaing stronghold, though others have relocated to villages in the Mulayit mountain range, roughly 20 km inside the border.

Following last year’s Myawaddy crackdown — widely dismissed as a publicity stunt — scammers reportedly flocked south to the Thai-Myanmar border town of Phaya Thonezu (Three Pagodas Pass) under the command of Colonel Saw A One.

Washington added him to its sanctions list Thursday, claiming he oversaw an expansion of scam operations and buildings.

“Tens of thousands of fraudsters flooded in here during the crackdown over there [in Myawaddy], turning this place into a large scam hub,” a resident of Phaya Thonezu told The Irrawaddy. “Since then, the scam buildings have expanded.”

He added that restrictions on movement make it difficult to determine the exact number of scam compounds and workers, though he confirmed the presence of two major compounds in the town and many more hidden nearby in restricted forest

The U.S. escalated its border scam crackdown in 2025, sanctioning leaders of the regime-allied Karen National Army (formerly the Karen Border Guard Force) including Saw Chit Thu and his two sons.

Washington has since formed the Scam Center Strike Force with Thailand to seize evidence, intercept fleeing scam bosses, and cut off cross-border supplies to compounds.

Jeanine Pirro, who oversees the Strike Force, met with Thai officials in Bangkok this week to discuss strengthening bilateral intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border crackdowns against the scam syndicates.

The Irrawaddy could not reach DKBA headquarters for comment.

World.title: ‘Ungrateful and Two-Faced’: Why a Chinese Analyst Slammed Myanmar’s Junta Chief
World.content:
Following Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, a Chinese commentator responded that the junta was attempting to dodge its own political failures by simply attributing its opponent’s combat effectiveness to external assistance.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that resulted in the seizure of the Myanmar military’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and eventually left the regime stripped of control over most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State. The offensive brought about one of the most humiliating defeats in the Myanmar military’s modern history.

The regime chief insisted the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), one of the alliance members, did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” Min Aung Hlaing said, his voice filled with rage.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

On Friday, the Chinese commentator, who claims to “specialize in Myanmar and Southeast Asia”, made the comments on Chinese social media platform WeChat under the title “The Myanmar Military’s Misunderstanding of China: An Analysis of Min Aung Hlaing’s Unspoken Accusations”.

The commentator, whom The Irrawaddy has learned is knowledgeable about Myanmar affairs and familiar with Naypyitaw, argued that Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks went beyond an assessment of the military’s battlefield defeats.

“He was not explaining his assessment of the enemy; he was assigning blame. He attributed the EAOs’ victory in Operation 1027 to ‘covert support from China,’” the author says.

The commentator also said the Myanmar military has never been on the pro-China end of the country’s political spectrum. From General Aung San, the founder of the Myanmar military, to successive generations of leaders like Than Shwe, Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing, all have been full of misunderstandings and suspicions toward China, the author said.

Regarding the junta’s loss in Operation 1027, the author said the Myanmar military failed to look inward for the cause of the collapse of its combat capability after 2021. “The real collapse occurred internally: troops were replenished through forced conscription, military officers’ families enjoyed special privileges, running businesses within the military was rampant, and grassroots morale was shattered. The Myanmar military has failed to rectify these long-accumulated bad habits,” the author pointed out.

“Shoving all the blame onto ‘external assistance’ is the easiest explanation, but also the one that solves absolutely nothing,” the author added.

China mediated a ceasefire between the alliance and the military in January 2024. In April 2025, under Chinese pressure, the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio, allowing the Myanmar military to re-enter the city.

The author says these developments should have encouraged the Myanmar military to rely more on China’s mediation efforts to facilitate negotiations and de-escalation. Instead, the junta leadership interpreted them differently.

“Instead, not only were they ungrateful, but they stubbornly believed: ‘Since the EAOs listen to China and stop fighting when told to, they must also be taking orders from them to attack the Myanmar military; therefore, any military action by the EAOs must be masterminded by China behind the scenes.’”

“If China were truly covertly supporting the EAOs, Lashio would never have been returned. This is the hardest evidence to refute the ‘covert support’ theory, but unfortunately, it is never mentioned in the Myanmar military’s narrative,” the author argues.

The commentator also pointed out that whenever the Myanmar military wants China to pressure ethnic armed groups, it invokes the concept of pauk-phaw, or fraternal, ties. When it needs China to support its economy, open border ports, or buy agricultural products, it repeats the slogan “China-Myanmar Community With a Shared Future.” Yet, the moment domestic governance goes wrong, it immediately shifts the blame to China, the author says.

“This two-faced mentality of simultaneous dependence and suspicion is currently the deepest rift in China-Myanmar relations.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Rejects ‘Unfair’ Rohingya Genocide Ruling at ICJ
World.content:
NAYPYITAW—A historic ruling by the top UN court that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority was “not fair,” the regime’s presidential spokeswoman said Friday.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, the court’s president said.

Asked about the ICJ decision at a press conference in the capital Naypyitaw, spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe called it unfair.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she said, noting the 9-6 vote.

“So this was not a unanimous decision,” she added. “I would say it is not fair.”

Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

But the ICJ ruling dismissed Myanmar’s argument that it was carrying out counter-insurgency operations.

“There is no evidence before the court that, in the conduct of the clearance operations, Myanmar distinguished between civilians and alleged (Rohingya) fighters,” the judgment said.

It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges have determined that a state committed genocide.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh during the crackdown, the court said.

Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, it said, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

No enforcement

The court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation, with specific sums to be determined later.

While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling may heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy.

China, an enduring partner after the coup, raised concerns of judicial overreach after the ICJ ruling.

One of the ICJ’s judges is from China and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.

The U.S. reacted with caution, stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the international court.

Despite determining in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Washington has more recently pushed back on another case before the court, involving accusations by South Africa that U.S. ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Lashes Out at Beijing, Scammer Whac-a-Mole Continues in Shan, and More
World.content:
Min Aung Hlaing hints at Chinese hand in resistance’s Operation 1027

Putschist president Min Aung Hlaing is still groping for an explanation for Operation 1027, the humiliating Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that stripped his regime of most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on the offensive.

He insisted the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

Then came the interesting part: “There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he added.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country, few observers were left in doubt that it was a swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance.

The comments echoed Min Aung Hlaing’s complaints at the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

They come after Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun delivered a body blow to Naypyitaw by urging “high-level autonomy” for ethnic minorities, a suggestion that flies in the face of the military regime’s centralization doctrine.

Regime chief fingers neighbors for sustaining ‘insurgents’

In the same outburst, Min Aung Hlaing also accused the two neighbors that have made the biggest effort to accommodate his regime—China and Thailand—of sustaining “insurgents” by encouraging trade through border crossings they control.

He started with Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and MNDAA, which now control much of Myanmar’s border with China. “In Kachin, the KIA runs border gates at the Chinese border. In northeastern Myanmar, the MNDAA runs Chinshwehaw gate,” he said.

“Taxation from illegal trade has sustained and financed insurgents,” he complained.

In Kachin, the regime has also lost control over the lucrative rare earth mines, which are now a major source of revenues for the KIA. The situation is not much different in northern Shan, where the regime has lost key border crossings with Yunnan as well as rare earth and other mineral resources.

On the surface, he was only accusing Thailand of directly facilitating trade through resistance-held territory at the Thaw Le Hta crossing in Hpapun, avoiding direct accusations against China except by inference and association.

Chinese Customs figures show a steady increase in cross-border trade through crossings controlled by the MNDAA and its allies. Trade through the Chinshwehaw border crossing alone reached 5.01 billion yuan (about US$700 million) so far this year. The central regime is reduced to heavy-handed efforts to “tax” this trade once goods reach military-controlled areas.

China steps up media ‘outreach’ in Myanmar to shape narrative

China stepped up efforts to shape Myanmar’s information space this week, gathering regime-aligned media figures, officials and commentators in Yangon to promote President Xi Jinping’s four flagship global initiatives.

Speaking at a symposium at the Wyndham Grand Yangon Hotel on Tuesday with over 160 participants, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia highlighted growing bilateral cooperation in security, governance and people-to-people exchanges. Myanmar is the first country to sign up to all four of Xi’s initiatives, which also include AI.

Ma listed the usual talking points, from law-enforcement cooperation to combat cross-border crimes, including online scam operations, to cultural and media exchanges aimed at strengthening “mutual understanding.” Echoing Chinese President Xi Jinping and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, she called for key projects of the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) to be hurried along.

The event brought together stalwart regime propagandists like Lower House MP Aye Chan, Myanmar Press Council Chairman Dr. Tin Tun Oo, Myanmar Narrative Think Tank chairman Ko Ko, plus figures from regime and regime-aligned media.

Days earlier, Myanmar Foreign Ministry-backed think tank MISIS and state-owned China Media Group gathered academics, media representatives and officials in Yangon to discuss future areas of China-Myanmar cooperation aligned with Beijing’s 15th Five-Year Plan.

The forums follow a similar gathering hosted by Ma in May, when she called on regime-linked media and opinion leaders to tell “beautiful stories” about China.

Chinese-run scam industry lives on in southern Shan

Myanmar’s regime says it arrested 23 Chinese nationals and seized three assault rifles in a raid on an alleged online scam and gambling operation in Laihka Township in southern Shan State on Wednesday.

They were detained at a makeshift compound deep in the forest comprising a workshop, living quarters and a kitchen. A tally compiled from regime media reports suggests some 90 Chinese scammers have been arrested in raids since February in Laihka, which has emerged as a new scam hotspot since 2025.

They take advantage of the lawless environment amid competing territorial claims of local militias as well as the Shan State Progressive Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), and the Restoration Council of Shan State/Shan State Army (RCSS/SSA).

Even as a docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry broadcast on Chinese state media last month sold the 2024 crackdown on scam hubs in northern Shan State’s Laukkai as an unmitigated success, the criminal gangs simply scattered across eastern and southern Shan instead. According to the independent Institute for Strategy and Policy–Myanmar, operations have since been identified in at least 17 Shan townships including Tangyan, Tachileik and Muse.

Meanwhile, ASEAN and the U.S., meeting in Manila this week, adopted what was billed as a “partnership work plan” to tackle online scams and thereby increase international pressure on Myanmar’s regime. Regime leader Min Aung Hlaing was not invited to the summit.

Complied by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Kazakhstan Supports Opening of 2026 World Chess Championship in Geneva
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan joined international efforts to promote chess diplomacy by supporting the opening of the 2026 World Chess Championship in Geneva on Nov. 22, bringing together diplomatic representatives, United Nations (UN) officials and two of the sport’s youngest title contenders.

The opening ceremony took place at the Palace of Nations, with support from Kazakhstan’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva, under the auspices of the International Chess Federation (FIDE).

Ahead of the ceremony, the Kazakhstan Hall hosted a press conference attended by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Office, Yerzhan Kazykhan; FIDE President Timur Turlov; UN representatives; reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju of India; and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, the permanent mission’s press service reported.

Addressing the participants, Kazykhan drew parallels between chess and diplomacy, noting that both require strategic thinking, respect for rules and the ability to find solutions acceptable to all sides. He also highlighted Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop chess and the growing interest in the game among young people.

The championship will run from Nov. 22 to Dec. 12 at the Martin Bodmer Foundation in Cologny, near Geneva. The first game is scheduled for Nov. 24.

At 20, both Gukesh and Sindarov will make history as the youngest players to compete in a match for the world chess title.

Kazakhstan’s support for the opening ceremony reflects its engagement in international chess initiatives and comes as the country strengthens its presence in the global chess community following Timur Turlov’s election as FIDE president.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Commission Five Solar Power Plants With 92 MW Capacity This Year
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to commission five solar power plants with a combined capacity of 92 megawatts (MW) by the end of this year, as the country continues to expand renewable energy generation and diversify its energy mix.

Kazakhstan’s installed renewable energy capacity currently stands at 3.7 gigawatts (GW), including 1.3 gigawatts (GW) of solar power. From January to September, renewable energy facilities generated 7.8 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity, with solar power plants accounting for 1.9 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh), the Energy Ministry reported on Nov. 23.

The country initially planned to commission 10 renewable energy facilities with a combined capacity of 245 megawatts (MW) this year. Seven facilities are already operational, including three solar power plants with a total capacity of 62.6 megawatts (MW). These include a 20-megawatt (MW) plant developed by Stellar Energy in the Mangystau Region, a 22.6-megawatt (MW) facility by Altyn Solar Energy in the Kostanai Region, and a 20-megawatt (MW) plant by Jetisu Terra Power in the Zhetisu Region.

Two additional solar power plants developed by Alkhena in the Kyzylorda Region, with a combined capacity of 30 megawatts (MW), are scheduled to begin operations by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan is building a pipeline of prospective solar energy projects with a combined capacity of approximately 900 megawatts (MW). Major initiatives include a 300-megawatt (MW) solar power plant by China Energy and projects by Tumar Commerce with a combined capacity of up to 1 gigawatt (GW).

By the end of 2035, Kazakhstan aims to commission at least 8.4 gigawatts (GW) of new renewable energy capacity, including approximately 1.8 gigawatts (GW) of solar generation.

The expansion comes as Kazakhstan moves into the next phase of its energy transition, with a growing focus on integrating renewable sources into the national power system. As solar and wind generation increase, developing transmission infrastructure, energy storage and grid flexibility will become increasingly important to ensure a stable electricity supply.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 13th Worldwide in Utility Model Applications
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 13th worldwide in utility model applications in 2025, with 1,914 applications filed that year, a 21.4% increase from 2024, according to the World Intellectual Property Organization’s (WIPO) World Intellectual Property Indicators 2026 report.

The country ranked among the world’s top 20 origins of utility model applications, placing ahead of several economies and close to Brazil, which recorded 2,584 applications, and Italy, with 2,253.

China topped the global ranking with approximately 2.65 million applications, followed by Russia with 13,147 and Germany with 7,338. Thailand, Indonesia, Ukraine, Japan, Türkiye, South Korea and Spain also featured in the top 10.

Global utility model applications decline

Kazakhstan’s growth came amid a broader decline in global utility model filings. According to WIPO, worldwide applications fell 16.3% in 2025 to nearly 2.7 million, after three consecutive years of growth, Kazinform reported.

The decline was driven primarily by China, where applications dropped by 534,640 compared with 2024, reaching approximately 2.65 million.

Despite the decrease, Chinese applicants accounted for 97.2% of all utility model applications worldwide, compared with 93% in 2015.

What are utility models?

A utility model is a form of intellectual property protection that grants its holder exclusive rights to commercially exploit a technical invention for a limited period. Unlike conventional patents, utility models generally have shorter protection periods, typically six to 10 years, and are granted without substantive examination in most jurisdictions, according to WIPO.

The World Intellectual Property Indicators 2026 report is WIPO’s annual review of global intellectual property activity. It covers 2025 statistics on patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs, microorganisms, plant variety protection and geographical indications.

World.title: Kazakhstan Moves to Expand Air Links With South Korea, Jordan and Algeria
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is advancing plans to expand air connectivity with South Korea, Jordan, Algeria and Germany through new flight routes and agreements with foreign aviation authorities.

Kazakh aviation officials discussed the developments during the Seventh International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7), where they held a series of bilateral meetings with counterparts from several countries.

Korean Air plans Seoul-Almaty flights

Korean Air plans to launch regular flights between Seoul and Almaty in summer 2027, reported the Transport Ministry on Nov. 19. The intention was discussed at a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev and South Korea’s Deputy Minister for Civil Aviation Jeong Chae-gyo.

Lastayev welcomed the airline’s plans to enter the Kazakh market, noting that a new carrier would increase passenger traffic, strengthen tourism ties and give travelers more options. Korean Air has also expressed interest in exploring flights between Seoul and Astana.

Currently, 12 regular passenger flights operate weekly between Kazakhstan and South Korea on the Astana-Seoul, Almaty-Seoul and Shymkent-Seoul routes.

The officials also discussed finalizing a draft air services agreement, which would establish a legal framework for further expanding air connectivity and cooperation between their aviation authorities.

Jordan, Algeria agreements open new opportunities

Kazakhstan and Jordan have signed a memorandum of understanding allowing designated airlines from each country to operate up to 14 flights per week. The agreement followed a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee Chairperson Saltanat Tompiyeva and Jordan’s Civil Aviation Regulatory Commission Chairperson Deifallah Farajat.

Jordanian representatives also confirmed national carrier Royal Jordanian’s interest in launching regular flights to Kazakhstan. The officials noted growing interest among Jordanian citizens in Kazakhstan as a tourism destination, creating opportunities to strengthen business and tourism ties.

A separate memorandum signed between Kazakhstan and Algeria also provides for up to 14 weekly flights for designated carriers from each country.

The agreement was reached during a meeting between Tompiyeva and Hassan Boulfelfel, director general of Algeria’s National Civil Aviation Agency.

The two officials also initialed a draft air services agreement to establish the legal framework for regular flights between the countries. Discussions covered practical cooperation between aviation authorities and the possibility of a separate memorandum on technical cooperation.

Germany talks focus on air connectivity and fleet development

Kazakhstan and Germany also discussed expanding air services and strengthening civil aviation cooperation during a meeting between Lastayev and Stefan Schnorr, state secretary at Germany’s Federal Ministry of Transport.

Lastayev highlighted the strong level of bilateral cooperation and Kazakhstan’s interest in expanding air links between the two countries.

The discussions also covered cooperation with European aircraft manufacturer Airbus. Air Astana and FlyArystan currently operate a combined fleet of 65 Airbus aircraft, including 36 operated by Air Astana and 29 by FlyArystan.

Another 23 Airbus aircraft are expected to join the fleet by 2030. In June, Air Astana and Airbus signed an agreement in Brussels to acquire up to 50 A320neo family aircraft, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2031.

The two officials also discussed cooperation between their competent authorities in investigating aviation accidents and incidents. They agreed to explore a new cooperation agreement to strengthen institutional ties and facilitate the exchange of expertise and best practices.

World.title: Almaty’s 45,000-Seat Stadium Undergoes Ground Testing Ahead of Foundation Work
World.content:
ASTANA – Construction of a new 45,000-seat stadium in Almaty remains in the preparatory stage, with engineers conducting geological surveys and testing trial piles before foundation work begins, the Kazinform news agency reported.

The stadium is being built on a 32-hectare site between the Kulja and Talgar highways. The facility is designed to meet UEFA Category 4 requirements and is expected to become one of the city’s main sports venues.

According to Almaty’s Construction Department, the site is located in an area with seismic activity reaching 10 points, making geological assessments essential to the project’s safety. In cooperation with the Kazakh Research and Design Institute of Construction and Architecture (KazNIISA), engineers are examining the soil’s physical and mechanical properties, including its strength and load-bearing capacity.

Foundation work awaits test results

Trial piles are currently being driven into the ground to assess their strength and stability and determine whether they can withstand the loads of the future stadium structures. The construction department said concrete work on the main foundation structures has not yet begun. Work will begin once the results of the pile tests and geological surveys are available.

Earthworks have also been partially completed. The topsoil has been removed, and initial site grading has been carried out, although full leveling remains unfinished. Excavation and backfilling will proceed in accordance with the project design and construction schedule, the department said.

Work planned by the end of 2026

Almaty Deputy Construction Department Head Nurbek Zhassybaiyev outlined several tasks scheduled for completion by the end of 2026.

These include completing the installation and testing of trial piles and preparing technical assessments based on the results. The project also provides for further earthworks, soil treatment and site grading across the stadium area and adjacent training fields.

The construction site is also expected to receive temporary and permanent utility infrastructure, including electricity, water supply and outdoor lighting. Pile installation and concreting are also planned in accordance with the project documentation.

The stadium’s capacity was initially announced at 35,000 seats. Following feedback from residents and the public, the planned capacity was increased to 45,000.

Construction is expected to be completed in spring 2028.

World.title: More Than 40 Startups to Compete for $50,000 at INMerge 2026 in Baku
World.content:
ASTANA – More than 40 startups will compete for a $50,000 cash prize at the INMerge Innovation Summit 2026, which will bring together 120 selected startups, over 200 international speakers and thousands of participants in Baku on Nov. 30-Dec. 1.

Organized by PASHA Holding, the region’s largest innovation platform will host the INBattle startup competition, with the winner also earning the opportunity to represent Azerbaijan at the Startup World Cup 2027.

This year’s summit attracted more than 1,300 startup applications from 94 countries. One of its key focuses will be developing the startup ecosystem, showcasing emerging technologies and expanding opportunities for international cooperation.

The summit will feature more than 200 internationally renowned speakers from the worlds of technology, business, economics and innovation. Among them are five-time Grand Slam champion and entrepreneur Maria Sharapova, former Chief Business Officer of Google X Mo Gawdat, former Nike Chief Marketing Officer Greg Hoffman, and 2025 Nobel Laureate in Economic Sciences Joel Mokyr.

The full list of speakers and ticket details is available here.

Founded and organized by PASHA Holding, the INMerge Innovation Summit is an annual innovation and technology summit held in Baku since 2021. By bringing together corporations, investors, startups and government representatives from Azerbaijan, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe, the summit fosters regional collaboration and contributes to Baku’s development as an innovation hub.

At its 2025 edition, the summit brought together more than 5,000 participants, over 180 speakers, 122 startups and 80 investors. For a closer look at last year’s atmosphere and key discussions, watch our special report from Baku on The Astana Times’ YouTube channel.

World.title: GITEX Global 2026 to Bring Together 6,000 Tech Companies, Startups and Government Entities in Dubai
World.content:
ASTANA – GITEX Global 2026 will bring together more than 6,000 technology companies, government entities and startups in Dubai on Dec. 7–11, with a focus on artificial intelligence (AI), data infrastructure, energy, robotics, cybersecurity and emerging technologies.

The event will open with a high-level summit on Dec. 7 at the Dubai World Trade Center. The four-day exhibition and conference program will take place from Dec. 8 to 11 at the Dubai Exhibition Center in Expo City Dubai. The event will reunite with Expand North Star, its startup and investor showcase, which will run from Dec. 8 to 10 at the same venue.

Organizers describe the 2026 edition as a new chapter for GITEX, with a new venue and format. More than 400 government entities and over 750 investors from more than 60 countries are expected to participate. The investors collectively represent nearly $2 trillion in assets under management.

The event will examine how geopolitical shifts, energy volatility and competition over critical infrastructure are reshaping global markets. Discussions will focus on the growing importance of data sovereignty, national AI strategies and investment partnerships as governments and businesses prepare for 2027.

AI, data infrastructure and energy in focus

Participating technology companies collectively represent approximately $20 trillion in market capitalization, according to the event overview. The lineup includes major global technology brands such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, IBM, Cisco, Huawei, Intel, Oracle, Salesforce, Dell, Lenovo and Siemens.

A central topic will be the relationship between AI development and the infrastructure needed to support it. Two dedicated showcases, GITEX Super Data Center and GITEX New Energy, will focus on data centers, energy supply, construction, industrial capacity and the role of infrastructure in national competitiveness.

The program will also address sovereign AI, frontier models and agentic AI, alongside intelligent connectivity and quantum technologies.

Institutions from the United Arab Emirates listed among the participants include the Ministry of Economy, Dubai Digital Authority, Dubai Police, Dubai Customs, the Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority, and the UAE Cybersecurity Council. International participants include government and trade organizations from Poland, India, Serbia, Greece, Hong Kong, Pakistan, South Korea, Cyprus, Latvia, Slovenia, Hungary and Georgia.

Robotics, mobility and cybersecurity

The newly launched GITEX World Robotix and GITEX MobX will focus on robotics, embedded AI and the commercial development of future mobility. Exhibitors include Unitree, Ant Group Robotics, Booster Robotics, Pudu Robotics, iFLYTEK and LimX Dynamics, as well as U.S.-based Joby Aviation.

The program will explore the deployment of humanoid and service robots, autonomous systems and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Joby Aviation is developing electric air taxis for Dubai through a planned network of four vertiports.

Cybersecurity will be another major focus. GITEX Cyber Valley will address AI security, dual-use cyber technologies and post-quantum readiness, with dedicated business meetings and briefings for international cybersecurity leaders. Participating companies include Acronis, Kaspersky, CrowdStrike, Fortinet, SentinelOne, Trellix and Palo Alto Networks.

The inaugural LIVX by GITEX will explore the application of AI in longevity research and healthcare, including drug discovery, genomics, precision diagnostics and regenerative medicine. Participants include the Institute for Healthier Living Abu Dhabi, the Buck Institute for Research on Aging and Insilico Medicine.

New companies and international startups

The event will feature companies working across AI infrastructure, enterprise software, mobility and quantum computing.

Among the highlighted enterprises is Abu Dhabi-based Neurovia AI, a subsidiary of Robo.ai, which develops technology for storing, optimizing and transmitting visual data. Its NeuroStream platform reportedly compressed a 12.15-gigabyte 4K video file to 421 megabytes while maintaining visual quality, reducing the file size by more than 96%.

Other featured companies include Workday, which develops finance and human resources software; Netris, a provider of network automation for AI infrastructure; and Monday.com, an AI-powered workflow management platform.

The event overview also lists six unicorn companies with a combined valuation of $76 billion: Swiss quantum software company Terra Quantum, French quantum computing company Pasqal, Chinese robotics company AGIBOT, AI data company Scale AI, AI workspace provider Genspark and Dutch AI chip developer Axelera AI.

Please note: The Astana Times is part of the event’s official international media delegation at GITEX Global. Follow for more exclusive content.

World.title: Kazakhstan Handles 84% of China-Central Asia Freight as Regional Trade Nearly Triples
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan handles approximately 84% of freight transported between China and Central Asia, placing it at the center of a rapidly expanding regional trade network. Trade between China and the five Central Asian countries nearly tripled between 2020 and 2025, rising from $23.5 billion to almost $70 billion, according to a Nov. 19 analytical brief by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB).

China has become the region’s largest trading partner, accounting for nearly 30% of its total merchandise trade in 2025, up from 17-18% in 2020-2021. All rail freight between China and Central Asia passes through Kazakhstan, primarily via the Dostyk and Altynkol border crossings.
