World.title: President Ilham Aliyev signs decree on January 2027 military conscription
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 23. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has signed an order on the conscription of citizens for compulsory active military service and the transfer of servicemen completing their compulsory service to the reserve from January 1 through 30, 2027.

The text of the document has been published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

Under the order, citizens of Azerbaijan born in 2009 who have reached the age of 18 by the date of conscription (inclusive), as well as those born between 1997 and 2008 who are under the age of 30, have not completed compulsory active military service in the Azerbaijani Armed Forces, and are not entitled to deferment or exemption from conscription, will be called up for compulsory active military service from January 1 through 30, 2027.

Servicemen who have completed the service period stipulated in Article 38.1.1 of the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan "On Military Duty and Military Service" will be transferred to the reserve from January 1 through 30, 2027.

The Cabinet of Ministers of Azerbaijan is tasked with taking the measures предусмотренные by law to implement this order.

World.title: Penny Wong sounds alarm over US-China rivalry and the risk of conflict
World.content:
The United States and China are increasingly willing to wield their power without regard for the rules that have helped prevent major conflict for decades, Foreign Minister Penny Wong will warn.

In a stark assessment of the world order, Senator Wong will use a major foreign policy speech on Tuesday to say international institutions are increasingly paralysed by tensions between powerful nations, weakening their ability to resolve or prevent disputes.

"Rules without power cannot secure peace. Power without rules cannot sustain it," she will say in an address to the Senate.

Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin emerged from their historic talks in Shenzhen with broad statements but few concrete details about how those ambitions would be achieved. (The Canadian Press: Adrian Wyld via AP)

The warning comes days after US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held landmark talks in China, emerging with a joint declaration that did not refer to the Ukraine invasion or the Iran war.

Meanwhile, the Albanese government has been focused on strengthening Australia's influence in the Indo-Pacific, deepening security and economic ties with neighbouring countries while maintaining the US alliance and managing its relationship with China.

The diplomatic push continues this week with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese expected to host Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, and Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale in Canberra, following a series of summits with world leaders across Asia.

US, China and the great power divide

In her speech on Tuesday, Senator Wong will say Beijing is seeking to reshape the world in its own interests, while Washington is redefining its role and what it expects of allies, leaving countries like Australia facing greater pressure to protect their sovereignty.

"The great powers, the United States and China, are competing across every domain, with less regard for the guardrails that once kept competition from tipping into conflict," she will say.

Senator Wong will say the competition between the US and China remains the "strategic dynamic of our time," particularly in Australia's region.

She will argue China is "intensifying" its efforts to "remake the multilateral system" and increasingly militarising disputed issues.

"China is undertaking the largest military build-up by any country since the Second World War, without the transparency and reassurance the region expects," she will say.

Australia strikes deal on AI talks with China Anthony Albanese has secured an agreement for new talks with China on artificial intelligence.

Senator Wong will also note the US National Security Strategy released this year specifically says the "days of the United States propping up the entire world order like Atlas are over".

In the wake of the midterm elections, which delivered a resounding loss to the Republican Party and Mr Trump's MAGA movement, Senator Wong will say the direction of US policy is "still being contested at home in ways that will affect the entire world".

Senator Wong will say Australia plans to continue to "clearly" state its views on areas of disagreement with China.

"We believe a stable relationship, in which differences can be managed, is better for Australia, better for China and better for our region," she will say.

Middle powers have strength in numbers

Senator Wong will argue that while the US and China remain the dominant global powers, countries like Australia, India, Indonesia, Japan and South Korea are gaining greater economic, diplomatic and military influence.

She will say the number of mid-sized powers has nearly doubled since the end of the Cold War, while the US and China's combined share of global GDP has largely plateaued over the past decade.

But Senator Wong will also warn growing international instability has made it harder for smaller nations to protect their independence, let alone expand their influence.

"It is increasingly costly for middle powers and smaller nations to simply hold the strategic space they have, let alone expand it," she will say.

Albanese meets Xi Jinping Anthony Albanese meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Senator Wong will argue Australia must deepen partnerships with like-minded countries to ensure the world's superpowers do not dictate its interests.

"Amplified middle power diplomacy characterises our approach, bringing together countries that can achieve more in partnership than any one of us could achieve alone," she will say.

In addition to working with other countries in the region and traditional allies in Europe, Senator Wong will say Australia is deepening its relationship with nations in Africa and Latin America.

Australia will not abandon international institutions

Senator Wong will pitch Australia as a "strong defender" of multilateralism and say the government cannot "pretend" global and regional institutions are "working as they should".

"The UN is facing serious financial pressures. Decision-making is too often paralysed by great power dynamics," she will say.

The foreign minister will argue the breakdown in international cooperation has made it harder to address global challenges, with countries increasingly unable to reach consensus.

"And when the capacity to act collectively is weakened, every other challenge becomes harder to manage," she will say.

But Senator Wong will reject abandoning the multilateral system, instead calling for reform, including the UN Security Council.

"Middle powers would not help themselves by walking away from multilateralism because it's imperfect," she will say.

"It would leave a vacuum, and vacuums are rarely filled by peace."

World.title: Ukraine strikes two Russian vessels off Libyan coast
World.content:
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for a series of drone strikes on two Russian vessels near the Libyan port of Benghazi.

In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said drones on Sunday sunk a Russian corvette Merkury and struck a cargo ship he said Moscow used to transport weapons.

A combat military helicopter was also destroyed in the attack, he said.

"It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," he wrote on X.

Russian officials made no immediate comment.

Mr Zelenskyy said the Merkury was one of Russia's newest ships commissioned during the 2023 invasion.

"Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit," he wrote.

"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attacks were executed in response to Russian aggression. (Reuters: Henry Nicholls)

Mr Zelenskyy described the assault as "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war".

He said he received detailed briefings on Sunday and Monday, adding that "the targets we set were achieved".

The attacks drew condemnation from the United Nations who warned against the prospect of a Libya still recovering from civil war becoming "a battleground for foreign conflicts".

It comes as Ukraine steps up its strikes against Russia away from the frontline.

At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.

A Russian strike on a five-storey apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people on Sunday morning, police said. A seven-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the attack, rescue services said.

Libyan officials say 10 people wounded

The strikes severely damaged the Russian navy corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw fire at the base early on Sunday.

Why Ukraine's Crimean Bridge destruction was significant in Russian war One expert says Ukraine's destruction of the Crimean Bridge marked a "huge blow to Putin's credibility as Russian leader".

Civil defence rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.

United Nations condemns attacks

The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, and called for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".

Ukrainian sea drones hit and sunk a Russian warship. (Security Service of Ukraine via AP)

"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UN mission wrote on X.

The government in eastern Libya has written to UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the UN Security Council, calling for an investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch the attack.

Sunday's strikes came after a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday, close to Finnish waters.

Kyiv has not commented on that attack but the Finnish military said it was likely to have been carried out by Ukraine. All 16 crew were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship, one of them slightly injured.

AP/AFP/Reuters

World.title: Meldrum remembered as 'the fan all artists wish to have'
World.content:
An "unwavering" champion. "Truly unique." An "enemy" turned ally. And "the fan all artists wish to have".

Australian musicians have been lining up to pay tribute to Ian "Molly" Meldrum, the music tastemaker, record producer, Countdown host and Hey, Hey It's Saturday regular who died at the age of 83 on Monday morning.

Meldrum, who leaves a lasting legacy as one of the most influential figures in the Australian media landscape, was introduced to a whole generation of Australians as the face of the ABC's Countdown TV show.

Among those watching at home was a young Kylie Minogue, who reflected on growing up watching the program "every single weekend" long before she was Australian pop royalty.

"[I was] in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room and dreaming of how music might become part of my life," Minogue wrote in a heartfelt Instagram tribute.

Loading Instagram content

"I was over the Moon to be in the Countdown audience one time, and by my late teens I was on the show."

Meldrum was an early, staunch supporter of Minogue's transition from Neighbours soap star to an international career in music.

She praised his "unwavering love and support" of her, as well as the way Meldrum "championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way".

" Vale Molly. I'm going to turn the music up in your honour. "

In his own online tribute, fellow Neighbours star turned solo artist Jason Donovan called Meldrum "a truly unique character, a great Australian and one of this country's greatest pioneers and ambassadors for music and entertainment.

"He was loved, recognised and respected around the world for the extraordinary contribution he made to Australian music and the artists he championed. There will never be another quite like him."

He also shared a memory of Meldrum appearing in a Neighbours episode alongside Minogue and Guy Pearce: "What a day that was!"

Jimmy Barnes said he and Meldrum "went through a lot", and initially considered him "the enemy", as the host of "the best music TV show in the country but insisting that we had to mime".

However, after appearing on Countdown, Barnes conceded the impact on Cold Chisel's career was immediate, catapulting them to bigger venues and wider popularity.

"We were always thankful to him for that," the frontman continued.

Loading Instagram content

Mysterious Girl hit-maker Peter Andre, who signed to Meldrum's label, Melodian Records, in the early 90s as a teenager, said his death "really hurts," calling him a "true icon [and] friend".

"If it wasn't for this man, I would not of had any of the chances I had to make it in any way in the entertainment industry back when it was near impossible to get noticed," he wrote.

"He believed in me from day one and I am forever grateful."

Loading Instagram content

ARIA Hall of Famer Kate Ceberano also praised Meldrum for helping elevate and amplify her career, saying his death marked the end of an era.

"He had no agenda he wanted, no praise, he never basked in any reflected glory or self pride," she wrote.

"He simply wanted the world to hear what he could hear, wanted you to see what he was looking at and then blow it up to 11. Way up sky high. No dream is too big. No cringe, withholding nothing."

" He was the fan all artists wish to have. "

Loading Instagram content

Before Countdown aired, Meldrum produced Russell Morris's 1969 single The Real Thing, transforming the song penned by the late Johnny Young into a six-minute, chart-topping epic

"He was a unique, and loveable individual," Morris wrote on Faceboook. "I was lucky enough to call him my friend, and mentor."

He added: "As can be witnessed by his incredible musical, and media career — he achieved things that were truly great… long live the king."

Icehouse frontman Iva Davies called Meldrum a "bright, larger than life figure", remembering his support in championing homegrown artists and their careers.

"Like the rest of the music community that owed so much to his support, the band and I are so thankful that Molly was a part of our lives and music," he wrote.

Similarly, Daddy Cool and Mondo Rock musician Ross Wilson wrote that Meldrum "selflessly helped me and so many other performers".

"The band and I are so thankful that Molly was a part of our lives and music."

World.title: Two guilty over cocaine plot that was 'embarrassment to organised crime'
World.content:
Two people have been found guilty for their roles in a failed attempt to bring nearly a tonne of cocaine into Western Australia, in what the prosecutor described as "disorganised crime".

The drugs, worth half a billion dollars, were found inside the bulk carrier St Pinot, which headed to Australia from Argentina with a load of animal feed in May 2023.

Ashley Vlotman, 40, and Meagan Rees, 35, were today found guilty of aiding the attempted importation of 850 kilograms of cocaine.

The court heard Vlotman and Rees were among the organisers of a plan to get a boat to rendezvous with the bulk carrier, but the operation came apart when the crew of the smaller vessel hit trouble in rough seas and had to be rescued.

Three men were on board that smaller boat, named No Fixed Address, and earlier this year one of them — Tamaohungia Joseph Tepatu-Edwards — was sentenced to 26 years in prison after pleading guilty over the attempted importation.

Authorities staged a press conference after the drugs were seized. (ABC News: Dave Weber)

One of the other men on board, Lithuanian Germanas Joneliunas, was acquitted over his involvement, saying he believed it was a tobacco importation.

The jury could not reach a unanimous verdict on the other man on No Fixed Address, Terrence Baker, who said he believed he was going on a fishing trip to Rottnest.

The captain of St Pinot, 46-year-old Milan Begovic, told the court he did not know there was cocaine on his vessel and the jury found him not guilty.

The WA Supreme Court heard the criminal scheme was beset by multiple failures and the cocaine did not actually make it to shore until after the authorities had taken control.

The roles of Vlotman and Rees were outlined in messages shown to the jury.

Meagan Rees pictured outside court during the trial. (ABC News: David Weber)

While there was no mention of cocaine, there were messages about buying a boat, with someone using the handle Meagan Elizabeth saying "I'm charging an administrator fee" for being a "messenger".

Sea sick

Tepatu-Edwards and Mr Baker set out on No Fixed Address with Mr Joneliunas, a man from Lithuania they had never met before.

Mr Baker and Mr Joneliunas told the court they became violently ill at sea, and some hours later, No Fixed Address itself was in trouble.

Loading...

Mr Baker called his mother and Water Police became involved with Tactical Response Group officers boarding the boat.

No drugs were found on No Fixed Address and the trio were released before being arrested again after the cocaine was found on St Pinot.

St Pinot had been boarded and directed to port by the authorities, with the cocaine discovered in packages inside a flooded ballast tank.

In messages to a friend after the arrests, Meagan Elizabeth referred to a "syndicate", and said the police already seemed to know a lot.

Prosecutor Steven Whybrow labelled the plot an "embarrassment to organised crime".

Prosecutor Steven Whybrow. (ABC News: David Weber)

After the jury delivered its verdicts, Justice Amanda Forrester said Mr Begovic and Mr Joneliunas were free to leave, although it's understood they do not have permission to stay in Australia.

Vlotman and Rees have a sentencing hearing in May.

World.title: Steve Smith labours on return from injury in Sheffield Shield
World.content:
Steve Smith has fallen cheaply in his batting comeback, making a laborious 12 for New South Wales against Queensland in their Sheffield Shield clash.

Smith had not played a innings since October 22, when he battled a neck injury in Australia's second Test in South Africa.

The star batter returned for NSW ahead of Australia's first Test against New Zealand starting on December 9 in Perth.

In reply to Queensland's 278 all out, the Blues were 7-195 at stumps at the SCG on Monday.

Smith's knock in tricky conditions was cut short by fringe Test paceman Michael Neser.

Smith struggled for touch on a rain-affected day and, with stadium lights on in the last session, faced 59 balls.

Smith was adjudged LBW when trapped on the crease to an in-dipping Neser delivery, though replays showed the ball perhaps would have missed leg stump.

The ex-Test captain, who has maintained a public silence amid the renewed furore over Australia's sandpaper scandal, cut Bulls spinner Mitchell Swepson (3-45) for four early and was six runs from eight balls.

He then was scoreless from his next 24 deliveries. His next run came when he almost chopped a Cameron Gannon short ball onto his stumps.

Steve Smith rarely displayed his fluid best shot-making. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Smith came to the crease to replace NSW opener Sam Konstas, who did no harm to his claims for a Test recall, making 42 from 86 balls.

Konstas, who has been in fine touch in the domestic season, struck a six and five fours before being dismissed in strange fashion.

Facing Swepson, Konstas attempted a half-hearted push to the leg-side but got a leading edge to pop a simple return catch to the Queensland tweaker.

Konstas fell after a 79-run opening partnership with Josh Philippe, who also departed when within reach of a half-century. He edged to keeper Jimmy Peirson from the bowling of Neser (2-28) when on 46.

The most remarkable dismissal of the day though came when Charlie Stobo was caught by Hugo Burdon at wide long on off the bowling of Marnus Labuschagne.

Stobo could have been caught on the rope by Burdon, only for the Queensland opener to put his hands up and acknowledge that he trod on the boundary rope in his attempt to throw the ball back in to himself.

Despite that reprieve, the very next ball Stobo went to hit Labuschagne to the exact same spot, where he was caught.

Earlier, Queensland were bowled out for 278 with Test spinner Nathan Lyon claiming a wicket in his first over on Monday. He finished with 1-86 from 29 overs.

Charlie Stobo (3-45) and Liam Hatcher (3-55) were the most successful bowlers.

AAP

World.title: No life jackets, lifeboat or functioning radio on airboat during 2023 crash
World.content:
A court has heard passengers on an airboat tour, operated by Matt Wright's outback adventure company, were forced to use their clothes and towels to treat injuries after a serious crash.

Today, Top End Safari Camp pleaded guilty to breaching NT WorkSafe laws over the May 2023 airboat crash.

Wright, a director of the company, attended Darwin Local Court for today's hearing, however, his wife and co-director, Kaia Wright, was unable to attend due to illness.

Matt and Kaia Wright leaving the NT Supreme Court last August, after he was found guilty on two counts of attempting to pervert the course of justice. (ABC News: Michael Parfitt)

The court heard the boat, which was carrying 13 passengers including six children, crashed into a semi-submerged tree while travelling along Sweets Lagoon in Bynoe, south-west of Darwin.

The force of the collision threw passengers forward out of their seats, causing injuries to several people.

One passenger, who the court heard was seated in the front row of the boat, hit her head on a step, which caused serious head injuries.

"A significant portion of her scalp was opened," prosecutor Nicholas Goodfellow said.

Nicholas Goodfellow says several passengers were injured in the accident. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

Other passengers suffered a "variety of lacerations and bruising".

The court heard in the immediate aftermath of the crash, crew realised the boat did not have a first-aid kit on board.

"Many resorted to using their own towels and items of clothing to care for the injured, even fashioning a makeshift neck brace for one of the passengers," Mr Goodfellow said.

At the time, the airboat was not fitted with life jackets, a lifeboat or a functioning radio, the court heard.

Matt Wright is widely known for his work as a celebrity crocodile wrangler, having appeared on multiple television shows. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

The lawyer representing Top End Safari Camp, Lyma Nguyen, said the company's failure to comply with its safety duties was "not systemic", describing the breach as an "anomaly" and a "one-off incident".

Ms Nguyen also told the court Mr and Mrs Wright were interstate on the day of the crash and were relying on their general manager, Tim Johnson, and the airboat master, Anton Pugliuca, to manage the tours.

Company 'close to liquidation': Lawyer

The maximum fine for the company's breach is $1.5 million, with Ms Nguyen urging the court to consider Top End Safari Camp's "precarious financial situation".

Ms Nguyen said Wright and the company were facing several civil claims in the NT Supreme Court and Federal Court, brought by several of the airboat passengers.

Lyma Nguyen urged the court to take the company's'precarious financial situation into account. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

"The company is close to liquidation," Ms Nguyen said.

"The company has been operating at a loss due to reputation damage arising out of the crash and the prosecutions, and the company has a very limited capacity to pay a fine.

" A hefty fine will force the company into liquidation. "

Judge Stephen Geary will hand down his sentence on December 22.

World.title: Giddey's historic triple-double rewrites 60-year Chicago Bulls record
World.content:
Josh Giddey has broken his own NBA record and rewritten 60 years of Chicago Bulls history with a remarkable triple-double in an overtime loss to Denver.

The point guard improved his own assist high for Australians in the NBA with 22, while adding 23 points and 14 rebounds in the Bulls' 151-145 loss to the Nuggets.

No Chicago player had notched more than 20 assists since 1985, and Guy Rodgers in 1966 was the last Bull to record at least 20 points, 20 assists and 10 rebounds in a game.

Giddey, who hit 10 of 17 field goals and scored seven late points to force overtime, recorded his 33rd NBA triple-double to move to 14th on the all-time list — equal with countryman Ben Simmons.

Remarkably, it came after he managed just two points and was benched by coach Tiago Splitter in the fourth quarter of a loss to Washington.

He had combined 18 points, 14 rebounds and nine assists in the game before that, rebounding from a four-point effort in the game prior to sum up a rollercoaster season for the battling 4-12 Bulls.

"He [Splitter] can relate to us. He was good about it and doesn't sugar-coat it. I wasn't surprised or confused as to why I wasn't out there," Giddey said post-game of his recent struggles.

"You appreciate it a lot more after the fact. During the moment, you don't want to hear those things.

"I have learnt you've got to be able to move on. I can't come into practice still pissed off and dwelling on things."

Nikola Jokić had 37 points, 18 rebounds and 11 assists for the 202nd triple-double of his career — closing the gap on NBA leader Russell Westbrook (209) — while Jamal Murray scored eight of his season-high 45 points in overtime.

Nikola Jokić (right) also registered a triple-double in a high-scoring game. (Getty Images: Jayden Mack)

Giddey's stat line came without their two leading scorers, the injured Norman Powell and Caleb Wilson (fractured metacarpal), who are averaging a combined 39.7 points per game this season.

"He played extremely well," Splitter said.

"We've got to give them flowers when they deserve and last game they didn't have it. Tonight they brought it."

Earlier on Sunday (Monday AEDT), Giddey's Boomers teammate Dyson Daniels put the brakes on Detroit star Cade Cunningham to hand Atlanta a fourth-straight win.

Daniels had 14 rebounds to go with eight assists, five steals and five points in his 39 minutes on court in the 107-97 win.

He kept Cunningham (five points) under wraps — the All-Star failed to hit double figures for the first time this season.

The 23-year-old leads the NBA in steals at three per game through 17 matches this season, and also tops the league in deflections and loose balls recovered.

The Hawks are now perched in third place in the Eastern Conference with an 11-6 record.

The Pistons led 85-74 at the start of the fourth quarter before the Hawks took a 92-85 lead with 18 unanswered points. Isiah Joe's three-pointer with 4 minutes and 52 seconds remaining ended Detroit's scoreless streak.

Nickeil Alexander-Walker posted 27 points, while Corey Kispert scored a season-high 18 points and Lu Dort 16 for the Hawks, who were without CJ McCollum (left calf strain) and Australian Jock Landale (right big toe ⁠strain).

AAP

World.title: Australia beats France in Billie Jean King Cup tie
World.content:
Sam Stosur's Australian team will be back for a crack at the Billie Jean King Cup crown next year after "unreal" Maya Joint joined the party with two victories to seal a crushing 4-0 win over France in their play-off tie at Le Portel.

Joint had watched her teammates Storm Hunter and national number one Talia Gibson give the visitors a convincing lead in the French seaside town after the first day on Saturday, but was thrust into the action alongside Hunter to try to seal victory in the key doubles rubber on Sunday, local time.

Even on the Le Chaudron clay court chosen by the hosts, the Aussie duo were in a different league to the home pairing of world number 38 Diane Parry and world No.8 doubles player Kristina Mladenovic, racing to a tie-sealing 6-2 6-4 victory.

Joint, who produced some spectacular tennis in that win, then got in on the singles action, swiftly outplaying Elsa Jacquemot 6-1 6-3 in under an hour. Victory in that "dead" rubber underlined the triumph before organisers scrapped the last scheduled match between Hunter and Clara Burel.

"Maya was unreal today. It was a really tough match against quality opponents," said Hunter, whose own game always seems to go up a notch when she wears the green and gold.

"We're really happy with the result."

Joint, delighted to be returning to her best at the end of a season when her Wimbledon triumph over Serena Williams proved the absolute highlight, added: "The vibes were high all week, we were just really happy and excited to all be here."

The three Australians, between them, had blasted through their four matches without dropping a set, and conceding just 20 games over the whole weekend of one-sided fare.

It was also a moment of revenge for captain Stosur, who played in the 2019 final, which she lost 3-2 on home soil in Perth against a French team that included Mladenovic.

If they had lost the tie, she knew Australia would have been condemned to relegation to its regional group next year, thus ruling it out of a chance to shoot for the 2027 title.

Instead, they will be back in April's qualifiers amid what looks like a renaissance in the Australian women's game, looking to seal a place in the week-long finals in Shenzhen where they could pursue a first title since 1974, when the World Cup of women's tennis was known as the Federation Cup.

"It's a fantastic feeling for us right now; we put in a lot of hard work to try and make this result happen," Stosur said.

"We put on these jackets in the green-and-gold, and it really does bring out the best in a lot of our players. If we can keep building the way we are, for sure we want to try and lift that trophy one day again."

The seven-time champions are looking to bounce back from a disappointing early exit in 2026 when they lost 3-1 in a home qualifier against Great Britain in Melbourne in April.

It's now four years since Australia last reached the final, losing 2-0 to Switzerland in Glasgow.

AAP

World.title: Georgie Prespakis wins AFLW’s top honour as unstoppable Garner breaks All-Australian record
World.content:
SportAFLAFLW Georgie Prespakis wins AFLW’s top honour as unstoppable Garner breaks All-Australian record Hannah Kennelly and Gabriela Sumampow Updated November 23, 2026 — 10:00pm ,first published 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The packed crowd at Melbourne’s Centrepiece held their breath. It was down to the final round of the best and fairest count for the league’s W Awards, and Geelong’s Georgie Prespakis and Charlie Rowbottom were each capable of taking the crown. Geelong’s Georgie Prespakis was crowned AFLW’s best and fairest for 2026. Getty Images It was Prespakis who prevailed, winning the league’s highest accolade with 30 votes, narrowly beating Rowbottom (28 votes) and Garner (24 votes) in a thrilling count on Monday evening. She joins her sister, Essendon’s Maddy Prespakis, as a fellow best and fairest winner. “It’s certainly some good genes, I’ll take those for sure,” Prespakis said.



“I can’t wait to celebrate this moment with my family.” “I feel so privileged to have parents that have always supported me … I’ve always wanted to follow in Maddie’s footsteps, and at times I feel like I’m in her shadows,” she said. “I know she’s looking at me [and being] like ‘shut up’“. Georgie embraces sister Maddy Prespakis after winning the top honour. Getty Images An emotional Prespakis thanked her coach Mick Stinear, Patrick Dangerfield, midfield coach Ryan Pendlebury and her family for guiding her throughout her career. She also gave a heartfelt address to her teammates.



“I want to thank my teammates. I’m not the player that I am without you guys. I feel like you guys understand me so well. You know the overthinker that I am, and you know that I just care so deeply about all you guys, and just want the best for all of us as a team. “You guys challenge me, make me better, not only on the field but off the field. So I’m very appreciative for that, and I love being able to come to work with you guys and see you guys most days of the week. I already miss it.” The Geelong premiership player had a career-best year with an average 30.2 disposals, but her team narrowly fell short in the semi-finals to a rampant Sydney. Prespakis trailed behind fellow favourites Tyla Hanks and Rowbottom until round 7 before polling three votes and skyrocketing up the leaderboard and taking the lead in round eight. Charlie Rowbottom finished second in the count. Getty Images



Once again, Garner missed out on the league’s top gong, despite teammate and last year’s best and fairest winner Ash Riddell singing her praises earlier in the night, saying “Justice for Jam”. The “generational player” – as coach Darren Crocker declared last week – has never received the best and fairest award, but won several other accolades during the night. Unstoppable Garner breaks All-Australian record at AFLW awards North Melbourne great Jasmine Garner has enhanced her reputation as an AFLW generational player, earning the captaincy of the All-Australian team for the third time and a record-breaking ninth selection in the team of the year during the league’s W Awards night on Monday night.



Garner moves clear of teammate Emma Kearney for the most AFLW All-Australian selections, after the pair were previously tied on eight. AFLW captain Jasmine Garner is interviewed by Lauren Wood at the W Awards. Getty Images Carlton’s Harriet Cordner, who was named vice-captain, alongside Sydney Swans livewire Zippy Fish – who stepped up after claiming the league’s Rising Star award last year. The continued impact of Irish players on the game was also recognised, with the Geelong Cats’ Aishling Moloney (County Tipperary) and Hawthorn’s Aine McDonagh (County Galway) awarded their second All-Australian blazers, while Carlton’s Erone Fitzpatrick (County Laois) and North Melbourne’s Erika O’Shea (County Cork) collected their first. Jasmine Garner was a dominant force at Monday’s W Awards. Getty Images



Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive. Following their rise from 13th on the ladder in 2025 to second in 2026, Geelong joined North

Melbourne in leading the team with four selections each, followed by Melbourne with three players. The Cats were among the leading premiership chances leading into the finals, bet they exited season 2026 in straight sets, losing agonisingly to the Demons and Sydney. Friday’s grand final will see Melbourne take on reigning premiers North melbourne in a primetime evening clash at Ikon Park.



In a boost for the Demons ahead of their tough assignment against the Roos, youngster Jordyn Allen was crowned the 2026 Rising Star. Allen, who turned 19 this month, won the award after receiving 37 of a possible 40 votes to finish ahead of Richmond’s Olivia Wolmarans (33 votes) and Collingwood’s Ash Centra (24 votes). She becomes the club’s first player to win the award since Tyla Hanks in 2021 after polling a maximum five votes from most of the eight-member voting panel. Gallery Gallery icon 19 images AFLW Marking the AFLW season at the W Awards The speedy midfielder debuted in round one against Hawthorn and featured in every match for the Demons, averaging nearly 19 possessions.



A beaming Allen said she couldn’t wait for Friday’s grand final and credited teammate Maeve Chaplin for helping her understood “how fun footy could be”. “Thank you to my parents, my family and friends ... the Melbourne footy club, thank you for drafting me. “Let’s get it done on Friday.” Gold Coast’s Dekota Baron pipped Carlton’s Darcy Vescio and Melbourne’s Tayla Harris to claim the Mark of the Year for her high-flying effort in Round 5. Dekota Baron competes for the ball via Getty Images



Goal of the Year went to fellow Gold Coast player Lucy Single with her sensational goal in round eight where she fended off Brisbane Lions’ Sophie Conway before producing an unbelievable finish on the run. The major came during the league’s Q-clash, which the Suns won for the first time. Single edged out Collingwood’s Ruby Schleicher and the Geelong Cats’ Georgie Prespakis to take home the honour at Monday night’s W Awards. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wong to Labor critics: Australians cannot ‘abandon the US’ despite Trump turmoil
World.content:
PoliticsFederalForeign relations Wong to Labor critics: Australians cannot ‘abandon the US’ despite Trump turmoil Matthew Knott November 23, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Foreign Minister Penny Wong will mount a vigorous defence of Australia’s alliance with the United States despite President Donald Trump’s transactional and unpredictable style, rejecting calls from Labor luminaries to scrap the AUKUS pact and distance the country from its closest security partner. Wong will deliver a major foreign policy speech to the Senate on Tuesday as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese prepares to finalise a sweeping new comprehensive treaty with his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale a day later. The treaty is expected to contain significant security clauses that move Solomon Islands closer to Australia in a blow to China’s efforts to expand its influence in the Pacific. Foreign Minister Penny Wong will address parliament on the national security challenges of a new world era. Alex Ellinghausen The treaty will represent a major turnaround from 2022 when then-prime minister Manasseh Sogavare stunned Canberra by signing a secretive security pact and ramping up policing cooperation with Beijing.



But bipartisanship over Pacific policy has broken down over the government’s $500 million Nakamal Treaty with Vanuatu, which was announced in June and blocks China from establishing a military base in the island nation. In dissenting remarks to a parliamentary committee examining the treaty, the Coalition said it opposed the deal because it imposed unacceptable restrictions on future governments’ ability to determine climate and energy policy. Echoing the Coalition’s complaints about the proposed Australia-European Union free trade deal, the Coalition said it opposed ratifying the Vanuatu agreement because its clauses create binding conditions related to achieving renewable energy and climate targets. A government spokesperson accused the Coalition of “putting an ideological opposition to climate change ahead of our national security” and disrespecting the Pacific’s priorities. A leaked message from Australia’s high commissioner in the Solomons, Jeffrey Roach, to Solomon Islands Deputy Prime Minister Francis Sade, released in July, shows that each Solomon Islands constituency would be granted an estimated $1.9 million over three years in funding for community priorities through the treaty.



A further $142 million would be provided over two years to help fund Wale’s free school education policy plus funding for visa improvements and security requests, with Australia providing a total of $980 million in funding by 2028. Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach In her speech to the Senate on Tuesday, Wong will say that the government is “finalising a new comprehensive treaty with Solomon Islands, which will elevate and deepen our partnership”. This follows a new alliance with Fiji inked in July and another with Papua New Guinea last year. “A more fragmented and complex world is emerging, one in which Australia must work to build alignment with partners who share our interests,” Wong will say, according to speech notes.



While acknowledging the Trump administration has said it is no longer interested in “propping up the entire world order”, Wong will argue: “This change in US strategic posture does not alter the formidable fundamentals of American power: a dynamic economy, unmatched global military power, and an indispensable role in maintaining stability in the Indo-Pacific. “As we have seen in recent weeks, the US is a vigorous democracy with the ability to remake and reimagine itself.” Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese are preparing to strike a new comprehensive treaty. Alex Ellinghausen Greens leader David Shoebridge has made curtailing the US alliance a centrepiece of his foreign policy, and a crowdfunded public inquiry led by former Labor minister Peter Garrett called for the government to cancel the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine pact. The report said that AUKUS threatens Australian sovereignty and risks dragging the nation into a war with China, reflecting criticisms of the pact by former Labor foreign ministers Bob Carr and Gareth Evans.



Wong will defend the US alliance in her speech, arguing it “enhances our security, gives us access to advanced technology and intelligence we could not acquire on our own, and bolsters our capacity to deter aggression”, including through AUKUS. Related Article AUKUS Former defence chief urges rethink of Australia’s relationship with China “President Trump has always been clear that he envisages a different role for America in the world, even before he was elected,” Wong will say. “There are those that say uncertainty about American policy means Australia should abandon America. “They ignore the vibrancy of American democracy, the dynamism of its economy and its contribution to the prosperity of our region.”



Wong will argue that critics of America “present a retreat from the alliance as a road to autonomy, ignoring and even undermining Australia’s standing as an already independent, sovereign nation”. “Such a policy would surrender a central source of Australian strategic weight at precisely the moment we need every opportunity for influence available to us,” she will argue. Meanwhile, Wong will say that Australia is pursuing “amplified middle power diplomacy” including deepening ties with Japan, India, the European Union and South-East Asia while stabilising relations with China. “Australia must retain the capacity to make our own choices in a world where others would make them for us,” she will say. “That means working with partners to make domination harder, coercion costlier and cooperation more valuable.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.content:

“It obviously wasn’t only oysters (C8) that the royals didn’t eat,” says Wendy Bull of North Turramurra. “In 1970, when the Queen and Princess Anne visited New Zealand, I attended a function where food was being served. Princess Anne suddenly and very loudly announced to her mother: ‘Not bloody mushrooms again!’ I shall never forget the look of horror on the Queen’s face as she quickly put her fingers up to her lips and said: ‘Anne – ssshhhhh’.”

Sandpapergate (C8) unearths a disclosure from within our own: “It’s now the moment I feel compelled to fess up that my 1970 feat of bowling four hapless tailenders of the Newington 15B XI in consecutive deliveries was ameliorated by a split seam affording me a once-in-a-lifetime spin opportunity,” admits Andrew Cohen of Glebe. “My only consolation assuaging my guilt was that I didn’t tamper with the ball. But, mea culpa, I didn’t ask for it to be replaced, either.”

“My local hardware store has run out of all things abrasive,” notes Jack Dikian of Mosman. “Could it be Cricket Australia has cornered the reverse-swing market?”

In noting recent bylines, Adela Parkes of Boat Harbour reckons “Tom Decent may be the only decent thing in the whole sorry saga”.

“Like Shane Nunan, I suffered under the cane (C8) for misdemeanours long forgotten,” writes Andrew Mowat of Beecroft. “The technique to minimise the pain circa 1961 was to rub your hands in your Brylcreemed hair and bend your fingers down. Things got tough at Brisbane Central School when the headmaster made you choose which cane you wanted from his substantial selection, which went from very thin to about half an inch thick: painful, no matter what you picked. And, interestingly, this was a teacher-training school!”

A 19-year-old has been taken to hospital after he was struck by a pole launched through his car windscreen from another vehicle on Monday afternoon.

The young man was driving a silver Toyota Corolla, travelling south-west along Breakfast Creek Road about 3pm when he stopped in traffic near Skyring Terrace, which allowed another vehicle to overtake his car.

Police said the driver of the second vehicle – a Toyota Hilux – then threw a metal pole at the Corolla, smashing the windscreen.

The pole hit the 19-year-old, who was taken to hospital for treatment.

Officers said urged anyone who might have CCTV or dashcam footage of the assault – or who might have seen it firsthand – to come forward.

World.content:

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week, a data centre race heats up, a key CFMEU inquiry witness takes the reins of a new regulator, and a potential audit of a victim support scheme. While it may not yet have translated into a surge of development activity, it’s clear Crisafulli and Co’s AI data centre push has sparked plenty of high-level action behind closed doors. And not just doors of the state’s ministerial offices. Public disclosures scoured by Circus have identified no less than three firms which have scored face time with key bureaucrats. Troubled Brisbane-based Australian data centre giant NextDC has been finding an audience with Premier David Crisafulli and his top bureaucrat. Peter Rae Since we first brought details about Viridis Green Data Centres’ efforts to spruik itself to the government, lobbyist-registered former conservative premier Rob Borbidge has been busy.



Another three meetings have been held by Borbidge on Viridis’ behalf with figures including state development deputy director-general Shaun Ferris. The most recent of these was a follow-up on October 14 to “discuss progress on regional data centres”, while late August saw a tour of the CSIRO’s Edge Data Centre in Brisbane. “The Edge Data Centre for the CSIRO was built by Viridis and a tour and inspection [was] arranged following earlier meetings and discussions,” the lobbyist register entry read. Meanwhile, proponents of the massive Anthropic-backed Western Downs data centre Zerra DC – via lobbyists GRA Cosway – have met with underlings of co-ordinator general Gerard Coggan.



Lobbying records show GRA Cosway have also nudged Water Minister Ann Leahy’s office trying to set up “meetings and events” following up on an “offer of briefing”. Related Article Public service LNP-sponsor data centre firm taps ex-premier to join major meetings Perhaps most interesting, however, is the trio of meetings landed by the troubled Brisbane-based NextDC – one of the country’s largest data centre operators. Chief executive Craig Scroggie has bagged not one but two meetings with Premier David Crisafulli, his director-general Damien Walker, and their staff, since late August. Both are described only under “portfolio matters”. In mid-September, Crisafulli and Walker then met the firm’s Rockhampton-raised rich-lister founder Bevan Slattery.



What has been discussed among the group is unclear, and neither Crisafulli’s office nor NextDC responded to our questions. Whether the firm’s recent share price dive might have a material impact on the topic is another question – but they could sure use some good news. Could that be a new site, or expansion to its existing modest Queensland locations under the LNP’s much-anticipated “rigorous approvals framework” under development? We’ll have to wait and see. One thing that is clear though, according to a spokesperson for billionaire businessman Clive Palmer, is that his recent rendezvous with Crisafulli has nothing to do with building one of the new coal-power stations the premier has said he’s open to for the electricity needs of such sites. Make of that what you will.



Key CFMEU inquiry witness handed interim reins of new regulator It came as little surprise when Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie told parliament last week that the government would take up recommendations for a new construction code and regulator. Sarina Wise giving evidence at the CFMEU inquiry. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry The code is designed to crack down on union flags and branding on worksites, but it was the second-half of Bleijie’s update which caught our ears. The new authority overseeing compliance with that code has already been set up as an independent body, reporting to David Mackie, who works under Bleijie as director-general (and before that, had him officiate his wedding).



Leading this initial team of six will be an interim general manager, Sarina Wise. Readers may know as the current executive director of compliance and field services within the department’s Office of Industrial relations. Wise has given evidence to the CFMEU inquiry that soon after she came to that role from one at NSW’s workplace safety regulator, it was clear that “there was deep regulatory capture by the CFMEU”. Bleijie told parliament the move was a “scalable response to implement recommendation two which will be monitored as the code takes effect”. Watch this space. Audit office could run ruler over alleged victim support scheme rort





That audit, not scheduled until the 2027-28 financial year, was still yet to be fully scoped, Vagg told the committee. “As we get closer to the time of delivering that performance audit, we’ll assess what has been happening within that department and broader risks associated with that particular delivery element,” she said. “If risks emerge or there’s been significant activities of government, I may adjust the timing, but I’m still working through that.” Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? World.title: Albanese stands by Bowen after failed COP amid global recriminations
World.content:
PoliticsFederalParis Agreement Albanese stands by Bowen after failed COP amid global recriminations Natassia Chrysanthos and Nick O'Malley November 23, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has maintained it was in Australia’s national interest for Energy Minister Chris Bowen to co-host this year’s COP31 in Turkey, despite the summit’s negotiations collapsing without any agreed outcomes. The Coalition hammered Labor over Bowen’s role on Monday as the energy minister travelled home from Antalya, where the climate talks reached a stalemate on Sunday night for only the third time in the conference’s 32-year history. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Getty Images The central sticking point was whether the final document should specify phasing out fossil fuels – oil-producing nations led by Saudi Arabia wanted to scrub those references, while nations seeking more ambitious action, including Europe and the Pacific, said they must be included. The deadlock has cast a shadow over both the future of the UN’s climate summit and the role of Bowen, who campaigned for his role as president of negotiations when Australia lost its bid to host the talks in Adelaide.



The Coalition on Monday called for Bowen to resign, with opposition energy minister Dan Tehan telling question time the minister had wasted “$150 million of our money on his big COP flop, including $30 million on a pre-COP [event in the Pacific that] no-one went to.” Opposition MP Dan Tehan has led the argument against Bowen’s joint COP presidency. Dominic Lorrimer Albanese defended Australia’s involvement, saying climate change was making weather events more extreme while the countries least responsible stood to lose the most, including Pacific neighbours. “The government believes that we have responsibility to this and future generations to act. [Critics argue that] one country acting alone won’t make a difference. We agree with that. We need to bring other nations with us on the journey,” Albanese said, to jeers from opposition MPs who asked how that was going. The prime minister also said there were links between environmental security and national security, referencing the interests of the Pacific. “I don’t think [the prime ministers of Fiji, Tuvalu, Samoa, Tonga and the Solomon Islands] thank the member opposite for the nature of that question, in which he said no-one was there at the pre-COP meeting held in the Pacific,” he said.



Tehan, however, argued Bowen had embarrassed Australia on the world stage. “The [COP] model as it currently stands is completely and utterly broken,” he said. “Chris Bowen should have known that, and then he would have spared Australians the expense of $150 million for an exercise, which became a vanity project for him.” There was jeering in Monday’s question time as Albanese stood by Australia’s investment in this year’s COP. Dominic Lorrimer Consensus approach the ‘root of the problem’: Bowen In the aftermath of the calamitous result, summit delegates are debating whether the joint co-hosting arrangement between Turkey and Australia, proposed by Bowen, backfired by muddying authority and slowing discussion in the conference’s final days.



Some critics questioned Bowen’s strategy of insisting all 198 parties agree to a final cover decision. The cover text, which captures the COP’s headline aims, is negotiated throughout the summit to achieve consensus, and sinks if any country objects. The death knell this year came when Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the European Union, rejected the text on Sunday night because it “does not even mention fossil fuels”. Photo: Matt Golding Bowen said he tried to strike a balance: instead of using explicit language, the draft text referred to previous agreements on fossil fuels. “It was good faith attempt. It wasn’t enough,” he said. The Australian Greens were scathing of Bowen’s approach. “At the end of COP 31, we have the Albanese Labor government choosing to side with Saudi Arabia and Trump, and not mention fossil fuels, rather than back in Europe and our Pacific neighbours,” said leader David Shoebridge.



“This is worse than disappointing.” Others argue that the requirement for consensus is a problem. The United Nations’ climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he was asking for advice on reforming the system on Sunday night. Bowen said the consensus rule was “the fundamental root of the problem”, not the joint presidency. Chris Bowen, president of COP31 negotiations, during the closing session at the climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. AP Photo/Khalil Hamra “When positions are so strong, that’s a very big challenge for any presidency – joint or individuals – to come to the global context,” he said in Turkey after the talks finished.



“Australia left nothing on the field, trying to find solutions to reach what I now see as unbridgeable red lines. The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory. Related Article Updated

Paris Agreement ‘Abject failure’: Coalition demands Bowen’s head as COP31 ends without a deal “Unfortunately, we’re unable to reach agreement on a cover decision, and that’s disappointing ... I take my share of responsibility. Ultimately, you know, people can judge what could have been done or couldn’t have been done. Ultimately, it’s a party-driven process.” Bowen pointed to positive outcomes, such as more than 90 countries signing an electrification pledge. “People of goodwill worked very hard. I haven’t slept in the last three nights. We’ve been negotiating all the way through,” he said. Fiji’s environment minister, Lynda Tabuya, said the failure to agree on a cover text was not Bowen’s. “It is a collective responsibility that rests with all parties. Consensus requires compromise, courage, and political will from all of us,” she said.



Failed COP talks create hope for better forums The stakes were raised at this year’s conference given the United Nations’ environment program had warned just weeks before that the world would overshoot the Paris Agreement of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees. Former president of Ireland, Mary Robinson, said that should have shaken leaders into action, but “instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership from the co-presidencies Turkey and Australia”. Former United States vice-president Al Gore, however, blamed the failure on a “handful of petro-states [who] have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels”. Other climate change advocates praised the EU and its allies for choosing to play hardball, including former UN climate change executive secretary Christiana Figueres, who said COP31 showed progress could be achieved without consensus.



“Let’s be clear about what happened in Antalya: more than 130 countries refused to sign a deal that would have belied the true state of our crisis,” she said. Related Article Analysis

Climate policy There is no getting around the scope of this failure – both for Chris Bowen and the world Matthew McDonald, a professor of international relations at the University of Queensland, said the longer-term legacy of this year’s talks could be a “recognition of the limits of this consensus-driven approach to climate negotiations, and the development of alternative sites for climate action.” Tuvalu’s climate change minister, Maina Talia, said the island nation would next year co-host with Ireland the second conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, alongside “a growing coalition of doers”. “Tuvalu cannot accept this as the final scenario. So we are putting our resolve where we can make an impact,” he said. “It is moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation.”

World.title: Melbourne’s ‘unacceptable’ $5.5m loss after payouts, collapse of major sponsor deal
World.content:
Updated SportAFLMelbourne Demons Melbourne’s ‘unacceptable’ $5.5m loss after payouts, collapse of major sponsor deal Michael Gleeson and Danny Russell Updated November 23, 2026 — 7:37pm ,first published November 22, 2026 — 7:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Melbourne posted an “unacceptable” $5.5 million loss after big payouts to staff and the collapse of their major sponsor deal, but president Steven Smith said he was confident the club had recovered to financial stability after what is now an $11.5 million loss over three years. “Today the club announced an operating loss of $2.9 million and statutory loss of $5.49 million following a challenging 2026 financial year,” Smith said in a letter to members. “Results like this are clearly not acceptable and the board and management are committed to returning the club to sustainable financial performances moving forward. We have already made significant changes to drive revenue growth and profitability. Our 2027-2031 Strategic Plan has been set with a clear path to financial stability and will be presented to members at the upcoming AGM on 16 December.” Melbourne Football Club president Steven Smith speaks to the media in 2026. Joe Armao While the Demons have turned things around on the field, the club has continued to be hit with big payouts to a range of staff and players, as well as unexpected financial losses.



The club’s major sponsor DriversDepot defaulted on their deal, leaving the club to tear up the sponsorship worth $1.5m a year for three years. The club also paid out six months on the $757,000 annual salary of former CEO Paul Guerra when they sacked him after seven months in the job. Guerra is still pursuing $1m in compensation through the court, which means, after other legal action against the club by former president Glenn Bartlett, the club continues to spend heavily on legal fees. Former Melbourne CEO Paul Guerra has landed a new job. Joe Armao The club made a payout to former player Steven May and his wife after personal information was revealed in an online meeting of players’ wives and families. The club also had to absorb most of the salary for Clayton Oliver leaving the club and instead playing for GWS. The club also did not have home games on King’s Birthday or Anzac Day eve this season, which hurt them in gate receipts.



Previously, the club paid premiership coach Simon Goodwin $1.3m after terminating his contract. The Demons have been resurgent under Steven King. AFL Photos The Demons made a $1.6m statutory loss in 2024 but declared a $1.6m operating profit, posted a $4.45m statutory loss in 2025 but an operating loss of $200,000, and two sources with knowledge of this year’s financials – speaking on condition of anonymity – said the Demons are poised to announce the $5m statutory loss for this year at a time when they are rallying funds for a new home base at Caulfield or elsewhere. Despite this, the club is confident of returning to the black next year, with the expectation of signing a new major sponsor and home games next season for blockbuster games. The revolving door of senior leaders is expected to stop, with respected new CEO Dan Taylor stepping off the board and away from his job as head of Stan (owned by Nine, the owner of this masthead) to take over the club after Guerra’s departure. Regardless, the financial performance will be a critical issue shaping the board election at the end of this month with one of the two club vice presidents, Geoff Porz, deciding he will not seek re-election, meaning there will be at least one vacancy to fill. Fellow vice president, former president and club captain, Brad Green, and sitting director Sarah Robinson, are seeking re-election ahead of the December 16 annual general meeting.



Smith said the club had endorsed Simon Harle, a founding partner of BGH Capital private equity firm, to replace Porz. At least two other candidates have announced they will contest the coming elections but not as a combined ticket. Finance expert Peter Lawrence, a chartered accountant who is standing for a fifth time, has been a strong advocate of governance change at Melbourne. Safety consultant Ted Dohrmann has also announced he will stand. The timing of Porz’s decision not to seek re-election was interesting as he had been the driving force behind the Demons’ proposed $100 million move to Caulfield, engaging FMRS Advisory in a bid to win state government support. Related Article AFL 2026 The final hurdle that forced the Demons to hit pause on long-awaited home The Age reported exclusively in September the project was on life support, while club president Steven Smith conceded last month the club was considering alternative options. Replacing Richmond, who have relocated to the former Hawthorn base at Waverley Park while they undertake the rebuild of Punt Road Oval, remains one option, but it is not considered a long-term solution by the club as it only has one oval and no capacity to grow the footprint.



Porz was contacted for comment. Lawrence called for the Demons to resolve their home-base future in a candidate statement posted on LinkedIn. “Members deserve clarity and progress,” he wrote. “This issue has dragged on for years, and we risk losing players if it isn’t addressed.” Simon Goodwin coached the Demons to the 2021 premiership. Getty Images



Dohrmann, who has run his own safety and ergonomics consultancy business since 2014, also posted a candidate statement on LinkedIn, saying he had engineering, major-project and risk management experience. “I understand that the board’s role is to govern the club, not to tell football professionals how to do their jobs,” he wrote. Green, 45, played the last of his 254 games in the red and the blue in 2012 before joining the board in November 2020 and filling the president’s role between Roffey’s 2024 departure and the arrival of Smith at the end of last year. Away from the club, he is the managing director of fire protection and safety company GMH Fire & Safety Australia. Robinson is a private banker with the Macquarie Group specialising in retirement planning, superannuation and investment advice.



She first joined the Demons board in 2023, and is a member of the club’s investment subcommittee. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.content:
WorldEuropeLive music Thousands evacuated after suspected tear gas let off at Manchester concert Kelly-Anne Taylor November 23, 2026 — 7:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: More than 50 people were seen by medics after suspected tear gas was released into the crowd at a concert in Manchester on Sunday night (London time). Police declared a “major incident” as thousands of concertgoers were evacuated from Co-op Live, an indoor arena, about 10pm during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver. Pictures circulating on social media show police cars circling the venue and emergency vehicles swarming the area. Armed police were also seen outside the arena. Concert-goers wrapped in emergency blankets walk outside Co-op Live as authorities respond to the incident. Getty Images The North West Ambulance Service said one person was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary and more than 50 people had been assessed by medics, with some reporting “eye and respiratory symptoms”.



Greater Manchester Police confirmed officers attended a “major incident” on Sunday night, explaining “a substance believed to be tear gas was let off in the crowd towards the end of a concert”. Police said in a subsequent statement that investigators were still working to identify the substance and the cause. View post on X Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker confirmed more than 12,000 people had been “safely evacuated”. “Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital,” she said.



“We understand the concern that this incident will have raised – particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night – and we’d like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it.” Earlier, the force said: “All attendees are currently being safely evacuated as a precaution. Those showing signs of being impacted are being supported by emergency services, with thankfully no serious injuries reported. View post on X “Please stay away from the arena whilst emergency services help those that have been at the concert safely make their way to their transport home. “A major incident has been declared to ensure emergency services and partner agencies can work together quickly and effectively to co-ordinate a safe response.”



Video from the concert showed the audience booing as a venue official announced that the event was ending early. Related Article 'I woke up shaking' - Manchester concertgoer recalls night of terror “Due to unforeseen circumstances, the show is now finished,” the official said. “In your own time, please make your way to the nearest exit. “If you require medical assistance, please speak to a member of staff or visit the level zero concourse.” Toliver is one of the world’s biggest rappers with over 45 million listeners a month, according to Spotify. He is set to continue his world tour, NITROUS, with performances at the O2 Arena and OVO Arena Wembley on Monday and Tuesday (London time).



In May 2017, 22 people were killed in a terror attack at the Manchester Arena, including an eight-year-old girl and an off-duty female police officer, moments after US singer Ariana Grande finished performing. Following the attack, emergency services were criticised for their response. A public inquiry concluded there were “very significant” failings by the police, “very substantial problems” with the ambulance service response and a “risk-averse” approach from the fire service. Armed police were also seen outside the arena. Getty Images The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Georgie Prespakis wins AFLW’s top honour as unstoppable Garner breaks All-Australian record
World.content:
SportAFLAFLW Georgie Prespakis wins AFLW’s top honour as unstoppable Garner breaks All-Australian record Hannah Kennelly and Gabriela Sumampow Updated November 23, 2026 — 10:00pm ,first published 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
