The packed crowd at Melbourne’s Centrepiece held their breath. It was down to the final round of the best and fairest count for the league’s W Awards, and Geelong’s Georgie Prespakis and Charlie Rowbottom were each capable of taking the crown. Geelong’s Georgie Prespakis was crowned AFLW’s best and fairest for 2026. Getty Images It was Prespakis who prevailed, winning the league’s highest accolade with 30 votes, narrowly beating Rowbottom (28 votes) and Garner (24 votes) in a thrilling count on Monday evening. She joins her sister, Essendon’s Maddy Prespakis, as a fellow best and fairest winner. “It’s certainly some good genes, I’ll take those for sure,” Prespakis said.



“I can’t wait to celebrate this moment with my family.” “I feel so privileged to have parents that have always supported me … I’ve always wanted to follow in Maddie’s footsteps, and at times I feel like I’m in her shadows,” she said. “I know she’s looking at me [and being] like ‘shut up’“. Georgie embraces sister Maddy Prespakis after winning the top honour. Getty Images An emotional Prespakis thanked her coach Mick Stinear, Patrick Dangerfield, midfield coach Ryan Pendlebury and her family for guiding her throughout her career. She also gave a heartfelt address to her teammates.



“I want to thank my teammates. I’m not the player that I am without you guys. I feel like you guys understand me so well. You know the overthinker that I am, and you know that I just care so deeply about all you guys, and just want the best for all of us as a team. “You guys challenge me, make me better, not only on the field but off the field. So I’m very appreciative for that, and I love being able to come to work with you guys and see you guys most days of the week. I already miss it.” The Geelong premiership player had a career-best year with an average 30.2 disposals, but her team narrowly fell short in the semi-finals to a rampant Sydney. Prespakis trailed behind fellow favourites Tyla Hanks and Rowbottom until round 7 before polling three votes and skyrocketing up the leaderboard and taking the lead in round eight. Charlie Rowbottom finished second in the count. Getty Images



Once again, Garner missed out on the league’s top gong, despite teammate and last year’s best and fairest winner Ash Riddell singing her praises earlier in the night, saying “Justice for Jam”. The “generational player” – as coach Darren Crocker declared last week – has never received the best and fairest award, but won several other accolades during the night. Unstoppable Garner breaks All-Australian record at AFLW awards North Melbourne great Jasmine Garner has enhanced her reputation as an AFLW generational player, earning the captaincy of the All-Australian team for the third time and a record-breaking ninth selection in the team of the year during the league’s W Awards night on Monday night.



Garner moves clear of teammate Emma Kearney for the most AFLW All-Australian selections, after the pair were previously tied on eight. AFLW captain Jasmine Garner is interviewed by Lauren Wood at the W Awards. Getty Images Carlton’s Harriet Cordner, who was named vice-captain, alongside Sydney Swans livewire Zippy Fish – who stepped up after claiming the league’s Rising Star award last year. The continued impact of Irish players on the game was also recognised, with the Geelong Cats’ Aishling Moloney (County Tipperary) and Hawthorn’s Aine McDonagh (County Galway) awarded their second All-Australian blazers, while Carlton’s Erone Fitzpatrick (County Laois) and North Melbourne’s Erika O’Shea (County Cork) collected their first. Jasmine Garner was a dominant force at Monday’s W Awards. Getty Images



Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive. Following their rise from 13th on the ladder in 2025 to second in 2026, Geelong joined North

Melbourne in leading the team with four selections each, followed by Melbourne with three players. The Cats were among the leading premiership chances leading into the finals, bet they exited season 2026 in straight sets, losing agonisingly to the Demons and Sydney. Friday’s grand final will see Melbourne take on reigning premiers North melbourne in a primetime evening clash at Ikon Park.



In a boost for the Demons ahead of their tough assignment against the Roos, youngster Jordyn Allen was crowned the 2026 Rising Star. Allen, who turned 19 this month, won the award after receiving 37 of a possible 40 votes to finish ahead of Richmond’s Olivia Wolmarans (33 votes) and Collingwood’s Ash Centra (24 votes). She becomes the club’s first player to win the award since Tyla Hanks in 2021 after polling a maximum five votes from most of the eight-member voting panel. Gallery Gallery icon 19 images AFLW Marking the AFLW season at the W Awards The speedy midfielder debuted in round one against Hawthorn and featured in every match for the Demons, averaging nearly 19 possessions.



A beaming Allen said she couldn’t wait for Friday’s grand final and credited teammate Maeve Chaplin for helping her understood “how fun footy could be”. “Thank you to my parents, my family and friends ... the Melbourne footy club, thank you for drafting me. “Let’s get it done on Friday.” Gold Coast’s Dekota Baron pipped Carlton’s Darcy Vescio and Melbourne’s Tayla Harris to claim the Mark of the Year for her high-flying effort in Round 5. Dekota Baron competes for the ball via Getty Images



Goal of the Year went to fellow Gold Coast player Lucy Single with her sensational goal in round eight where she fended off Brisbane Lions’ Sophie Conway before producing an unbelievable finish on the run. The major came during the league’s Q-clash, which the Suns won for the first time. Single edged out Collingwood’s Ruby Schleicher and the Geelong Cats’ Georgie Prespakis to take home the honour at Monday night’s W Awards. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wong to Labor critics: Australians cannot ‘abandon the US’ despite Trump turmoil
World.content:
PoliticsFederalForeign relations Wong to Labor critics: Australians cannot ‘abandon the US’ despite Trump turmoil Matthew Knott November 23, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Foreign Minister Penny Wong will mount a vigorous defence of Australia’s alliance with the United States despite President Donald Trump’s transactional and unpredictable style, rejecting calls from Labor luminaries to scrap the AUKUS pact and distance the country from its closest security partner. Wong will deliver a major foreign policy speech to the Senate on Tuesday as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese prepares to finalise a sweeping new comprehensive treaty with his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale a day later. The treaty is expected to contain significant security clauses that move Solomon Islands closer to Australia in a blow to China’s efforts to expand its influence in the Pacific. Foreign Minister Penny Wong will address parliament on the national security challenges of a new world era. Alex Ellinghausen The treaty will represent a major turnaround from 2022 when then-prime minister Manasseh Sogavare stunned Canberra by signing a secretive security pact and ramping up policing cooperation with Beijing.



But bipartisanship over Pacific policy has broken down over the government’s $500 million Nakamal Treaty with Vanuatu, which was announced in June and blocks China from establishing a military base in the island nation. In dissenting remarks to a parliamentary committee examining the treaty, the Coalition said it opposed the deal because it imposed unacceptable restrictions on future governments’ ability to determine climate and energy policy. Echoing the Coalition’s complaints about the proposed Australia-European Union free trade deal, the Coalition said it opposed ratifying the Vanuatu agreement because its clauses create binding conditions related to achieving renewable energy and climate targets. A government spokesperson accused the Coalition of “putting an ideological opposition to climate change ahead of our national security” and disrespecting the Pacific’s priorities. A leaked message from Australia’s high commissioner in the Solomons, Jeffrey Roach, to Solomon Islands Deputy Prime Minister Francis Sade, released in July, shows that each Solomon Islands constituency would be granted an estimated $1.9 million over three years in funding for community priorities through the treaty.



A further $142 million would be provided over two years to help fund Wale’s free school education policy plus funding for visa improvements and security requests, with Australia providing a total of $980 million in funding by 2028. Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach In her speech to the Senate on Tuesday, Wong will say that the government is “finalising a new comprehensive treaty with Solomon Islands, which will elevate and deepen our partnership”. This follows a new alliance with Fiji inked in July and another with Papua New Guinea last year. “A more fragmented and complex world is emerging, one in which Australia must work to build alignment with partners who share our interests,” Wong will say, according to speech notes.



While acknowledging the Trump administration has said it is no longer interested in “propping up the entire world order”, Wong will argue: “This change in US strategic posture does not alter the formidable fundamentals of American power: a dynamic economy, unmatched global military power, and an indispensable role in maintaining stability in the Indo-Pacific. “As we have seen in recent weeks, the US is a vigorous democracy with the ability to remake and reimagine itself.” Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese are preparing to strike a new comprehensive treaty. Alex Ellinghausen Greens leader David Shoebridge has made curtailing the US alliance a centrepiece of his foreign policy, and a crowdfunded public inquiry led by former Labor minister Peter Garrett called for the government to cancel the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine pact. The report said that AUKUS threatens Australian sovereignty and risks dragging the nation into a war with China, reflecting criticisms of the pact by former Labor foreign ministers Bob Carr and Gareth Evans.



Wong will defend the US alliance in her speech, arguing it “enhances our security, gives us access to advanced technology and intelligence we could not acquire on our own, and bolsters our capacity to deter aggression”, including through AUKUS. Related Article AUKUS Former defence chief urges rethink of Australia’s relationship with China “President Trump has always been clear that he envisages a different role for America in the world, even before he was elected,” Wong will say. “There are those that say uncertainty about American policy means Australia should abandon America. “They ignore the vibrancy of American democracy, the dynamism of its economy and its contribution to the prosperity of our region.”



Wong will argue that critics of America “present a retreat from the alliance as a road to autonomy, ignoring and even undermining Australia’s standing as an already independent, sovereign nation”. “Such a policy would surrender a central source of Australian strategic weight at precisely the moment we need every opportunity for influence available to us,” she will argue. Meanwhile, Wong will say that Australia is pursuing “amplified middle power diplomacy” including deepening ties with Japan, India, the European Union and South-East Asia while stabilising relations with China. “Australia must retain the capacity to make our own choices in a world where others would make them for us,” she will say. “That means working with partners to make domination harder, coercion costlier and cooperation more valuable.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. “It obviously wasn’t only oysters (C8) that the royals didn’t eat,” says Wendy Bull of North Turramurra. “In 1970, when the Queen and Princess Anne visited New Zealand, I attended a function where food was being served. Princess Anne suddenly and very loudly announced to her mother: ‘Not bloody mushrooms again!’ I shall never forget the look of horror on the Queen’s face as she quickly put her fingers up to her lips and said: ‘Anne – ssshhhhh’.”

Sandpapergate (C8) unearths a disclosure from within our own: “It’s now the moment I feel compelled to fess up that my 1970 feat of bowling four hapless tailenders of the Newington 15B XI in consecutive deliveries was ameliorated by a split seam affording me a once-in-a-lifetime spin opportunity,” admits Andrew Cohen of Glebe. “My only consolation assuaging my guilt was that I didn’t tamper with the ball. But, mea culpa, I didn’t ask for it to be replaced, either.”

“My local hardware store has run out of all things abrasive,” notes Jack Dikian of Mosman. “Could it be Cricket Australia has cornered the reverse-swing market?”

In noting recent bylines, Adela Parkes of Boat Harbour reckons “Tom Decent may be the only decent thing in the whole sorry saga”.

“Like Shane Nunan, I suffered under the cane (C8) for misdemeanours long forgotten,” writes Andrew Mowat of Beecroft. “The technique to minimise the pain circa 1961 was to rub your hands in your Brylcreemed hair and bend your fingers down. Things got tough at Brisbane Central School when the headmaster made you choose which cane you wanted from his substantial selection, which went from very thin to about half an inch thick: painful, no matter what you picked. And, interestingly, this was a teacher-training school!”

A 19-year-old has been taken to hospital after he was struck by a pole launched through his car windscreen from another vehicle on Monday afternoon.

The young man was driving a silver Toyota Corolla, travelling south-west along Breakfast Creek Road about 3pm when he stopped in traffic near Skyring Terrace, which allowed another vehicle to overtake his car.

Police said the driver of the second vehicle – a Toyota Hilux – then threw a metal pole at the Corolla, smashing the windscreen.

World.title: Whatever happened to the Fair Go?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Whatever happened to the Fair Go? November 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. TRUST Sean Kelly’s latest considered analysis, (“Preaching certainty is full of risk”, 23/11), draws an analogy between the culture in the Australian cricket team a decade ago and that in national politics.

Both involved cheating (sandpaper, Robodebt and policies permitting corruption and favouring inequality). Both cricket fans and voters feel betrayed, but voters are particularly angry.

We can only hope that anger will not blind voters to constructive choices in expressing it at the ballot box, as your correspondent implies (Letters: “Crime and Education” 23/11), drawing attention to major parties’ “tough on crime” simplistic faux-solution proposals while ignoring complex contributory causes including poverty, family disadvantage and poor education outcomes.

Kelly nails the issue with these words: “This is exactly what has happened in national politics as growing numbers of people come to understand the country no longer works in the way we were led to believe. You cannot work hard and expect to buy a house.

“The rich are not playing the same game as the rest of us. Meanwhile, those in charge continued to assure us things are working exactly as they are supposed to.“

No, it is certainly not cricket.

Joe Di Stefano, Geelong Labor Party’s shame

It’s such a shame the Labor Party under Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan let alleged corruption occur. I’m no fan of the Liberal Party, and even less of the Greens and One Nation.

However, the Andrews and Allan governments have left me with no choice but to kick their party out, so the party can take a hard look at itself after, I believe, the majority of Victorians will vote the Liberal Party in.

Margaret Summers, Carnegie



An era of bitter disappointment in leaders

We are almost at the end of this lacklustre election campaign and many commentators believe the result a foregone conclusion.

But does anyone seriously believe that their lives will be changed as a result of this election or that the many promises made during the course of the campaign will be kept?

It has been an era when we all are bitterly disappointed by political leaders who have failed in their responsibilities to provide many services to the cities and regions that taxpayers are entitled to, but have not received. A shameful loss of trust.

Bruce MacKenzie, South Kingsville My crystal ball tells me ...

Whoever wins the election, the number of billionaires will continue to increase as will the number of poor.

Richard Crago, Burwood East Welcome to the ‘me first and only’ mentality

The Age makes for depressing reading at times (“Dave Hughes lets F-bombs fly as war on tax changes lands in Melbourne,” 23/11), telling of Get Ahead’s war on tax.

Its main thrust is to reverse the federal government’s capital gains tax and negative gearing tax changes, to the benefit of wealthier people and leaving less tax revenue for essential services for those in need.

Other reports tell of a government service having to close, so another essential service can be housed, and the cutting of essential funding for family court victims. Taxes are the price to be paid for living in a civilised society, where those who are fortunate enough to have plenty help those who are need.

It is distressing because it seems we live in an Australia where the notion of “good for society as a whole” is being replaced by a “me first and only” mentality.

Those attending the Get Ahead event appear to have significant wealth – surely they can spare a little for a single mother being terrorised by her ex?

Louise Kloot, Doncaster THE FORUM The sorry state

The most glaring aspect of the sorry state of Victoria’s finances is that it was so unnecessary (“State must swing the axe: experts”, 23/11).

We would not be in what one leading economist calls an “appalling mess”, if the Labor government had not undertaken the so-called Big Build. As well as the maladministration of specific infrastructure projects, the reasons behind the entire concept should be investigated.

That might show the Big Build was really about providing a never-ending supply of work for the building industry, rather than a well planned and coordinated project based on demonstrated social and economic benefits.

The next government must stop, or at least limit as many Big Build projects as possible. Debt reduction must now take priority over an addiction to providing jobs.

Ironically, the one project Victorians were calling for long before anyone suggested tunnels from Cheltenham to Box Hill or Watsonia to Bulleen remains incomplete: a fast, efficient rail link to Melbourne Airport.

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills



Tough on crime costs

A productivity commission report shows that nationally we spend an average of $3600 per child on youth detention. In Victoria, this jumps to more than $7100 per day per child.

While all parties are in full ″⁣tough on crime″⁣ election mode they should ask themselves why they are prepared to spend more on locking up children than keeping them out of jail in the first place.

It seems every time budgets need cutting, it impacts social services and, paradoxically, politicians seem more than willing to spend more on incarceration than prevention.

The headline of Shane Wright’s article “Cut and cut now, economists urge next government to swing the axe” (23/11) does not bode well in this regard as we anticipate a Liberal Party win and the threat of Victoria being ″⁣Jeffed″⁣ once more.

Stephen Farrelly, Donvale Andrews’ achievements

Whatever the election outcome on Saturday, we should not lose sight of the magnificent achievements over the past 12 years of Victorian Labor government. Gaining government after four years of Liberal inaction and infighting, Daniel Andrews and his team set about revitalising the state.

I am so proud of our Treaty with First Nations people, an Australian first. All around my local area, I see the results of the Big Build with multiple level crossings removed.

New trams and trains and the Metro rail project among other transport works. Free TAFE, free nursing degrees, new hospitals and schools. The list is enormous.

My children and grandchildren will be benefiting from all of this for many years to come.

Steve Griffin, West Coburg Who keeps nodding?

On Saturday, Victorians may have a new government. We know who the leader might be, but very little about the new ministers or their capabilities. Over the past few years almost all political issues are handled publicly by the premiers and prime minister and leaders of the opposition, regardless of the nature of the issue. In the background on the news, the responsible minister or shadow minister nods in agreement .

The voting public need to know the leaders and the government ″⁣team″⁣ that make future policy decisions. Many of us barely know current ministers, let alone the shadow ministers

Rod Mackenzie, Marshall ALP’s strong record

I am finding it very depressing how little Victorians know about what has been achieved in this state.

Many people are unaware of how many new schools have been built. Nineteen new schools have been opened in 2026, and 121 schools in the past 10 years, which is more than half the new schools built in the whole of Australia.

Likewise, the ignorance about new hospitals, even if someone lives only three kilometres away. Have we seen any stories of how life has changed significantly, for the better, by users of the Metro rail system?

Victorians have been fed a barrage of negative and critical journalism, so are ignorant of the significant improvements that have been achieved.

Sadly, it seems we are facing a future of not just inaction, but of disastrous reactionary policies that will take our society backwards, especially in relation to renewable energy.

Margery Renwick, Brighton Female councillor threats

I welcome the release of the Fit to Lead Study (″⁣MPs reveal toll on mental health″⁣ (23/11). Its findings are shocking, but will not come as a surprise for many of us. As a councillor in local government (Yarra), I have faced calls for a journalist to do a ″⁣hit job″⁣ on me because I dared to discharge my duties diligently and voted against a particular proposal.

My own experience confirms that there are no effective mechanisms to challenge unacceptable conduct; councillors are expected to tolerate abuse. The worst is directed at women, mostly by men.

The data doesn’t lie and it seems that the underlying intent is to drive women from public life and positions of leadership. There is a heavy toll for those who do step up to represent the community.

This begs the question: Why would anyone want to step up and lead, when elected representatives and their families are seen as fair game?

Sharon Harrison, Richmond



Zero tolerance sometimes

The ramification of social media is listed as a cause in the ″⁣Fit to Lead″⁣ study by the international Better Politics Foundation. Perhaps it could extend the survey to local government councillors (of which I am one, at the City of Stonnington) who have less support than state, territory and federal government MPs.

While the foundation report calls for “greater accountability for social media companies”, it seemingly ignores the perpetrators’ who deliver a slew of insults at (mainly female) councillors without regard for the impact on their mental health or their families’ wellbeing.

Are they the same people who have initiated the ubiquitous ″⁣zero tolerance″⁣ signs in shops, cafes, businesses – even hospitals?

I often wonder.

Sally Davis, Malvern East Cop 31 result is good

Under the circumstances, failure to produce a “consensus” agreement at COP31 is the best possible outcome. (“‘Abject failure’: Coalition demands Bowen’s head as COP31 ends without a deal″⁣, 23/11).

With Saudi Arabia, Russia and a handful of nations refusing to endorse a deal that mentioned fossil fuels (and the Saudis also spruiking expensive and unproven carbon capture and storage), the worst possible result would have been the majority of countries being bullied into accepting a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel. The division is stark and had to be declared.

And what would the LNP do? Having already ditched their own commitment to net zero emissions, deputy opposition leader Jane Hume immediately rushes onto News24 calling for Minister Bowen to resign.

As the world faces an increasingly dangerous climate, the LNP rushes further into irrelevance. It seems they just don’t get it.

Rob Firth, Red Hill, ACT Turn up the volume

The death of Molly Meldrum marks the end of an era. For those of us who grew up with Countdown, Sunday nights were never complete until Molly appeared in his cowboy hat, enthusiastically telling us what records to buy.

He wasn’t always articulate, occasionally got his words hopelessly tangled and conducted interviews that could leave both the interviewer and interviewee wondering what had just happened.

But what Molly lacked in polish, he more than made up for in passion. He championed Australian music, helped launch careers and introduced us to music that might have passed us by. Today, the music industry has algorithms, streaming services and carefully packaged presenters. We had Molly.

So, Molly, wherever you are, do yourself a favour. Put on a record, turn up the volume and enjoy the applause.

Darren Grindrod, Glenroy All good in Dingley

There are good young people in the world; and certainly in Dingley Village.

I am 83 years and quite fit. I was walking with my husband around the local streets last week when I tripped and skidded on my nose and top lip, and landed on my hand and knee. There seemed to be a lot of blood. A car driving towards us stopped and a young man leapt out, grabbed his first aid kit from the boot and rushed to assist. He was not a medic, just a very thoughtful person. My heartfelt thanks to him and to all those who rush to assist when help is needed.

Lynette Ellis, Dingley Village Henry Higgins update

I went to see My Fair Lady at the newly refurbished State Theatre. It was a beautiful, sumptuous show and the performers didn’t put a foot wrong ... as far as I could tell. But maybe it is time the ending was ″⁣updated″⁣ to suit modern times and notions of gender relationships.

Perhaps the ending could be changed to how it was portrayed in the play Pygmalion, on which it was based. When George Bernard Shaw wrote it, Professor Higgins received his comeuppance as an overbearing bully by being dumped in favour of the doting Freddy.

During one of the songs denigrating women, there was an audible gasp from the audience. I’d hate to see this musical disappear; perhaps it’s time for Professor Higgins to be dragged into the 21st century with a feminist makeover.

Cheryl Day, Beaumaris



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Molly Meldrum

So sad to hear of Molly. I grew up watching Countdown and even attended several times, which made me feel like the luckiest person in the world. So many classic moments with Iggy, Prince Charles, JPY and more. Molly told us to do ourselves a favour, and we all did. You were a one-off, and will always be remembered.

Samantha Keir, East Brighton Farewell, Molly, and well done. The man who put the ″⁣um″⁣ in Meldrum.

Donald Hirst, Armadale Furthermore

Having lived through the Kennett blitz of social cohesion, savage cutting of the public service and rapid sell-off of resources, I have genuine fear of the next year in Victoria. Gen X and younger generations are in for a shock.

Jenni King, Camberwell



Your correspondent (Letters, ″⁣Matthew Flinders Day″⁣, 23/11) can’t have his cake and eat it too. Without Invasion Day, there cannot be a Matthew Flinders Day.

Tom Stafford, Wheelers Hill Reading the opinion piece by Michelle Goldberg on what drives Elon Musk (23/11), the old saying about money being the root of all evil comes to mind, but with Musk it’s the other way round.

Henry Herzog, East St Kilda As the tide turns on Donald Trump, history may see him as more King Canute then Henry VIII.

Peter Thomas, Pascoe Vale At last an article highlighting the damage war inflicts on habitat and wildlife (“Endurance swimmer tackles Strait of Hormuz”, 23/11). All hail the intrepid Lewis Pugh. Meanwhile, back home the Liberals and One Nation have vowed to bring back logging of native forests.

Michael Read, Carnegie With the dismal failure of the COP, all I can do now is continue to recycle diligently, charge my EV with my solar panels and then sip margaritas in the sunshine, pretending that all is fine.

Sue Peterken, Berwick



And to those who commute by e-bikes, a big thank you. Role modelling of this healthy and clean way of transport is important too.

Ruth Davis, Carrum The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Mad about Harry: Superstar Harry Styles shops up a storm in Brighton
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Mad about Harry: Superstar Harry Styles shops up a storm in Brighton Fiona Byrne November 23, 2026 — 7:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. What is it with visiting music superstars and supermarkets in Melbourne’s bayside suburbs? First, Liam Gallagher of iconic band Oasis was spotted late last year buying ice-cream at the Mount Martha IGA during the Melbourne leg of the group’s world tour. Now, British star Harry Styles, one of the biggest touring acts in the world, has been sighted picking up a few groceries at the Mint supermarket in leafy Brighton. Harry Styles is in town for a string of sold-out Aussie shows. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images The means streets of Brighton, particularly the shopping strips of Bay and Church streets, were buzzing on Monday after word spread that Styles had popped into Mint to pick up some pantry essentials that morning.



We put in a call and a Mint employee, who claimed to have served Styles, told us that yes, he had done a quick shop, spending about 15 minutes in the store, “first thing in the morning”. “He looked like he had been for a run; he was wearing shorts. He kept to himself but was lovely. It was a lovely start to the week,” we were told. Apparently, no watermelon made it into his grocery basket. A screen grab reportedly of Harry Styles in Melbourne. TikTok That supermarket sighting came after it emerged the singer, who performs the first of his four shows at Marvel Stadium on Friday as part of his Together Together tour, had caught a film, by himself, no less, at the Elsternwick Cinema on Sunday afternoon – the 3.50pm screening of Wild Horse Nine, to be exact.



Brighton and Elsternwick … bayside has definitely called Styles. Editor's pick CBD Harry Styles concert creates havoc for AFLW stars vying for grand final berth Social media claims by breathless “Harries”, the name given to Styles’ fans, also put him at the Prahran Market and Albert Park Lake over the weekend, as well as Chapel Street and the CBD on Monday. We can’t say if these “sightings” are correct but there’ll certainly be more. On his most recent tour in early 2023, Styles was photographed grabbing a bite to eat at Cibi, a Japanese cafe and design store in Collingwood. The cafe was subsequently inundated by influencers wanting to snap themselves at Style’s snack spot, prompting the venue to place a ban on customers taking photos and videos. Harry Styles has been spotted in Brighton and Elsternwick in Melbourne. Getty Images



Looping back to Oasis, the reason Liam Gallagher made his way down to the local supermarket in the Mount Martha village was that he was staying in a private home rather than a hotel while in Melbourne. The property he bunked down in was – and still is – owned by embattled reality-TV star turned fitness entrepreneur Sam Wood, who had rented it out to the Oasis star. Meanwhile, Wood’s other bayside home in Hanby Street, Brighton, is on the market and under offer as Wood cools his heels in custody in Queensland over two domestic violence-related charges. Oh, blue hue: Dumped Liberal Lindemann recycles polling booth fashion Former Liberal now independent candidate for Williamstown Paul Lindemann may have been disendorsed by the party, but you could be forgiven for thinking he is still flying the Liberal flag.



Decked out in what looks like Liberal blue and seen last week holding a Liberal-branded umbrella, Lindemann has been working the early voting booths in his electorate under his new Team Paul guise, a shift that was necessitated after he was dumped earlier this month by Jess Wilson’s party when posts containing offensive racist tropes were discovered on his private Facebook page. Independent candidate for Williamstown Paul Lindemann and supporters wear Team Paul shirts with the Liberal logo taped over. He apologised via social media to his supporters for his “inappropriate” language and continued on with his campaign to snare the inner-west seat, even wearing the shirts that were printed when he was standing for the Liberals, just with black tape over the party’s logo. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Liberals dump candidate over Indigenous slurs on secret Facebook account Put it down to a case of waste not, want not, or perhaps recycle and reuse, but Lindemann told us he had 170 of the tops printed and wanted to get some use out of them, rather than chucking them out, after he was dumped by the party.



It seems he still feels an affinity with the party that quickly washed its hands of him once his off-putting social media posts were revealed, telling CBD he still holds a Liberal Party membership. Paul Lindemann on the campaign trail last month before he was disendorsed by the Liberal Party. Jason South In a video taken last week at a Williamstown booth and seen by this column, Lindemann can be heard telling prospective voters there is “no hostilities” between himself and the Liberals and that he is confident things will “be sorted” out if or when he gets into parliament. In holding fast to the distinctive blue hue, the independent Lindemann seems to have rattled some of the other candidates for the seat. Labor even trotted out a sign at one of the polling booths late last week that identified Lindemann and stated in capitals, “This election there is no Liberal candidate”, just in case anyone needed reminding.



Lindemann, a junior basketball coach, has had a rough couple of weeks. Apart from his ugly Facebook posts, it was revealed earlier this month he had been suspended from coaching or attending any games run by Basketball Victoria for six weeks last year for “bringing the game into disrepute” after a parent accused him of mocking an opposition under-14s player during a game. Related Article Victorian election Video shows dumped Williamstown candidate chasing down alleged vandal And just last week, a video emerged showing Lindemann confronting and accusing a man of vandalising his campaign corflutes. World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic Circus Troubled data centre firm lands major face time atop Tower of Power Matt Dennien November 23, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week, a data centre race heats up, a key CFMEU inquiry witness takes the reins of a new regulator, and a potential audit of a victim support scheme. While it may not yet have translated into a surge of development activity, it’s clear Crisafulli and Co’s AI data centre push has sparked plenty of high-level action behind closed doors. And not just doors of the state’s ministerial offices. Public disclosures scoured by Circus have identified no less than three firms which have scored face time with key bureaucrats. Troubled Brisbane-based Australian data centre giant NextDC has been finding an audience with Premier David Crisafulli and his top bureaucrat. Peter Rae Since we first brought details about Viridis Green Data Centres’ efforts to spruik itself to the government, lobbyist-registered former conservative premier Rob Borbidge has been busy.



Another three meetings have been held by Borbidge on Viridis’ behalf with figures including state development deputy director-general Shaun Ferris. The most recent of these was a follow-up on October 14 to “discuss progress on regional data centres”, while late August saw a tour of the CSIRO’s Edge Data Centre in Brisbane. “The Edge Data Centre for the CSIRO was built by Viridis and a tour and inspection [was] arranged following earlier meetings and discussions,” the lobbyist register entry read. Meanwhile, proponents of the massive Anthropic-backed Western Downs data centre Zerra DC – via lobbyists GRA Cosway – have met with underlings of co-ordinator general Gerard Coggan.



Lobbying records show GRA Cosway have also nudged Water Minister Ann Leahy’s office trying to set up “meetings and events” following up on an “offer of briefing”. Related Article Public service LNP-sponsor data centre firm taps ex-premier to join major meetings Perhaps most interesting, however, is the trio of meetings landed by the troubled Brisbane-based NextDC – one of the country’s largest data centre operators. Chief executive Craig Scroggie has bagged not one but two meetings with Premier David Crisafulli, his director-general Damien Walker, and their staff, since late August. Both are described only under “portfolio matters”. In mid-September, Crisafulli and Walker then met the firm’s Rockhampton-raised rich-lister founder Bevan Slattery.



What has been discussed among the group is unclear, and neither Crisafulli’s office nor NextDC responded to our questions. Whether the firm’s recent share price dive might have a material impact on the topic is another question – but they could sure use some good news. Could that be a new site, or expansion to its existing modest Queensland locations under the LNP’s much-anticipated “rigorous approvals framework” under development? We’ll have to wait and see. One thing that is clear though, according to a spokesperson for billionaire businessman Clive Palmer, is that his recent rendezvous with Crisafulli has nothing to do with building one of the new coal-power stations the premier has said he’s open to for the electricity needs of such sites. Make of that what you will.



Key CFMEU inquiry witness handed interim reins of new regulator It came as little surprise when Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie told parliament last week that the government would take up recommendations for a new construction code and regulator. Sarina Wise giving evidence at the CFMEU inquiry. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry The code is designed to crack down on union flags and branding on worksites, but it was the second-half of Bleijie’s update which caught our ears. The new authority overseeing compliance with that code has already been set up as an independent body, reporting to David Mackie, who works under Bleijie as director-general (and before that, had him officiate his wedding).



Leading this initial team of six will be an interim general manager, Sarina Wise. Readers may know as the current executive director of compliance and field services within the department’s Office of Industrial relations. Wise has given evidence to the CFMEU inquiry that soon after she came to that role from one at NSW’s workplace safety regulator, it was clear that “there was deep regulatory capture by the CFMEU”. Bleijie told parliament the move was a “scalable response to implement recommendation two which will be monitored as the code takes effect”. Watch this space. Audit office could run ruler over alleged victim support scheme rort





That audit, not scheduled until the 2027-28 financial year, was still yet to be fully scoped, Vagg told the committee. “As we get closer to the time of delivering that performance audit, we’ll assess what has been happening within that department and broader risks associated with that particular delivery element,” she said. “If risks emerge or there’s been significant activities of government, I may adjust the timing, but I’m still working through that.” Have a curiosity for the Circus tent?
