World.title: Albanese stands by Bowen after failed COP amid global recriminations
World.content:
PoliticsFederalParis Agreement Albanese stands by Bowen after failed COP amid global recriminations Natassia Chrysanthos and Nick O'Malley November 23, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has maintained it was in Australia’s national interest for Energy Minister Chris Bowen to co-host this year’s COP31 in Turkey, despite the summit’s negotiations collapsing without any agreed outcomes. The Coalition hammered Labor over Bowen’s role on Monday as the energy minister travelled home from Antalya, where the climate talks reached a stalemate on Sunday night for only the third time in the conference’s 32-year history. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Getty Images The central sticking point was whether the final document should specify phasing out fossil fuels – oil-producing nations led by Saudi Arabia wanted to scrub those references, while nations seeking more ambitious action, including Europe and the Pacific, said they must be included. The deadlock has cast a shadow over both the future of the UN’s climate summit and the role of Bowen, who campaigned for his role as president of negotiations when Australia lost its bid to host the talks in Adelaide.



The Coalition on Monday called for Bowen to resign, with opposition energy minister Dan Tehan telling question time the minister had wasted “$150 million of our money on his big COP flop, including $30 million on a pre-COP [event in the Pacific that] no-one went to.” Opposition MP Dan Tehan has led the argument against Bowen’s joint COP presidency. Dominic Lorrimer Albanese defended Australia’s involvement, saying climate change was making weather events more extreme while the countries least responsible stood to lose the most, including Pacific neighbours. “The government believes that we have responsibility to this and future generations to act. [Critics argue that] one country acting alone won’t make a difference. We agree with that. We need to bring other nations with us on the journey,” Albanese said, to jeers from opposition MPs who asked how that was going. The prime minister also said there were links between environmental security and national security, referencing the interests of the Pacific. “I don’t think [the prime ministers of Fiji, Tuvalu, Samoa, Tonga and the Solomon Islands] thank the member opposite for the nature of that question, in which he said no-one was there at the pre-COP meeting held in the Pacific,” he said.



Tehan, however, argued Bowen had embarrassed Australia on the world stage. “The [COP] model as it currently stands is completely and utterly broken,” he said. “Chris Bowen should have known that, and then he would have spared Australians the expense of $150 million for an exercise, which became a vanity project for him.” There was jeering in Monday’s question time as Albanese stood by Australia’s investment in this year’s COP. Dominic Lorrimer Consensus approach the ‘root of the problem’: Bowen In the aftermath of the calamitous result, summit delegates are debating whether the joint co-hosting arrangement between Turkey and Australia, proposed by Bowen, backfired by muddying authority and slowing discussion in the conference’s final days.



Some critics questioned Bowen’s strategy of insisting all 198 parties agree to a final cover decision. The cover text, which captures the COP’s headline aims, is negotiated throughout the summit to achieve consensus, and sinks if any country objects. The death knell this year came when Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the European Union, rejected the text on Sunday night because it “does not even mention fossil fuels”. Photo: Matt Golding Bowen said he tried to strike a balance: instead of using explicit language, the draft text referred to previous agreements on fossil fuels. “It was good faith attempt. It wasn’t enough,” he said. The Australian Greens were scathing of Bowen’s approach. “At the end of COP 31, we have the Albanese Labor government choosing to side with Saudi Arabia and Trump, and not mention fossil fuels, rather than back in Europe and our Pacific neighbours,” said leader David Shoebridge.



“This is worse than disappointing.” Others argue that the requirement for consensus is a problem. The United Nations’ climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he was asking for advice on reforming the system on Sunday night. Bowen said the consensus rule was “the fundamental root of the problem”, not the joint presidency. Chris Bowen, president of COP31 negotiations, during the closing session at the climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. AP Photo/Khalil Hamra “When positions are so strong, that’s a very big challenge for any presidency – joint or individuals – to come to the global context,” he said in Turkey after the talks finished.



“Australia left nothing on the field, trying to find solutions to reach what I now see as unbridgeable red lines. The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory. Related Article Updated

Paris Agreement ‘Abject failure’: Coalition demands Bowen’s head as COP31 ends without a deal “Unfortunately, we’re unable to reach agreement on a cover decision, and that’s disappointing ... I take my share of responsibility. Ultimately, you know, people can judge what could have been done or couldn’t have been done. Ultimately, it’s a party-driven process.” Bowen pointed to positive outcomes, such as more than 90 countries signing an electrification pledge. “People of goodwill worked very hard. I haven’t slept in the last three nights. We’ve been negotiating all the way through,” he said. Fiji’s environment minister, Lynda Tabuya, said the failure to agree on a cover text was not Bowen’s. “It is a collective responsibility that rests with all parties. Consensus requires compromise, courage, and political will from all of us,” she said.



Failed COP talks create hope for better forums The stakes were raised at this year’s conference given the United Nations’ environment program had warned just weeks before that the world would overshoot the Paris Agreement of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees. Former president of Ireland, Mary Robinson, said that should have shaken leaders into action, but “instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership from the co-presidencies Turkey and Australia”. Former United States vice-president Al Gore, however, blamed the failure on a “handful of petro-states [who] have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels”. Other climate change advocates praised the EU and its allies for choosing to play hardball, including former UN climate change executive secretary Christiana Figueres, who said COP31 showed progress could be achieved without consensus.



“Let’s be clear about what happened in Antalya: more than 130 countries refused to sign a deal that would have belied the true state of our crisis,” she said. Related Article Analysis

Climate policy There is no getting around the scope of this failure – both for Chris Bowen and the world Matthew McDonald, a professor of international relations at the University of Queensland, said the longer-term legacy of this year’s talks could be a “recognition of the limits of this consensus-driven approach to climate negotiations, and the development of alternative sites for climate action.” Tuvalu’s climate change minister, Maina Talia, said the island nation would next year co-host with Ireland the second conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, alongside “a growing coalition of doers”. “Tuvalu cannot accept this as the final scenario. So we are putting our resolve where we can make an impact,” he said. “It is moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation.”

World.title: ‘River of filth’ - Motueka residents want action on wastewater problems
World.content:
Motueka residents fed up with sewage overflows and persistent wastewater odours say the problems are taking a toll on their community and not enough is being done to fix them.

A filter failure at Motueka's Goodman Ledger Park pump station caused weeks of pungent odour earlier this year, while last winter's flooding led to a sewage overflow, with some private bores contaminated and residents reporting illness.

Tasman District Council records show six sewage overflows have occurred at the pump station during heavy rain and flooding, while odour complaints stretch back more than a decade.

Audio player for " Tasman locals struggling as ageing wastewater infrastructure causes stink " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2752376%2Friver-of-filth-motueka-residents-want-action-on-wastewater-problems

Tasman locals struggling as ageing wastewater infrastructure causes stink Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Motueka resident Dave Oliver said he first became aware of the problem in January, when he noticed a pungent smell.

"You ever been in a toilet, a bathroom, when the fan wasn't working? It was the smell of poo, the neighbourhood smelled like sewage."

Ledger Avenue resident Feebee Newlands said during last winter's floods, wastewater overflowed from the pump station, creating a "river of filth".

Sewage overflowed from the Goodman Ledger Park pump station during flooding in Motueka during June 2025. Supplied / Feebee Newlands

The odour issue in January led Newlands and other residents to form the Motueka Wastewater Action Group. The group want to hear from other communities around the country who are facing similar issues so they can advocate for change.

She said she was "so wild about the smell" and what was happening to the community, that she began knocking on doors, asking people about their experiences.

"I felt like I was going to vomit, that's how bad it was, it was disgusting.

"Hearing people's stories of children being sick with headaches, animals itchy and scratchy and can't stop licking, cats not well, people not sleeping, people stressed, people have not been able to open their doors and their windows."

She said residents had been dealing with the issue for 15 years and some people had chosen to leave the area due to the ongoing issues.

Motueka residents have erected their own signs after odour issues with the Goodman Ledger Pump Station. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Motueka resident Helen Bro used to volunteer in the garden at the Ledger Goodman Park, but said she stopped after last June's flooding, because of the difficulty getting information about what to do after a sewage overflow, and concerns over how people were alerted to the health risks.

She also had concerns that new wastewater standards would effectively permit overflows of raw sewage to land.

"We're really worried that what we're fighting for now for the pumping station will be permitted in two years' time."

A network overwhelmed in heavy rain

Tasman District Council water and waste manager Mike Schruer said the Goodman Ledger pump station was built 70 years ago and now dealt with 95 percent of Motueka's wastewater.

Odour issues at the pump station had led to a filter being installed in 2019. The filter cartridge had failed in January, and the order for its replacement was lost by the supplier, and it was six weeks before it was replaced.

The Goodman Ledger Pump Station was built in 1949, upgraded in 2004 and now deals with 95 percent of Motueka's wastewater. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Schruer said the filter had been upgraded, the wet well level adjusted and the location of the hydrogen sulfide sensors changed, which reduced the risk of odours.

In regard to overflows, Schruer said there was a "significant" inflow and infiltration problem in Motueka, with stormwater and groundwater entering the wastewater network, overloading it during heavy rain, as occurred during the June 2025 flood.

"That pump station is designed to take 400 cubic meters an hour and in the June 2025 storm event we were getting 800 cubic meters an hour, so significantly more."

Alongside that, he said the stormwater network in Motueka was "lagging well behind" where it needed to be.

A new pump station as part of development in West Motueka would ease the load on the Goodman Ledger pump station, and there would be further changes to the network as the Motueka Wastewater Treatment Plant needed to be upgraded or replaced by 2035, before its consent expires, Schruer said.

The council was working to identify where water was entering the wastewater network and had funding to investigate private properties where surface water was being diverted into gully traps. It could issue property owners with notices requiring the problem to be fixed.

Feebee Newlands, Dave Oliver and Helen Bro are some of the residents affected by sewage overflows and odour issues from the Goodman Ledger Pump Station. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Schruer said two-thirds of Motueka relied on private bores, instead of being connected to a reticulated water system, which was a problem during heavy rain, as overland flow led to contamination.

The Motueka Wastewater Action Group said it had been difficult to find out who was responsible for public health after a sewage overflow, with responsibility shared by Health NZ, emergency management, water regulators and local councils.

Health New Zealand national public health service medical officer of health Dr Cheryl Brunton said there were 12 reports of campylobacter infection in Nelson and Tasman after the June/July 2025 flooding, but it could not say how many of those were in Motueka.

Brunton said during floods, public health advice was issued to help protect communities from health risks, regardless of whether specific sewage overflows had been identified, while local councils were responsible for issuing boil water notices if any of the water supplies they manage may be contaminated.

Will new rules legitimise overflows?

Residents are also worried the new rules could legitimise sewage overflows by allowing them to be consented.

The Water Services Authority head of system strategy and performance Sara McFall acknowledged the situation in Motueka and said the environmental and public health harm caused by sewage overflows was a nation-wide problem. Recent reporting showed there had been more than 11,000 sewage overflows in the last year, but it was likely that didn't show the full scale of the problem.

"What we know is making an overflow prohibited activity hasn't worked because they're still happening. But what it means is they're not being monitored, there's no risk assessment. We don't have management plans in place so that we can start getting on top of the issues."

Flooding in Ledger Ave, Motueka during June 2025. Supplied / Feebee Newlands

She said the current rules varied around the country, in some places an overflow was a prohibited activity while in other places it was consented.

McFall said the new national standards that come into effect in 2028 would give a more comprehensive picture of what was going on, with greater scrutiny of overflows through monitoring, reporting and public notification.

She said overflow points would need to be mapped, and a risk assessment plan will be needed to show how they are monitored, managed and reported.

"It's going to take some years before we're on top of the infrastructure challenges that we're seeing with our wastewater networks but this will really strengthen the oversight and management of overflows and it means that if they have to get a consent then you can put in conditions and you can put in conditions around odour and other things."

She said wastewater networks across the country were in poor condition and it was hoped the introduction of new standards would help to incentivise investment in infrastructure, where it was needed.

"Our aim is that we have fewer overflows and that they're better managed and I think this should be a really important first step in getting operators to understand where their risks are, prioritise investment in their infrastructure and in their networks to get on top of the issue."

An odour filter was installed in the pump station in 2019 after complaints, and an issue with replacing it in early 2026 led to a six-week long odour problem. RNZ / Samantha Gee

The Water Services Authority had also consulted on a proposed national odour standard, which Sara McFall said would set national requirements around wastewater treatment plant odour for the first time.

In the meantime, Newlands said the Motueka Wastewater Action Group wanted to hear from other communities around the country facing similar issues.

"That's the national call out, we want to gather as many people around New Zealand with the same sort of issues, whether they're past or they're present, to formulate a strong, movement around New Zealand.

World.title: Hutt Valley locals concerned over potential pool closures as council tries to balance rate caps
World.content:
And Eva Perese-Wood, RNZ Intern

Hutt Valley locals are shocked and disappointed by the potential loss of public pools as the council works to balance the government's proposed rates cap.

Hutt City Council is weighing its options - including potential closures to public pools, libraries, and community hubs - as it tries to keep rates affordable while providing public services.

For local man Craig Williams, losing the Wainuiomata pool would be a "slap in the face" after the community fundraised for it and dug it themselves.

He worried about what children would do without access to it.

"Well, they're going to hang out here, get into crime, all sorts of things. I mean, at the moment, you get kids hanging around here now with nothing to do.

"If there's no pool in the summer, it's going to get even worse."

He said closing the pool would be "ridiculous".

Audio player for " Hutt Valley Coucil to close pools and libraries in proposal " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/regions/2752346%2Fhutt-valley-locals-concerned-over-potential-pool-closures-as-council-tries-to-balance-rate-caps

Hutt Valley Coucil to close pools and libraries in proposal Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Water Safety New Zealand chief executive Glen Scanlon said he recognised the tough situations councils were in.

But he said pools were important places for teaching the community about water safety in an accessible, affordable way.

"So we'd be urging ratepayers if they value them and we hope they do to really get involved in that consultation process and give their thoughts to the council."

He advised people to consider their abilities before swimming in open water.

Wainuiomata Intermediate principal Craig Sharp also worried about what children would do without the pool, as there wasn't much to do in the area.

"[It] means that most of them will just go to the river and the river's unsupervised and potentially a lot more dangerous."

He joked it had given the school a real-world scenario to teach the children about persuasive writing as they wrote to the mayor.

Lower Hutt Mayor Fauono Ken Laban said they were facing difficult options.

"Nobody wants to close a pool, nobody wants to close a library, nobody wants to close a community hub, and nobody wants to spend less on roads and on rubbish," he said.

"But the reality is we need to find ways to reduce our costs and reduce our expenditure."

Locals Linda and David Grime wanted to know what the council was doing with the money from their rates.

"They're going up every year anyway, like horrendous amounts. Where's all the money going?," asked David Grime.

The couple said the news was "shocking" and it would be "awful" to lose the pool.

Over by the Eastbourne pool, locals felt similarly.

Muritai School teacher Sraah Bleier said the community was "up in arms" and already starting petitions.

In fact the local Eastbourne community had gathered more than 2000 signatures on a petition by time of writing.

She said 118 kids were signed up for the swim club at the pool.

"It would also mean less learning time, because it would have to take at least half an hour to bus [to Naenae] and half an hour back and then a half an hour lesson."

She said would be a loss to the community.

"We're an island nation, we need all our kids to swim.

"And there's nothing more Kiwi than launching off a bridge or a rock or Days Bay Wharf, so they've got to be able to swim back around minimum, right?"

Another resident told RNZ she'd be open to paying higher rates to keep the pool open.

But the plans did not solely target pools - libraries were also at risk.

World.title: Seeds grown in simulated atmosphere secured in Arctic Circle doomsday vault
World.content:
Hundreds of New Zealand seeds grown in a simulated future atmosphere have been secured in a doomsday vault in the Arctic Circle.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault safeguards more than 1.4 million seed samples from around the world. The vault, located in the mountain permafrost, stores copies of important seeds in a bid to preserve agricultural biodiversity and ensure there will be enough food in the future.

The latest shipment from the Margot Forde Genebank - based in Palmerston North and managed by the Bioeconomy Science Institute Maiangi Taiao - marked 10 years since New Zealand's first deposit.

According to Genebank director Kioumars Ghamkhar the 300 seed samples contained "vital genetic material".

This year, the deposit included seeds from grasses grown for more than 25 years in an enriched carbon dioxide atmosphere - "just in case disaster happens", he said.

Dr Ghamkhar with former Crop Trust executive director Marie Haga in 2016. The Crop Trust manages and funds the Svalbard. Supplied / Bioeconomy Science Institute

Ghamkhar said the seeds could help develop future varieties capable of withstanding extreme climate shifts.

The climate-resilient varieties came about through natural change, rather than genetic modification, he said.

"When you impose some conditions on plants, they adapt and their genetics changes over time."

He said future deposits could include drought-resistant varieties that had adapted to growing in wetter conditions, for example.

While accepting that he and his small team played "an important role" Ghamkhar rejected the idea that New Zealand's future was in his hands.

"I wouldn't put that much credit on myself and the team."

Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway. Supplied / Bioeconomy Science Institute

So, how does the team choose what to send to the underground vault on a Norwegian archipelago?

"Basically, the criteria for us is what is important for New Zealand as its heritage, let's say, in agriculture. And then what is important for the world? And of course, climate change is nowadays an important factor."

The Genebank's long-term goal was to secure about 18,000 seed samples in the Arctic vault - about 10 percent of its entire collection.

Ghamkhar said the focus was on "backing up seed material" with economic and climate adaptive value, with ryegrass and white clover among the core species.

So far, the Genebank had shipped close to 3500 seed samples, dried and sealed inside double-layered aluminium pouches.

Ghamkar said visiting the Svalbard Global Seed Vault with the first deposit in 2016, was "unreal".

Entering the vault in 2016. Supplied / Bioeconomy Science Institute

Everything from the "snow-covered land" in the height of summer and the long hours of daylight, "was just amazing," Ghamkhar said.

"The hotel I was staying at, the lady at the reception said that a week before there was a polar bear hitting the door trying to get in.

"So this is just fascinating and I think it was a privilege, really, to do that 10 years ago and one of my best experiences."

Ghamkhar said the seed vault, which has been up and running since 2008, was a realistic, rather than defeatist or pessimistic, project.

He said things disappeared and changed over time - sometimes due to human intervention, sometimes not.

"If they disappear and you don't collect and bring them in, you won't have any record of it. It's gone and it's gone forever.

World.title: Final defendant in alleged mortgage and investment fraud pleads not guilty
World.content:
The final defendant charged in a Serious Fraud Office (SFO) investigation into an alleged mortgage and investment fraud involving members of the same family has pleaded not guilty.

Gerard Peters is charged with obtaining by deception in connection with the $1.8m scheme which involved fraudulently obtaining credit and properties.

He is the fifth defendant in the case, and was arrested at the border last month after being overseas for seven years.

His brothers, Christopher and Francis Peters, and family associate Gur Raj Singh Bhachu had previously pleaded guilty to charges associated with the scheme.

Their mother, Serene Peters, has denied one charge of obtaining by deception.

Christopher Peters has pleaded guilty to four charges of obtaining by deception related to a $4.47m mortgage fraud scheme and one charge of obtaining by deception related to the 1.8 million dollar investment fraud. He is due to be sentenced in April.

Francis Peters was sentenced to nine months and two weeks' home detention after pleading guilty to three charges of obtaining credit by deception and one charge of obtaining property by deception.

Bhachu was sentenced to nine months' home detention after pleading guilty to 12 charges relating to four properties involved in mortgage fraud.

World.title: Mercury cuts ribbon on Northland's $287m Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm
World.content:
Northland's first wind farm has been officially opened today as the region continues its transformation from energy importer to significant producer of renewable power.

Mercury's Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm, with 12 towers producing 77 megawatts (MW) of electricity in a good breeze, is not the biggest in the country by any means - but its turbines are by far the tallest.

Each measures 206m from ground to rotor tip, making them taller than any structure in New Zealand bar Auckland's Sky Tower.

The project, at Omamari, on the wild west coast north of Dargaville, cost $287 million.

The expected annual output of 220 gigawatt-hours (GWh) is roughly equivalent to the power used by 31,000 homes.

Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton opened the wind farm this afternoon with Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambert and Northland MP Grant McCallum.

Hamilton said the first turbines started generating power in July, with final commissioning, testing and site rehabilitation expected to continue until early 2027.

The project was on track to be completed on time and on budget.

Hamilton thanked mana whenua Te Roroa, landowner Pāmu and the Kaipara community for their support.

Getting the 80-metre-long turbine blades from Northport, on the east coast, to Dargaville and then up the west coast to Omamari was a major transportation feat. Supplied / Viv Trounson

About 180 people worked on site each day at the peak of construction. More than 250,000 hours of work had been clocked up without any serious accidents.

Kaiwaikawe boosted Mercury's generation diversity with wind farms in Northland, central North Island, Otago and Southland complementing the company's hydro and geothermal generation, Hamilton said.

"The wind blows differently across the country. Having wind farms spread across multiple regions reduces reliance on the weather in any one place, contributing to a more resilient and secure electricity system for New Zealand."

One of the objections raised when the wind farm was first mooted was its proximity to wetlands frequented by the endangered bittern or matuku-hūrepo.

The company had set up a $640,000 Bittern Management Fund to support DOC and iwi programmes protecting the birds, and made a $360,000 commitment to GPS tracking, Hamilton said.

The company was also contributing $30,000 a year to the Kaiwaikawe Community Fund.

The first two funding rounds had paid for, among other things, bikes for tamariki at Kaihu Valley School, science equipment for Dargaville Primary School and operating costs for Dargaville Menz Shed.

Just last month, Mercury opened the South Island's largest wind farm, the 46-turbine Kaiwera Downs near Gore. It cost just over $600 million, produced enough power for 96,000 homes, and was built in two stages.

Earlier this month the company broke ground on the $506m, 40-turbine Puke Kapo Hau Wind Farm in Otago.

Getting the enormous Kaiwaikawe turbine blades from Northport, on the opposite coast, to Omamari was a major transportation feat, with only one known mishap when a truck veered off a metal road into a drain.

Each blade is 80m long, making a rotor diameter of 162m.

Ngāwhā geothermal power station remains Northland's biggest producer of renewable energy. Peter de Graaf

The rise of an energy exporter

The opening of Kaiwaikawe continues Northland's evolution from a power-importing region - reliant on electricity transported large distances over vulnerable transmission lines, as seen in the 2024 pylon collapse - to a significant producer of renewable energy.

The Far North is already a net exporter of energy, thanks to Top Energy's geothermal power plant at Ngāwhā, near Kaikohe, and Lodestone Energy's Kohirā Solar Farm just outside Kaitāia.

Ngāwhā produces 57MW and operates 24 hours a day, unlike wind or solar plants.

Top Energy plans to boost its output to 89MW in coming years. Its current annual generation is around 450GWh.

Kohirā, which produces about 55GWh a year, was New Zealand's first utility-scale solar farm when it started operating in 2023.

The ability to export much more power from the Far North to Auckland, where it is most needed, is limited by a lack of capacity in the transmission lines between Kaikohe substation and Marsden Point.

There are no such issues in the Whangārei district thanks to spare capacity in the lines from Marsden Point to Auckland, built to accommodate oil-fired power stations that have long since been dismantled.

Marsden Point also has New Zealand's first grid-sized battery and a major solar farm under construction by Meridian Energy.

Why are they so tall?

Hamilton said the tallest structure in New Zealand was still the Sky Tower at 328 metres.

However, the second tallest through to the 13th tallest structures were now the 12 turbines at Kaiwaikawe.

The 12-turbine, $287 million Kaiwaikawe is Northland’s first wind farm. Supplied / Mercury

They were tall for a reason, he said.

"The idea with wind is that if you get higher up off the ground and into the wind currents, the wind is stronger, but also more consistent," he said.

"So the best thing to do is to get the wind turbines nice and tall off the ground, and then to have really long blades, so they can capture as much wind as possible and turn it into electricity."

Hamilton said they were not just the tallest in the country, they also had the highest output with each turbine producing up to 6MW.

The site had been chosen for its consistently high wind speeds, proximity to a grid connection, and suitable land for access and construction - in this case a Pāmu farm.

Cutting the ribbon at Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm are, from left, Te Roroa’s Snow Tane, Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth, Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton, Northland MP Grant McCallum, Mercury chairman Scott St John, and Pāmu chief executive Mark Leslie. Supplied / Mercury

Transporting the blades about 110km from one side of Northland to the other was "pretty challenging", he said.

As well as negotiating various towns and roundabouts and getting past houses, the transport crews had to check bridges to make sure they could take the weight, and lift more than 100 power lines so the giant blades could pass underneath.

Hamilton said the company was proud to have brought the wind farm online on time and on budget.

World.title: Waikato water company has a barge on stand by in preparation for El Niño
World.content:
Audio player for " Waikato's water company warns El Niño could put pressure on supply " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/regions/2752046%2Fwaikato-water-company-has-a-barge-on-stand-by-in-preparation-for-el-nino

Waikato's water company warns El Niño could put pressure on supply Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Waikato's water company says there's a barge on stand by to act as a floating pump station if expected drought conditions cause river levels to drop too far.

IAWAI is preparing for a predicted severe El Niño to put significant pressure on the region's supplies and water quality.

Its chief executive Peter Winder told Checkpoint that they were concerned because the Waikato River is the major source of water for the region.

"We're at the point of making sure that we have all of the necessary contingency plans in place," he said.

"Low flows in the river itself are problematic, as would be changes in water conditions."

Winder said if the river level drops below the fixed intake at the side of the river, IAWAI can use a barge to pump water but that would still be within its consented intake.

"There is a barge that Hamilton City Council invested in, which can be lowered into the river to allow us to take water from a deeper base than the fixed intake on the side of the river. That has never had to be used so we're hoping we can avoid that."

IAWAI would make such a decision in consultation with the council and Mercury Energy, if needed.

Winder said the water company has other demand management and water restriction plans that can be put in place.

This included working with the major water users, including Fonterra, Dairy Goat, coolstores and the council. Waikato Hospital's water supply is protected from any restrictions.

"Part of the plan is demand management across households as well as major users if that is necessary."

Winder said holiday hotspots could feel the impact of drought conditions due to the influx of visitors.

"Raglan's supplied by a spring, it has a finite capacity, demand can exceed supply we just need to be careful."

A report tabled with the IAWAI board this week sets out the wide-ranging readiness programme covers risk monitoring, demand management, operational contingency plans, communications, escalation and incident response.

The water company is working closely with both Hamilton City Council and Waikato District Council, as well as local Civil Defence and the Smart Water education programme.

The report notes another potential issue is water quality, such as algae blooms and natural arsenic levels which have increased in recent years during late spring and early summer.

"A water-quality event occurring at the same time as peak demand would create the most significant challenge because treatment output could reduce when demand is highest," the report said.

World.title: 'It's going to waste' - poverty advocate appalled by Fonterra's plan to dump millions of litres of raw milk
World.content:
Fonterra's application to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk in Canterbury is "quite grim" when so many New Zealanders do not have enough to eat, says a poverty researcher.

While almost nine Olympic-sized swimming pools of raw milk could go down the drain, a third of people in some parts of the country are struggling to keep food on the table.

"The hunger monitor report from the New Zealand food network is showing that one in three families in the Waikato, which is a strong dairy producing region, don't have enough to eat and going hungry," poverty researcher Dr Rebekah Graham says.

"To hear that Fonterra, want to dump millions of perfectly fine milk simply to increase corporate profits is quite grim.

"I think it's a terrible indictment on our society, that we have normalised this and allowed this to happen, that somehow it's now acceptable for the largest company in terms of dairy, to just dump millions of litres of milk, because that's easier and cheaper for them, than actually considering how that milk might be used, to feed people, to nourish people."

Audio player for " Fonterra plans to dump 22 million litres of raw milk alarms experts " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2751368%2Fit-s-going-to-waste-poverty-advocate-appalled-by-fonterra-s-plan-to-dump-millions-of-litres-of-raw-milk

Fonterra plans to dump 22 million litres of raw milk alarms experts Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

She said while the proposal allowed for the dumping of 22 million litres of raw milk, for many even one litre was out of reach.

"If I was one of those families. struggling to pay $4 for a bottle of milk to then hear that it's all being poured out and going to waste. It would be heartbreaking."

Graham said the news reminded her of a woman she spoke to for her PHD on food insecurity, who was horrified that people tipped out their milk before heading on holiday.

"I thought of what it was like for her, who couldn't afford to feed her kids, but her milk was eked out. It was watered down. It was really valued. And I thought, imagine what that must be like, having to do that, and then hearing that this company's just simply doesn't care, and it's just going to throw it all away."

Environmental Law Initiative legal researcher Eliza Prestidge-Oldfield agreed. It has asked Environment Canterbury to reject the application.

"That's seven and a half thousand milk tankers full of milk. That's more milk than Fonterra has donated for the Kickstart Breakfast Programme in the 15 years that programme has been running. So you know, the quantities here I think are just staggering."

She said one of the ways Fonterra could dispose of the milk was by irrigating it to farmland.

"And so what we might end up seeing is something like bacterial changes in rivers, we might see algal blooms, we might see oxygen depletion, and also that soil the productivity of that soil is significantly affected, because it's having to sort of process this milk."

Prestidge-Oldfield said the dairy giant was trying to bypass scrutiny by the way it had applied for a variation of its existing wastewater discharge consents.

She said rejection would require Fonterra to apply for a new discharge consent.

The dairy giant said the move was necessary to manage a potential surplus caused by production constraints across the South Island.

It declined RNZ's request for an interview today.

Dairy sector commentator and Agri-Women's Development Trust general manager Julia Jones said it did not sound bad in perspective.

"Last year Fonterra collected 16.5 billion litres of milk and so its roughly about 0.14 per cent of all of that, or one litre in every 740 litres. I know nine Olympic swimming pools sounds huge. I know that 22 million litres sounds massive, but I just sort of wanted to bring that number back into perspective."

While farmers planned with military precision, she said there were factors out of their control.

"You can't predict the weather within a degree, you don't necessarily know how much grass is going to grow and that impacts the production or how much milk will come from the cow which is how much will be collected and then we have a finite amount of processing capacity, so factories."

Senior lecturer in agribusiness management at Lincoln University Dr Nick Lees said no one wanted to see milk wasted.

"I don't think Fonterra wants to see milk wasted either. Probably one point to make clearly is applying for a resource consent is not actually the same as actually dumping milk. This is primarily a contingency plan."

He said there were situations when this could be needed, particularly in the peak.

World.title: 'She wanted to go on her terms': Auckland mum, 93, fulfils wish of assisted dying in Zurich
World.content:
*Warning: This story contains details of assisted dying and may be upsetting for some readers

A family forced to take their elderly mother to Switzerland to fulfil her wish of assisted dying are calling for a law change so others do not have to go through the same ordeal.

Margaret Topzand, of Auckland, died in Zurich on 2 July. She was 93.

Justin Topzand said his mother had led a full and happy life, and was still in good health.

"There was nothing wrong with her. She was starting to show mild dementia and forgetfulness, but she was basically sick of living," he said.

"She felt that she'd done and seen everything and that it was time for her to go. And she wanted to go on her terms, without having to linger in a retirement home for years and years."

Margaret, a long-time supporter of voluntary euthanasia, called her sons together - Peter, Justin and Allister - to explain her wishes.

However, that request turned out to be far more difficult than anyone expected.

Margaret Topzand, seen here with son Peter, enjoying the sun during one of her last walks in the Swiss countryside. Supplied

The brothers discovered that New Zealand's End of Life Choice Act, which became law in 2021, only allowed assisted dying for people who had a terminal illness and were expected to die within six months.

"She was upset and really frustrated," Justin said.

"She had a few meetings with the three of us brothers, and said: 'Can't you help me?' And we realised we couldn't. Legally, we could not help her until Peter, my older brother, discovered that we could go to Switzerland with her."

What Peter Topzand had read in a newspaper article was that Swiss not-for-profit organisation Dignitas offered doctor-assisted suicide for foreign nationals - provided they met strict criteria.

Peter said his mother was still living independently, but finding that increasingly difficult.

Audio player for " Strict criteria sees people seeking assisted dying overseas " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/health/2751692%2Fshe-wanted-to-go-on-her-terms-auckland-mum-93-fulfils-wish-of-assisted-dying-in-zurich

Strict criteria sees people seeking assisted dying overseas Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Realising she needed a higher level of care, they visited a rest home to see if that would be a good option.

"There were all these old ladies in their wheelchairs, dribbling into their laps. It looked awful, even though it was a nice and expensive rest home, and mum said as we got in the car, 'I'm not doing it, I'm not going to be an old lady in a wheelchair, who doesn't know her own name, dribbling into her lap'. Her words were: 'Can't you help me to step out?'."

It was then that Peter mentioned, just as conversation, what he had read about in Switzerland.

"And she said, 'Well, let's do that, I want you to organise that', and I thought: 'shit'. I agonised over it a bit and spoke to my wife and to friends, and I came to the conclusion that while it was not my job to talk her out of it or prevent her from doing it, I wasn't prepared to be the one who actually orchestrated and facilitated my own mother's death. I just didn't want that."

Justin Topzand says his mother Margaret was a positive and inspirational woman who embraced life - and wanted the right to decide when to end it. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

However, during his research, Peter had also stumbled onto the concept of death doulas, professionals who guide people through the process of dying.

It did not take long to find an end-of-life doula whose values meshed with their own.

The doula took Margaret to the many medical and psychiatric check-ups the Swiss authorities demanded, and handled the mountain of reports and documentation.

In particular the Swiss wanted to be certain Margaret was not suffering from depression, and that she was capable of making the decision to end her life.

Justin said when they finally got a green light to travel to Switzerland, their plans were derailed by the war on Iran.

They then had to repeat part of the process once it was safe to travel again, because too much time had passed since the psychiatrist's all-clear.

"So then we had to rush around trying to find airfares and hotels. But what was really good is in the last two weeks before mum went, a lot of family and friends came to see her and say goodbye," he said.

"She never changed her mind. She was stoic, she was happy that she was finally able to end her life. There were a lot of tears from the other side but she just said: 'Yes, this has been good, it's been nice knowing you, thank you'. And when we left her apartment the morning that we flew, she just looked back and said: 'This has been a great apartment', and closed the door and walked away. And it made our job so much easier."

Margaret Topzand hiking with her son Justin Topzand. Supplied

'It was bloody tough'

Once in Switzerland, Margaret and her sons filled in the days waiting for final approval by going for walks in the countryside.

Justin said the procedure took place in a clinic on the outskirts of Zurich.

It was almost derailed again when the exacting officials checking Margaret's identity said her passport photo was too old.

"She'd aged considerably in the eight years since the photo was taken so initially they said: 'No, we can't accept this'. But within five minutes the Swiss police were there, they asked her who she was, got her to hold up her passport, took a photo of her and said: 'Yes, we accept that, off you go'."

Peter Topzand became emotional as he recalled his last moments with his mother, his arm around her shoulders.

"It was bloody tough. But I'm very happy that she's got her wish."

Justin said she never hesitated, even when the end was very close.

"Her last words were: 'I wonder if I'm going to heaven? I don't believe in heaven'. And within seconds, she was unconscious, and within minutes, she was dead… It was hard, but it's what she wanted. She also wanted tūī bird song so my brother had recorded some, and we had that for the last minutes. It was lovely and she died a happy old lady. Quickly."

Justin Topzand says his mother Margaret loved New Zealand and was forever grateful to the International Red Cross for helping her emigrate after the horrors of a World War Two concentration camp in what is now Indonesia. Supplied

'It's appalling': Family says law change needed

Justin Topzand said he was grateful New Zealand had an assisted dying law but believed the criteria were too narrow.

"It seems ridiculous that you have to travel halfway across the planet to do a pretty simple procedure that could be done in New Zealand. I think we need to catch up with the Europeans and accept that a lot of people in New Zealand want to have options and they haven't got them."

The ACT Party has a private members bill before Parliament that could ease the restrictions on assisted dying, by removing the requirements for a terminal illness and a six-month prognosis.

However, opponents of a law change fear disabled people could then opt for assisted dying - not because they wanted it, but because they felt they were a burden on their families or were unable to get the support, housing and care they needed, especially in an era of cuts to health and disability services.

Justin said there would always be concerns the law could be abused.

"And that's why you need psychologists and psychiatrists involved to talk to the individual and make sure this is what they want, not what the family wants."

Peter Topzand said if someone was 93 and had demonstrated support for voluntary euthanasia for decades, they should have that option.

Many people could not afford to travel to Switzerland, he said.

"I think it's appalling that she had to spend all that time and money going to Switzerland when, by rights, that service should have been provided here, probably at a fraction of the cost," he said.

"A lot of people wouldn't be able to afford it, the tickets to Switzerland and the Dignitas fees and the doula's fees and the psychiatrist's fees and the hotels. It all adds up."

Margaret and Hajo Topzand on their wedding day. Supplied

'She embraced the beauty of what was around her'

Margaret Topzand was born in the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia, in 1933, and somehow survived years in a Japanese internment camp during World War II.

Justin Topzand said she was one of the few people he knew who said the atomic bomb had saved her life, because it hastened the end of the war.

The family was reunited in the Netherlands after the Japanese surrender, then emigrated to New Zealand with help from the International Red Cross.

They arrived with little money, but Margaret trained as a nurse and worked in hospitals around the country.

She married Hajo Topzand and eventually settled in Titirangi, Auckland, where they raised their three sons.

She travelled extensively, even visiting Madagascar and going hiking in Australia in her 80s.

Justin put his mother's positivity down to surviving the concentration camp as a child.

"She always saw the better side of life, and embraced the beauty of what was around her," he said.

"She became a New Zealander through and through. She just loved it here, and was always thankful to New Zealand and the Red Cross for getting her here. She was an amazing woman, an inspiration."

* The second part of this story, to be published tomorrow, will examine some of the arguments for and against changing New Zealand's assisted dying law.
